recipes.name: Ackee and Saltfish
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Canned ackee (drained) or fresh ripe ackee
Neutral vegetable oil or coconut oil

steps: Place the salt cod in a large bowl and cover with cold water. Soak for 12–24 hours, changing the water at least twice. For a faster desalt, bring the fish to a gentle boil in fresh water, drain, and repeat twice. Taste a small flake after the final soak — it should be pleasantly salty, not aggressively so. Flake into rough pieces, removing any bones.

Heat the oil in a wide skillet over medium heat until shimmering. Add the onion and cook for 4–5 minutes until softened and translucent. Add the garlic and Scotch bonnet and cook for 1 minute more. Add the tomatoes and cook, stirring, until they soften and release their juices — about 3 minutes. The mixture should look jammy and fragrant.

Add the flaked cod to the sofrito and stir well to combine, cooking for 2 minutes. Then add the drained ackee and fold in very gently with a wide spatula — ackee breaks apart easily and should remain in identifiable golden chunks, not mashed. Season with black pepper. Taste before adding any salt; the fish likely provides enough. Heat through for 2 minutes on medium-low.

Scatter sliced scallions over the top and serve immediately from the pan. Ackee and saltfish waits for no one — it loses its textural distinction as it sits. Accompany with fried Johnny cakes, hard dough bread, breadfruit, or boiled green banana.

recipes.name: Pesce all'Acqua Pazza
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Whole sea bream or sea bass (gutted, scaled, 500–700 g each)
Dried red chili flakes (or fresh peperoncino)

steps: Score each fish with 3–4 deep diagonal cuts on each side, cutting through to the bone — this allows seasoning to penetrate and ensures even cooking. Season inside and out with salt, including into the cavity and the score marks. Allow to rest at room temperature for 10 minutes while you prepare the broth base. Pat the exterior dry with paper towels before adding to the pan.

In a wide, lidded pan large enough to hold the fish flat, warm the olive oil over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and chili flakes. Cook gently for 1–2 minutes, stirring, until the garlic is softened and just beginning to turn pale gold at the edges — not brown. Add the halved cherry tomatoes, pressing a few gently with the back of a spoon to release their juice. Cook another 2 minutes until the tomatoes begin to soften and the oil takes on their color.

Pour the wine and water into the tomato base and raise heat to bring to a brisk simmer. Lay the seasoned fish flat in the pan — they can overlap slightly if necessary. Spoon some of the broth and tomatoes over the fish. Cover with a lid and cook on medium heat for 12–15 minutes, depending on the size of the fish. The fish is done when the flesh at the deepest score mark pulls away from the bone cleanly and is opaque white all the way through.

Scatter the roughly chopped parsley over the fish and pan. Drizzle a final generous stream of your best extra-virgin olive oil directly over the fish and broth. The raw olive oil added at the end is essential to the dish's character — it emulsifies into the broth as you spoon it over. Serve the fish whole in the pan or carefully transferred to a deep platter with all the broth ladled around it. Provide good bread to mop the pan.

recipes.name: Adjika
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Fresh hot red peppers (serrano or cayenne, stemmed, seeded)

steps: Halve the peppers and remove seeds and membranes — wear gloves throughout. Toss with half the salt and spread on a clean kitchen towel or paper towels. Leave uncovered for 1–2 hours to draw out excess moisture. This salting and dehydration step concentrates the pepper flavor and removes the water content that would otherwise make the adjika too thin and watery. The peppers will visibly shrink and become slightly translucent.

Traditional adjika is made in a stone mortar — a food processor is acceptable but produces a slightly less vibrant paste. Pound or pulse the garlic and remaining salt until a rough paste forms. Add the macerated peppers and pound/process until the peppers break down into a rough paste. Add the blue fenugreek, cilantro, and vinegar. Continue pounding or processing until a coarse, fibrous paste forms — not entirely smooth, with some texture from the pepper skins and herb stems remaining. Taste: it should be fiercely hot, salty, herbal, and slightly sour.

recipes.name: Filipino Chicken Adobo

ingredients.name: Bone-in, skin-on chicken pieces (thighs and drumsticks)

steps: Combine chicken pieces with vinegar, soy sauce, crushed garlic, bay leaves, and black peppercorns in a bowl or zip bag. Toss to coat. Marinate at room temperature for 30 minutes, or refrigerate for up to 4 hours. The vinegar and soy will begin to lightly cure the surface of the chicken.

Remove chicken from the marinade (reserve the liquid). Heat oil in a wide, heavy pan or wok over high heat until just smoking. Sear the chicken pieces skin-side down for 4–5 minutes without moving, until the skin is deeply golden and releases cleanly from the pan. Flip and sear the bone side for 2 minutes. Work in batches if needed.

Return all chicken to the pan. Pour in the reserved marinade and the water — the liquid should come halfway up the chicken. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cover and cook for 25 minutes, turning the chicken once halfway through.

Uncover and increase heat to medium-high. Continue cooking, turning the chicken occasionally, for 10–15 minutes until the sauce has reduced to a thick, glossy glaze that coats the chicken rather than pooling in the pan. The skin, having softened during the braise, will re-crisp slightly in the rendered fat as the liquid disappears.

recipes.name: Agedashi Tofu
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Grated daikon, grated ginger, katsuobushi, green onion

steps: Remove the tofu from its packaging and wrap in 3-4 layers of paper towels. Place on a flat surface with a small plate on top as a weight — do not use heavy books, which will crush silken tofu. Let rest for 15 minutes to draw surface moisture. Cut into 6-8 cubes, approximately 4x4cm. Very gently pat each cut face dry with paper towels. This step is essential: surface moisture causes the starch coating to dissolve before frying, resulting in a bald, oil-soaked cube rather than a crisp shell.

Combine dashi, usukuchi soy sauce, and mirin in a small saucepan. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring to combine. Cook for 2 minutes. Taste — it should be lightly salty, savory with a background sweetness, and clean. The pale soy sauce is traditional for agedashi to preserve the golden color of the sauce; regular soy makes a darker, deeper version. Keep warm until needed.

Heat oil to 180°C (355°F) in a deep, narrow pot or small wok. Working quickly, roll each tofu cube in potato starch, pressing gently to adhere, then shake off excess — you want a thin, even dust, not a thick coat. Lower cubes into oil one at a time using chopsticks or a spider. Fry 3-4 pieces at a time for 2-3 minutes, turning once, until the coating is set and very pale gold. The coating should be almost translucent, not deeply browned.

Place 2-3 fried tofu cubes in a small, deep bowl. Ladle hot tentsuyu sauce over and around them immediately — the sauce should come about halfway up the sides of the cubes. Garnish the top of each cube with a small mound of grated daikon, a pinch of grated ginger, a few strands of katsuobushi (which will wave in the heat), and thinly sliced green onion. Serve within 60 seconds. The entire magic of agedashi is the moment when the crisp coating begins to absorb the broth — this process starts the second you pour the sauce.

recipes.name: Agrodolce
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Shallots or red onion, thinly sliced

steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the sliced shallots and the rosemary sprig. Cook gently, stirring occasionally, for 6-8 minutes until the shallots are completely soft, translucent, and just beginning to take on a light golden color. They must not brown — agrodolce's sweetness comes from the sugar, not caramelized onion.

Pour in the white wine and let it bubble and reduce by half over medium heat, 3-4 minutes. Add the raisins. Continue simmering until the wine is nearly evaporated and the raisins have plumped in the liquid. The pan will look jammy and slightly reduced.

Add the sugar to the pan and stir for 30 seconds until it begins to dissolve in the heat of the base. Pour in the red wine vinegar all at once — it will bubble sharply. Stir to combine and simmer over medium heat for 8-10 minutes until the sauce reduces to a syrupy consistency that coats a spoon. Taste throughout: the ratio of sweet to sour should feel balanced, not one-sided.

Off the heat, fold in the toasted pine nuts and season with salt and black pepper. The salt will sharpen the sweet-sour contrast dramatically — taste after each pinch. Remove the rosemary sprig. Serve warm over duck, pork tenderloin, pan-roasted chicken thighs, or roasted winter squash.

recipes.name: Akara (Black-Eyed Pea Fritters)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Dried black-eyed peas, soaked overnight and skins removed
Fresh scotch bonnet or habanero pepper, chopped
Water (for blending batter to correct consistency)

steps: Soak the dried black-eyed peas in cold water for at least 6 hours or overnight. Drain, then rub the beans vigorously between your palms in a bowl of fresh water — the skins will loosen and float to the top. Skim off the skins and drain, repeating 3–4 times until most skins are removed. Clean, skin-free beans produce a white, fluffy akara batter; beans with skins still on make the fritters dense and grey-tinged. Even a 20-minute soak and aggressive rubbing will remove most skins.

Combine the peeled beans, onion, scotch bonnet, salt, and just enough water to help the blender run — start with 2 tablespoons and add more sparingly. Blend until very smooth, about 2–3 minutes. The goal is a thick, smooth, fluffy paste, not a thin pourable liquid. Transfer to a bowl and beat the batter vigorously with a wooden spoon or hand mixer for 3–5 minutes — this incorporates air and gives akara its characteristic lightness. The batter should double slightly in volume and turn paler as air is worked in.

Heat enough oil in a medium saucepan to give a depth of at least 5 cm. Heat to 175 °C (a small drop of batter should sizzle and rise immediately). Using two spoons or a small ice cream scoop, drop spoonfuls of batter gently into the oil — do not crowd the pot, 4–5 at a time. Fry for 3–4 minutes total, turning gently halfway, until deep golden-brown on all sides. The fritters will puff and become round as they fry. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels.

Remove akara with a slotted spoon and drain on a paper towel-lined plate. Serve immediately — hot akara at peak crisp is the entire point of the dish. In Lagos, akara is sold from street stalls in the early morning alongside ogi (fermented corn porridge). Serve with a dipping sauce of tomato, onion, and pepper if desired. Akara made to order, eaten in the street, still crackling from the oil, is one of the great breakfast experiences of West Africa.

recipes.name: Al Pastor Achiote-Guajillo Marinade
steps: Heat a dry comal or cast-iron skillet over medium-high heat until very hot. Press each guajillo and ancho chile flat on the dry surface with a spatula for 10 to 15 seconds per side — you want the flesh to darken from bright brick-red to a deeper reddish-brown with small blistered spots, releasing a bloom of sweet, slightly smoky aroma. Guajillo chiles toast faster than anchos — watch them carefully. The moment you smell something fruity and slightly toasty, they are done. Transfer immediately to a bowl and cover with 2 cups of very hot (not boiling) water. Weigh them down with a plate and soak for 20 to 25 minutes until completely soft and pliable. The soaking water turns a vivid brick-orange. Reserve 3 tablespoons of the soaking liquid — it carries flavor that will be added to the marinade. Drain the chiles and use immediately.

Combine the drained soaked chiles, reserved chile soaking liquid, achiote paste, onion, garlic, fresh pineapple, white vinegar, orange juice, toasted cumin seeds, dried oregano, black peppercorns, ground cloves, and salt in a blender. Blend on high for 2 full minutes until the marinade is completely smooth. Stop the blender and rub a small amount between your fingers — if you feel any graininess from the seeds, peppercorns, or chile skins, blend for another minute. The finished marinade should be vivid orange-red to deep brick-red, completely smooth, and will stain anything it touches. Taste it now: the raw marinade will be quite sharp — bright from the pineapple and vinegar, with a building chile heat and an earthy, almost floral depth from the achiote. It will mellow considerably during the marinating period, losing its rawness and integrating into the meat. Use immediately: apply to thinly sliced pork shoulder (3 to 5 mm slices), coating every surface generously. Marinate refrigerated for at least 4 hours, ideally 12 to 24 hours.

recipes.name: Al Pastor

ingredients.name: Dried guajillo chilies, stems and seeds removed
Dried ancho chili, stem and seeds removed

steps: Tear the guajillo and ancho chilies open and remove all seeds and veins. Heat a dry comal or cast-iron skillet over medium heat until very hot. Press each chili flat with a spatula and toast for 20–30 seconds per side — until fragrant and pliable, with a couple of small dark spots. Do not let them turn black, or the entire marinade will taste of ash. Transfer immediately to a bowl and cover with just-boiled water. Weight them down with a small plate and soak for 20 minutes until completely soft and yielding.

Drain the chilies, reserving 60ml of soaking water. Combine soaked chilies, achiote paste, pineapple, onion, garlic, vinegar, oregano, cumin, salt, and oil in a blender. Add the reserved soaking water. Blend on high for 2–3 minutes until completely smooth — there should be no visible chili skin or fibre. Taste and adjust: it should be deeply smoky, mildly tangy from the vinegar and pineapple, pleasantly spiced, and the salt should be at the front of your tongue. If too thick to blend, add soaking water one tablespoon at a time.

Place the thinly sliced pork shoulder in a large bowl or zip-lock bag. Pour all of the marinade over the pork and toss thoroughly until every surface is evenly coated in the deep red paste. The pineapple enzymes (bromelain) will begin tenderizing the meat almost immediately — this is why the marinating time should not exceed 8 hours or the pork surface will become mushy. Cover and refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours, ideally overnight (but not more than 8 hours for thin-cut shoulder).

Position the oven rack at the highest position and set the broiler to its highest setting. Line a heavy baking sheet with foil. Lay the marinated pork slices in a single layer — they may overlap slightly. Broil for 4–5 minutes until the top surface is caramelised, blistered in places, and the edges are beginning to char. Flip each slice and broil for another 2–3 minutes. Remove and shave or chop into small pieces for tacos. Traditionally, the caramelised, slightly charred bits (the chicharitas off the trompo) are the best part — do not avoid the char.

recipes.name: Alfajores de Maizena
steps: Beat the room-temperature butter and sifted powdered sugar together in a stand mixer with the paddle attachment on medium speed for 4–5 minutes until the mixture is very pale, almost white, and light in texture. The prolonged creaming incorporates air and fully dissolves the powdered sugar, which is essential to the eventual melt-in-the-mouth texture. Scrape the bowl and paddle halfway through. The final mixture should look like whipped cream cheese — not the dense, yellow paste of under-creamed butter.

With the mixer on low, add the eggs one at a time, then the extra yolk, beating well after each addition. The extra yolk enriches the dough and contributes to the sandy, crumbly texture. Add the vanilla extract and lemon zest. Sift together the cornstarch, flour, and baking powder and add in two additions with the mixer on low, mixing only until just combined — as soon as no dry flour is visible, stop. Over-mixing develops gluten and will make the cookies tough rather than tender. The dough will be soft and slightly sticky.

Preheat the oven to 170°C (340°F). On a lightly floured surface, roll the chilled dough to 5mm thickness — not thinner, or the cookies will be too fragile. Cut 4cm rounds with a cookie cutter and arrange on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spaced 2cm apart. Bake for 12–14 minutes. The key indicator is what should NOT happen: the cookies must not take on any color. They should look almost exactly as they did going in — pale and matte, just dried and set. This near-invisible bake is the secret to their dissolving tenderness.

Ensure the cookies are completely cool — even slight warmth will melt the dulce de leche and cause them to slide apart. Match cookies into same-sized pairs. Spoon or pipe a generous amount of dulce de leche (about 1 teaspoon) onto the flat side of one cookie. Press the matching cookie on top, flat-side down, and rotate very gently to spread the dulce de leche to the edge without cracking the fragile cookies. Roll the exposed dulce de leche edge through the coconut, pressing lightly so it adheres all the way around. Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days.

recipes.name: Aloo Gobi

ingredients.name: Waxy potatoes (Yukon Gold), cut into 2 cm cubes
Cauliflower, cut into small 2–3 cm florets
Kashmiri chili powder or mild red chili powder

steps: Heat the ghee in a wide, heavy skillet or karahi over medium-high heat. Add the cumin seeds — they should sizzle immediately and begin to darken within 30 seconds. Add the sliced onion and cook, stirring frequently, for 8–10 minutes until deep golden and soft. Add the minced garlic and grated ginger and stir for another 60 seconds until the raw smell of the garlic has mellowed to sweet-savory. The entire pan should smell of toasted cumin and caramelizing onion — this is the flavor foundation everything else will absorb.

Add the ground turmeric, ground coriander, and Kashmiri chili powder to the golden onion in the pan. Stir constantly over medium heat for 45–60 seconds, cooking the spices directly in the ghee. The mixture will become very fragrant and stiff; if it begins to stick, add a tablespoon of water and stir to release. Season with salt. The spice paste is ready when the raw dusty aroma of the spices has transformed into a roasted, warm, complex fragrance and the fat has separated slightly at the edges of the paste.

Add the potato cubes to the spiced base and toss to coat every surface in the turmeric-orange spice paste. Spread into a single layer and cook over medium-high heat, stirring every 2–3 minutes rather than constantly — this allows the potato to develop golden sear marks rather than just steaming. Cook for 8–10 minutes until the potato cubes are golden on several sides and half-tender when pierced with the tip of a knife. They should still have a little resistance at this stage; they will finish cooking with the cauliflower.

Add the cauliflower florets to the pan and toss to coat in the spiced ghee. Sprinkle the garam masala over everything now — added at this mid-stage, it blooms gently in the residual fat rather than burning in an empty pan. If the pan looks very dry, add a tablespoon of water and cover with a lid for 3–4 minutes to steam-cook the cauliflower through. Then remove the lid and cook uncovered for another 5 minutes, tossing every 2 minutes, until both the potato and cauliflower are fully tender and the pan is dry — this is a dry curry; no sauce, only fragrant, spiced fat.

Remove the pan from the heat. Squeeze the lemon juice over the entire pan and toss immediately — the acid brightens all the spices and cuts through the richness of the ghee. Scatter the fresh cilantro over the top and give one final toss. Taste for salt and add a pinch more if needed. The finished aloo gobi should taste of nothing but the vegetables themselves and the spices — deeply savory, warmly spiced, with a clean lemony lift. Serve immediately with roti or paratha. It does not hold well; the vegetables lose their texture as they sit.

recipes.name: Pasta all'Amatriciana

ingredients.name: Guanciale (cured pork cheek, cut into lardons or thick batons)
San Marzano tomatoes (crushed by hand from a 400 g can)
Dried red chilli flakes (or 1 small dried peperoncino, crumbled)

steps: Place the guanciale in a cold, dry, heavy skillet — a wide sauté pan or frying pan works well. Set over medium-low heat and cook slowly, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the fat renders out completely and the pieces are golden, amber, and slightly crisp but still yielding at the centre. The guanciale releases its fat slowly — starting in a cold pan allows the fat to liquefy gradually and coat the pieces evenly as they cook. Remove the guanciale with a slotted spoon, leaving all the rendered fat in the pan.

Add the chilli flakes to the guanciale fat in the pan over medium heat and stir for 30 seconds until the chilli blooms in the fat — it will sizzle gently and the fat will turn faintly orange-red. Immediately pour in the white wine and stir vigorously to dissolve any fond and combine the chilli into the liquid. Let the wine reduce by half over 2–3 minutes until the raw alcohol smell cooks off and is replaced by a mellow, slightly fruity fragrance.

Crush the San Marzano tomatoes through your fingers into the pan — keeping them in rough, irregular pieces rather than a smooth purée. Return the guanciale to the pan. Stir well to combine, then let the sauce simmer uncovered over medium heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the tomatoes have broken down, the sauce has thickened to a rich, rust-red slick, and the fat from the guanciale is beginning to float in orange droplets on the surface — a sign of proper concentration.

Cook the bucatini in heavily salted boiling water to just shy of al dente (1–2 minutes less than the package says). Reserve 120 ml of the starchy cooking water before draining. Transfer the pasta directly to the sauce in the pan using tongs, bringing some cooking water naturally. Add a splash of reserved water and toss vigorously over medium heat for 1–2 minutes until the pasta finishes cooking in the sauce and the sauce clings to every tube. Add more water as needed — the sauce should coat, not pool. Finish with a grinding of black pepper.

Divide the pasta into warmed bowls. Scatter a generous amount of finely grated Pecorino Romano over each portion — it should be enough to see as a visible, snowy layer over the sauce. The cheese will soften and partially melt into the hot pasta, providing a sharp, salty counterpoint to the rich, sweet-porky sauce. Serve immediately. No additional oil, cream, or butter. The dish is complete.

recipes.name: Cast-Iron Skillet Cornbread
steps: Place a 25 cm (10-inch) cast-iron skillet in the oven and preheat both to 220 C (425 F). This step is non-negotiable: the blazing hot skillet creates the lacy, crackling bottom crust that defines cast-iron cornbread. While the oven heats, melt the skillet butter and the batter butter, then prepare your dry and wet ingredients separately.

In a large bowl, whisk together cornmeal, flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt, and sugar. In a separate bowl, whisk buttermilk, eggs, and melted-and-cooled butter together. Pour the wet ingredients into the dry and stir with a spatula just until combined — 10–15 strokes. Lumps are expected and correct. Do not overmix. The batter should be pourable but thick, like a loose pancake batter.

Remove the smoking skillet from the oven. Add the skillet butter — it will sizzle and foam violently. Swirl to coat, then pour in all the batter at once. The edges should crackle and set immediately on contact. Return to the oven and bake at 220 C for 20–25 minutes until the top is golden-brown and a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean. The cornbread will pull away from the skillet sides slightly. Let cool 5 minutes in the pan, then invert onto a cutting board.

recipes.name: Anticuchos de Corazón

ingredients.name: Beef heart, trimmed of fat, membrane, and ventricle tubes, cut into 3cm cubes
Ají panca paste (or dried ají panca, soaked and blended)
Boiled Peruvian corn (choclo) or corn on the cob, cut into rounds

steps: Working on a sturdy board, examine the beef heart carefully. Using a sharp boning knife, trim away any visible pockets of exterior fat — they are tallow-flavored and won't render in the short grill time. More importantly, feel for and cut out the firm white connective tissue tubes (the aorta and pulmonary vessels) that run through the top of the heart, and peel away the tough outer membrane that sheathes the ventricle walls. The actual muscle of the heart is unlike any other cut — it is deep red, extremely fine-grained, and dense, with almost no intramuscular fat. Slice the cleaned muscle across the grain into pieces roughly 3cm thick. They should look like small, irregular medallions, darker and more uniform than a steak.

In the bowl with the trimmed heart pieces, combine the ají panca paste, red wine vinegar, minced garlic, ground cumin, salt, and black pepper. Mix thoroughly with your hands, massaging the marinade into every surface and crevice of the meat. The vinegar begins a gentle acid tenderization immediately, and the ají panca — which is smoky, mild, and fruity in a distinctly different way from ají amarillo — stains the meat a deep, brick-red purple. Cover the bowl tightly and refrigerate for a minimum of 3 hours, ideally overnight. The longer it marinates (up to 24 hours), the more the vinegar softens the tight muscle fibers and the more deeply the spices penetrate. An hour before cooking, thread the pieces onto metal skewers — two or three pieces per skewer, leaving a little space between them.

Prepare your grill for extremely high direct heat — charcoal is authentic and optimal, gas works but lacks the smoke. The grill grate should be so hot that the skewers sizzle immediately and loudly on contact. Brush the grate with a little oil to prevent sticking. Lay the skewers perpendicular to the grate bars and leave them absolutely still for 2–3 minutes to develop a deep char. Turn once; grill the second side for 2 more minutes. Total cooking time is 4–5 minutes — beef heart is best eaten medium, with a faint blush of pink in the very center of the thick pieces. If you cook it beyond that, the muscle fibers contract violently and the texture goes from pleasantly chewy-tender to genuinely tough. While grilling, baste once with oil to create additional flare-ups and the characteristic flame-kissed char marks of street-cooked anticuchos.

Let the skewers rest 2 minutes off the heat. Plate in the traditional Lima street-food style: the skewers laid directly over rounds of boiled choclo (or corn on the cob cut into rounds) and boiled potato — the mild starchiness of both counterbalances the charred, acidic, deeply savory heart. In Lima, an anticucho vendor will hand you the skewer with the corn and potato already impaled at the base, so each bite can alternate between meat and starch. No additional sauce is strictly necessary, but a spoonful of remaining marinade warmed and reduced makes an excellent quick dipping sauce, or serve with additional ají amarillo paste on the side.

recipes.name: Classic Double-Crust American Apple Pie

ingredients.name: Granny Smith and Honeycrisp apples (mixed), peeled, cored, sliced 5 mm
Light brown sugar + granulated sugar (mixed equal parts)

steps: In a large bowl, whisk flour and salt. Add cold butter and lard. Using your fingertips, work the fats into the flour until the mixture looks like coarse crumbs with some larger, flat butter flakes — those flakes create the flaky layers. Do not overwork. Drizzle in ice water 1 tablespoon at a time, tossing with a fork. Stop adding water when the dough just holds together when pinched. Divide in two, flatten into discs, wrap, and refrigerate at least 2 hours or overnight.

Combine the sliced apples with sugar, cinnamon, cornstarch, and lemon juice. Toss to coat. Let stand 30 minutes at room temperature — the sugar will draw liquid out of the apples. Drain off the released juice into a small saucepan, reduce it to a thick syrup over medium heat, and pour it back over the apples. This pre-reducing step prevents the gap that forms between crust and filling when juices boil away during baking.

On a lightly floured surface, roll the first dough disc to a 30 cm circle, about 3–4 mm thick. Drape into a 23 cm pie dish, pressing into the corners without stretching. Pile the apple filling into the shell, mounding it higher than the rim — it will settle during baking. Roll the second disc and lay it over the top, or cut into strips for a lattice. Trim to 1.5 cm overhang, fold under, and crimp the edge. Cut steam vents if using a full top crust. Refrigerate the assembled pie for 30 minutes before baking.

Preheat oven to 220 C (425 F) with a sheet pan on the lower rack (this conducts heat to the bottom crust). Brush the top crust with egg wash and scatter a pinch of granulated sugar over it. Bake at 220 C for 20 minutes until the edges begin to set and color. Reduce heat to 190 C (375 F) and continue baking 35–45 minutes until the crust is deeply golden and the filling is visibly bubbling through the vents. Cool on a wire rack for at least 3 hours before slicing — the filling thickens as it cools.

recipes.name: Apple Strudel
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: High-gluten bread flour or all-purpose flour
Tart apples (Granny Smith or Cox), peeled, thinly sliced

steps: Combine flour, warm water, oil, and salt, mixing until a shaggy dough forms. Knead vigorously for 10 full minutes — this dough requires serious development of gluten, which is what allows it to be stretched to an almost impossible thinness without tearing. Knead by slapping the dough against the work surface and folding it. The finished dough should be smooth as silk, warm from the kneading, and extremely elastic. Shape into a ball, brush with oil, and rest covered for 45 minutes at room temperature. The rest is not optional — it relaxes the gluten to the point where stretching becomes possible.

Toss the thinly sliced apples with sugar and cinnamon and let macerate for 15 minutes — the sugar draws out juice. Drain the excess juice thoroughly, as too much moisture will make the strudel soggy. Toast the breadcrumbs in butter until golden and fragrant — these absorb any residual apple moisture during baking, keeping the pastry crisp from inside. Combine the drained apples and buttered breadcrumbs just before filling the stretched dough.

Cover a large table with a clean cloth and dust lightly with flour. Place the rested dough in the center and roll it out with a pin to about 40x60cm. Then begin stretching by hand: place both hands under the dough, palms down, and stretch outward from the center using the backs of your knuckles. Walk around the table, stretching in all directions, until the dough is paper-thin (about 1mm) and almost transparent — roughly 60x80cm. The dough must be so thin you can read text through it. Brush thoroughly with melted butter as you work.

Spread the buttered breadcrumbs across two-thirds of the dough, leaving a 5cm border. Pile the apple filling evenly over the breadcrumbs. Using the tablecloth to assist, roll the strudel into a tight log, using the cloth to lift and fold rather than your hands. Place seam-side down on a parchment-lined baking sheet, curving into a horseshoe if needed. Brush generously with melted butter. Bake at 190°C (375°F) for 35–40 minutes, brushing with butter once more at the 20-minute mark. Dust with powdered sugar and serve warm.

recipes.name: Apple Tarte Tatin
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Firm apples (Golden Delicious or Braeburn), peeled, halved, cored
Unsalted butter, cold, cut into pieces
Puff pastry or shortcrust, rolled to 3 mm
Vanilla pod, split and seeds scraped

steps: Scatter the caster sugar in an even layer across the base of a heavy 24–26 cm oven-safe skillet or tarte tatin mold. Set over medium heat without stirring. The sugar will begin to liquefy at the edges — let it pool before swirling the pan gently to even the color. Continue until the liquid caramel reaches a deep amber, the color of dark mahogany. Remove from heat.

Off the heat, drop the cold butter pieces into the amber caramel one at a time. Add the vanilla seeds and pod. The mixture will bubble furiously — this is correct. Stir with a heatproof spatula until the butter is fully incorporated and the caramel is smooth, glossy, and homogeneous.

Remove the vanilla pod. Arrange the apple halves cut-side up over the caramel, packing them as tightly as possible in a circular pattern — they will shrink during cooking, so crowding is correct. Set the pan over medium heat and cook 15–20 minutes until the apples are partially softened and the caramel has deepened and thickened around them.

Cut the pastry into a circle 2 cm wider than the pan diameter. Drape it over the apples and tuck the overhanging edge down into the pan, hugging the apple perimeter. Prick the pastry six times with a fork. Preheat the oven to 190°C (375°F) fan-assisted.

Bake at 190°C for 25–30 minutes until the pastry is deeply golden and puffed, and caramel is visibly bubbling at the pan edges. Remove and rest on a wire rack for exactly 5 minutes — no longer, or the caramel will seize and the tart will stick on inversion.

Place a large, lipped serving plate firmly over the pan. Grip both plate and pan securely, count to one, then invert with confidence. Hold for three seconds, then lift the pan away. Any apples that have shifted can be pressed gently back into place with a spoon. Serve warm with crème fraîche alongside.

recipes.name: Arancini al Ragù
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Warm water or light chicken stock
Saffron threads, steeped in 2 tbsp warm water
Low-moisture mozzarella, cut into 1 cm cubes

steps: Combine the rice and warm stock or water in a medium saucepan. Add the saffron water and a generous pinch of salt. Bring to a boil, stir once, then reduce to a low simmer and cover. Cook for 16-18 minutes until all liquid is absorbed. The rice should be slightly firmer than eating-rice — it will continue to absorb and compact as it cools. Immediately spread the rice onto a large rimmed baking sheet in a thin, even layer to cool. Do not cover — you want steam to escape. Let cool completely at room temperature, at least 45 minutes, until the rice is sticky, compact, and cold to the touch. Cold rice is non-negotiable for forming arancini.

Cook the diced onion in a little oil over medium heat until soft and translucent, about 8 minutes. Add the ground meat and cook, breaking it up with a wooden spoon, until no pink remains and the meat is lightly browned in spots, about 10 minutes. Add the tomato paste and stir to coat. Cook for 3 minutes, stirring constantly, until the paste darkens and smells sweet and caramelized. Add a splash of water or wine to deglaze. Season well with salt and pepper. Simmer on low heat for 20 minutes until the mixture is thick, cohesive, and not at all wet — a wet filling will burst the rice shell during frying. Cool completely before filling.

Transfer the cold, spread rice to a large bowl. Beat one egg and add it to the rice. Mix thoroughly with your hands until the egg is fully distributed and the rice feels even more cohesive and slightly sticky. This binding step makes the arancini hold their shape during breading and frying. Test by pressing a handful firmly — it should hold a firm ball that doesn't crumble.

Wet your hands lightly. Scoop about 100g of rice into one palm and flatten it into a disc roughly 10 cm across. Place a heaped teaspoon of cooled ragù in the center and press a cube of mozzarella alongside it. Carefully cup your hand and bring the edges of the rice disc up and around the filling, pressing firmly to enclose it completely. Use both hands to roll into a tight sphere. Press firmly — any air pocket or thin spot will cause the arancini to burst in the fryer. Repeat. Rest the formed balls on a parchment-lined tray as you go.

Set up a breading station: beaten egg in one bowl, fine breadcrumbs in another. Roll each arancino first in beaten egg until completely coated, letting the excess drip off. Then roll immediately in the breadcrumbs, pressing firmly on all sides to create a complete, even crust with no bare patches. Roll a second time through egg and breadcrumbs for a double coat — this double layer is the secret to a shatteringly crisp shell that won't crack in the oil. Place on a parchment-lined tray and refrigerate for at least 20 minutes before frying.

Heat the neutral oil in a deep, heavy pot to 175 C (350 F) — use a thermometer. The oil depth should be at least 8 cm to allow the arancini to be submerged. Gently lower 2-3 arancini into the oil at a time — do not crowd the pot, which drops the temperature and causes greasy, pale results. Fry for 4-5 minutes, turning gently with a spider skimmer every 90 seconds to ensure even color on all sides. Remove when deeply golden-brown all over and transfer to a wire rack lined with paper towels. Allow the oil to return to 175 C between batches. Serve within 5 minutes while the cheese is still molten.

recipes.name: Arepas
steps: In a large bowl, combine masarepa, warm water, salt, and softened butter. Stir with a fork until the butter is distributed and the water has been absorbed, then knead the masa with your hands for 2-3 minutes. Masarepa is precooked flour — it hydrates very quickly, unlike raw cornmeal. The resulting dough should be smooth, non-sticky, and pliable — the consistency of moist Play-Doh. If adding cheese, knead it into the dough now. Allow the masa to rest for 5 minutes, covered with a damp cloth. During this brief rest, the starch continues to absorb water and the dough firms slightly to the ideal forming consistency.

Divide the masa into 6-8 equal portions (about the size of a golf ball). Roll each between your palms into a smooth sphere, then press between flat palms to form an even disc approximately 1 cm thick and 8-10 cm across. The disc should have smooth, uncracked edges — run a wet fingertip along any cracks and press them closed. Thicker arepas (1.5 cm) cook slower and have a more doughy interior; thinner arepas (0.7 cm) develop more crust relative to interior. Colombian arepas are typically about 1 cm.

Heat a dry cast-iron griddle, comal, or heavy skillet over medium heat (no oil — arepas are cooked dry on the surface, though a light brush of butter adds flavor). When the griddle is hot enough that a drop of water skitters and evaporates in 2-3 seconds, add the arepas in a single layer without crowding. Cook for 5-7 minutes per side without disturbing, until a well-defined golden-brown crust has formed on each face. Resist pressing or moving them — the crust needs uninterrupted contact with the hot surface to develop properly. An arepa is finished when it sounds hollow when tapped with a knuckle and the crust is firm rather than soft.

recipes.name: Arroz con Leche
steps: Rinse the rice briefly under cold water. Combine milk, rice, cinnamon stick, lemon zest strips, and salt in a heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a gentle simmer, stirring frequently to prevent the milk from scorching on the base. Once it simmers, reduce to the lowest heat setting.

After 10 minutes, add the sugar and stir to dissolve. Continue cooking on the lowest heat, stirring every 3–4 minutes, for a total of 30–35 minutes from the point of adding the rice. The pudding is done when it has thickened to a loose, flowing cream — it should still look slightly underdone in the pot, as it will thicken further as it cools.

Remove the cinnamon stick and lemon zest strips. Stir in the butter until melted — it adds a silkiness that enriches the finish. Pour into individual serving bowls or one large dish. Press a piece of plastic wrap directly onto the surface of the pudding to prevent a skin from forming. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours, or until fully cold and set.

Remove the plastic wrap. Dust the surface with ground cinnamon through a fine sieve, tracing a neat stripe or covering the entire surface evenly. Serve immediately from the refrigerator — arroz con leche is best cold. Do not stir the cinnamon in; it sits on top as both flavour and visual mark of completion.

recipes.name: Arroz Rojo (Mexican Red Rice)
steps: Combine the tomatoes, garlic, and onion quarter in a blender with 100ml of the broth and blitz to a completely smooth purée. You should have approximately 350ml of liquid. The raw purée will be bright orange-red; it will deepen during cooking. Set aside.

Heat the oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the dry (unrinsed) rice all at once and stir constantly with a wooden spoon for 4–6 minutes. The grains will gradually turn from white to pale blond, then to a warm golden color. Do not walk away — toasting is what keeps Mexican rice grains separate rather than clumping. The room will fill with a nutty, popcorn-like aroma.

Add the carrot and serrano chile to the toasted rice and stir for 30 seconds. Pour in the tomato purée — it will hiss and spatter as it hits the hot oil — and stir immediately to coat all the grains. Add the remaining broth, cumin, and salt. Bring to a boil, stirring once, then reduce to the lowest possible heat, cover tightly, and cook undisturbed for 18–20 minutes.

Remove from heat. Scatter the frozen peas over the surface, re-cover, and let rest 5 minutes — the residual steam will thaw and warm the peas without cooking them to mush. Then use a fork to fluff gently from the edges inward, pulling the grains apart. Remove the serrano chile before serving if desired. Taste for salt.

recipes.name: Arroz Verde
steps: Combine the poblano, jalapeño, cilantro (stems and all), onion, and garlic in a blender. Add 250 ml of the stock. Blitz on high for 60-90 seconds until completely smooth with no visible pieces. The purée will be a vivid, almost neon green at first — it will darken as it cooks. Season the purée lightly with salt before adding it to the rice. Measure it — you need approximately 500 ml of purée total; if you have more, reserve it. If less, add a little more stock.

Rinse the rice under cold water until the water runs clear, then spread it out on a clean kitchen towel and pat as dry as possible — wet rice will spatter violently in the hot oil and steam instead of toasting. Heat the oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot with a tight-fitting lid over medium-high heat until the oil shimmers. Add the dry rice and spread into an even layer. Cook, stirring constantly, for 4-5 minutes until the grains turn from white to a pale, even golden color and smell nutty and toasted.

Pour the entire green purée over the toasted rice all at once — it will hiss and spatter as it hits the hot oil and rice, so stand back. Stir immediately to prevent any rice from sticking. Cook over medium-high heat, stirring frequently, for 3-4 minutes as the purée dries out and the rice absorbs the green color. You are essentially frying the purée into the rice — when it no longer looks wet and the rice has absorbed the vivid green color, it is ready for the remaining stock.

Pour the remaining stock (250 ml) over the rice, add the salt, and stir once to distribute. Bring to a full boil over high heat. Once boiling, reduce to the absolute lowest heat, cover tightly, and cook for 15 minutes without lifting the lid. The rice needs to steam in this final stage — every time the lid is lifted, you lose steam and the rice will cook unevenly. Set a timer and do not open the pot.

Remove from heat and let the rice rest, covered, for 5 minutes to allow the steam to redistribute evenly through the grains. Uncover and fluff gently with a fork, using a lifting and separating motion from the bottom of the pot. Taste and adjust salt. The rice should be a deep, even green throughout each grain — not just surface-stained. Serve as a side dish alongside chicken, fish, or beans, or as a base for a grain bowl.

recipes.name: Sachertorte
steps: Preheat oven to 170°C (340°F). Butter and flour a 23cm springform pan, line the base with parchment. Beat the softened butter and icing sugar on medium speed until light and pale — about 5 minutes. Add the melted (but cooled) chocolate and beat until fully incorporated. Add the egg yolks one at a time, beating well after each. The mixture will look slightly curdled — this is normal. Sift the flour into the mixture and fold in gently with a spatula.

In a scrupulously clean bowl, beat the egg whites on medium speed until foamy. Increase to high speed and add the caster sugar gradually in a slow, steady stream. Beat to stiff, glossy peaks — the meringue should hold a firm peak that barely curves at the tip and looks like shaving foam. The sugar must be fully dissolved — rub a small amount between fingers: it should feel smooth, not gritty.

Add one-quarter of the meringue to the chocolate base and stir vigorously to lighten it. Then add the remaining meringue in two additions, folding with a large rubber spatula using slow, deliberate J-strokes — cut to the bottom, sweep under, fold over. Rotate the bowl between each fold. Stop as soon as no white streaks remain. The batter should be airy but still noticeably heavy. Pour into the prepared pan, smooth the top, and bake immediately.

Bake at 170°C for 45-55 minutes. The Sachertorte should bake relatively flat with a very slight dome. It is done when a skewer inserted in the center comes out clean and the top springs back when lightly pressed. Cool in the pan for 15 minutes, then release and invert onto a wire rack to cool completely. When fully cold, slice horizontally through the center to make two equal layers.

Warm the apricot jam with 2 tbsp of water and pass through a sieve to make it smooth. Brush a very thin layer over the cut surface of the bottom layer and assemble the two layers. Then brush the entire outside of the assembled cake — top and sides — thoroughly with the warm jam. Allow to set for 15 minutes. For the glaze: combine sugar and water in a saucepan, bring to a boil, and cook to exactly 103°C (217°F). Remove from heat and add the chopped chocolate all at once. Stir until fully smooth and glossy. Pour immediately over the jam-coated cake on a wire rack over a tray. Use a palette knife in a single sweep to smooth the top — do not go back and forth. Allow to set fully at room temperature.

recipes.name: Avgolemono
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Fresh lemon juice (about 2 large lemons per 4 eggs)

steps: Crack the eggs into a medium bowl and whisk vigorously for 1–2 minutes until completely homogeneous and slightly frothy — no streaks of white or separated yolk should remain. While still whisking, pour in the fresh lemon juice in a slow, steady stream. The mixture will turn paler and slightly thicker as the acid begins to partially denature the egg proteins — this is intentional and helps the emulsion hold under heat. The finished base should be a pale, foamy, uniformly yellow-cream liquid that smells intensely of fresh lemon with an underlying egg richness. Have the hot broth already simmering in a pot nearby before you begin the temper.

Have the hot broth at a bare simmer (just below boiling, about 85–90C). Using a ladle, pour a single ladle of hot broth into the egg-lemon mixture while whisking constantly and rapidly. The egg mixture will lighten and thin slightly as the first ladle hits. Add a second ladle, still whisking. Then a third. By the time you have added 3–4 ladles, the egg mixture will be warm and the temperature differential will be small enough that adding it back to the pot will not scramble it. Pour the tempered mixture back into the pot of broth in a slow stream while whisking the broth continuously. The temperature must remain below 85C throughout — if the broth is at a hard boil, remove from heat first.

With the tempered egg-lemon mixture now in the pot, heat over medium-low while stirring gently and constantly with a wooden spoon or spatula, making sure to reach the bottom and corners of the pot. The sauce will thicken gradually over 3–5 minutes as the egg proteins set at a low temperature, coating the spoon progressively more. Do not boil — the moment you see bubbles beginning to form at the edges, reduce heat immediately. The finished sauce should coat the back of a spoon with a smooth, velvety layer and leave a clean line when a finger is drawn through it. Taste and adjust salt. The sauce should taste brightly of lemon with a rich, savory broth behind it — neither element should dominate. Serve immediately or keep at around 70C to hold.

recipes.name: Baba Ghanoush
steps: Place whole eggplants directly on a gas burner set to high flame, or as close as possible to a very hot grill or broiler element. Char on all sides, turning with tongs every 3–4 minutes, until the entire exterior is blackened and the eggplant has completely collapsed and feels hollow. This takes 15–20 minutes total. The more thoroughly charred, the deeper the smoke.

Place the charred eggplants in a colander over a bowl. Cover the colander and let them steam for 10 minutes — this loosens the skin and allows the eggplant to release bitter liquid. Peel away all the charred skin with your fingers, working carefully to remove any large patches of black. Discard the liquid that has collected. Allow the drained flesh to sit for a further 5 minutes to shed more liquid.

Using a fork or pestle, mash the garlic with the salt to a smooth paste. Add the eggplant flesh and mash roughly — some texture is welcome. Beat in the tahini and lemon juice in alternating additions, tasting as you go. The dip will tighten and turn creamy as the tahini emulsifies with the eggplant. Adjust salt and lemon aggressively — it needs more than you expect. Transfer to a serving plate, make a well with the back of a spoon, drizzle with olive oil, dust with paprika, and scatter parsley.

recipes.name: Bacalhau à Brás
steps: Place the salt cod in a large bowl of cold water, skin side up. Refrigerate and change the water three times over 24 hours — at 8-hour intervals is ideal. The fish should taste of the sea, not of brine. After soaking, pat thoroughly dry and remove any remaining bones with tweezers.

Lower the cod into a wide pan of barely simmering water (no rolling boil — the water should just tremble). Poach for 5–7 minutes until the flesh is cooked through but still moist. Remove with a slotted spoon and let cool enough to handle. Peel away the skin, then use your fingers and two forks to shred the cod into fine, thread-like pieces — as thin as you can manage without reducing it to mush.

Cut the peeled potatoes into matchstick julienne — about 2mm × 2mm × 6cm — using a mandoline or sharp knife. Rinse in cold water, then dry completely on towels (wet potato steams rather than fries). Heat 2–3cm of the olive oil in a wide pan to 180°C (a test straw should sizzle immediately). Fry the potatoes in batches until light gold and crisp, about 3–4 minutes per batch. Drain on a wire rack, not paper towels, which soften the bottom.

In the same pan (wipe out excess frying oil, leave a thin film), warm 2 tablespoons of fresh olive oil over medium heat. Add the onion and cook slowly for 10–12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until deeply soft, translucent, and faintly golden at the edges — this is the aromatic backbone of the dish. Add the garlic in the last 2 minutes and stir until fragrant but not coloured.

Add the shredded cod to the onions and garlic. Toss gently over medium-low heat for 1 minute to warm through and marry the flavours. Add the potato straws and toss again — you want them still crisp at this stage. Beat the eggs lightly with a fork (do not season — the cod does that) and pour over the mixture. Fold continuously with a spatula over low heat, pulling the eggs through the mixture in slow waves. Remove from the heat while the eggs are still a little underdone — they will carry-cook.

Scatter the roughly chopped parsley generously over the top — it is not just a garnish here but a bright, herbal counterpoint to the salt and richness. Add the olives, either scattered whole or halved. Drizzle with a thread of your best olive oil. Taste and adjust salt only if needed — it rarely will be. Serve immediately in the pan or on warm plates; this dish does not wait.

recipes.name: New York Bagel
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine all dough ingredients in a stand mixer with a dough hook. Mix on low 2 minutes to bring together, then medium for 10 minutes. Bagel dough is intentionally stiff at 55% hydration — stiffer than almost any other bread. The low hydration is what creates the characteristic dense, chewy crumb. Add water only 1 teaspoon at a time if the dough is cracking and won't come together.

Divide into 8 pieces (~110 g each). To shape: roll each piece into a smooth ball, then poke a floured finger through the center. Stretch the ring out to 3–4 cm diameter in the center — it will shrink back. Alternatively, roll into a 25 cm rope and join the ends around your hand, rolling the seam to seal. Place on oiled parchment. Cover and refrigerate 8–12 hours — cold retarding develops flavor and firms the bagels for boiling.

Bring a large wide pot of water to a rolling boil. Add barley malt syrup. Boil bagels 2 bagels at a time: 30 seconds per side for a thin, soft crust; 60 seconds per side for a thicker, chewier crust (New York style). The bagels will float to the surface almost immediately from the oven spring — that is correct. Remove with a slotted spoon, drain briefly, then roll in toppings or leave plain. Place on a wire rack set over a baking tray.

Preheat oven to 240 C (465 F) with a baking stone or heavy baking sheet inside. Bake the boiled, topped bagels directly on the hot surface for 18–22 minutes, rotating once at the 10-minute mark, until the surface is a deep, even golden-brown and the crust feels firm when tapped.

recipes.name: New York–Style Bagels
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine the water, malt syrup, and instant yeast in a large bowl and stir briefly to dissolve. Add the flour and salt. Mix by hand or with a dough hook until the ingredients come together into a stiff, rough ball — about 3 minutes. This dough is intentionally very stiff: 55% hydration is on the low end for bread, and that stiffness is what gives the bagel its characteristic chewiness. The dough will feel almost too dry and will not fully smooth out during mixing. Turn out onto an unfloured surface.

Knead the dough on an unfloured surface for 8–10 minutes by hand (or 6 minutes in a stand mixer with a dough hook on medium speed). The stiff dough won't be as extensible as focaccia or sourdough, but it should become smooth and develop enough elasticity to pass the windowpane test: stretch a small piece between your fingers into a thin membrane without it tearing. Divide into 8 equal portions (about 110–120g each). Roll each into a smooth ball, cover with a damp towel, and let rest 15 minutes to relax the gluten before shaping.

To shape each bagel: roll each ball into a rope about 9 inches long, slightly thicker in the middle. Wrap the rope around your palm and four fingers, overlapping the ends by 1–2 inches on your palm. Roll your palm back and forth on the counter while pressing down — the ends will fuse together under the pressure. The resulting ring should have a hole about 1.5–2 inches in diameter (it will close significantly during boiling and baking). Alternatively, poke a floured thumb through the center of each ball and gently stretch the hole. Place shaped bagels on a parchment-lined sheet pan.

Cover the pan of shaped bagels with plastic wrap and refrigerate for 10–14 hours (overnight). The cold proof develops flavor while keeping the dough very firm, which helps the bagels hold their shape during boiling. To test if they are ready: drop one bagel into a bowl of cold water. If it floats within 10 seconds, it's ready to boil. If it sinks and stays down, it needs more time at room temperature (30–60 minutes out of the refrigerator).

Bring a wide pot of water to a rolling boil. Add the barley malt syrup and baking soda and stir to dissolve — the water will foam slightly. Working in batches of 2–4 (do not crowd), lower the bagels into the water. Boil 1 minute per side (2 minutes total) for a chewier crust, or 30 seconds per side for a slightly softer result. Remove with a slotted spoon and transfer to a parchment-lined baking sheet. Immediately apply toppings (sesame seeds, poppy seeds, everything seasoning) while the surface is wet.

Bake the boiled bagels at 500°F (260°C) for 18–22 minutes, rotating the pan once halfway through, until they are a deep mahogany-brown all over — including the bottom. They will darken more than you expect and more than you might be comfortable with. Do not pull them early; the color is the flavor. Cool on a wire rack for at least 10 minutes before cutting — the interior is still finishing and will be slightly gummy if cut hot.

recipes.name: Bagna Cauda
steps: Place the peeled garlic cloves in a small saucepan and cover with cold milk. Bring gently to a simmer over low heat and cook for 10-12 minutes until the garlic is completely tender and has lost most of its sharp bite. Drain and discard the milk. This step transforms raw garlic's aggression into something sweet and mellow — it is not optional if you want an approachable bagna cauda.

In a wide, low saucepan or terracotta bagna cauda pot, combine the warm olive oil and drained mellowed garlic over the lowest possible heat. Add the rinsed anchovy fillets. Cook gently, stirring occasionally, for 10-15 minutes. The anchovies will dissolve completely into the oil; press them with a wooden spoon to help. The garlic should also gradually break down — mash it against the pan with the spoon. Neither should fry or sizzle aggressively.

Off the lowest possible heat, stir in the cold butter piece by piece until it melts into the warm oil, giving the sauce a slightly creamier, richer texture. Season with white pepper. Transfer to a terracotta serving vessel over a tea light or candle to keep it warm at the table. Serve with raw and briefly blanched vegetables — cardoons, fennel, radicchio, peppers, carrots.

recipes.name: Baguette
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: The night before, build a poolish: stir together 100 g of the flour, 100 g of the water (room temperature), and a tiny pinch of the yeast — about 1/16 teaspoon — into a loose, batter-like paste. Cover and leave at cool room temperature for 12 to 16 hours. This slow pre-ferment builds the wheaty, faintly nutty flavor and the organic acids that give a real baguette its character, long before the main dough is mixed.

Add the remaining flour, the remaining water, and the rest of the yeast to the poolish and mix to a shaggy mass with no dry flour left. Rest it 20 to 30 minutes (an autolyse) so the flour fully hydrates and gluten begins forming on its own. Then sprinkle the salt over the top and squeeze and fold it in until fully incorporated. The dough will be wet and sticky at this high hydration — resist adding flour. Knead briefly or use slap-and-folds just until it comes together into a rough, cohesive ball.

Bulk-ferment the dough in a lightly oiled, covered container. Over the first 2 hours, give it three or four sets of stretch-and-folds spaced about 30 minutes apart: wet your hand, lift one side of the dough up and over itself, rotate the bowl, and repeat around all four sides. Each fold builds strength and traps gas. After the folds, let it rise undisturbed until nearly doubled and visibly airy — about 2 to 3 hours at room temperature total, or refrigerate overnight for deeper flavor.

Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and divide into three pieces of about 250 g each. Pre-shape each loosely into a rectangle and rest 15 to 20 minutes covered, so the gluten relaxes. To shape, gently flatten one piece into a rectangle, fold the top third down and seal, fold the bottom third up and seal, then roll and taper from the center outward into a slender 14-inch baton with pointed ends. Settle the loaves seam-side up in the folds of a heavily floured couche (use the rice flour to prevent sticking) and proof 45 to 75 minutes until puffy.

Preheat a baking stone or steel to 475°F (245°C) with an empty tray on the bottom rack. Transfer the proofed loaves seam-side down onto parchment. With a razor or lame held at a low 30-degree angle, make three or four long overlapping diagonal slashes down the length of each loaf — almost parallel, not crosswise. Slide the loaves onto the stone and immediately pour the boiling water into the hot bottom tray to flood the oven with steam, then close the door. Bake 12 minutes with steam, then remove the tray, vent any excess, and bake 8 to 12 minutes more until deep golden and crackling. Cool on a rack at least 20 minutes — the crumb is still setting.

recipes.name: Baja Fish Tacos
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: White fish fillets (cod, halibut, or tilapia), skin off
All-purpose flour and cornstarch, equal parts combined
Mexican lager beer (Modelo Especial or Pacifico), cold
Cayenne pepper and garlic powder, equal parts
Neutral oil for deep-frying (vegetable or canola)
Shredded white cabbage, Mexican crema, lime wedges, and hot sauce

steps: Combine the flour-cornstarch blend, cayenne, garlic powder, and salt in a medium bowl. Pour in the cold beer all at once and stir with a fork just until combined — 8 to 10 strokes at most. The batter must be lumpy, not smooth. Lumps of unmixed flour are your friend: they create uneven pockets that fry into extra-crunchy patches. Do not over-mix. Keep the batter cold — set the bowl over ice if your kitchen is warm. Cold batter hits hot oil and creates maximum shatter.

Heat at least 5 cm of oil in a heavy pot or deep skillet to 180°C (350°F). Use a thermometer — temperature precision matters here. Cut the fish into 2 x 8 cm strips along the grain. Pat them bone-dry with paper towels, then season with salt. Working in batches of 3–4 strips (never crowd the pot), dip each strip into the batter, let the excess drip off for 3 seconds, then lower it into the oil away from you. Fry for 3–4 minutes, turning once, until the batter is a deep golden amber and the fish floats freely in the oil. Drain on a wire rack — not paper towels, which steam the crust soft.

Set a dry cast-iron skillet or comal over high heat. Toast each corn tortilla directly on the hot surface for 20–30 seconds per side until it puffs slightly, smells of toasted masa, and develops faint char spots. Stack and wrap in a clean cloth to keep warm and pliable — cold, stiff tortillas crack when folded around the fish.

Working quickly while the fish is still hot and crisp, lay two warmed tortillas slightly overlapping on a plate (Baja style uses two per taco for structural support). Add a strip of fried fish down the centre. Top with a loose mound of shredded cabbage, a generous drizzle of crema, a squeeze of lime, and a dash of hot sauce. Eat immediately — batter crust softens within 5 minutes of contact with moist toppings.

recipes.name: Baked Feta with Greens and Beans

ingredients.name: Cannellini beans, cooked and drained (about 2 cans)
Feta, one block (vegetarian rennet), patted dry
Lacinato kale, stems removed, leaves torn

steps: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). In a 23 x 33 cm baking dish, toss the beans, cherry tomatoes, garlic, 45 ml of the olive oil, oregano, pepper flakes, and stock. Season with a small pinch of salt (the feta will add plenty) and lots of black pepper. Spread in an even layer.
Bake uncovered for 15 minutes, until the tomatoes begin to split and the liquid is bubbling at the edges.

Nestle the feta block in the center. Toss the kale with the remaining 15 ml oil and a pinch of salt and pile it around the feta. Bake 15–20 minutes more until the kale is wilted with crisp tips and the feta is soft. Then switch to broil (high) for 2–3 minutes, watching closely, to brown the top of the cheese.

Grate the lemon zest over the top and squeeze over half the juice. Gently break up the feta with a spoon, swirling it into the beans and greens so it thickens the juices into a creamy sauce. Taste, add more lemon if needed, and serve with torn crusty bread.

recipes.name: Turkish Baklava
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine the sugar and water in a heavy saucepan over medium heat. Stir only until the sugar dissolves, then stop stirring entirely. Bring to a boil and simmer for 8 to 10 minutes until slightly thickened — it should coat a cold spoon lightly. Remove from heat, add the lemon juice and rosewater, and stir once. The syrup must be made first and cooled completely to room temperature before the baklava comes out of the oven. Hot syrup on hot baklava makes it soggy rather than crisp.

Pour the hot syrup into a wide, shallow vessel and leave it uncovered at room temperature until completely cold — this takes at least 45 minutes. Do not rush it in the fridge (condensation dilutes it). While it cools, set up your workspace: unwrap the phyllo and keep it under a damp cloth to prevent drying, prepare the chopped pistachios, and butter and line the baking pan.

Brush the base of the baking pan generously with clarified butter. Lay a sheet of phyllo, brush with butter, repeat until half the sheets are used. Scatter the pistachios evenly across the surface in a level layer. Continue layering and buttering the remaining phyllo sheets on top. Brush the very top sheet with extra butter. Using a sharp knife, cut the baklava all the way to the bottom of the pan in a diamond or square grid pattern — the cuts must go all the way through before baking, not after.

Bake in a preheated oven at 160°C (320°F) for 50 to 60 minutes until the entire surface is evenly deep golden and the pastry sounds hollow when tapped. Do not rush the bake at higher heat — a low, steady temperature renders all the butter and crisps every layer without burning the surface before the interior sets. Remove from the oven and immediately pour the cooled syrup evenly over the hot baklava — pour slowly and in a steady stream so every part receives syrup. The sizzle will be violent. Leave undisturbed for at least 4 hours before cutting along the pre-made lines.

If any syrup remains unpoured, add it now, tilting the pan gently to distribute. Do not cover the baklava while it rests — covering traps steam and softens the crust. After at least 4 hours (overnight is better), re-cut along the original lines, wiping the knife clean between cuts. Serve at room temperature. Store uncovered or very loosely tented at room temperature for up to 5 days — never refrigerate.

recipes.name: Banana Bread
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Overripe bananas, mashed (3–4 large, very black)
Fine salt, vanilla extract, ground cinnamon

steps: Peel the overripe bananas into a large bowl. Mash thoroughly with a fork until almost completely smooth — a few small lumps are fine and add texture. The bananas must be very overripe: deep brown to black on the exterior, soft to the point of being nearly liquid. Underripe yellow bananas lack the concentrated sweetness and starch conversion that makes banana bread work.

To the mashed banana, add the brown sugar, melted (and cooled) butter, eggs, vanilla, and spices. Whisk until fully combined and the sugar is mostly dissolved. The butter must be cooled — if it's still hot, it will scramble the eggs. The mixture will look thick and glossy, like a loose caramel sauce.

Sift the flour, baking soda, and salt together over the wet mixture. Using a rubber spatula, fold gently with a J-stroke motion — scrape under, fold over — just until no dry flour streaks remain. Do not stir vigorously or beat. Overworking the batter develops gluten and creates a tough, rubbery loaf rather than a tender, moist one. Ten to fifteen folds should be enough.

Preheat the oven to 175°C. Pour the batter into a greased and floured 23x13cm loaf pan. Optionally, sprinkle the top with 1 tablespoon of brown sugar for a crackly crust. Bake for 55–65 minutes until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean or with just a few moist crumbs. The top should crack along the center — this is correct. Cool in the pan for 10 minutes before turning out.

recipes.name: Banana Oat Snack Cake
steps: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease an 8 × 8 in (20 × 20 cm) square pan and line it with a parchment sling. In a large bowl, mash the bananas with a fork until mostly smooth. Whisk in the brown sugar, eggs, melted butter, yogurt, and vanilla until evenly combined.

Add the flour, oats, baking soda, salt, and cinnamon directly to the bowl (sprinkle the baking soda evenly so it doesn't clump) and fold with a spatula just until no dry flour remains. Rest the batter 5 minutes so the oats begin to soften, then scrape into the pan, smooth the top, and scatter with the walnuts.

Bake on the middle rack 30–38 minutes, until the top is golden brown and domed, the edges pull from the pan, and a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean or with a few moist crumbs. Cool in the pan on a rack at least 20 minutes, then lift out with the parchment and cut into 9 or 16 squares.

recipes.name: Bánh Mì Caramelized Pork
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Pork belly or pork shoulder, thinly sliced (5mm)
Lemongrass, bruised and minced (inner stalk only)

steps: Combine sliced pork with fish sauce, shallots, lemongrass, and black pepper. Toss to coat every surface thoroughly. Marinate at room temperature for 30 minutes, or refrigerate up to 4 hours. The fish sauce begins drawing moisture out of the meat, concentrating the brine.

In a wide heavy skillet or wok over medium heat, add oil then sugar in an even layer. Do not stir — let it melt and color. When the edges turn amber, gently swirl the pan. Pull from heat at a deep amber that smells like butterscotch, not burnt coffee. Work fast; caramel moves through its stages in seconds.

Add marinated pork to the caramel in a single layer, working quickly. The mixture will spit and bubble violently — step back. Do not stir for the first 90 seconds so a crust can form. Then toss and cook over medium-high for 4-5 minutes total, until edges char and sauce clings like lacquer.

Remove from heat. Add 2 tablespoons of water to deglaze any stuck caramel from the pan and toss the pork to coat in the loose sauce. Let rest in the pan for 2 minutes — the residual heat melds the glaze and the resting reduces the risk of burning your mouth on the caramelized edges.

recipes.name: Bánh Xèo Batter

ingredients.name: Neutral oil, for frying each crepe

steps: In a large mixing bowl, combine the rice flour, cornstarch, turmeric, and salt. Whisk together the dry ingredients first so the turmeric is evenly distributed — it tends to clump and will cause yellow streaks in the finished crepe if not fully dispersed in the flour before liquid is added. Pour in the coconut milk while whisking, then add the cold water in a steady stream, continuing to whisk until completely smooth and lump-free. The batter should be very thin — thinner than pancake batter, closer to the consistency of heavy cream. The turmeric will dye the batter a vivid golden-yellow. Rest the batter for at least 30 minutes to allow the rice flour to fully hydrate and the starches to relax.

After the 30-minute rest, stir the sliced spring onions into the batter. The rested batter will have settled slightly with a thin waterier layer on top — stir it back together before stirring in the scallions. The spring onions are added to the batter rather than the filling so that they get lightly crisped by the pan heat during cooking, adding a gentle allium sweetness and a faint char to the crepe itself. Stir just before pouring each crepe, as the scallions and starch will continue to settle.

Heat a 28 cm non-stick frying pan over high heat until smoking hot — this is not negotiable. Add the oil and swirl to coat. Pour in one ladleful (about 80–100 ml) of batter, immediately lifting the pan and tilting in a circular motion so the batter spreads thinly across the entire surface, almost like making a crepe. The batter should sizzle explosively the instant it hits the pan — the Vietnamese name bánh xèo literally refers to that sizzling sound. Reduce heat to medium and add the filling (shrimp, pork, bean sprouts) to one half of the crepe. Cover with a lid and cook for 2–3 minutes until the edges of the crepe are golden and lifting away from the pan spontaneously, then uncover and cook for 1 more minute to crisp the edges fully. Fold the unfilled half over the filled half and slide onto a plate.

Serve each bánh xèo immediately as it comes from the pan. In the traditional Southern Vietnamese style, the diner tears off pieces of the crisp crepe, wraps each piece in a large lettuce leaf with fresh herbs (mint, perilla, Vietnamese coriander) and rolls the whole thing into a bundle to dip into nước chấm. The contrast between the crisp, hot crepe and the cool, fresh herbs wrapped around it is the defining pleasure of the dish. The crepe will soften within 2 minutes of folding — bánh xèo cannot be held; it must be eaten the moment it is made.

recipes.name: Classic American Sweet-Smoky BBQ Sauce
steps: Measure all ingredients into a medium heavy-bottomed saucepan — the heavy bottom is important, as the sugars in this sauce will scorch on thin stainless or aluminum. Whisk everything together thoroughly before applying any heat. Start with the ketchup as your base, then add molasses (pour it slow — it's stubborn), brown sugar, apple cider vinegar, and water. Add all the dry spices: smoked paprika, salt, black pepper, dry mustard, cayenne, garlic powder, and onion powder. Finish with the Worcestershire sauce. Whisk until the sauce is completely uniform — no streaks of molasses spiraling through lighter ketchup, no pockets of dry spice clinging to the bottom. Taste the raw mixture: it should taste harsh, aggressively vinegary, and a little medicinal from the dry mustard. This is correct. The heat will transform it.

Place the saucepan over medium heat and bring to a gentle simmer, stirring frequently to prevent the sugars from catching on the bottom. Once bubbling, reduce heat to low-medium. Simmer uncovered for 20–25 minutes, stirring every 2–3 minutes throughout. As the sauce cooks, it will deepen from bright brick-red to a darker, redder-brown mahogany. The raw vinegar sharpness will round and mellow; the molasses will gain caramel depth; the dry mustard will bloom and integrate. Watch the edges of the pot — this is where scorching begins. If you see any darkening at the edges, immediately reduce heat and stir from the bottom. The sauce is done when it coats the back of a spoon and a line drawn through it with your finger holds its shape for 2–3 seconds before slowly filling in.

Remove from heat and let cool in the pan for 10 minutes. Taste and adjust: if too sweet, add apple cider vinegar by the teaspoon; if too sharp, add a pinch more brown sugar; if flat, add a small pinch of salt and another drop of Worcestershire. Transfer to a glass jar or squeeze bottle. The sauce will thicken further as it cools — a sauce that seems slightly thin off the heat will be perfectly glossy and coating when it reaches room temperature. Refrigerate for up to 3 weeks. The flavor improves markedly after 24 hours in the refrigerator, as the spices continue to bloom and integrate. Reheat gently before serving — never boil again once made, or the vinegar balance will shift.

recipes.name: Basque Burnt Cheesecake
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Beat cream cheese with sugar and salt in a stand mixer with the paddle attachment on medium speed — or with a hand mixer — until the mixture is completely smooth, fluffy, and light, about 3 minutes. Scrape down the bowl twice. No lumps are acceptable here — cold cream cheese leaves clumps that never fully dissolve in the oven.

Add eggs one at a time on low speed, mixing until just incorporated before adding the next. Add vanilla with the final egg. Do not rush this step — adding eggs too quickly causes the emulsion to break. Scrape the bowl after each addition.

Sift flour directly into the batter. Add heavy cream. Whisk gently by hand until everything is incorporated — do not use the electric mixer at this stage. The batter should be thin, pourable, and completely smooth. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve into a jug for easy pouring.

Preheat oven to 230 C (450 F) conventional, or 210 C (410 F) fan. Line a 20 cm (8 inch) springform pan with two sheets of parchment, pushing them up the sides — the paper will ruffle and buckle and that is perfectly traditional. Pour in the batter. Bake for 28–32 minutes, until the top is deeply scorched — nearly burnt — with a dark mahogany center and the entire interior wobbles dramatically when the pan is nudged.

Cool the cheesecake in the pan at room temperature for at least 1 hour — it will deflate dramatically as it cools, developing the characteristic sunken center. Refrigerate for a minimum of 3 hours (overnight is ideal) to allow the custard to fully set. Serve at room temperature for the most custardy texture: remove from fridge 30 minutes before slicing.

recipes.name: BBQ Pulled Pork
