Lift out with tongs and immediately transfer to a plate, cut-side up, to prevent the flat cut surface from sitting in any pooled water. Do not run under cold water unless you are staging this dish more than 10 minutes in advance — the residual heat from within the stems will gently finish the leaves, and rinsing with cold water will wash away the natural sweetness from the cut surface. Arrange the halves on a serving plate in a fan or rows, all facing the same direction.

While the bok choy is being plated, add the neutral oil to a small saucepan or wok over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and let it cook slowly, stirring occasionally, for 2–3 minutes. You are not trying to brown the garlic hard — the goal is fragrant, softened slices that are golden at the edges but pale gold overall, and that have released their pungent aroma into the oil. Fully browned garlic will taste bitter in the finished sauce. The oil will smell intensely of sweet, mellow roasted garlic within 2 minutes. Watch closely: thin slices go from pale to golden to burnt in under 60 seconds once browning begins. As soon as the majority of the slices are pale gold with golden-tan edges, remove from heat — the residual heat in the pan will continue cooking them for another 30 seconds.

Add the oyster sauce, light soy sauce, and hot water or stock to the pan with the garlic oil. The liquid will sizzle aggressively against the hot oil — stand back. Stir quickly to combine into a smooth, glossy sauce. Let it bubble for 15–20 seconds until the water has partially evaporated and the sauce has thickened slightly to a syrupy consistency. Remove from heat and add the sesame oil. Stir once. Pour the entire contents of the pan — oil, garlic slices, and sauce — directly over the plated bok choy. The sauce should pool around the base of the stems and coat the cut surface. The garlic slices will settle over the leaves. The heat of the sauce will warm the already-cooked bok choy without cooking it further. Serve immediately — this dish does not hold and must be eaten within 3 minutes of saucing, while the contrast between the crisp-silky bok choy and the warm glossy sauce is still live.

recipes.name: Börek (Turkish Phyllo Pastry)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Yufka sheets or thin phyllo dough (thawed if frozen)
White Turkish cheese (beyaz peynir) or Greek feta, crumbled
Fresh spinach, washed and roughly chopped
Olive oil or melted butter (for brushing and filling)
Dried red chilli flakes and black pepper

steps: If using fresh spinach, place in a dry skillet over high heat for 2 minutes until wilted. Transfer to a clean kitchen towel and squeeze hard — the spinach must be as dry as possible or it will make the börek soggy. Roughly chop the squeezed spinach. Combine with crumbled cheese, chilli flakes, and black pepper in a bowl. Mix until evenly combined. Do not add salt — the cheese provides enough.

Whisk together the eggs, milk, and olive oil in a bowl until completely combined. This brushing mixture is what makes the börek layers fuse into a coherent pastry rather than staying as separate dry sheets. It should be pale yellow, slightly frothy, and pourable. Prepare this just before assembling.

Brush a 30x20cm baking dish with the egg-milk mixture. Lay a sheet of yufka in the dish, letting it overhang the sides. Brush generously with the egg mixture. Repeat with 2 more sheets, brushing each. Spread the filling across the center in an even layer. Fold the overhanging edges over the filling. Layer 3 more sheets on top, brushing each generously. The top layer should be brushed last. For a cigar or spiral börek, lay filling along the long edge of a sheet and roll tightly, then coil into the dish.

Preheat the oven to 190°C (375°F). Brush the top of the börek generously with the remaining egg-milk mixture and scatter sesame seeds if desired. Bake for 30–35 minutes until the top is a deep, uniform golden-brown and the pastry sounds hollow when tapped. The edges should be pulling away from the dish slightly. Rest 5 minutes before slicing — this allows the layers to set slightly so the börek holds its shape when cut.

recipes.name: Ukrainian Borscht

ingredients.name: Green or white cabbage, finely shredded
Waxy potatoes, peeled and cut into 2 cm cubes
Carrots, peeled and grated or cut into matchsticks
Whole peeled tomatoes (canned) or 3 fresh ripe tomatoes, chopped
Apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar
Fine sea salt and black pepper
Smetana or sour cream, for serving

steps: Preheat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Wrap the whole, unpeeled beets tightly in aluminum foil and roast directly on the oven rack for 45–60 minutes, depending on size (pierce with a skewer to test — it should slide in with no resistance). Let cool in the foil for 15 minutes. The skins will slip off effortlessly with a paper towel or gloved hand. Grate two-thirds of the roasted beets on the large holes of a box grater; cut the remaining third into small cubes. Roasting — rather than boiling raw beets — concentrates their sweetness and earthy flavour and is the difference between a flat borscht and a magnificent one. Save all the roasting juices from the foil.

In a large, heavy soup pot, heat the oil over medium heat. Add the diced onion and a pinch of salt and soften for 7–8 minutes until translucent and sweet-smelling, stirring occasionally. Add the carrot and cook for 3 more minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the tomato paste and fry it into the vegetables for 2 minutes, stirring constantly — it should darken and begin to stick before you deglaze. Add the canned tomatoes, crushing them with your hand as you add them. Cook for 5 minutes, breaking them down. The base should smell sweet, rich, and deeply tomato-forward.

Pour in the stock, add the bay leaves, and bring to a boil. Add the potato cubes and season generously with salt. Simmer for 10 minutes until the potatoes are half-cooked. Add the shredded cabbage and continue simmering for 10 more minutes — the cabbage should be tender but still have a faint, pleasant bite. Do not overcook the cabbage to mush. While the vegetables simmer, taste the broth constantly: adjust salt, and think about the balance of sweet and sour you are building toward.

Add the grated and diced roasted beets (and their reserved foil juices) to the simmering pot. Stir in the vinegar and sugar. The borscht will immediately turn a stunning, brilliant crimson — a colour no raw beet soup achieves. Simmer for just 5 minutes; long cooking after the beets are added causes the colour to fade toward brown. Taste: it should be deeply sweet-earthy from the beet, brightly sour from the vinegar, and rich and salty. Adjust all three. Remove from heat. Ladle into deep bowls. Finish each bowl with a generous tablespoon of smetana and a heavy shower of fresh dill. Serve with dark rye bread.

recipes.name: Bouillabaisse
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Whole small rockfish & fish frames (gurnard, conger, wrasse, scorpionfish — gilled, gutted, rinsed)
Firm fish for serving (monkfish, John Dory, sea bass — cut into thick steaks)
Garlic (half crushed for broth, half raw for rouille)
Ripe tomatoes (chopped) & a spoon of tomato paste
Strip of dried orange peel & bouquet (thyme, bay, parsley stalks)
Boiled potato & egg yolk (for rouille body)

steps: Warm a generous slick of olive oil in a wide, heavy pot over medium heat. Add the sliced onion, leek and fennel with half the garlic and sweat gently, stirring, until soft and translucent but uncoloured, 8-10 minutes. You are building a sweet vegetable foundation, not browning it — colour here turns the broth muddy and bitter.

Stir in the chopped tomatoes and tomato paste and cook 3-4 minutes until they break down and lose their raw edge. Add the dried orange peel and bouquet garni, then pile in the whole rockfish and frames. Stir to coat everything in the oily, tomato-stained aromatics and cook 2-3 minutes so the fish begins to firm and its flavours bloom into the fat.

Pour in just enough water to cover the fish by a finger, add the bloomed saffron and its soaking water, and season with salt. Bring to a rolling, vigorous boil — this is the secret of true bouillabaisse, the hard boil that emulsifies the olive oil into the broth so it turns opaque and golden rather than splitting. Boil hard, uncovered, for 20-25 minutes.

Discard the bouquet and orange peel. Tip the broth and softened fish through a coarse sieve or food mill set over a clean pot, pressing the solids firmly to extract every drop of golden liquor — but stop before forcing through bones and skin. You want a pourable, intensely flavoured broth, not a purée. Discard the spent solids and return the strained broth to a clean pot.

Make the rouille: pound the remaining raw garlic with the chilli and a pinch of salt to a paste, work in the boiled potato and egg yolk, then drizzle in olive oil whisking constantly until it builds into a thick, rust-red emulsion, loosening with a spoonful of the hot broth. Taste the strained broth and correct salt, pepper and saffron. Hold both warm — the broth at a bare simmer, the rouille at the ready.

Bring the broth to a gentle simmer and slide in the firm fish steaks, thickest first, so all finish together. Poach barely — 6-10 minutes depending on thickness — until the flesh turns opaque and flakes at the touch but is still juicy. Serve in two acts: first the golden broth ladled over toasts spread with rouille, then the poached fish, with more rouille alongside.

recipes.name: Braised Chicken with Green Olives & Lemon

ingredients.name: Fennel bulb, cored and cut into thin wedges
Lemon, scrubbed, half thinly sliced and seeded, half juiced

steps: Pat chicken dry and season all over with salt and pepper (ideally 1–24 hours ahead, uncovered in the fridge). Heat oil in a 30 cm oven-safe braiser or Dutch oven over medium heat. Lay thighs skin-side down, in batches if needed, and cook undisturbed 8–10 minutes until the fat has rendered and the skin is deep gold. Flip for 1 minute, then set aside skin-side up. Pour off all but about 30 ml of fat.

Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). In the remaining fat, cook onion and fennel over medium heat 8–10 minutes until soft and lightly golden. Add garlic, coriander, and paprika and stir 1 minute. Pour in the wine and simmer 2–3 minutes, scraping the fond, until reduced by about half.

Add stock, olives, lemon slices, and herb sprigs and bring to a simmer. Nestle the thighs in skin-side up with the skin above the liquid. Braise uncovered in the oven 40–45 minutes, until the thickest thigh reads at least 165°F (74°C) — ideally 185–195°F (85–90°C) for tender meat near the bone — and the sauce has reduced by about a third.

Rest 5 minutes, then squeeze in the reserved lemon juice to taste (start with half) and scatter with parsley. Serve with bread, rice, or potatoes to soak up the sauce. To freeze: cool the chicken submerged in its sauce, refrigerate within 2 hours, and freeze up to 3 months. The skin softens on freezing — reheat covered at 350°F (175°C) until the chicken reaches 165°F (74°C), then uncover under the broiler 2–3 minutes to recrisp.

recipes.name: Braised Red Cabbage (Rotkohl)

ingredients.name: Red cabbage (Rotkohl), cored and finely shredded
Tart cooking apple, peeled and grated
Goose fat, duck fat, or neutral vegetable oil

steps: Warm the fat in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the diced onion with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the onion is completely soft, translucent, and just starting to take the faintest golden edge at the tips. The onion should be sweet-smelling and collapsed, not browned — this is a sweet-sour dish and caramelised onion would make it too sweet.

Add the shredded cabbage to the pot in large handfuls, turning with tongs — it will seem like far too much but will collapse dramatically. Add the grated apple, vinegar, sugar, cloves, juniper berries, bay leaves, salt, and water or wine. Stir everything together, pressing the cabbage down into the liquid. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat, then reduce to a low simmer. Cover tightly and braise for 45–55 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes, until the cabbage has fully collapsed to a silky, tender mass. The cabbage will transform from bright purple-magenta to a deep, jewel-toned garnet as the acid reacts with the anthocyanin pigments and then mellows through cooking.

Remove the whole cloves, juniper berries, and bay leaves. Taste the Rotkohl critically: it should hold both its sweetness and its sharpness in balance, with the spice of clove and juniper humming in the background. Adjust with more vinegar for brightness, sugar for mellowness, or salt to lift everything. Rotkohl improves dramatically with resting: made a day ahead, refrigerated, and gently reheated, it loses any remaining sharpness and all the flavours meld into a beautifully integrated whole. Serve warm alongside roast pork, duck, sauerbraten, or bratwurst.

recipes.name: Red Wine Braised Short Ribs

ingredients.name: Fine sea salt and black pepper

steps: Pat the short ribs completely dry — surface moisture is the enemy of crust formation. Season aggressively with salt and pepper. Heat a heavy Dutch oven or braising pot over high heat until the oil just smokes. Sear ribs in batches, 3–4 minutes per side, until a deep mahogany crust forms on all surfaces. Do not crowd the pan; steam will prevent browning. Remove and set aside.

In the same pot, cook onion, celery, carrot, and garlic in the rendered fat over medium heat until softened and beginning to caramelize, about 8 minutes. Add tomato paste and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes until it darkens to a brick-red. Pour in the red wine and scrape up all the fond from the bottom. Simmer until the wine has reduced by half, about 10 minutes.

Return the seared ribs to the pot. Add beef stock and thyme and bay until the liquid comes two-thirds up the ribs — do not submerge. Bring to a bare simmer, then cover and transfer to a 150 C (300 F) oven. Braise for 3.5–4 hours, turning the ribs once halfway. The oven provides even, gentle heat from all sides that stovetop simmering cannot match.

recipes.name: Wine-Braised Beef Short Ribs
steps: Pat each short rib completely dry with paper towels — any surface moisture will steam rather than sear. Season aggressively on all six sides with kosher salt and coarse black pepper, pressing the seasoning into the meat. Rest at room temperature for at least 30 minutes, or salt the day before and refrigerate uncovered overnight for deeper seasoning and a drier surface (which sears better). Preheat the oven to 160 C (325 F).

Heat a large Dutch oven or heavy braiser over high heat. Add the oil and heat until smoking. Working in batches of two or three ribs at a time — never crowd the pan — sear each rib on all four meaty sides and the two bone-end faces. Allow each side 3 to 4 minutes undisturbed contact with the pan before turning. Total searing time per batch: 15 to 18 minutes. Transfer the seared ribs to a plate. Do not clean the pot — the fond is critical.

In the same pot with all the accumulated fond, reduce heat to medium. Add the onion, carrot, and celery. Cook for 8 minutes, stirring occasionally and scraping the brown bits from the bottom, until the vegetables are deeply softened and beginning to brown. Add the garlic and cook 1 more minute. Push everything to the sides and add the tomato paste to the center. Cook the paste for 2 to 3 minutes until it darkens from red to brick-brown (pinçage). Stir into the vegetables.

Pour in the entire bottle of red wine. Bring to a boil, scraping every dark bit from the pot bottom. Let the wine reduce by half over medium-high heat — about 15 minutes — until the raw alcohol smell has burned off and the liquid smells of dark fruit and structure rather than vinegar. Add the beef stock and the bouquet garni.

Nestle the seared short ribs into the wine base, bone-side down. They should be at least two-thirds submerged — add more stock or water if not. Add the bouquet garni. Bring to a simmer on the stovetop, then cover with a tight-fitting lid and transfer to the preheated oven at 160 C (325 F). Braise for 3 to 3.5 hours, turning the ribs once halfway through. They are done when the meat has fully separated from the bone and a skewer or cake tester passes through with zero resistance.

Transfer the ribs to a warm plate, tented loosely with foil. Strain the braising liquid through a fine-mesh strainer into a wide saucepan, pressing the spent vegetables to extract every drop. Bring to a vigorous simmer and reduce until the sauce coats a spoon cleanly and has a lacquered appearance — typically reducing by half to two-thirds over 15 to 20 minutes. Adjust salt. Spoon the glossy sauce over the ribs and serve immediately, or rest the ribs in the strained sauce in the refrigerator overnight (they reheat better the next day).

recipes.name: Brigadeiro
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: In a medium heavy-bottomed saucepan (not non-stick — you need to see the color change on the pot bottom), combine the condensed milk, butter, sifted cocoa powder, and salt. Stir together with a heat-proof spatula before turning on the heat, making sure the cocoa is fully incorporated before any heat is applied — this prevents scorching lumps. Place over medium-low heat.

Cook the mixture over medium-low heat, stirring continuously with the spatula in long, slow strokes across the entire bottom of the pan — never stop stirring. The mixture will gradually thicken. After 8–12 minutes, it will begin to pull away from the sides and bottom of the pan as you drag the spatula through. This is the critical test: drag a line across the bottom of the pan with your spatula. If the line holds clear for 3 seconds before the mixture flows back together, it is ready. Remove from heat immediately.

Pour the cooked mixture onto a greased plate or into a shallow bowl. Do not scrape the pot — the bottom layer that stuck will taste bitter. Spread slightly with the spatula. Let cool completely to room temperature (30 minutes minimum), then refrigerate for at least 30 minutes. Cold brigadeiro is essential for rolling — warm brigadeiro will stick to your hands and cannot form clean spheres. The mixture should be firm enough to scoop and hold its shape.

Lightly grease your hands with butter. Using a small spoon or melon baller, scoop portions of about 1.5 tablespoons each. Roll each portion between your greased palms in a circular motion, applying gentle, even pressure to form a smooth sphere. Work quickly — the warmth of your hands begins to soften the brigadeiro. Roll each ball immediately in the chocolate sprinkles, pressing gently to adhere, then place in a paper candy cup. If the mixture becomes too soft to roll, chill your hands under cold water and pat dry before continuing.

recipes.name: Brigadeiros

ingredients.name: Unsweetened cocoa powder (or 70% dark chocolate, finely grated)

steps: Place the butter in a medium, heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium-low heat. Once melted, add the condensed milk, cocoa powder, and a pinch of salt. Stir immediately to combine — use a heat-proof rubber spatula or wooden spoon. The mixture will look smooth and glossy at first. Stir continuously to prevent any part of the base from scorching, especially at the edges where heat is most intense.

Continue cooking over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for 8–12 minutes. The mixture will gradually thicken, and you will begin to see it pulling away from the sides and bottom of the pan in a clean line as you stir. This is the critical 'ponto de brigadeiro' — the brigadeiro point. Test it by running the spatula down the center of the pan: if the track stays open for 2–3 seconds before the mixture flows back, it is ready. Remove from heat and stir in the vanilla extract. The mixture will thicken further as it cools.

Lightly butter a flat plate or shallow dish with unsalted butter. Pour the hot brigadeiro mixture onto the plate in a single flat layer. Do not scrape the pan — any dried or burnt bits stuck to the sides should be left behind. Allow to cool completely at room temperature for 20–30 minutes, then refrigerate uncovered for 30–60 minutes until firm enough to roll — it should feel like stiff clay, not soft putty.

Spread the chocolate sprinkles onto a flat plate. Lightly butter your palms with a tiny amount of unsalted butter. Scoop roughly 1 tablespoon (15g) of the brigadeiro mixture and roll it between your palms in quick circular motions to form a smooth, round sphere. Immediately place it in the sprinkles and roll gently to coat completely, pressing lightly so the sprinkles adhere. Transfer to a paper cup or parchment-lined tray. Work quickly — the warmth of your hands softens the brigadeiro fast. Re-butter your palms every 3–4 truffles.

recipes.name: Brioche
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, cool but pliable (82% fat)
Egg yolk beaten with a splash of cream (egg wash)

steps: In a stand mixer with the dough hook, combine the flour, cold eggs, cold milk, crumbled fresh yeast, sugar, and salt. Keep the salt and yeast from touching directly until they hit the flour. Mix on low for 3 to 4 minutes just until there is no dry flour and a rough, sticky dough forms. Everything stays cold — brioche is a battle against heat, and the dough should never climb past about 24°C / 75°F before the butter goes in.

Knead on medium speed for 8 to 12 minutes until the dough is smooth, very elastic, and pulls cleanly off the sides of the bowl in one slapping mass. You are building a strong gluten network NOW, before the fat coats the proteins. Stop and stretch a small piece into a windowpane — it should thin to translucency without tearing. Develop the gluten fully here; you cannot build it once the butter is in.

With the mixer on medium-low, add the cool, pliable butter a tablespoon-sized knob at a time, letting each piece disappear into the dough before adding the next — this takes 5 to 10 minutes. The dough will look broken and slick at first; keep going and it re-gathers into a glossy, supple mass. Add the butter slowly so it laminates into the gluten rather than greasing it out. Finish when the dough is satiny, fully homogeneous, and pulls off the bowl again.

Give the dough a 1-hour rest at room temperature, then fold it over on itself, press flat, cover tightly, and refrigerate for at least 8 hours and up to 24. This long cold ferment is non-negotiable: it firms the butter so the dough is workable, deepens flavor with a faint tang, and slows the yeast for an even, fine crumb. The next day, divide, shape (a braid, a fluted mold, or balls in a tin), and proof at warm room temperature, 24–26°C / 75–79°F, until nearly doubled and jiggly.

Brush the proofed loaf gently and thoroughly with the egg-yolk wash, getting into every seam without deflating it. Bake at 180°C / 350°F for 25 to 40 minutes depending on size, until deep mahogany-brown and the internal temperature reads 88–90°C / 190–195°F. Tent loosely with foil if it browns too fast — the high sugar and egg make brioche colour quickly. Cool fully on a rack before slicing; cutting it warm tears the tender crumb.

recipes.name: Brown Butter Chocolate Chip Cookies

ingredients.name: Egg yolk, from a large egg
Water (to replace moisture lost from browning)

steps: Melt the butter in a light-colored saucepan over medium heat. It will foam and sputter as the water cooks off, then quiet down. Swirl constantly for 5–8 minutes total until the milk solids at the bottom turn a toasty brown and it smells nutty. Immediately pour into a large heatproof bowl, scraping in all the brown bits. Stir in the water and let cool 20–30 minutes until warm but no longer hot (about 100°F / 38°C).
Add both sugars to the cooled brown butter and whisk 1 minute. Add the egg, yolk, and vanilla and whisk vigorously for about 1 minute more until thick, glossy, and lighter in color.

Whisk the flour, baking soda, and salt in a separate bowl, add to the wet mixture, and fold with a spatula just until a few streaks of flour remain. Add the chocolate and fold until no dry flour is visible. Cover and refrigerate at least 1 hour (up to 72 hours for deeper flavor) so the flour hydrates and the cookies spread less.

Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) and line two sheet pans with parchment. Scoop 50 g balls (about 3 tbsp), spacing them 7 cm apart — about 8 per pan, for roughly 22 cookies. Bake one pan at a time on the middle rack 10–12 minutes, until the edges are golden brown and set but the centers look puffy and slightly underbaked. Sprinkle with flaky salt as soon as they come out. Cool 10 minutes on the pan to finish setting, then transfer to a rack.

recipes.name: Brussels Sprouts with Pancetta

ingredients.name: Brussels sprouts, halved through the stem
Pecorino Romano or Parmesan, finely grated
Flaky salt and coarse black pepper

steps: Preheat the oven to 220°C (425°F) with a heavy baking tray inside — a preheated tray is the key to immediate searing contact. Toss the halved Brussels sprouts with olive oil, salt, and pepper in a bowl. Spread them in a single layer on the hot tray, cut-side down without exception. Do not turn them for the first 15 minutes — the direct contact with the hot metal is what produces the deep, caramelized fond on the cut face. After 15 minutes, check the cut side: it should be deeply golden-brown. At that point, roast a further 5 minutes without turning, until the outer leaves are charred and crunchy.

While the sprouts roast, place the diced pancetta in a cold dry skillet. Set the skillet over medium heat and allow the fat to render slowly as the pan heats up. This cold-pan start renders the fat gradually without burning the exterior before the interior is cooked. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the pancetta lardons are deeply golden-brown, crispy, and the fat has rendered out fully. Remove with a slotted spoon to a paper towel. Reserve 1 tablespoon of the rendered fat in the pan.

In the same pan with the residual pancetta fat, add the roughly chopped walnuts over medium heat. Toss constantly for 2–3 minutes until they are golden, fragrant, and the walnut fat begins to be visible as a slight sheen on the pan surface. Toasting in pancetta fat rather than plain oil adds a deeply savory dimension to the nuts. Watch closely — walnuts go from golden to burnt very quickly. Remove as soon as they smell deeply nutty and look dry and lightly golden.

Transfer the hot roasted sprouts to a large serving bowl. Add the crispy pancetta, toasted walnuts, and thinly sliced garlic (the residual heat from the sprouts will gently perfume the raw garlic without fully cooking it — this is intentional). Add the lemon zest, lemon juice, half the pecorino, and a drizzle of honey if using. Toss gently but confidently — some of the outer leaves will break off into crunchy chips, which is desirable. Taste and adjust with salt, pepper, lemon juice, or honey to balance. Scatter the remaining pecorino and serve immediately while warm.

recipes.name: Buffalo Hot Sauce

ingredients.name: Frank's RedHot Original Cayenne Pepper Sauce
Unsalted butter, cold, cut into 1/2-inch cubes

steps: Combine the Frank's RedHot, garlic powder, salt, white wine vinegar, and Worcestershire sauce in a small saucepan. Set over medium-low heat and warm gently, stirring once or twice, until the sauce is just steaming — about 3–4 minutes. You are not cooking it, just warming it to the precise temperature where butter will emulsify smoothly. The target temperature is 130–140°F (54–60°C): hot enough to melt cold butter quickly but not so hot that it drives off the butter fat before it can emulsify. A kitchen thermometer is helpful here, but you can judge by steam: gentle wisps rising from the surface, no bubbles. Do not let it boil — boiling drives off the volatile acids that give Frank's its characteristic sharp tang.

Remove the saucepan from the heat — the residual heat from the pan is all you need. Working quickly with a whisk, add the cold butter cubes one or two at a time, whisking constantly and vigorously in small, tight circles. Each cube should melt and be incorporated before the next goes in. The technique is called 'mounting with butter' (monter au beurre): the cold butter pieces maintain enough fat crystal structure to create a stable emulsion with the water-based hot sauce. As you add each cube, the sauce will transform: it goes from thin and watery to silky and coating, and its color deepens from bright orange-red to a rich, glossy terracotta. If at any point the sauce looks greasy or the butter is pooling in orange puddles rather than integrating, the sauce is too hot — add another cold butter cube and whisk off the heat until it comes back together. The finished sauce should be smooth, glossy, and coat a spoon completely.

recipes.name: Buffalo Wings
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Chicken wings, split into flats and drumettes
Celery sticks and blue cheese dressing (for serving)

steps: Pat the wings completely dry with paper towels — press firmly on all surfaces. In a large bowl, toss the dry wings with kosher salt and baking powder until evenly coated. The baking powder raises surface pH, which accelerates browning and draws moisture to the surface over time. Spread in a single layer on a wire rack over a sheet pan.

Heat oil in a deep pot or fryer to 190°C. Fry the wings in batches — do not crowd the pot — for 10–12 minutes, turning occasionally, until deep golden-brown and fully cooked through. Between batches, let the oil return to 190°C. Alternatively, bake at 220°C on a wire rack for 40–45 minutes, flipping halfway.

In a small saucepan over low heat, melt the butter. Remove from heat and whisk in the hot sauce and garlic powder until fully combined and glossy. The sauce should be warm but not boiling — boiling will break the emulsion, leaving a greasy, separated sauce. The ratio is roughly 2 parts hot sauce to 1 part butter by volume.

Transfer hot wings to a large bowl. Pour the warm buffalo sauce over them and toss vigorously until every surface is evenly coated. Work quickly — the heat from the wings will keep the sauce fluid and help it adhere. If the sauce starts to congeal, add a splash of hot sauce and toss again.

Arrange the glazed wings on a platter. Serve immediately with celery sticks and a generous pool of blue cheese dressing for dipping. Do not cover — the steam will destroy any remaining crispness. These are best eaten within 5 minutes of saucing.

recipes.name: Butter Chicken (Murgh Makhani)

ingredients.name: Kashmiri chili powder (or mild chili for colour)
Kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves), crushed between palms

steps: In a large bowl, combine the yogurt, ginger-garlic paste, Kashmiri chili powder, half the garam masala, and salt. Mix well. Score the chicken thighs with three shallow diagonal cuts on each side — this allows the marinade to penetrate and creates more surface for charring. Add the chicken and turn until every piece is evenly coated in the deep orange-red marinade. Cover and refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours, and ideally overnight. The yogurt's lactic acid tenderises the protein fibres; the chili colours the crust; the ginger-garlic penetrates deep.

Set the oven rack at the highest position and preheat the broiler to its maximum setting. Line a heavy baking sheet with foil and place the marinated chicken pieces in a single layer, shaking off any excess marinade. Broil for 8–10 minutes, turning once halfway, until the chicken is cooked through and the marinade has charred in dark brown-black spots across the surface. These char marks are non-negotiable — they are not just visual, they are an intrinsic flavour element of makhani (the char that occurs in a tandoor at 450°C). Remove and rest 5 minutes, then cut into large chunks.

In a wide, heavy pot, melt the butter over medium heat. Add the crushed cardamom pods and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant — the butter will foam and the cardamom will sizzle. Add the sliced onion and cook, stirring regularly, for 15–18 minutes until deeply golden-brown (not just translucent) — this is the single most time-critical step. The Maillard reaction in the onion provides sweetness and body to the sauce. Add the passata, Kashmiri chili powder, and remaining garam masala. Cook over medium-high heat for 15–20 minutes, stirring frequently, until the butter visibly separates from the tomato mass — this is 'bhunoing', and signals the sauce is cooked rather than raw.

Remove the cardamom pods. Allow the sauce to cool for 5 minutes, then blend until completely smooth using an immersion blender or by transferring to a stand blender in batches. A properly blended makhani sauce is silky and coat-thick, with no visible onion or tomato fibres. If using a stand blender, hold the lid with a folded tea towel and start on the lowest speed — hot liquids expand in sealed blenders. Pass through a fine-mesh strainer for an ultra-smooth finish if desired (restaurants do; home cooks need not).

Return the smooth sauce to the pot over medium-low heat. Add the charred chicken pieces and stir to coat. Simmer gently for 10 minutes — the chicken finishes cooking and the char flavour permeates the sauce. Pour in the heavy cream and stir. Add the remaining butter in small cubes, stirring until it melts into the sauce in a glossy emulsion. Crush the kasuri methi between your palms directly over the pot — it releases a distinctive bittersweet, mapley aroma that is the hallmark of makhani. Add sugar to balance acidity. Taste: the sauce should be creamy, mildly spiced, faintly smoky, and perfectly balanced between sweet and acid.

recipes.name: Butter-Poached Lobster (Beurre Monté)

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, cold, cubed (1 cm cubes)

steps: Bring a large pot of heavily salted water to a rolling boil. The water should taste like mild seawater. Dispatch each lobster humanely by driving the tip of a heavy chef's knife through the cross on the back of the head. Plunge the lobsters headfirst into the boiling water. Blanch for exactly 2 minutes — this sets the shells to brilliant red and makes the meat release from the shell cleanly, but leaves the interior essentially raw. Transfer immediately to an ice bath. Once cool enough to handle, twist off the claws and knuckles. Using kitchen shears, cut down the underside of the tail shell and pull the raw tail meat out in one piece. Crack the claws with a lobster cracker or the back of a heavy knife and extract the claw meat in whole pieces. Keep the knuckle meat connected to the claw if possible. Pat all meat very dry with paper towels. Season lightly with fine salt. Any moisture on the surface will break the beurre monté when you add the lobster.

In a small, deep saucepan, bring the water to a simmer over medium heat. Once simmering, begin whisking in the cold butter cubes two or three at a time, adding each new addition only after the previous cubes have almost entirely emulsified — the liquid in the pan should remain creamy-yellow and opaque, never separating into a greasy pool. Maintain a temperature between 82–88°C (180–190°F) — hot enough to melt butter, cool enough to keep the emulsion intact. Use an instant-read thermometer. Add the smashed garlic clove and tarragon sprigs to infuse while you build the emulsion. The finished beurre monté should be glossy, homogeneous, and coating — holding on a spoon like a loose cream sauce. Make at least 450 g of butter's worth to ensure enough depth in the pan to submerge the lobster meat completely. Keep warm over the lowest possible heat, or a double boiler.

Using a thermometer, verify the beurre monté is holding at 82–85°C (180–185°F). Gently lower the lobster tails and claw meat into the butter, making sure they are fully submerged. Baste continuously with a large spoon, ladling the warm butter over any exposed surfaces. Poach for 5–7 minutes for tails, 3–4 minutes for claws. The goal is internal temperature of 60°C (140°F) measured at the thickest part of the tail — this produces silky, just-set meat. Do not let the pan exceed 90°C or the proteins will seize and the texture will become rubbery. Remove from heat and allow to rest in the butter off heat for 1 minute. Lift with a slotted spoon. Squeeze a few drops of lemon juice into the remaining beurre monté, whisk briefly, and spoon it over the plated lobster as a sauce. Finish with a pinch of fleur de sel and fresh tarragon leaves.

recipes.name: Buttermilk Biscuits
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, very cold, cut into 1cm cubes

steps: Whisk together the flour, baking powder, baking soda, and salt in a large bowl. Add the cold butter cubes. Using your fingertips, quickly break the butter into the flour — smear each cube between your thumbs and fingers, working fast so body heat does not soften the butter. Stop when the largest pieces are the size of small peas and the smallest are sandy. Cold, intact butter pieces are what create layers.

Pour the cold buttermilk into the flour-butter mixture all at once. Using a fork or your hands, stir and fold just until the dough comes together — it will look shaggy and rough, with dry flour still visible. Do not knead. Overworking develops gluten and creates tough, flat biscuits. Dump the shaggy mass onto a lightly floured surface.

Pat the shaggy dough into a rough rectangle about 2cm thick. Fold it in thirds like a letter — left third over the center, then right third over that. Rotate 90 degrees, pat out to 2cm again, and repeat the fold. Do this 4–5 times total. These folds create the distinct layers. After the final fold, gently pat to about 2.5cm thick.

Preheat oven to 220°C. Using a sharp, round cutter (never twist — press straight down and pull straight up), cut biscuits. Place them touching each other on a parchment-lined sheet pan — this forces them to rise upward rather than spread outward. Brush tops with buttermilk or melted butter. Bake 12–14 minutes until deeply golden on top.

recipes.name: Fluffy Buttermilk Diner Pancakes

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly

steps: In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt, and sugar until evenly combined. Make a well in the center. The dry ingredients do not need sifting, but must be fully blended before adding liquid.

In a separate medium bowl, whisk together the buttermilk, eggs, and melted (but not hot) butter until combined. The melted butter should be warm enough to remain liquid but not so hot it begins to cook the eggs. The mixture will look slightly curdled or broken — this is normal and fine.

Pour the wet ingredients into the well in the dry ingredients. Using a rubber spatula, fold together with large circular strokes — scraping the bottom of the bowl with each pass — until just barely combined. Stop the moment no streaks of dry flour remain. The batter should be thick and lumpy with visible bumps and pockets. Lumps are mandatory: they are pockets of flour and gas that create the signature fluffy interior. Let the batter rest 5 minutes before cooking.

Heat a cast-iron griddle or non-stick skillet over medium heat. Add a small pat of butter and let it foam, then subside. When the foam dies and the pan smells faintly of toasted butter, it is ready. Pour 1/3 cup batter per pancake. Cook until bubbles form across the entire surface and the edges look set and matte — not shiny — about 2–3 minutes. Flip once and cook until the second side is golden-brown, 1–2 minutes more. Do not press down on the pancakes.

recipes.name: Butternut Squash Pasta with Brown Butter and Sage

ingredients.name: Butternut squash, peeled, seeded, cut into 2 cm cubes
Rigatoni or other short, ridged pasta

steps: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Toss the squash with the olive oil, 1 teaspoon salt, and pepper, and spread on a large sheet pan in one layer. Roast 25–30 minutes, flipping once halfway, until completely tender and caramelized at the edges.

While the squash finishes, bring a large pot of well-salted water to a boil (212°F / 100°C). Cook the pasta 1–2 minutes short of the package time. Scoop out 300 ml of the starchy cooking water before draining.

Melt the butter in a large, light-colored skillet over medium heat. When it foams, add the sage leaves and fry 1–2 minutes until crisp; lift them out onto a paper towel. Keep swirling the butter for another 1–2 minutes until the milk solids turn hazelnut brown, then add the garlic and pepper flakes for 30 seconds and pull the pan off the heat.

Put two-thirds of the roasted squash in a blender with 200 ml of the pasta water and the nutmeg. Blend until completely smooth, adding more pasta water if needed to reach a thick, pourable consistency. Vent the blender lid — hot liquid expands.

Return the skillet to medium heat, add the squash sauce to the brown butter, and stir to combine. Add the pasta and toss for 1–2 minutes, adding pasta water as needed, until glossy. Off the heat, stir in the cheese and lemon juice and season. Serve topped with the reserved squash cubes, crumbled crisp sage, and walnuts.

recipes.name: Butternut Squash Veloute

ingredients.name: Butternut squash, peeled, seeded, and diced
Creme fraiche or a drizzle of cream

steps: Preheat oven to 200 C (400 F). Spread the diced squash, sliced shallots, and unpeeled garlic cloves on a large baking sheet. Drizzle generously with olive oil and season with salt. Toss to coat. Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, turning once at halfway, until the squash is deeply caramelized on the cut surfaces and completely tender.

Squeeze the roasted garlic cloves from their skins into a blender. Add all the roasted squash and shallots. Pour in half the hot stock. Blend on high until completely smooth, adding more stock until you reach a pourable but thick consistency. Pass through a fine-mesh sieve if you want the most refined texture.

Pour the puree into a medium saucepan over low heat. Stir in the remaining hot stock to adjust consistency — the final soup should flow like heavy cream, not sit like a stiff porridge. Season carefully with salt, white pepper, and freshly grated nutmeg. Simmer on the lowest heat for 5 minutes, stirring, to marry the flavors.

Stir the heavy cream into the hot soup off the heat and taste once more for seasoning. In a small saucepan, melt the butter over medium heat, swirling the pan. Continue cooking until the butter solids turn nut-brown and the butter smells of toasted hazelnuts — about 3 minutes. Pour immediately into a small bowl. Ladle the soup into warmed bowls, drizzle with a thread of brown butter, and finish with toasted pepitas and a dot of crème fraîche.

recipes.name: Cá Kho Tộ (Caramelized Braised Fish)

ingredients.name: Catfish steaks, bone-in, 3 cm thick (cá tra or swai)
Young green coconut water (nước dừa tươi)
Spring onion greens, sliced into 3 cm pieces

steps: In a clay pot (or heavy-bottomed saucepan), add the sugar in an even layer over medium heat. Do not stir. Watch it carefully — sugar caramelizes unevenly and can go from perfect to burnt in seconds. As the edges begin to melt and turn amber, tilt the pot gently to encourage even melting. Once about two-thirds of the sugar has melted and turned a deep amber-brown, you can stir very gently. Continue until the entire mass is a dark mahogany color, just beginning to smoke at the edges, and smells deeply bitter-sweet with a trace of smoky bitterness. This darker-than-usual caramel is intentional — the slight bitterness it carries is what gives cá kho tộ its distinctive complexity when balanced against the fish sauce and coconut water. Immediately and carefully pour in the coconut water (it will hiss violently) and stir to combine.

Once the caramel and coconut water have combined into a smooth, dark liquid, add the fish sauce, sliced shallots, garlic, halved chilies, and cracked black pepper. Stir gently and bring to a simmer over medium heat. Let the aromatics cook in the braising liquid for 3–4 minutes — the shallots should begin to soften and the garlic should turn translucent. The braising liquid at this stage should taste intensely salty, bitter-sweet, and funky from the fish sauce, with a spicy undercurrent from the chili and pepper. It will seem aggressively seasoned — this is correct, because the fish will dilute it during the braise.

Gently lay the catfish steaks into the braising liquid in a single layer. The liquid should come about halfway up the sides of the fish. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, then reduce to medium-low. Do not stir the fish — catfish steaks break apart easily and the intact shape is important both aesthetically and texturally. Instead, use a spoon to baste the top of the fish every few minutes with the braising liquid. Cook for 15–20 minutes, occasionally tilting the pot to redistribute the sauce. As the liquid reduces, it will thicken and darken further, beginning to glaze the bottom of the fish. The fish is done when it is just cooked through and the sauce has reduced by about half and coats the fish in a thick, glossy lacquer.

Scatter the spring onion greens over the finished fish while it is still in the pot, directly before serving. In Vietnamese tradition, cá kho tộ is served in the clay pot it was cooked in, placed on a small trivet at the table, so the sauce continues to very gently simmer from the residual heat of the clay. Each diner spoons the fish and sauce generously over their bowl of plain steamed rice. The correct way to eat it is to spoon the sauce first — it is intensely flavored and should be used to season the rice — and then eat the fish in pieces, dipping each into the pooled sauce on your rice. The bittersweet, salty, fish-sauce complexity of the reduced caramel is the entire point of the dish.

recipes.name: Cacio e Pepe
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Pasta cooking water, starchy and salted
Extra-virgin olive oil (optional, for the pan)

steps: Add the coarsely cracked black pepper to a dry, wide skillet — ideally one large enough to hold all the pasta later. Toast over medium heat for 60-90 seconds, stirring constantly, until the pepper is fragrant and just beginning to smoke at the edges. You should smell a warm, woody, almost floral intensity — distinct from raw pepper. Add the olive oil if using, swirl to coat. Remove from heat and let the pan cool slightly. The pepper is now bloomed and will perfume the entire dish. Do not clean the pan — the pepper stays.

Cook the pasta in a smaller pot of water than usual — less water means more concentrated starch in the pasta water, which is critical for the sauce. Use well-salted water but go slightly lighter than usual since the Pecorino is very salty. Cook to 2 minutes less than the package al dente time — the pasta will finish in the pan. Reserve at least 1 cup (240ml) of the pasta cooking water before draining. The water should look slightly milky and opaque with dissolved starch. Drain without rinsing.

While the pasta cooks, combine the finely grated Pecorino and Parmigiano in a bowl. Add 2-3 tablespoons of the hot pasta water to the cheese and stir rapidly with a fork to form a paste — it should look like thick spackle or a very stiff béchamel. This pre-hydration prevents the cheese from clumping into stringy knots when it hits the hot pasta. The paste should be smooth and pliable, with no dry lumps of cheese. If too thick, add a few more drops of pasta water. This step is the structural key to lump-free cacio e pepe.

Return the pan with the bloomed pepper to medium heat. Transfer the drained pasta directly into the pan. Add 3-4 tablespoons of the hot pasta water and toss vigorously with tongs for 1-2 minutes. The pasta should finish cooking in this starchy liquid, which will become slightly creamy as the starch from the pasta dissolves into it. The pan should be very active — continuous tossing creates the emulsification. When the liquid looks slightly creamy and most has been absorbed, remove the pan from heat.

Off the heat, add the cheese paste to the pasta in two additions, tossing energetically between each. Add pasta water a tablespoon at a time as needed to loosen the sauce — it should flow and cling simultaneously, not sit as a gummy solid. The combination of heat, starch, and fat will emulsify the Pecorino into a seamless sauce. Work quickly and continuously. If the sauce begins to tighten and clump, a small splash of hot pasta water and vigorous tossing will usually bring it back. Plate into warm bowls immediately. Finish with a final twist of cracked pepper and a dusting of grated Pecorino.

recipes.name: Caesar Salad
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Toss the bread cubes with a portion of the olive oil and a smashed garlic clove, season with a little salt, and spread on a sheet pan. Bake at 190°C / 375°F for 12 to 15 minutes, tossing once halfway, until deep gold and crisp through the center. Discard the garlic clove. Let them cool on the pan so they crackle and stay crunchy.

In a wide wooden salad bowl (or a mortar), mash the remaining garlic with the anchovy fillets and a pinch of salt, grinding against the wood with the back of a fork until you have a smooth, sticky beige paste with no visible chunks. The salt acts as an abrasive; the anchovies dissolve almost entirely. This paste is the savory backbone of the dressing.

Whisk the coddled egg yolk, lemon juice, Worcestershire, and Dijon into the anchovy-garlic paste until smooth and pale. Then, whisking constantly, drizzle in the remaining olive oil in a thin stream so it emulsifies into a creamy, pourable dressing — thin like cold honey, not stiff like mayonnaise. Whisk in about half the grated parmesan. Taste: it should be bracingly tangy, salty, and savory. Adjust with more lemon for brightness or oil to soften.

Tear the cold romaine into large bite-sized pieces or leave small inner leaves whole. Add to the bowl with the dressing and toss thoroughly with your hands or tongs, lifting from the bottom, until every leaf is glossed and lightly coated — not drowned. Add the croutons and most of the remaining parmesan and toss once more. Plate, then finish with parmesan shavings and a heavy crack of black pepper. Serve immediately while the leaves are crisp and the croutons still crackle.

recipes.name: Calamari Fritti

ingredients.name: Fine semolina (or half 00 flour, half semolina)
Vegetable oil, for deep frying (sunflower or peanut)

steps: Pull the tentacles from the tubes and discard the quill (the clear plastic-like spine inside the tube). Pull away the purple-grey skin from the tubes if it has not already been removed by the fishmonger. Cut each tube into rings about 1cm wide. Keep the tentacles whole if small, or cut the crown in half if large. Now — this is the most important step — pat everything bone-dry in multiple changes of paper towels and leave spread on a rack for 10 minutes. Wet squid = steamed, rubbery calamari. Dry squid = crisp, tender calamari.

Whisk together the semolina, cornstarch, salt, black pepper, and cayenne in a wide, shallow bowl or a paper bag. Working in two batches, add the squid and toss to coat thoroughly, then lift each piece and shake off every excess grain of coating — only a thin, even film should remain. Excess coating falls off in the oil, burns, and pollutes the oil while making the calamari heavy and doughy. Lay the coated pieces in a single layer on a plate until ready to fry.

Heat the oil in a wide, deep, heavy pot to 180–185°C (a pinch of coating dropped in should sizzle immediately and rise to the surface). Fry the squid in small batches — no more than a handful at a time — for exactly 60 to 90 seconds. Do not walk away. The rings cook very fast and overcooking by even 30 seconds makes them rubbery. They are done when golden-amber all over and floating freely in the oil. Remove with a spider strainer and place on a wire rack immediately — never paper towels on the bottom, which trap steam.

The instant the calamari comes off the rack — within 10 seconds — season generously with fine salt while the oil on the surface is still hot and the salt will adhere. Arrange on a warm plate lined with a paper napkin (paper underneath is fine at this stage since the calamari is already on a wire rack; the napkin is for tableside aesthetics, not to re-steam them). Serve immediately with lemon wedges alongside. Calamari fritti waits for no one — it has a window of perfection measured in minutes.

recipes.name: Camarones al Mojo de Ajo
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Jumbo shrimp, head-on if possible (deveined, shells on or off)
Neutral oil or light olive oil
Guajillo chili (dried, stemmed and seeded, cut into strips or crumbled)
Fresh cilantro and lime wedges (for serving)

steps: In a wide, heavy skillet over medium-low heat, combine the butter and oil. Add all the sliced garlic and the guajillo strips at once. Cook, stirring gently every minute, for 8-12 minutes until every garlic slice has turned a deep, even golden — not pale tan, not brown. The goal is a deep amber gold that smells of caramelized sweetness, not bitterness. The oil will turn a warm amber color from the guajillo. This is the mojo de ajo and it is the soul of the dish — do not rush it.

Season the shrimp generously with salt. Increase heat to high. Add the shrimp to the pan in a single layer — do not crowd. Sear without moving for 90 seconds until the bottom edge turns pink and the shell (if on) begins to char. Flip each shrimp and cook 60-90 seconds more until the second side is pink and the shrimp just curls into a C shape. Do not overcook — shrimp go from perfect to rubbery in 30 seconds.

With the pan still on high heat, squeeze the lime juice directly over the shrimp — it will spit and steam instantly. Add a final small knob of cold butter and swirl the pan constantly for 30-45 seconds until the butter emulsifies into the pan juices, creating a glossy, cohesive sauce rather than separated oil. Remove from heat and scatter cilantro over the top. Serve immediately with warm tortillas and more lime.

recipes.name: Canelé de Bordeaux
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter (mixed with beeswax for moule coating)

steps: Combine the milk, butter, and the split vanilla bean with its scraped seeds in a saucepan. Warm over medium heat until the mixture just reaches a simmer — small bubbles around the edge and steam rising, but not a full boil. Remove from heat and allow to infuse for 10 minutes, then remove the vanilla pod. The milk should be warm to hot — it will be whisked into the egg-flour mixture and the heat helps hydrate the flour and temper the eggs simultaneously.

In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the whole eggs and yolks and whisk to a smooth, thick paste — no lumps. Pour the warm (not boiling) infused milk into the flour mixture in a thin, steady stream, whisking constantly as you go. The batter will loosen from a paste to a fluid, thin liquid as the milk is added. Finally, whisk in the rum. The critical technique: do not incorporate air — stir rather than whisk aggressively. Air creates an uneven, bubbly interior rather than the dense custard the canelé is famous for. Cover and refrigerate for 48 hours minimum — 72 hours is better. The flour absorbs the liquid and the batter settles.

Melt the beeswax pellets and butter together in a small saucepan over very low heat until fully liquid. The mixture should be around 70 C / 160 F — liquid but not so hot it burns the hand on contact. Using a small brush or by pouring and swirling, coat the inside of each copper canelé mould with the wax-butter mixture — a thin, even film. Place the moulds on a baking tray and allow the wax to set slightly — 1-2 minutes in the freezer. The beeswax creates the dramatically dark, shatteringly crisp shell that defines the canelé; butter alone gives a softer crust. Preheat the oven to 250 C / 480 F with the mould-lined tray inside.

Stir the cold batter very gently — no whisking — and ladle or pour it through a fine-mesh sieve into the waxed moulds, filling to 1 cm below the rim. The batter must be cold from the refrigerator. Place immediately in the preheated 250 C / 480 F oven. Bake at this high temperature for 10 minutes, then reduce to 180 C / 355 F without opening the oven door and bake for a further 50-60 minutes. The high initial heat sets the shell instantly and creates the dark crust; the lower temperature cooks the custard interior through without burning. The canelés are ready when they are a deep mahogany — almost approaching black — and have pulled away from the mould edges slightly. Unmould immediately onto a wire rack.

recipes.name: Cannoli Cream
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Line a fine-mesh sieve or colander with a double layer of damp cheesecloth and set it over a bowl in the refrigerator. Tip the ricotta into the lined sieve and leave to drain for at least 1 hour (or up to overnight for the driest result). Discard the liquid in the bowl. Properly strained ricotta should feel grainy and dry — like thick cottage cheese rather than yogurt. The water content of commercial ricotta is the single biggest reason cannoli cream turns out runny: drain it without mercy.

Transfer the strained ricotta to a bowl. Sift the powdered sugar over it and beat together with a spatula or hand mixer on low speed until completely smooth, with no sugar lumps and no ricotta curds remaining. This step breaks down the grainy texture of the ricotta into a creamy, cohesive mass. Taste for sweetness — the sugar level here is modest to allow the ricotta's flavour to come through. Add more sugar by the tablespoon if desired, but remember that the chocolate chips will add additional sweetness.

Add the orange zest, vanilla extract, and cinnamon to the sweetened ricotta and fold in with a spatula until fully distributed — the zest should be dispersed throughout, not clumped. Fold in the mini chocolate chips last, using three or four strokes to distribute evenly without crushing them. The chips should remain whole and provide textural contrast. Taste once more: the orange should be present but not dominant, the cinnamon a background whisper.

Cover the bowl tightly with cling film pressed directly onto the surface of the cream to prevent a skin forming. Refrigerate for at least 20 minutes before use. Fill cannoli shells at the very last moment by piping from both ends to ensure even filling — shells pre-filled more than 30 minutes ahead will soften and lose their crunch. For each filled cannoli, finish the exposed cream at both ends with a small pinch of chopped pistachios. Alternatively, serve the cream in small bowls or cups with crushed wafer for dipping.

recipes.name: Cannoli Siciliani
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: In a large bowl, combine the flour, sugar, and salt. Rub in the cold lard with your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs, like a shortcrust pastry. Make a well and add the Marsala, vinegar, and egg yolk. Mix with a fork until the dough comes together, then turn onto an unfloured surface and knead firmly for 5–8 minutes until smooth, supple, and homogeneous. The dough will be stiff — firmer than bread dough. This stiffness is correct: a stiff dough rolled thin enough will bubble and blister in the oil. Wrap tightly in cling film and rest at room temperature for 30 minutes.

Roll the rested dough on a lightly floured surface to 1–2 mm thickness (as thin as a pasta sheet). Using a floured 10–12 cm round cutter, cut circles. Wrap each circle around a cannoli tube mold, overlapping the edges by 1 cm. Brush the overlapping edge with beaten egg white and press firmly to seal — a loose seal will open in the oil and the shell will unfurl. If molds are limited, fry in batches and reuse. Do not crowd molds.

Heat the oil to 180°C (355°F) in a deep, heavy pan. Lower the mold-wrapped shells gently into the oil in batches of 2–3. They fry quickly — 2 to 3 minutes total, turning with tongs. You are looking for deep, even mahogany-brown with the characteristic blistered surface from the wine in the dough. When golden, lift and grip the mold with a cloth, then slide the fried tube off carefully onto a rack. The shell will release easily — do not force it. Cool the molds before re-using. Drain the shells on a rack.

The ricotta must be very well drained. The night before, set it in a fine-mesh sieve over a bowl in the refrigerator to drain for 12–24 hours; excess moisture makes a thin, weeping filling that immediately softens the shell. Beat the cold drained ricotta with the icing sugar, orange zest, and vanilla until smooth and creamy — start slow, then increase speed for 1 minute until light. Fold in the chocolate chips. Taste: it should be sweetly creamy, citrus-forward, and rich. Refrigerate until cold and firm. Transfer to a piping bag with a plain 1 cm nozzle.

Fill the cannoli only at the moment of serving — even 15 minutes in advance softens the shell. Hold a shell and pipe the filling in from one end until it appears at the other. Press a piece of candied orange or a pinch of chopped pistachios into the filling at each exposed end. Dust lightly with icing sugar if desired. Serve immediately, standing upright or tilted elegantly. A cannoli eaten an hour after filling is not a cannoli.

recipes.name: Caponata
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Toasted pine nuts and torn basil

steps: Salt the eggplant cubes lightly and let them sit 20 to 30 minutes, then blot dry — this draws out bitter liquid and keeps them from drinking the whole bottle of oil. Heat the olive oil in a wide pan until it shimmers and fry the eggplant in batches over medium-high heat, turning, until each cube is deeply golden on several faces and tender to the center. Lift onto a rack or paper to drain. Crowding the pan steams the eggplant grey and slick — give them room and patience.

In the same pan with a film of the frying oil, cook the sliced celery and onion over medium heat with a pinch of salt until softened and translucent but not browned, 8 to 10 minutes. The celery should lose its raw crunch while keeping a little bite — it is the textural backbone of caponata. Stir often and lower the heat if anything threatens to color.

Add the crushed tomatoes to the sweated vegetables along with the torn olives and rinsed capers. Simmer gently, stirring now and then, for 10 to 12 minutes until the tomato loses its raw edge, tightens, and turns from bright red to a deeper brick. You want a thick, glossy base that just coats the vegetables, not a soupy sauce — caponata should mound on a spoon, never pool.

Stir the sugar and vinegar together until the sugar dissolves, then pour it over the tomato base and let it bubble hard for a minute so the harsh edge of the vinegar cooks off and the sauce turns glossy — this is the agrodolce, the sweet-and-sour signature. Gently fold in the fried eggplant, taking care not to crush it, and warm everything through for 2 to 3 minutes. Taste and balance: it should land sweet, then sour, then savory. Off the heat, scatter pine nuts and torn basil over the top. Crucially, let it rest at least a few hours, ideally overnight, and serve at room temperature — caponata is always better the next day.

recipes.name: Dry-Method Caramel Sauce
steps: Place the sugar in a wide, heavy-based saucepan (light interior colour is ideal so you can see the caramel). Set over medium heat — do not stir. As the sugar melts at the edges, gently swirl the pan to even out the heat, but never use a spoon. Allow the sugar to melt slowly and evenly, swirling occasionally, until the entire mass is molten and a deep amber colour — the colour of dark honey or old whisky. Watch it carefully from the moment it fully liquefies: it will go from perfect to burnt in 15–20 seconds. The target temperature is 175–180 C.

Remove the pan from the heat and immediately add the warm cream in a slow, steady pour — stand back, the mixture will bubble violently and steam dramatically as the cold cream hits the hot sugar. Stir or whisk continuously as you add it. The caramel will seize and harden around the cream at first — keep stirring. Return to low heat and stir until any hardened caramel lumps have dissolved and the mixture is smooth.

Remove the pan from the heat. Add the cold cubed butter, flaky salt, and vanilla extract. Stir or whisk until the butter is fully melted and incorporated — the sauce will turn from thin to glossy and slightly thickened as the butter emulsifies. Taste: it should be deeply sweet, properly bitter at the back of the throat, and finished with a definite hit of salt. Pour into a clean jar or bowl. The sauce thickens as it cools; reheat gently to serve.

recipes.name: Pasta Carbonara

ingredients.name: Guanciale (cured pork cheek, cut into lardons or batons)
Egg yolks (4 yolks plus 1 whole egg)
Pecorino Romano (very finely grated, almost powdery)
Black pepper (very coarsely cracked — not finely ground)
Pasta cooking water (heavily salted, starchy — reserved just before draining)

steps: Place the guanciale in a cold, dry, heavy skillet and set over medium-low heat. Cook slowly, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the fat renders out completely and the pieces are golden and crisp but still slightly supple at the centre — not brittle and hard. Remove the guanciale with a slotted spoon, leaving all the rendered fat in the pan. Turn the heat off and allow the fat to cool slightly. It should be a clear, pale amber liquid in the pan.

Cook the pasta in a large pot of generously salted water — it should taste of the sea. Cook 1–2 minutes less than the package directions: you want the pasta just shy of al dente, since it will continue cooking in the pan. One minute before draining, ladle at least 200 ml of the cloudy, starchy cooking water into a heatproof cup and reserve. Drain the pasta but do not rinse.

Add the drained pasta directly to the pan with the guanciale fat over medium-low heat. Add the guanciale back in. Toss vigorously for 1–2 minutes, adding splashes of reserved pasta water as needed to build an emulsion — the starchy water and fat will combine into a glossy coating. Toast the cracked black pepper in the fat for 30 seconds until fragrant. The pasta should be glistening, glossy, and fully coated in the emulsified fat-and-water sauce. Remove the pan from all heat.

In a bowl, whisk the 4 egg yolks and 1 whole egg together with the very finely grated Pecorino and Parmesan until combined into a thick, pale yellow paste. With the pan completely off all heat, pour the egg-and-cheese mixture over the pasta. Toss continuously and vigorously — the residual heat of the pasta will gently cook and thicken the eggs without scrambling them. Add pasta water a tablespoon at a time as needed: the final sauce should be fluid, glossy, and cream-like in consistency. Taste and adjust black pepper. Serve immediately in warmed bowls.

recipes.name: Carnitas

ingredients.name: Pork shoulder (boston butt, cut into 5 cm chunks)

steps: Pat the pork chunks thoroughly dry and toss with the salt until every surface is coated. Let them sit at room temperature for 15-20 minutes while you assemble the aromatics. Dry, well-salted meat is the foundation — surface moisture steams instead of browns and dilutes the rendering fat.

Nestle the pork in a single layer in a heavy wide pot or Dutch oven. Add the lard, squeeze in the orange juice and drop in the spent shells, then add onion, garlic, bay, and cinnamon. Add just enough water to barely reach the top of the meat. Bring to a gentle simmer, then drop to the lowest heat that keeps lazy bubbles rising. Cook uncovered 1.5-2 hours, undisturbed, until the water has cooked off and the pork is fork-tender, now submerged in clear rendered fat.

Once the water is gone and the pork sits in clear fat, raise the heat to medium-high. If using, drizzle in the sweetened condensed milk now — the trace of sugar and dairy boosts browning the Michoacán way. Let the pieces fry in their fat, turning them only every few minutes, until deeply golden and crisp at the edges, 8-12 minutes. Resist over-stirring; contact time with the hot pot is what builds the crust.

Transfer the carnitas to a board and let them rest 5 minutes so the juices settle. Roughly chop or pull into a craggy mix of crisp shards and tender shreds, spooning over a little of the warm rendered fat to keep them glossy. Taste and add a pinch more salt and a squeeze of fresh lime if it needs brightening. Serve hot on warm corn tortillas with onion, cilantro, and salsa.

recipes.name: Carottes Vichy (Glazed Carrots)

ingredients.name: Carrots, peeled and sliced into 5 mm rounds

steps: Arrange the carrot rounds in a single layer in a wide sauté pan. Add butter, sugar, salt, and just enough water to barely cover the carrots — no more. Bring to a vigorous simmer over medium-high heat, uncovered. Cook, swirling the pan occasionally, until the liquid has almost entirely evaporated and a syrupy glaze remains.
Off the heat, scatter the chopped parsley over the glazed carrots. Toss gently to coat, then taste and adjust salt. Serve immediately — the glaze tightens as it cools.

recipes.name: Cassoulet

ingredients.name: Dried Tarbais beans (or flageolet, soaked overnight)
Duck confit legs (2 legs, from confit-duck-legs)
Pork belly (skin-on, cut into large lardons)
Day-old white bread (blitzed into coarse crumbs)

steps: Drain the soaked beans and place in a large pot with fresh cold water to cover by 5 cm. Add the bouquet garni. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook for 60–90 minutes until the beans are tender but still hold their shape completely — they must not be mushy, as they will continue cooking in the cassoulet. Season with salt only in the last 10 minutes of cooking, as salting too early toughens the skins. Reserve the cooking liquid.

In a large, heavy cassole or Dutch oven, render the pork belly lardons over medium heat until golden and their fat has run. Remove the lardons. In the same fat, brown the Toulouse sausages all over for 5–6 minutes until deeply coloured — do not cook through. Remove. Add the onion and garlic to the remaining fat and cook over medium-low heat for 8 minutes until softened and golden. Stir in the tomato purée and cook 2 minutes more until it darkens slightly. The fond (browned bits) on the bottom of the pot is the backbone of the cassoulet's depth.

Preheat the oven to 150 C (300 F). Add the cooked beans, lardons, and stock to the pot with the onion-tomato base. Stir gently to combine without breaking the beans. Nestle the browned sausages and the duck confit legs (skin-side up) into the beans. Add enough additional stock or bean cooking liquid to just reach the top of the beans. The duck skin should be poking just above the surface — it will form the first crust layer. Bring to a simmer on the stovetop, then transfer to the oven and bake uncovered for 2.5–3 hours.

In the final 30 minutes of baking, scatter the bread crumbs evenly over the surface in a thin, continuous layer. Increase the oven temperature to 180 C (350 F) and bake until the crumbs are deeply golden and crunchy. This final crumb crust is the defining textural element of a proper cassoulet — it should shatter when a spoon cuts through, giving way to the creamy, smoky, herb-scented beans beneath. Rest for 10 minutes before serving directly from the terrine at the table.

recipes.name: Cauliflower Shawarma
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Shawarma spice blend (cumin, coriander, turmeric, smoked paprika, cinnamon, allspice)

steps: In a large bowl, whisk together the olive oil, shawarma spice blend, and salt into a thick, fragrant paste. The oil should be fully absorbed by the spices — no separation. This paste needs to coat each floret generously, so make sure the consistency is thick enough to cling rather than drip.

Add the cauliflower florets to the bowl of paste and toss thoroughly, using your hands to work the paste into every crevice. The more surface area covered, the more caramelisation you will get. Let the cauliflower rest in the marinade for at least 10 minutes while the oven preheats to 220°C (425°F).

Spread the coated florets in a single layer on a large baking sheet, cut-side down where possible. Roast at 220°C for 25–30 minutes, without stirring for the first 20 minutes. The high heat and stillness are what create the deep caramelised crust. After 20 minutes, check and flip any pieces that are very dark underneath.

Transfer the roasted cauliflower to a serving platter immediately. Squeeze the fresh lemon juice over the top while still hot — the acid will sizzle on contact and lift the caramelised spices. Scatter with chopped flat-leaf parsley. Serve immediately as the crust softens as it sits.

recipes.name: Causa Limeña
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Yellow-fleshed potato (papa amarilla or Yukon Gold, peeled)
Black olive slices, hard-boiled egg, fresh parsley sprigs

steps: Place the peeled, halved potatoes in a pot of well-salted cold water and bring to a boil. Cook until completely tender and a knife slides through without any resistance — about 20–25 minutes depending on size. Drain immediately and spread on a tray to steam-dry for 5 minutes. This step is critical: wet potatoes produce a gluey causa that will not hold its shape. The potatoes must be very dry when mashed.

While the potatoes are still hot, pass them through a potato ricer or press them through a fine-mesh strainer with a spatula — never use a food processor, which will make them gluey. Transfer the riced potato to a large bowl. Add the ají amarillo paste, lime juice, and oil. Fold and work with a flexible spatula until completely homogenous, with no white streaks of unmixed potato. Season with salt. The causa dough should taste boldly of lime and ají, with a vibrant orange-yellow color throughout and the texture of soft, pliable clay.

Mix the drained tuna with the mayonnaise and season with salt and a squeeze of lime — it should taste well-seasoned and creamy. Line a loaf pan or individual ring molds with plastic wrap. Press one-third of the causa dough firmly into the base in an even, compact layer. Lay the avocado slices in a single, slightly overlapping layer. Spread the tuna mixture evenly over the avocado. Press the remaining two-thirds of causa dough over the tuna in two equal layers, pressing firmly between each addition to eliminate air gaps. The layers must be dense and cohesive or the causa will crumble when sliced.

Refrigerate the assembled causa for at least 1 hour, or up to 24 hours — it only improves as it firms and the flavors meld. When ready to serve, unmold onto a cutting board or serving plate by inverting the mold and gently lifting. Remove the plastic wrap. With a sharp knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between cuts, slice into clean portions. Garnish each serving with sliced black olives, hard-boiled egg quarters, and parsley. Serve cold — causa is a cold dish.

recipes.name: Ceviche Clásico

ingredients.name: Sushi-grade sea bass (corvina or lenguado), cut into 2 cm cubes
Fresh lime juice (from 14–18 limes, freshly squeezed)
Red onion, very thinly sliced into half-moons
Ají amarillo paste (or 2 fresh ají amarillo, seeded, minced)
Cancha (toasted Peruvian corn) or chifles (fried plantain chips)
Ají limo or habanero, seeded and very finely minced

steps: Slice the red onion as thinly as humanly possible — ideally 1 mm or less, using a mandoline or a very sharp knife. Place in a bowl of cold, lightly salted water. Soak for 10 minutes — this draws out sulfurous compounds and raw bite while preserving the clean onion flavor and brilliant purple-pink color. Drain, rinse, and drain again. In the same bowl, toss the drained onion slices with a pinch of salt and a small squeeze of lime juice. The salt seasons while beginning to macerate the onion, making each slice supple and bright. Set aside. Properly prepared onion is the texture counterpoint that makes ceviche: it must be crisp enough to have presence, soft enough to not be harsh. The soaking step is non-negotiable for a refined result.

In a chilled glass or ceramic bowl, combine the sea bass cubes with the salt and toss gently to season. Pour the lime juice over the fish — the juice must completely cover every piece. Add the ají amarillo paste, grated ginger, grated garlic, and ají limo. Toss very gently with a spoon, turning the fish once or twice without breaking the cubes. Do not mix vigorously — you are not making a salad. Place the bowl directly on ice or in the freezer for exactly 2–3 minutes. In Lima, ceviche marinates for only 2–3 minutes — the fish is barely touched by the acid, remaining almost raw at the center while the outermost layer turns opaque. This is the Limeño style: vital and immediate, consumed the moment it's ready. The remaining lime juice, now loaded with fish essence, ají heat, ginger, and brine, is the leche de tigre — tiger's milk. It is one of the most flavourful liquids in all of cooking.

Working quickly — the moment you stop moving, the fish continues to cure — add the macerated onion slices directly to the ceviche bowl. Add the cilantro leaves whole or gently torn, never chopped (chopped cilantro bruises and turns dark). Toss everything together with two spoons, using three or four gentle, lifting motions. Taste the leche de tigre and adjust seasoning: it should be explosively sour-salty-hot, but the heat should build rather than ambush. If it's too sour, a pinch of sugar helps; if too flat, more salt. Divide immediately among two chilled bowls. Fan slices of boiled sweet potato along one side — the camote's gentle sweetness is the traditional counterweight to the acidic fish and the textural rest your palate needs. Scatter cancha or chifles over the top for crunch. Serve within 30 seconds of plating. Ceviche does not wait. Invite your guests to drink the leche de tigre from the bowl.

recipes.name: Ceviche de Camarones
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Large shrimp (21–25 count), peeled and deveined
