steps: Bring a pot of well-salted water to a boil. Remove from heat completely and wait 2 minutes — the water should be around 80 C (176 F), no longer boiling. Drop the shrimp in. Stir once. Leave undisturbed for exactly 90 seconds, then immediately drain and transfer to a bowl of ice water to stop cooking. The shrimp should be just barely opaque in the very center — they will continue to firm as they cool. A shrimp that is fully pink and curled tight is already overcooked.

Slice red onion paper-thin on a mandoline or by hand. Place in a bowl, toss with a generous pinch of salt, and rub between the palms for 30 seconds. Cover with cold water and soak for 10 minutes — this removes the harsh sulfur compounds that make raw onion sharp without destroying their crunch and color. Drain and squeeze dry in a clean cloth.

Combine the cooled shrimp, macerated onion, lime juice, ají amarillo paste, grated ginger, garlic, and cilantro in a cold bowl. Toss gently to combine. Season with salt. Marinate for 15–20 minutes in the refrigerator — enough time for the leche de tigre (tiger's milk — the curing liquid) to develop body and for the lime to finish the surface of the shrimp. Serve immediately after marination in chilled bowls, with choclo corn on the side for textural contrast.

recipes.name: Ceviche
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Firm white ocean fish, skinless and boneless (corvina, sea bass, halibut, or fluke)
Fresh lime juice (key/Mexican limes preferred, never bottled)
Aji limo or fresh habanero, seeded and minced
Garlic clove, grated to a paste
Fresh ginger, finely grated (optional Nikkei accent)
Red onion, sliced paper-thin (sliced with the grain)
Sweet potato (camote), boiled and sliced into rounds
Choclo or boiled corn kernels / toasted cancha

steps: Boil the unpeeled sweet potato whole until a knife slides through with no resistance, 20 to 30 minutes, then cool, peel, and slice into thick rounds — it must be ready to serve before the fish ever touches lime. Meanwhile slice the red onion paper-thin and soak it in ice water for 10 minutes to strip its raw bite, then drain and dry it well. Cold, sweet camote and crisp, mellow onion are the counterweights to the acid and heat that come next.

Squeeze the limes gently by hand — never wring them to the rind, which releases bitter pith oils. In a bowl, whisk the fresh lime juice with the grated garlic, minced aji, optional ginger, and the salt until the salt dissolves. This is the leche de tigre, the tiger's milk: it should taste aggressively bright, garlicky, hot, and a touch too salty on its own, because the fish will quickly pull it into balance.

Cut the chilled, scrupulously fresh fish into even half-inch cubes — uniform pieces cure at the same rate. Fold the fish into the leche de tigre so every cube is bathed, then let it sit just 2 to 5 minutes for the modern Limeño style. The acid denatures the surface proteins, turning the edges opaque and firm while the centers stay tender and almost raw. Do not walk away — over-curing turns ceviche chalky and tough.

Off the heat of the acid, gently fold the drained red onion and most of the cilantro into the cured fish so they stay crisp and bright. Taste the leche de tigre one last time and correct the salt, lime, and heat. Spoon the fish and its cloudy liquid into a cold shallow bowl, lean the sweet potato rounds against one side, scatter the corn or toasted cancha, and crown with the remaining cilantro. Serve immediately, while everything is icy and the cure is at its peak.

recipes.name: Braided Challah
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: In a large bowl, whisk together warm water, beaten eggs, oil, and honey. Add yeast and stir briefly. Add flour and salt. Mix with a wooden spoon until the dough comes together, then switch to hand-mixing. The dough will be soft and slightly sticky — richer and more pliable than lean bread dough from the eggs and oil. It should not pour but it will cling to your hands. Do not add extra flour yet — challah needs this initial softness.

Knead on a lightly floured surface for 10 minutes by hand, or 7 minutes on medium speed in a stand mixer with a dough hook. Enriched dough takes longer to develop than lean dough because the fat coats the gluten strands. The dough will begin tacky and gradually become smooth and supple. It is fully developed when the surface is silky, slightly shiny, and pulls away from your hands cleanly. The windowpane test: stretch a small piece — it should thin to a nearly translucent membrane.

Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, turning once to coat. Cover with plastic wrap. Let rise in a warm spot (26–28 C) for 90 minutes until doubled. Challah dough rises more slowly than lean dough because of the oil and eggs, which inhibit yeast slightly. Patience is essential. Do not rush with extra heat — slow rising builds more complex flavor in the enriched crumb.

Gently punch down the dough and divide into 6 equal strands (or 3 for a simple braid). Roll each strand on a lightly floured surface into a rope 35–40 cm long, tapered at both ends. For a six-strand braid: lay strands parallel, pinch at the top. Number them 1 (far left) through 6 (far right). Move strand 6 over strand 1. Move strand 1 over strands 3 and 4. Move strand 6 under strand 4, then over strand 5. Repeat: always moving the far-right strand over the far-left, then the far-left strand over strands 3–4, the far-right strand under strand 4 and over strand 5. Pinch at the bottom and tuck both ends under. Lay on a parchment-lined pan. Cover and proof 45 minutes until visibly puffy.

Preheat oven to 190 C (375 F). Beat the egg yolk with 1 teaspoon water until smooth. Gently brush the entire surface of the proofed braid — get into all the crevices between strands. Apply two coats for a deeper mahogany. Bake for 30–35 minutes until deeply golden-brown. Check internal temperature: 88–90 C (190–195 F). If the braid is browning too fast on top after 20 minutes, tent loosely with foil. Cool on a wire rack at least 30 minutes before tearing.

recipes.name: Chana Masala
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Whole spices (2 black cardamom, 1 cinnamon shard, 2 cloves, 1 tsp cumin seed, 2 bay leaves)
Ground spice blend (1 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp Kashmiri chile, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp garam masala)

steps: Heat the oil or ghee in a heavy pot over medium-high until it shimmers and a cumin seed dropped in sizzles immediately. Add all the whole spices at once — black cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, cumin seed, bay leaves. Let them bloom for 20-40 seconds until the cumin darkens a shade and the kitchen fills with a sweet, woody aroma.

Add the chopped onion and a pinch of salt to the tempered oil. Cook over medium heat, stirring often, for 12-15 minutes until deep golden-brown. Add the ginger-garlic paste and slit green chiles and fry for another 2 minutes until the raw garlic smell is gone. This patient browning is the backbone of the dish — don't rush it.

Stir in the tomato puree and the ground spice blend. Lower the heat slightly and bhuno (fry-stir) for 8-12 minutes, scraping the pot, until the tomato breaks down and the oil pools and separates from the masala. This is the most important step: cooking the ground spices into the fat removes their raw, dusty taste and builds the dish's color and depth.

Add the cooked chickpeas along with enough of their cooking liquid (or water) to make a loose gravy — about equal volume to the masala. Add salt. Bring to a simmer, partially cover, and cook 20-25 minutes, mashing a spoonful of chickpeas against the side to thicken the gravy. The chickpeas should drink in the color and turn from pale to a warm tan-red.

Stir in the amchoor and let it cook for 1-2 minutes — taste and adjust, you want a clear tangy lift, not a flat sourness. Kill the heat, scatter cilantro and slivered raw ginger over the top, and rest 5 minutes covered before serving so the flavors settle. Serve with bhatura, naan, or steamed rice.

recipes.name: Chapati

ingredients.name: Ghee or neutral oil (optional, for finishing)

steps: Combine atta and salt in a deep bowl (the traditional thali shape is ideal — high sides help contain the kneading). Add warm water gradually, mixing with your fingers as you pour. Atta absorbs water differently from all-purpose flour — it can take more than expected. Add water until the dough just comes together, then turn onto the surface and knead for 8-10 minutes with the heel of your palm, using a rhythmic push-fold-rotate motion. The finished dough should be very soft — softer than bread dough, noticeably softer than pizza dough. It should not stick, but it should be yielding under the lightest pressure.

Cover the dough tightly with a damp cloth and rest at room temperature for 20-30 minutes. During this rest, the gluten relaxes (enabling the rolling out of very thin rounds without spring-back) and the whole-wheat bran in the atta absorbs water fully and softens. This rest is more important for chapati than for any other flatbread — without it, the rolled rounds spring back and the finished chapati will be tough rather than soft. Divide the rested dough into 10-12 golf-ball-sized portions.

On a lightly floured surface (atta is best for dusting), roll each dough ball with a thin rolling pin (the traditional belan is narrow and lighter than a Western rolling pin, allowing fast rotation). Roll from the center outward with light, quick strokes, rotating the round 45-60 degrees after each pass to keep the circle even. The target is a circle 20-22 cm in diameter and 1.5-2 mm thin — about the thickness of two stacked credit cards. It should be translucent in the thinnest spots. Dust only as much as needed to prevent sticking — excess atta makes the tawa smoke and the chapati tough.

Heat a dry tawa (cast-iron flat griddle) or heavy skillet over high heat until a drop of water skitters and evaporates within 1 second. Place a chapati on the dry surface and cook for 45-60 seconds until the surface begins to show matte dry spots and small bubbles form. Flip using tongs and cook the second side for 30-45 seconds until it shows similar matte spots and slightly larger bubbles. Now transfer directly onto a gas flame with tongs or use a wire flame tamer: hold the chapati over the open flame for 5-10 seconds per side. The trapped steam inflates the chapati into a full balloon — this is the sign of a well-made chapati and indicates the interior is cooked through. Remove immediately, brush with ghee if using, and stack under a clean cloth to keep soft.

recipes.name: Char Siu Glaze
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Red fermented bean curd (nam yu), mashed
Shaoxing rice wine or dry sherry

steps: Mash the red fermented bean curd to a smooth paste with a fork. Combine all ingredients in a saucepan and whisk together until uniform. The fermented bean curd will resist — work it in thoroughly. The glaze at this stage will be a dark, muddy reddish-brown.

Heat the glaze in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring constantly. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 4–5 minutes until the glaze has thickened, the sugar has fully dissolved, and it coats the back of a spoon heavily. Remove from heat — it will continue to thicken as it cools. Use warm for marinating and glazing, or store refrigerated for 3 weeks.

recipes.name: Char Siu (Cantonese BBQ Pork)

ingredients.name: Pork shoulder or pork neck (with some fat marbling)
Fermented red bean curd (nan ru), mashed smooth

steps: Slice the pork shoulder into strips approximately 4 cm wide, 4 cm thick, and 15–20 cm long, following the grain of the meat. Mix all marinade ingredients — honey, hoisin, soy sauce, mashed red bean curd, Shaoxing wine, brown sugar, five spice, and garlic — in a bowl and whisk until smooth. The fermented red bean curd (nan ru) should fully dissolve into the mixture, turning it a distinctive reddish-brown that will deepen to the characteristic char siu red during roasting. Add the pork strips to the marinade and turn to coat every surface thoroughly. Press the marinade into any crevices with your fingers. Transfer to a zip-lock bag or covered container and refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours — overnight is strongly preferred and will produce a markedly more complex result. The longer marinade time allows the salt to penetrate deep into the meat and the sugars to begin their chemical interaction with the proteins, which accelerates Maillard browning during roasting.

Preheat your oven to 220°C (425°F). Place a wire rack over a foil-lined baking tray — the rack elevates the pork so heat circulates underneath, and the foil catches the inevitable sugary drips that would otherwise carbonize directly on your tray. Remove the pork from the marinade, reserving all of the marinade, and lay the strips on the rack with at least 2 cm of space between each. They should not touch. Roast for 15 minutes. Meanwhile, pour the reserved marinade into a small saucepan and bring to a boil for 2 minutes — this makes it safe to use as a glaze on cooked meat. After the first 15 minutes, flip each strip using tongs and brush the top generously with the cooked marinade. Return to the oven for another 10 minutes. The alternation of high heat and glaze application is what builds the layered, crackling lacquer that defines char siu.

Brush the reserved honey (the second portion set aside for glazing, not the used marinade) generously over every surface of the still-hot pork strips. Return to the oven under the broiler — with the oven rack in the upper third — for 3–4 minutes, watching constantly. The honey will bubble and caramelize at the surface in real time, producing the final high-shine lacquer glaze that char siu is famous for. Pull the strips out when the glaze is bubbling vigorously and the surface looks wet and glossy but the edges nearest the heat are just beginning to turn very dark. The glaze will set and harden slightly as it cools. Do not skip this step — the pre-glaze roasting develops the crust; this final honey application provides the shine and the final layer of sweetness.

Transfer the rested strips to a cutting board. Slice each strip across the grain into pieces 8–10 mm thick — cutting with the grain produces tough, stringy pieces; cutting across it produces the clean, yielding bite that is the whole point. Each slice should reveal a cross-section of pale-pink, juicy interior ringed by a band of deep mahogany glaze. Fan the slices slightly overlapping on a plate. Drizzle any drippings from the pan over the top. Serve with steamed white rice, or use as a filling for steamed bao buns, over lo mein noodles, or alongside congee.

recipes.name: Chard with Currants and Pine Nuts

ingredients.name: Rainbow chard, stems separated and sliced into 2 cm pieces, leaves roughly torn

steps: Place the pine nuts in a dry skillet over medium-low heat. Shake or stir constantly for 2–3 minutes until they turn a deep golden color. Watch without distraction — they go from pale to burnt in under 30 seconds. Tip immediately onto a cool plate to stop cooking.

In a large, wide pan over medium heat, warm the olive oil until it shimmers. Add the garlic slices and cook, stirring, until they are pale gold and fragrant — about 1 minute. Do not let them brown. Add the chard stems and cook, stirring, for 3 minutes until beginning to soften. Add the chard leaves in large handfuls, wilting each before adding the next. Once all leaves are wilted, add the golden raisins, white wine vinegar, and red pepper flakes. Stir to combine and cook for 1 more minute. Season with salt.

Taste for seasoning — the agrodolce balance should be present but subtle. If it tastes flat, add a few more drops of vinegar; if too sharp, a small pinch of sugar. Transfer to a serving plate and scatter the toasted pine nuts over the top. Serve warm or at room temperature.

recipes.name: Chawanmushi
steps: Beat the eggs gently with chopsticks or a fork in a cutting, slicing motion — do not whisk vigorously. The goal is to break the yolks and blend the whites and yolks into a uniform mixture without incorporating any air, which would create bubbles in the steamed custard. In a separate bowl or jug, combine the warm dashi, soy sauce, mirin, and salt and stir to blend. Pour the seasoned dashi into the beaten eggs gradually, stirring gently as you pour. The dashi-to-egg ratio of roughly 2.5:1 by volume is what produces the barely-set, trembling consistency — more egg and the custard becomes firm; less and it won't set. Strain the entire mixture through a fine-mesh sieve into a pouring jug, pressing the chalazae through with a spoon, then strain once more through cheesecloth if possible for an impeccably smooth result.

Divide the shrimp and kamaboko slices evenly among 4 chawanmushi cups (or any deep, heatproof cups or ramekins with lids). Arrange them with some care — in traditional service, the shrimp curl attractively against the cup wall where they can be seen through the custard once it sets, acting as a visual indicator of quality. If using shiitake, place them cap-side down. Leave space at the top — fill cups only to 80% capacity, as the custard needs room to set without touching the lid. Do not add the mitsuba yet; it will go on just before serving.

Pour the strained egg mixture slowly into each cup over the back of a spoon to prevent disturbing the fillings or creating bubbles. Fill to about 1 cm below the rim. Skim any bubbles off the surface with a paper towel or the edge of a spoon — any bubble on the surface will leave a crater when it pops during steaming. Cover each cup with its lid (or foil wrapped tight). Place in a bamboo steamer or a pot with a steaming rack. Steam over medium-low heat — not a rolling boil, just a gentle, steady steam. A violent boil will cause the custard to cook too fast at the edges, creating a pocked, spongy texture called 'su' (holes). Steam for 12–15 minutes. Check at 12 minutes: the custard should tremble as a single unit when gently shaken, with the center just barely set.

Remove the cups from the steamer and let them sit for 2 minutes — the custard will firm the final degree of setting from residual heat. Remove the lids and add 1–2 mitsuba sprigs to each cup, pressing the stems gently into the custard surface so they stand slightly upright. Serve immediately in the cup, with small spoons. Chawanmushi is eaten with a spoon by breaking through the smooth surface and scooping custard and filling together. It is served hot in winter and chilled (cold chawanmushi requires a firmer egg ratio) in summer. The mitsuba will wilt quickly — serve without delay.

recipes.name: Chermoula
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Fresh cilantro, leaves and tender stems
Flat-leaf parsley, leaves and tender stems

steps: Place the garlic cloves in a mortar with the salt. Pound with a circular and downward motion until the garlic breaks down completely into a sticky, smooth paste — the salt acts as an abrasive, drawing out the garlic's moisture and accelerating the process. This should take about 90 seconds of sustained effort. The paste should show the faint translucency of crushed raw garlic with no visible fibrous strands.

Add the cilantro and parsley to the garlic paste in the mortar and pound together — the herbs will release their oils quickly and the mixture will turn bright green almost immediately. Add the ground cumin, paprika, cayenne, and lemon zest. Continue pounding and working the pestle, alternating between crushing and stirring motions. The goal is a coarse, fragrant paste: not a smooth puree, but not a rough chop either — something with visible herb texture and fully integrated spices. If the mortar is too small, transfer to a food processor and pulse briefly, being careful not to over-process.

Add the lemon juice and olive oil to the herb and spice paste. Fold and stir together — the acid and fat will loosen the paste into a spreadable, saucy consistency. Add the oil in increments, stirring after each addition, until you reach the texture you need: thicker if using as a marinade or rub, looser if spooning over cooked fish. Taste and adjust: more salt if it tastes flat, more lemon if it needs brightness, more cayenne if it needs heat. Chermoula is immediate — use it within an hour for the brightest color and freshest flavor.

recipes.name: Chicken Katsu
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Neutral oil for shallow frying (rice bran or canola)

steps: If using skin-on thighs, leave the skin on — it fries up into a crackling layer that contrasts beautifully with the panko crust. Open the thigh flat and trim any large pockets of fat from the interior that would not render during shallow frying. Place between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound gently with the flat face of a meat mallet from the center outward until the thigh is an even 1.5 cm thickness throughout — thick patches will not cook through by the time the crust reaches full color. Season both sides with fine salt and white pepper immediately before dredging.

Combine the Worcestershire sauce, ketchup, and oyster sauce in a small bowl. Stir well to combine. Taste — the sauce should be sweet, tangy, and deeply savory with a slight fermented undertone. Adjust ratios to personal taste: more Worcestershire for depth and tang, more ketchup for sweetness and body, a touch more oyster sauce for umami. This is a quick approximation of commercial Bull-Dog sauce. Allow to sit for 5 minutes for the flavors to integrate.

Set up three shallow dishes: flour, beaten egg, and panko. Dredge each thigh in flour, patting off every trace of excess. Dip into beaten egg, letting the excess drip for 2 seconds. Press firmly into the panko, then flip and press again — unlike schnitzel, katsu benefits from a thick, pressed panko coating that builds a robust, shattering crust rather than a delicate one. The coating should be visibly thick. Heat oil to 170°C / 340°F in a heavy pan — enough oil to come halfway up the thigh. Fry skin-side down (or top-side down) for 4 minutes until deep golden. Flip carefully and fry 3 minutes on the second side until deep golden and the thickest part reads 74°C / 165°F. Drain on a rack.

Rest the fried katsu on the rack for 2 minutes — this allows the crust to set and the interior to equilibrate. Using a sharp, heavy knife with one clean downward press per cut (not a sawing motion, which tears the crust), slice into 2–3 cm strips across the width, keeping the slices in the original shape of the thigh. Reassemble the sliced pieces on the cutting board and slide as a unit onto warmed plates beside a mound of shredded cabbage. Drizzle tonkatsu sauce across the slices or serve alongside for dipping.

recipes.name: Chicken Marsala

ingredients.name: Boneless skinless chicken breasts, pounded to 1/4 inch

steps: Season pounded cutlets with salt and pepper. Dredge in flour, shaking off all excess. Heat 2 tablespoons butter and all the olive oil in a large, wide skillet over medium-high heat until the butter foam subsides. Sear the cutlets in a single layer, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply golden on both sides. Do not crowd the pan — work in batches. Transfer to a plate and loosely tent with foil.

Add remaining butter to the pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer — do not stir for the first 2 minutes, letting them make contact with the hot pan. Once browned on one side, stir and add shallots and garlic. Cook, stirring, until the shallots are soft and the mushrooms are fully golden and have released and reabsorbed their liquid, about 4-5 minutes total. Add thyme.

Pour the Marsala into the hot pan all at once — it will spatter and steam dramatically. Scrape up all the fond from the pan bottom. Add the chicken stock. Bring to a boil and reduce by half over high heat, about 3-4 minutes. The sauce should thicken enough to coat a spoon and turn a deep amber color as the Marsala's sugars concentrate.

Nestle the seared chicken cutlets back into the Marsala sauce. Simmer over low heat for 2-3 minutes to rewarm the chicken and meld the flavors. Off heat, swirl in the remaining butter until the sauce becomes glossy and unified. Scatter fresh parsley. Serve immediately over egg noodles, polenta, or mashed potatoes.

recipes.name: Pollo en Mole Poblano

ingredients.name: Chipotle chiles in adobo (or 2 dried morita chiles)
Dark chocolate (70% cacao minimum), roughly chopped
Stale white bread slice, fried in lard until golden
Ripe roma tomatoes (charred whole under broiler until blackened)
White onion half (charred cut-side down in a dry skillet)
Garlic cloves (charred unpeeled in a dry skillet, then peeled)

steps: Heat a dry comal or heavy skillet over medium heat until it almost smokes. Working one or two at a time, press each dried chile flat against the hot surface with a spatula for 10–15 seconds per side. They will puff slightly, release an intoxicating roasty-chocolate aroma, and turn a shade darker — not black, not soot, just a shade. Transfer each toasted chile immediately to a large bowl and pour boiling water over them. Weight them down with a small plate and soak for 20 minutes until completely softened and pliable.

Drain the soaked chiles, reserving the soaking liquid. In a blender, combine the chiles, fried bread, toasted pumpkin seeds, sesame seeds, charred tomatoes and onion, peeled charred garlic, cinnamon, cloves, cumin, peppercorns and dark chocolate. Add 200 ml of the warm chicken stock. Blitz at high speed for 3 full minutes, scraping down twice, until completely smooth — the paste should have the consistency of thick hummus. For a silkier mole, pass through a medium sieve.

Heat the lard in a deep, wide pot over medium-high heat until shimmering. Carefully pour or spoon the mole paste into the hot fat — it will spatter and spit violently as the moisture hits the oil. Fry the paste, stirring and scraping constantly, for 5–8 minutes. This is the most important step: frying drives off water, deepens the colour from brown to nearly black, concentrates the flavour and marries the fat with the solids into a unified paste that will later emulsify with the stock.

Add the warm chicken stock to the fried mole paste in three additions, whisking thoroughly after each to fully incorporate before adding the next. Season with salt. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered, stirring frequently, for 30 minutes until the sauce reduces slightly and the individual flavours knit into something unified, complex and rounded. Taste: mole should be bitter (chile), sweet (chocolate and dried fruit), earthy (spices), with heat in the back of the throat — adjust with a pinch more salt or a small square of chocolate.

Nestle the raw chicken thighs into the mole sauce, skin-side up. The sauce should come about two-thirds of the way up the chicken. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover loosely with a lid slightly ajar, and cook for 35–40 minutes until the chicken is cooked through and beginning to pull from the bone. Remove the lid and simmer 10 more minutes to caramelize the exposed skin. Taste the sauce one final time and adjust salt. Let the pot rest off the heat for 10 minutes before serving.

recipes.name: Pollo en Mole Negro

ingredients.name: Bone-in chicken pieces (legs, thighs, and drumsticks)
Mole negro paste (Oaxacan or commercial, e.g. Doña Maria)

steps: Pat the chicken pieces completely dry and season all over with salt. Heat the lard or oil in a wide, heavy pot (Dutch oven or cazuela) over medium-high heat until shimmering. Working in batches, sear the chicken skin-side down for 4–5 minutes without moving it until the skin is golden-brown and releases cleanly from the pan. Flip and sear the underside for 2 minutes. Remove and set aside. This browning is not about cooking the chicken through — it is about building Maillard-browned fat and fond in the pot that will marry into the mole.

In the same pot over medium heat, add the mole negro paste directly into the remaining fat. Fry the paste, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, for 3–5 minutes. The paste will sputter and spit at first, then gradually quiet as its moisture evaporates. You are frying out the raw, flat flavour of the paste ingredients and developing a deeper, more complex base. The paste will darken by one shade and smell toasted, smoky, and bittersweet — like dark chocolate and dried chile.

With the fried mole paste over medium heat, add the warm chicken stock one ladle at a time, whisking each addition fully into the paste before adding the next. This gradual incorporation prevents lumping and helps the sauce develop a smooth, velvety body. After all the stock is incorporated, bring the sauce to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered for 15 minutes, stirring frequently to prevent the thick sauce from catching on the bottom. Taste and adjust salt.

Nestle the browned chicken pieces into the mole sauce, turning each piece to coat. The sauce should come three-quarters up the sides of the chicken. Cover with a lid, reduce to the lowest possible simmer, and cook for 1.5 hours, turning the chicken gently every 20 minutes and spooning the sauce over any exposed skin. The low heat is critical — a rolling boil will make the chicken tough and crack the mole sauce. Uncover for the last 15 minutes to thicken the sauce slightly and glaze the chicken.

Transfer the chicken pieces to warm plates or a warm serving platter. Ladle the mole sauce generously over each piece — the chicken should be nearly submerged in sauce. Scatter toasted sesame seeds over the top. Serve immediately with freshly made white rice (which absorbs the mole beautifully), warm corn tortillas for tearing and scooping, and a garnish of finely chopped white onion. Mole negro is meant to be tasted in quantity — do not be restrained with the sauce.

recipes.name: Chicken Piccata

ingredients.name: Boneless skinless chicken breasts (pounded to 1/4 inch)

steps: Butterfly each chicken breast or halve horizontally to create two thin cutlets. Place between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound with a meat mallet or rolling pin to an even 1/4-inch thickness. Season both sides generously with salt and pepper. Dredge in flour, shaking off all excess — a bare, dusty coat is what you want, not a thick crust.

Heat 2 tablespoons butter and all the olive oil in a wide, heavy skillet over medium-high heat until the butter foam subsides and the pan shimmers. Lay cutlets away from you in a single layer. Do not crowd — cook in batches if needed. Sear 3-4 minutes without moving until deep golden. Flip and cook 1-2 more minutes. Transfer to a warm plate and tent loosely.

Pour off excess fat from the pan, leaving the golden fond. Return the pan to medium-high heat. Add the white wine and stock, scraping all the browned bits from the bottom with a wooden spoon. Reduce by half — about 2 minutes of vigorous boiling. The liquid should concentrate and the alcohol smell should have fully cooked off.

Reduce heat to low. Add lemon juice and capers to the reduced sauce base. Return the chicken cutlets to the pan and simmer 1 minute to rewarm. Remove from heat and add the remaining cold butter in pieces, swirling the pan constantly until each piece melts and incorporates. Add parsley. The sauce should look glossy and slightly thickened — opaque, not transparent. Serve immediately.

recipes.name: Austrian Chicken Schnitzel

ingredients.name: Eggs, beaten with a splash of milk
Fine sea salt and white pepper

steps: Butterfly each chicken breast by cutting horizontally almost through and opening it flat. Place between two sheets of plastic wrap. Using a meat mallet or heavy rolling pin, pound outward from the centre in sweeping motions until the cutlet is a uniform 4–5 mm thick — thin enough to be almost translucent when held up to light. Season both sides with salt and white pepper.

Set up the classic crumb station: flour, egg wash (egg beaten with a splash of milk), and fine dry breadcrumbs. Dust each cutlet in flour, shaking off every trace of excess. Dip into the egg wash, lifting and letting it drip for 3 seconds. Lay in breadcrumbs and toss crumbs over the top — then gently press the crumbs on with the flat of your hand. Crucially: do not press hard. The loose crumb is what creates the characteristic souffled, billowing crust.

Heat the clarified butter in a very wide, shallow pan over medium-high heat to 160–170 C (320–340 F). The butter should be deep enough to come halfway up the schnitzel. Lay the cutlet in the butter. Immediately start tilting and spooning the hot butter over the top surface. Cook for 2–3 minutes, then flip — the bottom should be deep golden. Continue basting and cook 2 more minutes. The characteristic Viennese schnitzel will soufflé away from the meat as it fries.

Drain the schnitzel briefly on a paper towel — 10 seconds only, not longer, or the crust will steam and soften. Transfer to a warm plate and serve immediately with a wedge of lemon and a scattering of parsley. The traditional accompaniment is potato salad (Erdäpfelsalat) or simply cucumber salad.

recipes.name: Chicken Shawarma
steps: Combine yogurt, lemon juice, garlic, all spices, olive oil, and salt in a large bowl. Whisk until fully integrated — the turmeric will turn it golden-yellow, the paprika orange, and the cinnamon will deepen it to a warm amber. The yogurt acts as both a tenderizer and a coating that holds the spices against the meat during roasting. Taste: it should be boldly spiced and slightly sharp.

Using a sharp knife, score each chicken thigh with three deep diagonal cuts through the flesh to the bone, about 1 cm deep. This allows the spice marinade to penetrate and dramatically increases surface area for charring. Coat the thighs thoroughly in the marinade, working it into the score cuts. Pack tightly in a container or zip-lock bag, press out air, and refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours — overnight produces noticeably deeper flavor penetration.

Preheat the oven to 230°C (450°F) with a rack in the upper third. Lay the marinated thighs skin-side up on a wire rack set over a foil-lined baking sheet — the rack allows hot air to circulate and the fat to drip away, concentrating the crust. Roast for 25–30 minutes until the internal temperature reads 75°C and the skin is deeply charred and caramelized at the edges. The spice coating should be almost burnt at the highest points.

Rest for 5 minutes. Slice the thighs thinly on the bias, cutting across the grain, collecting the slices into a pile on the board. Drag the blade flat across the cutting board to pick up any charred spice crust that flakes off — these intensely flavored bits are the best part. Serve in flatbread with garlic sauce (toum), pickled vegetables, and fresh parsley.

recipes.name: Chicken Tikka Masala
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Boneless chicken thigh (cut into 4 cm pieces)
Kashmiri red chili powder (deep red, mild)

steps: Whisk the yogurt with half the ginger-garlic paste, one third of the garam masala, two thirds of the Kashmiri chili, and half the salt. Coat the chicken thigh pieces thoroughly, cover, and refrigerate for at least 4 hours — overnight is better. The acid and live cultures in the yogurt tenderize the meat while the chili stains it a deep brick red.

Char the chicken hard and fast under a grill, in a screaming-hot cast-iron pan, or over open flame. You want deep blackened spots while the inside stays just cooked — about 3-4 minutes per side. Do not cook it through to dry; it will finish in the gravy. The scorched marinade is the soul of 'tikka' and brings the smoke.

Heat the ghee and fry the onion until deep golden, 8-10 minutes. Add the remaining ginger-garlic paste and cook off its rawness, 1 minute. Add the remaining Kashmiri chili and the passata with the remaining salt. Bhuna — fry and stir over medium heat — until the tomato darkens, tightens, and the fat splits out at the edges, about 10-12 minutes. This frying, not mere simmering, is what builds depth.

Fold the charred chicken (and any resting juices) into the masala base with enough water to make a coating gravy. Simmer gently 6-8 minutes until the chicken is cooked through and has soaked up the sauce. Stir in the cream and the remaining garam masala, then crush the dried fenugreek leaves between your palms and scatter them in. Simmer 2 more minutes — do not boil hard once the cream is in — and rest off the heat before serving.

recipes.name: Chicken Tortilla Soup

ingredients.name: Chipotle chiles in adobo, minced with their sauce
Black beans, cooked (or canned, rinsed and drained)
Corn kernels, frozen or cut from the cob
Corn tortillas, cut into thin strips
Cilantro, avocado (diced), and crumbled queso fresco

steps: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Toss the tortilla strips with 15 ml of the oil and a pinch of salt, spread them in a single layer on a sheet pan, and bake 10–14 minutes, stirring once halfway, until crisp and golden. They firm up further as they cool. Store at room temperature, uncovered — never in the soup you plan to freeze.

Heat the remaining 30 ml oil in a 5–6 litre Dutch oven over medium heat. Add onion, poblano, and jalapeño with a pinch of salt and cook 7–9 minutes, stirring often, until soft and translucent. Add garlic, cumin, and oregano and stir 45–60 seconds until fragrant, then stir in the chipotle and adobo for 30 seconds.

Add tomatoes with their juices and the stock; bring to a boil. Lower in the whole chicken thighs, reduce to a gentle simmer (small bubbles breaking steadily), cover partially, and cook 20–25 minutes until the thickest thigh reads at least 165°F (74°C). Thighs are most tender around 175–185°F (79–85°C). Transfer chicken to a board.

Shred chicken with two forks into bite-size pieces and return it to the pot with the beans and corn. Simmer 5 minutes to heat through. Off the heat, stir in lime juice and season with salt — usually 1–2 tsp with low-sodium stock. Serve topped with tortilla strips, cilantro, avocado, and queso fresco. To freeze: cool the soup (no lime garnish, no strips) in shallow containers to below 70°F (21°C) within 2 hours and refrigerate, then freeze up to 3 months. Reheat to a simmer and add fresh lime.

recipes.name: Chickpea Spinach Coconut Curry
steps: Heat the oil in a wide, heavy pot over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle 30–45 seconds until a shade darker and fragrant. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and cook 8–10 minutes, stirring often, until soft and light golden at the edges.

Add the garlic, ginger, and green chile and cook 1 minute. Add the coriander, turmeric, and garam masala and stir constantly for 45–60 seconds so the spices fry in the oil without scorching. Splash in a tablespoon of water if they start to stick.

Add the crushed tomatoes and cook 5 minutes until they darken and thicken slightly. Stir in the coconut milk and chickpeas, season with 1 teaspoon salt, and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens and some chickpeas begin to crack. Mash a few against the pot wall to thicken the gravy.
Stir in the spinach a handful at a time; it wilts in 1–2 minutes. Take off the heat, squeeze in the lime, and adjust salt. Serve over basmati rice scattered with cilantro.

recipes.name: Picadillo Filling for Chiles en Nogada

ingredients.name: Ripe tomatoes, peeled, seeded, and diced
Fresh peach or pear, peeled and finely diced

steps: Heat the lard or oil in a large, wide skillet or sauté pan over medium heat. Add the finely diced onion and cook, stirring regularly, for 8 to 10 minutes until completely translucent and beginning to turn golden at the edges. Do not rush this step — the onion must be properly softened to contribute sweetness rather than rawness to the picadillo. In the last 2 minutes, add the minced garlic and stir constantly to prevent it from burning. The garlic should turn pale golden and fragrant — not brown. The mixture should smell sweet and deeply onion-y, with a thread of toasty garlic. If the garlic browns before the onion is soft, reduce the heat. The proper foundation of the picadillo begins here: under-sweated aromatics produce a sharp, harsh filling, while properly softened ones produce a round, sweet base that supports the complexity of the spices and dried fruit.

Add the ground pork to the pan, breaking it up immediately into very small pieces with a wooden spoon or a stiff spatula — the goal is the finest possible mince texture. Add the ground cinnamon, cloves, and black pepper directly onto the pork as it hits the pan. Cook over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking up continuously, for 8 to 10 minutes until the pork is completely cooked through and has developed some color and browning rather than just steaming. Picadillo gets its depth from browning — if the pan is overcrowded or the heat too low, the pork will steam in its own moisture and turn grey and flat. If the pan seems crowded, cook the pork in two batches. The fat rendered from the pork will combine with the lard and the spices to create an aromatic base. When the pork is brown and fragrant, reduce the heat to medium.

Add the diced tomatoes to the pork and stir to combine. Cook over medium heat for 5 minutes until the tomatoes have softened and given up their liquid. Add the diced dried apricots, raisins, and chopped almonds, stirring to distribute evenly throughout the meat mixture. Add the diced fresh peach or pear. Season with salt and the sherry vinegar, stirring well. Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer, stirring occasionally, for 15 to 20 minutes until most of the tomato liquid has evaporated and the mixture is relatively dry — it needs to be dry enough to hold its shape when stuffed into a chile, not wet enough to leak out during plating. The dried fruit will have plumped and become jammy, the fresh fruit will have softened and nearly dissolved into the meat, and the almonds will be just barely tender with a faint crunch. Remove from heat and fold in the fresh parsley. Taste and adjust: the picadillo should be sweet, savory, spiced, and subtly tart all at once — complex enough to be interesting on its own and dramatic enough to hold its own against the walnut cream sauce and the poblano chile.

recipes.name: Argentine Chimichurri
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Wash and thoroughly dry the parsley — wet herbs make a muddy chimichurri. Gather the leaves and tender stems into a tight bundle and chop finely with a sharp knife. Do not use a food processor — the blade bruises the cell walls and turns it into a paste. You want a rough, hand-cut texture.

Peel garlic cloves and mince them very finely by hand. Chimichurri is not cooked, so large garlic pieces will deliver harsh, burning bites. The mince should be almost a paste, but achieved with a knife, not a press.

In a bowl, combine the parsley and garlic. Add red pepper flakes and salt, then pour in the vinegar and olive oil. Stir gently with a fork — do not whisk. The chimichurri should be loose and broken, not emulsified. The oil and vinegar should remain slightly separated.

Cover and let the chimichurri rest at room temperature for at least 30 minutes, or refrigerate for up to a week. The flavors need time to marry — the vinegar softens the garlic's bite, the oil carries the herb flavors, and the pepper flakes bloom. Stir before serving.

recipes.name: Cantonese Garlic-Braised Eggplant
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Chinese or Japanese eggplant, cut into 5 cm batons
Dried chilli flakes and white pepper

steps: Toss eggplant batons with a generous pinch of salt in a colander. Set over the sink for 20 minutes. The eggplant will release significant moisture. Pat completely dry with paper towels before frying — wet eggplant absorbs three times as much oil.

Heat oil in a wok over high heat until smoking. Add eggplant batons in a single layer — do not crowd, fry in batches. Cook without moving for 90 seconds until the contact side is deeply golden. Toss and fry the other sides, 1–2 minutes total. The eggplant should be golden and softened but not falling apart. Remove with a slotted spoon.

Pour off all but a thin film of oil from the wok. Reduce heat to medium. Add garlic, ginger, and chilli flakes. Stir-fry for 30–45 seconds until deeply fragrant and the garlic turns pale gold at the edges. Do not let the garlic go brown — in a quick braise, bitter garlic has no time to mellow.

Add soy sauce, rice wine, and stock to the wok and stir to combine. Return the fried eggplant to the wok. Toss gently to coat. Bring to a simmer and cook 2–3 minutes until the eggplant has absorbed the sauce flavours. Stir the cornstarch slurry and drizzle into the simmering sauce while tossing continuously. Cook 30–60 seconds until the sauce thickens and clings to every piece like a glaze. Serve over white rice.

recipes.name: Hong Shao Rou (Shanghai Red-Braised Pork Belly)

ingredients.name: Pork belly, skin-on, cut into 4cm cubes

steps: Place the pork belly cubes in a pot of cold water. Bring to a boil over high heat. Boil for 5 minutes — you will see grey foam rising. This is myoglobin and impurities. Drain, discard the water, and rinse each cube of pork under cold running water. This step is not optional — it ensures a clear, clean-tasting braising liquid rather than a murky, funky one. Pat the pork dry with paper towels.

Heat the oil in a wok or heavy pot over medium heat. Add the rock sugar and stir until it melts into a golden caramel — about 3 minutes. The caramel should be amber, not dark. Immediately add the pork belly cubes and turn them to coat in the caramel. The skin side should spend the most time in contact with the pan. Cook for 3–4 minutes, turning, until the pork is lightly caramelized and the skin is turning golden.

Add the Shaoxing wine to the pot — it will sizzle and steam dramatically. Add the dark soy, light soy, scallion knots, ginger coins, star anise, cinnamon stick, and enough water to just cover the pork. Bring to a boil, then reduce to the lowest possible simmer. Cover and braise for 1.5 hours, turning the pork every 30 minutes. Remove the lid for the final 20–30 minutes and increase heat to medium-low to reduce the sauce to a glossy, lacquer-like consistency that coats each cube heavily. Remove the whole spices and scallions before serving.

recipes.name: Chinese Steamed Egg Custard

ingredients.name: Spring onion, finely sliced on the bias

steps: Beat the eggs gently with chopsticks using a side-to-side motion — the goal is full integration without incorporating air. Add the warm (not hot) water and soy sauce. The water must be warm, not boiling: hot liquid pre-cooks the proteins and cold water sets them unevenly. Beat gently to combine, then strain through a fine-mesh sieve into the steaming bowl or individual cups. The sieving is non-negotiable — it removes chalazae and bubbles that create pitting and air holes in the finished custard. Skim off any foam from the surface with a spoon and cover tightly with cling film to prevent condensation from dripping onto the surface.

Set up your steamer with boiling water but immediately reduce to the lowest possible simmer before adding the custard. The enemy of smooth custard is aggressive steam. Place the covered bowl in the steamer, then turn the heat down so only a whisper of steam circulates. Steam on low for 12–15 minutes. Do not open the lid more than once to check. The custard is done when it no longer sloshes as one liquid but jiggles as a unified, soft gel. If your stove cannot sustain low enough heat, crack the steamer lid open 1–2 cm to let excess steam escape — this keeps the temperature from climbing too high.

Remove the cling film carefully — the accumulated steam and condensation will roll off. Drizzle the finishing soy sauce and sesame oil across the surface in two or three passes — they will pool into dark, fragrant islands on the pale custard. Scatter the spring onion across the top. Serve immediately in the steaming bowl, scooping portions at the table with a spoon. The custard is best the moment it's made; it begins to weep liquid as it cools.

recipes.name: Chocolate Fondant (Molten Lava Cake)

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing
Plain flour, plus extra for dusting

steps: Melt butter and chocolate together in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water (bain-marie). Do not let the bowl touch the water. Stir gently until fully melted and glossy. Remove from heat and set aside to cool slightly — you want it warm, not hot (around 40 C). Meanwhile, butter and flour six individual dariole moulds or ramekins (100 ml), tapping out excess flour.

In a large bowl, whisk together the whole eggs, egg yolks, and caster sugar vigorously by hand (or with an electric whisk) for 3–4 minutes until the mixture is pale, thick, and falls from the whisk in a wide ribbon that holds its shape on the surface for 2–3 seconds before dissolving. This aeration is what gives the fondant its thin, souffle-like shell.

Pour the warm chocolate-butter base into the egg-sugar ribbon. Fold with a large spatula using wide, deliberate scooping motions from the bottom of the bowl — do not stir. When almost combined, sift over the flour and salt, then fold until just incorporated with no dry streaks visible. The batter should be glossy, fluid, and airy. Divide evenly between the prepared moulds, filling to 1 cm below the rim. Refrigerate for at least 20 minutes (up to 24 hours).

Preheat oven to 200 C (fan 190 C). Place moulds on a baking tray and bake for exactly 10–12 minutes (10 for a very liquid centre, 12 for a fudgey-flowing one). The exterior should be set and pulling away from the mould sides very slightly; the centre should still wobble. Run a knife around the edge, invert onto warmed plates, and wait 5 seconds before lifting the mould. Serve immediately — the centre begins to set within 2 minutes of leaving the oven.

recipes.name: Dark Chocolate Ganache
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Light corn syrup (for gloss and shelf life)

steps: Pour the heavy cream and corn syrup into a small heavy-bottomed saucepan. Set over medium heat and bring to a full simmer — you want small, insistent bubbles breaking across the entire surface, not a rolling boil that would scorch the fat. Watch the edges of the pan: cream scalds quickly once it reaches a gallop. The moment you see a confident simmer with steam rising in a column, remove from heat. The corn syrup dissolves invisibly but is doing important work: it disrupts sugar crystallisation and gives the finished ganache that jewel-like sheen that makes mirror glazes sing. Do not stir once it approaches heat — just watch. Total time on heat: 2–3 minutes.

Place the finely chopped chocolate in a deep, heatproof bowl — a deep bowl concentrates the heat and prevents splashing. Pour the hot cream over the chocolate in one confident pour, making sure all the chocolate is submerged or in contact with the cream. Do not stir yet. Wait 90 seconds, letting the residual heat of the cream melt the chocolate from the outside in. This patience is the secret: if you stir immediately, you introduce cold air before the chocolate has melted, risking a grainy, broken ganache. After 90 seconds, begin stirring with a silicone spatula from the very center of the bowl, making small, tight concentric circles. You will see a glossy, dark emulsion form in the center — keep working outward until the ganache is completely uniform, glossy, and no streaks of cream remain. This should take about 2 minutes of gentle, deliberate stirring.

While the ganache is still warm (but not burning hot — ideally around 40°C / 104°F), drop in the room-temperature butter cubes one at a time, stirring each in completely before adding the next. Room-temperature butter is critical: cold butter will not emulsify smoothly and can make the ganache seize. Add the pinch of flaky sea salt and stir it through — the salt performs two functions: it amplifies the chocolate's fruitiness and balances the sweetness so the ganache tastes complex rather than simply sweet. The finished ganache should be poured immediately if using as a glaze, or left at room temperature for 2 hours until it firms to a spreadable truffle consistency. For chocolate truffles, cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours until scoopable. The ganache keeps at room temperature for 48 hours or refrigerated for two weeks.

recipes.name: Chocolate Lava Cake
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, plus extra for ramekins

steps: Butter four 180ml (6oz) ramekins generously and dust with cocoa powder or flour, tapping out the excess. The butter-cocoa coating must be thorough and even — any bare spot and the cake will stick, ruining the unmolding. Refrigerate the prepared ramekins while you make the batter. Cold ramekins help the outer shell set quickly in the oven, creating the temperature differential that keeps the center liquid.

Combine the butter and chopped chocolate in a heatproof bowl over a pot of barely simmering water (bain-marie). The water should not touch the bottom of the bowl. Stir gently and frequently until the mixture is completely melted and smooth — remove from heat the moment the last solid piece has melted, as continuing to heat will make the chocolate grainy. The finished mixture should be glossy, fluid, and smell deeply of dark chocolate.

In a large bowl, whisk the whole eggs, yolks, powdered sugar, salt, and vanilla vigorously by hand for 2 full minutes until the mixture is pale, thick, and ribbon-like. This step aerates the batter and gives the outer shell its slightly cakey structure — without this whipping, the cake will be more like set ganache throughout rather than having a defined shell. The mixture should lighten in color noticeably.

Pour the cooled chocolate mixture into the egg mixture and fold gently with a spatula until just combined. Sift the flour over the top and fold again with minimal strokes — 8–10 folds maximum. Overmixing develops gluten and toughens the exterior shell. The batter should be smooth, dark, and just barely homogenous — stop the moment no flour streaks remain.

Fill each prepared ramekin three-quarters full. Bake at 220°C (425°F) for exactly 10–12 minutes — the timing is everything. The edges should be set and pulling away from the ramekin walls, but the center should visibly jiggle when the pan is shaken. Run a thin knife around the edge of each cake, place a warm plate on top, and invert in one decisive movement. Wait 10 seconds, then lift the ramekin. Serve immediately — the center will continue to set within 2 minutes.

recipes.name: Chocolate Mousse
steps: Set the chopped chocolate and butter in a bowl over a pan of barely steaming water — the bowl should not touch the water. Stir gently and let them melt together into a single, glossy mass. Pull the bowl off the heat the moment the last shards disappear; chocolate scorches and grain the instant it overheats. Let it cool to just warm to the touch, around 40°C, before anything else goes in.

Whisk the egg yolks, vanilla, and salt together, then whisk them into the warm (not hot) chocolate in one go. The mixture will thicken and pull together into a dense, deeply shiny paste — almost like a soft ganache. Work quickly and confidently; if the chocolate is too hot the yolks will scramble, and if it sits too long it stiffens. You want a base that is supple and pourable, ready to receive air.

In a spotlessly clean, grease-free bowl, whip the egg whites until frothy, then rain in the caster sugar a spoonful at a time as you beat. Continue to a soft, glossy meringue that holds a peak which curls gently at the tip. Stop short of stiff and dry — an over-beaten meringue turns grainy and refuses to fold in smoothly, leaving white specks through the mousse.

Whip the cold cream to soft, droopy peaks — barely past pourable, what the French call 'à la chantilly molle'. It should mound but still flow when the bowl is tilted. Stop early; cream that is whipped stiff makes a heavy, buttery mousse and risks turning grainy when folded.

First whisk a third of the meringue vigorously into the chocolate base to slacken it — this sacrificial third makes the rest fold in without deflating. Then add the remaining meringue and the whipped cream together and fold with a large spatula, cutting down through the center, sweeping along the bowl, and turning over, rotating the bowl as you go. Stop the instant no streaks remain. Spoon into glasses or a serving bowl and chill at least 3 to 4 hours, or overnight, until set but still pillowy.

recipes.name: Choucroute Garnie
steps: In a large, deep pot or Dutch oven over medium heat, cook the lardons for 5 minutes until the fat begins to render and they are lightly golden. Add the sliced onions and continue cooking, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the onions are soft and translucent. They should not colour significantly — keep the heat medium at most.

Add the rinsed and well-squeezed sauerkraut to the pot, nestling the smoked pork knuckle into the center. Scatter the juniper berries and bay leaves over the top. Pour the Riesling over everything — it should come about halfway up the sauerkraut. Bring to a simmer, then cover tightly and cook over very low heat (or in a 150 C / 300 F oven) for 2 hours. The sauerkraut should braise gently, not boil.

Nestle the smoked sausages into the sauerkraut so they are half-submerged. Cover and cook for a further 20–25 minutes at a gentle simmer until the sausages are heated through and have absorbed some of the kraut perfume. To serve, make a bed of sauerkraut on a large warmed platter, tear the pork knuckle meat from the bone in large pieces, and arrange everything — knuckle, sausages, lardons — over the sauerkraut. Serve with boiled potatoes and Dijon mustard.

recipes.name: Churros con Chocolate
steps: Combine water, butter, and salt in a medium heavy-bottomed saucepan over high heat. Bring to a full rolling boil, stirring until the butter is completely melted and incorporated. The entire surface should be turbulent — no butter slicks should float on top. Remove from heat the moment it hits a full boil; a moment of over-boiling evaporates too much water and throws off your flour ratio.

Tip all the flour into the boiling liquid in one go. Switch immediately to a stiff wooden spoon or silicone spatula and stir vigorously, pressing the dough against the sides of the pan. Within 60–90 seconds the mixture will pull away from the sides and form a single cohesive ball. Continue drying the dough over medium heat for another 2 minutes, stirring constantly. This step drives out excess moisture and cooks the starch so the dough can absorb eggs without becoming soupy.

Beat the eggs one at a time into the cooled panade using a hand mixer, stand mixer with a paddle, or strenuous hand-beating with a wooden spoon. After each egg the dough will look broken and slippery — keep beating until it fully absorbs before adding the next. When both eggs are incorporated the dough should be smooth, glossy, and just stiff enough to hold a piped shape. Test by lifting the spoon: the dough should fall in a slow, thick ribbon and hold a V-shape at the tip.

Heat vegetable oil to 175–180°C (350°F) in a deep saucepan or wok — use a thermometer. Pipe 15–20 cm lengths of dough directly into the hot oil using scissors or a knife to snip each rope. Fry in small batches of 3–4 without crowding, turning once with tongs after 2 minutes. Total fry time is 4–5 minutes per batch until deeply golden. The oil temperature will drop when you add dough; adjust heat to maintain 170°C. Drain on a wire rack, not paper — paper traps steam and softens the crust.

Mix the caster sugar and ground cinnamon in a wide, shallow bowl — about 10 parts sugar to 1 part cinnamon. Roll each hot churro through the mixture immediately after draining, turning to coat every ridge. The residual oil acts as a binder; if the sugar slips off, the churro has cooled too much. Work quickly. Arrange on a plate without stacking to preserve the crust.

Whisk the cornstarch into about 50 ml of the cold milk until fully dissolved — no lumps. Pour the remaining milk and sugar into a small saucepan over medium heat and warm until steaming. Add the dissolved cornstarch slurry, whisking constantly. When the mixture begins to steam and thicken, reduce heat to low and add the finely chopped dark chocolate all at once. Stir slowly until the chocolate fully melts and the sauce coats the back of a spoon thickly — this is meant to be far thicker than hot cocoa. It should mound slightly when dropped from a spoon.

recipes.name: Spanish Churros
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Bring water to a rolling boil in a saucepan. Add the salt and oil and let them dissolve in the water, then pull the pan off the heat and tip in all the flour at once. Stir immediately and vigorously with a wooden spoon — the boiling water cooks the starch in the flour (this is a pâte à choux relative), creating a smooth, stiff dough that pulls away from the sides of the pan cleanly. Continue stirring for 1 to 2 minutes until no raw flour remains and the dough forms a single cohesive mass.

Transfer the dough to a large piping bag fitted with a large star nozzle — a 6-point or 8-point star with at least a 1.5 cm opening. Twist the top shut and rest for 5 minutes. The brief rest allows the dough to cool just enough that it will not soften the bag, and gives the gluten a moment to relax so the dough extrudes evenly. Meanwhile, mix the cinnamon and sugar in a shallow tray and set it next to the stove. Heat the frying oil in a deep, wide pot to 180°C (356°F).

Holding the piping bag over the hot oil, pipe 10–15 cm lengths directly into the oil, using scissors or a knife to snip the dough cleanly at the nozzle. Fry in small batches — no more than 4 to 5 at a time — for 2 to 3 minutes per side, turning once, until deep golden-brown on all sides. The ridges from the star nozzle are the churro's crust — they crisp before the dough's interior sets. Lift with a spider or tongs and drain on a rack or paper towel for no more than 30 seconds before coating.

Drop the hot drained churros immediately into the cinnamon-sugar mixture and toss to coat, or roll them quickly in the tray. The residual oil on the surface is the glue — the coating will not adhere well once they cool. Serve within 10 minutes of frying. Churros do not keep well: they begin losing their snap within 20 minutes as steam migrates from the interior to the crust.

recipes.name: Ciabatta
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Water (cool, for the poolish and dough)

steps: The night before, build a poolish: whisk together a third of the flour, an equal weight of the water (so roughly 30% flour at 100% hydration), and a pinch of the yeast — about a fifth of the total. It should be a loose, pancake-thick batter. Cover and leave at cool room temperature for 12 to 16 hours. This long, slow pre-ferment is where the bread's flavor and extensibility are built; rushing it gives a bland, tight loaf.

Add the remaining flour, water, yeast, and the olive oil to the poolish and mix to a shaggy, sticky mass — no real kneading, just enough to hydrate every bit of flour. Cover and rest 20 minutes (an autolyse) so the flour fully absorbs water and the gluten begins to organize on its own. Then sprinkle the salt over the top and squeeze it through the dough with wet hands until evenly distributed. The dough will be very wet and slack; that high hydration is what makes ciabatta's open crumb, so resist adding flour.

Bulk-ferment in an oiled tub for about 2 to 3 hours at warm room temperature, building strength with stretch-and-folds instead of kneading. With a wet hand, grab one side of the dough, stretch it up, and fold it over the center; rotate the tub and repeat on all four sides. Do a full set of four folds every 30 minutes for the first 90 minutes, then leave the dough to rise undisturbed. Each fold tightens the gluten and traps gas; over the session the slack dough transforms into something jiggly, billowy, and full of air.

Generously flour your work surface and a couche or floured towel with the semolina or rice flour. Tip the dough out without punching it down — you want to keep the gas. Dust the top, then with a bench knife cut it into two or three rough rectangles, handling as little as possible. Stretch each gently into a slipper shape, transfer (flour-side down, then flipped at baking) onto the floured couche, and pleat the cloth between loaves. Proof 30 to 45 minutes until puffy and pillowy. Meanwhile heat the oven to 245°C (475°F) with a baking stone or steel and a steam pan.

Flip each loaf flour-side up onto a peel or parchment and slide onto the hot stone, keeping the slipper shape. Pour boiling water into the steam pan (or spritz the oven walls) and shut the door fast. Bake with steam for the first 10 minutes for maximum oven spring and blistering, then vent the steam and bake another 10 to 15 minutes until deeply golden and crackling. The loaves are done at an internal temperature of about 96-99°C (205-210°F). Cool fully on a rack — at least an hour — before tearing; the crumb is still setting inside.

recipes.name: Cider-Braised Pork Shoulder with Apples

ingredients.name: Pork shoulder (butt), boneless, cut into 4 large pieces
Yellow onions, sliced into thick half-moons
Firm, tart apples (such as Granny Smith), cored and cut into eighths

steps: Season the pork all over with salt and pepper — ideally the night before, uncovered in the fridge. Pat dry. Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C). Heat oil in a heavy 6–7 litre Dutch oven over medium-high heat and brown the pork pieces on all sides, 3–4 minutes per side (about 15 minutes total), in two batches. Set aside and pour off all but 2 tbsp fat.

Over medium heat, cook onions and carrots in the pork fat 8–10 minutes until the onions are soft and golden at the edges. Add garlic for 1 minute. Pour in the cider, scraping up all the fond, and boil 3–4 minutes to reduce by about a third.

Add stock, thyme, and bay; return the pork and its juices. The liquid should come about halfway up the meat. Bring to a simmer, cover, and braise in the oven 2 hr 30 min–3 hr, turning the pieces once halfway, until fork-tender (around 200°F / 93°C inside). Add the apple wedges for the final 30 minutes, tucking them into the liquid.

Transfer pork, apples, and carrots to a platter and tent with foil. Remove herb stems and bay. Skim fat from the liquid, then boil it 6–10 minutes until reduced to about 500 ml and lightly syrupy. Whisk in mustard and vinegar, taste for salt, and spoon over the pork. Scatter with parsley. Serve with mashed potatoes or crusty bread. To freeze: pack pork and vegetables fully covered in the sauce, cool, refrigerate within 2 hours, and freeze up to 3 months. Reheat covered at 325°F (165°C) or on the stove until steaming hot throughout.

recipes.name: Cioppino

ingredients.name: Dungeness crab, cracked into sections (or king crab legs)
Firm white fish (halibut or sea bass), 4 cm chunks
Canned whole San Marzano tomatoes, hand-crushed

steps: Heat the olive oil in a very large, wide pot (at least 8 litres — cioppino is generous) over medium heat. Add the diced onion and fennel and cook, stirring regularly, for 10–12 minutes until both are completely soft, translucent, and slightly golden at the edges. The fennel will lose its licorice sharpness and become sweet and yielding. Add the crushed red pepper and cook 1 minute more. The base should smell sweet, savory, and faintly of anise.

Add the minced garlic and dried oregano to the softened vegetables and cook for 2 minutes, stirring, until the garlic is fragrant but not browned. Pour in the white wine — it will hiss and steam dramatically. Scrape up any caramelized fond from the base of the pot. Raise the heat to high and cook the wine vigorously for 4–5 minutes until it has reduced by roughly half and the raw alcohol smell has dissipated, leaving a clean, fruity, slightly acidic aroma.

Add the hand-crushed tomatoes with their juices, the fish stock, bay leaves, and salt. Stir everything together. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a lively simmer (small, frequent bubbles). Cook uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the tomatoes have broken down fully and the broth has deepened in flavor and color. The broth will reduce and concentrate. Taste and adjust salt — this is also your last opportunity to balance the broth before the seafood goes in.

Add the crab sections to the broth first and cover. Cook for 5 minutes. Add the clams, cover, and cook 4 minutes more. When the clams begin to open, add the mussels and shrimp. Cover and cook 3 minutes. Add the fish chunks last — they need only 3 minutes. Gently submerge the fish in the broth, being careful not to break the pieces. When the fish is just opaque throughout and flakes gently at the edge, remove from heat. Discard any clams or mussels that have not opened.

Tear the fresh basil over the surface of the finished cioppino and stir once, very gently, to distribute without breaking up the seafood. Toast the sourdough slices while the cioppino finishes. Ladle into very large, warmed bowls — each bowl should hold a piece of crab, several clams and mussels, shrimp, and a piece of fish. Pour extra broth over generously. The toast goes alongside the bowl, not in it, for dragging through the broth between bites.

recipes.name: Cherry Clafoutis
steps: In a large bowl, whisk eggs and sugar together until pale and slightly thickened. Sift in the flour and whisk until smooth with no lumps. Add milk, vanilla, salt, and melted butter and whisk until the batter is completely uniform — it will be very thin, like crêpe batter. For an extra-silky result, strain through a fine sieve and let the batter rest for 15 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 180 C (350 F). Butter a 10-inch ceramic baking dish generously. Pour a thin layer of batter (about 1/3 of the total) into the dish and bake for 5 minutes until just set — this prevents the cherries sinking to the bottom. Remove from the oven, arrange the cherries in a single layer across the surface, then pour the remaining batter over the top.

Bake at 180 C (350 F) for 35–40 minutes, until the clafoutis has puffed dramatically around the edges, set in the centre with only the faintest wobble, and turned golden-brown on top. It will deflate slightly on cooling — this is normal and correct.

Allow the clafoutis to cool in the dish for at least 10 minutes so it settles and the custard firms slightly. Dust generously with powdered sugar through a fine sieve just before serving. Serve directly from the dish, warm or at room temperature. In the Limousin tradition, the cherry pits are left in during baking to release a faint almond bitterness.

recipes.name: Clams Casino
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: In a skillet over medium heat, cook the diced bacon until the fat has rendered and the edges begin to crisp — about 5 minutes. Do not cook to full crispness; it will finish under the broiler. Add the diced pepper and shallots and cook another 3 minutes until softened. Remove from heat. Stir in the softened butter and red pepper flakes. The mixture will look loose and greasy — correct.

Scrub the clams under cold water to remove grit. Shuck each clam: hold it in a folded towel, insert an oyster or clam knife at the hinge, twist to pop, then slide the knife along the top shell to sever the muscle. Discard the top shell. Sever the bottom adductor muscle to loosen the clam in the shell but leave it resting in the cupped bottom shell. Reserve all the clam liquor that pools in the shell.

Preheat the broiler to high. Arrange the shucked clams on a foil-lined baking sheet; crumple the foil into ridges to keep the shells level. Place a generous teaspoon of the casino stuffing on top of each clam, mounding it slightly. Broil 4–6 inches from the heating element for 4–6 minutes, until the clam edges curl, the liquor bubbles, and the bacon on top is deeply golden and just starting to crisp at the edges. Watch constantly — broilers vary wildly.

recipes.name: Cochinita Pibil

ingredients.name: Bitter orange juice (or equal parts orange and lime)
Habanero chili, seeds removed for moderate heat

steps: Combine the achiote paste, bitter orange juice, garlic, habanero, cumin, oregano, cinnamon, pepper, and salt in a blender. Blitz to a smooth, brick-red recado (marinade paste). The color should be a deep, vivid red-orange from the annatto — nearly the color of brick dust. Taste: it should hit sour first from the citrus, then earthy and faintly bitter from the achiote, with building heat. Add more bitter orange if it tastes flat.

Score the pork shoulder deeply with a knife — 3–4 cm cuts all over the surface, including through any fat cap, to allow the recado to penetrate the muscle. Coat the pork completely with all the achiote recado, working it vigorously into every score mark. Meanwhile, quickly pass the banana leaves over a gas flame or electric burner for 3–5 seconds per side — they will turn from matte to shiny and become pliable. Line a deep roasting dish or Dutch oven with overlapping banana leaves. Place the pork in the center, pour over any remaining marinade, and wrap the leaves up and over the pork to create a sealed parcel. Marinate in the refrigerator overnight (minimum), or 4 hours minimum.

Preheat the oven to 150°C (300°F). Cover the roasting vessel tightly with a lid or heavy-duty foil — no steam should escape. Roast for 4 to 5 hours until the pork is completely tender and pulls apart with no resistance. At the 3-hour mark, carefully open the parcel and check: a fork inserted at the thickest part should slide in with zero resistance. If there is any pushback, rewrap and continue. The internal temperature should reach 93°C (200°F) for complete collagen breakdown.

Open the banana leaf parcel at the table if serving whole, or transfer the pork to a wide board and shred using two forks — pull with the grain in long strokes for large, silky shreds rather than mushy chunks. Pour all the braising liquid over the shredded meat and toss to coat. The fat, collagen-rich liquid will absorb into the shreds and keep them moist. Serve with warm corn tortillas, pickled red onion in habanero brine, and fresh cilantro.

recipes.name: Thai Coconut Ice Cream

ingredients.name: Palm sugar, grated or broken (not refined white)
Condensed coconut milk (or regular sweetened condensed milk)
Pandan leaf, tied in a knot (optional)

steps: Combine the coconut cream, grated palm sugar, fine salt, and the tied pandan leaf in a medium saucepan. Warm over medium-low heat, stirring regularly, until the palm sugar is completely dissolved — about 5 minutes. The palm sugar will dissolve slowly and the liquid will shift from pure white to a warm ivory-amber as the sugar's caramel compounds integrate. Do not rush this over high heat — the coconut cream scorches easily on the bottom of the pan and can develop a cooked, tinny taste. Once the sugar is fully dissolved, taste the base: it should be distinctly sweet, lightly salty, and carry the palm sugar's characteristic mild molasses note underneath the coconut richness. Remove the pandan leaf and remove from heat.

Whisk the egg yolks and condensed milk together in a medium bowl until the mixture is pale yellow and smooth. Now temper the hot coconut base into the yolks: pour a thin, slow stream of the warm coconut base into the yolk mixture, whisking constantly and vigorously. Add the first few tablespoons in a very thin stream — the yolks must gradually equalize in temperature with the hot liquid before you add the bulk. Once you have added about one-third of the hot coconut base, the yolk mixture will be warm and safe to combine quickly — pour in the remainder in a steady stream while continuing to whisk. This technique prevents the yolks from scrambling. Return the combined mixture to the saucepan and cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a silicone spatula in figure-eight strokes, until the mixture thickens slightly and coats the back of the spatula — about 3 to 4 minutes.

Allow the custard base to cool to room temperature, then refrigerate for at least 1 hour until completely cold — ideally overnight. This pre-chilling dramatically reduces the freezing time and improves the final texture. Pour the cold custard into a shallow, freezer-safe container (a metal loaf pan works well). Freeze for 2 hours until the edges are solidly frozen but the center is still soft and slushy. Remove from freezer and beat vigorously with a fork or hand mixer, breaking up the ice crystals and incorporating air throughout. Return to freezer for another 2 hours. Repeat this beat-and-freeze cycle one more time for the smoothest result. For the final freeze, leave undisturbed for at least 2 hours until fully set. The no-churn method is slower than a machine but the beating cycles break down large ice crystals into fine ones — the difference between grainy and creamy.

Scoop the ice cream into small bowls, wafer cones, or — authentically — into a small portion served over steamed sticky rice. Scatter the toasted coconut flakes over the top of the scoop and add the crushed peanuts if using. The contrast of cold, creamy ice cream against warm or room-temperature sticky rice is a classic Thai street combination. Serve immediately — the ice cream will melt quickly in warm environments. The toasted coconut adds crunch and amplifies the coconut flavor, while the peanuts provide a salty, roasted counterpoint to the sweetness. At street stalls, this ice cream is sometimes served with sweet corn, kidney beans, or taro — do not be surprised by these additions, which are traditional.

recipes.name: Coconut Prawn Curry

ingredients.name: Tiger prawns, shell-on and heads on
Lemongrass stalks, outer layers removed, bruised
Palm sugar or soft brown sugar
Fresh red chilies, deseeded and sliced

steps: Heat the coconut oil in a wide wok or pan over medium-high heat. Add the shallots and cook, stirring, for 3 minutes until softened and slightly golden. Add the garlic, galangal slices, and sliced lemongrass. Cook 1 minute. Add the fresh turmeric and chili slices. Stir-fry for another 2 minutes — the kitchen should fill with a sharp, citrusy, spicy fragrance. The aromatics should be softened and fragrant but not browned — you are blooming, not frying.
