Fill each mould three-quarters full with the cold batter — do not overfill or the crust will not form properly. Bake for 12-14 minutes until the edges are deep golden-brown, the centre has puffed slightly, and a toothpick inserted in the centre comes out with just a few moist crumbs. The dramatic colour contrast — dark gold edges, lighter domed centre — is the hallmark of a properly baked financier.

recipes.name: Beer-Battered Fish and Chips
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Thick cod fillets (skin removed), 200 g each
Maris Piper or King Edward potatoes, peeled and cut into 1.5 cm batons
Beef dripping or neutral frying oil (enough to deep fry)

steps: Cut the potatoes into thick, irregular batons — chip shop chips are never perfect rectangles. The variation in thickness gives you a range of textures from pure-crunchy thinner pieces to fluffy-centered thicker ones. Rinse the cut chips in cold water for 5 minutes to remove excess surface starch (which causes sticking and uneven browning), then dry thoroughly with clean kitchen towels — any residual water causes dangerous oil spatter. Heat the frying oil or dripping in a deep, heavy pot to exactly 140 C (285 F). Fry the chips in batches for 5–6 minutes — they will be soft, pale, and just barely beginning to color at the edges. They must not brown at this stage. Lift out with a spider or slotted spoon and drain on a rack. At this stage you have par-cooked chips; they can sit at room temperature for up to 1 hour before the second fry.

In a large cold bowl (chill it in the freezer for 10 minutes), combine the flour, baking powder, and salt. Make a well in the center and pour in the ice-cold beer in one go. Whisk briskly until just combined — the batter should be slightly lumpy, like thick pancake batter. A few visible flour streaks are fine and even desirable; overworking the batter develops gluten, which makes it dense and rubbery rather than light and shattering. The beer provides carbonation (bubbles expand in the hot oil, creating a lacey, open crust) and the alcohol lowers the boiling point of water in the batter, helping it set faster and crisp sooner. If the batter feels too thick to pour in a thin, even coating, add 1–2 tablespoons more ice-cold beer. Keep the batter cold until the moment of frying.

Raise the oil temperature to 190 C (375 F). Pat the cod fillets completely dry — moisture prevents the batter from adhering. Dust each fillet in plain flour, shaking off any excess (this gives the batter a surface to grip). Dip one fillet into the beer batter, letting the excess drip for 2 seconds, then lower it slowly into the hot oil, holding it just beneath the surface for 5 seconds before releasing — this sets a thin exterior crust that prevents the fillet from sinking to the pan bottom and sticking. Fry for 4–5 minutes (for a 200 g fillet) until the batter is a deep, even amber-gold. Do not crowd the pot — fry maximum two fillets at a time or the oil temperature will drop and the batter will absorb oil and go greasy. Remove with a spider and drain on a rack, never on paper towels (which create steam and soften the crust).

While the fish drains, raise the oil to 190 C (375 F) — the same temperature as the fish, but the second fry of the chips is where the magic happens. Fry the par-cooked chips in batches for 3–4 minutes until they are a deep golden brown with a crisp, blistered exterior. The par-frying already cooked the interior fully, so this second fry is entirely about crust formation — you are dehydrating the surface and driving the Maillard reaction. Do not walk away: at 190 C the chips go from golden to burnt within 90 seconds. Remove when deeply golden and drain on a rack.

Salt the chips and fish immediately while they are blistering hot — salt adheres only to a hot, fat-coated surface. Serve the fish draped across a pile of chips on a sheet of the traditional newspaper-substitute greaseproof paper, or on warm plates. Put the malt vinegar on the table and let people apply their own: the correct amount of vinegar to fish and chips is entirely personal and fiercely debated in Britain. Serve with tartar sauce, mushy peas, or both. Eat within 5 minutes — the batter crust is at its maximum crunch for only a brief window before the steam from the fish within softens it from inside.

recipes.name: Flamiche aux Poireaux
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Leeks (white and pale green parts only, sliced 1 cm thick)

steps: In a large bowl, combine flour and salt. Add the cold cubed butter and rub quickly between your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse, pea-sized breadcrumbs — work fast to keep the butter cold. Drizzle in the ice-cold water one tablespoon at a time, mixing with a fork until the dough just comes together without being wet or sticky. Press into a disc, wrap in plastic, and refrigerate for 30 minutes. Roll to a 3 mm circle and line a 24–26 cm tart tin. Prick the base all over with a fork. Refrigerate again for 15 minutes, then blind-bake at 190°C (375°F) lined with parchment and beans for 15 minutes; remove the beans and bake a further 8–10 minutes until the base is pale gold and set.

Wash the sliced leeks thoroughly in cold water and drain well. Melt the butter in a wide pan over low heat. Add the leeks with a pinch of salt and stir to coat. Cook over the lowest possible heat, covered, for 20–25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the leeks are completely soft, sweet, and yielding — they should have no bite whatsoever. Remove the lid and cook for a further 5 minutes to evaporate any remaining moisture. The leeks should look translucent and silky, not watery.

In a bowl, whisk together the cream, eggs, and half the Gruyère until fully combined. Season generously with salt and white pepper. Fold the cooled stewed leeks into the custard mixture until evenly distributed. The mixture should look creamy and cohesive — not separated.

Pour the leek custard into the blind-baked shell. Scatter the remaining Gruyère evenly across the surface. Place on a baking sheet and bake at 180°C (355°F) for 30–35 minutes, until the custard is just set with only a very slight tremor in the center, the surface is golden, and the cheese has formed patches of deep golden-brown.

recipes.name: Flan de Leche
steps: Combine sugar and water in a small, heavy saucepan over medium-high heat. Do not stir — swirl the pan gently if needed. The syrup will bubble, then turn golden. Watch carefully once the colour begins to develop; it darkens rapidly. Remove from heat when it reaches a deep amber (the colour of old whiskey). Immediately pour into the base of a 20 cm round cake pan or 6 individual ramekins. Tilt to coat evenly before the caramel sets.

In a large bowl, whisk eggs and yolks gently — do not beat aggressively, as you want to avoid incorporating air. Whisk in condensed milk, whole milk, vanilla, and salt until smooth. Strain the entire mixture through a fine-mesh sieve to remove any chalazae or egg threads. This is what gives flan its flawlessly smooth surface.

Preheat the oven to 160 C (325 F). Pour the custard gently over the set caramel in the pan. Place the pan in a roasting tin. Pour boiling water into the roasting tin to come halfway up the sides of the flan pan — this is the bain-marie that ensures even, gentle heat. Bake for 50–60 minutes. Start checking at 45 minutes.

Run a thin knife around the edge of the flan to loosen it. Place a deep-lipped serving plate — larger than the pan — over the top. In one confident motion, invert the pan onto the plate. Hold for 10 seconds, then lift the pan. The caramel will flow down the sides and pool on the plate. If the flan doesn't release, return to the refrigerator for 30 minutes and try again.

recipes.name: Mexican Flour Tortillas
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Whisk flour, salt, and baking powder together in a large bowl. Add lard or shortening in small pieces. Using your fingertips or a pastry cutter, work the fat into the flour until it resembles coarse, irregular breadcrumbs with pea-sized fat pockets still visible — like a pie crust. Do not over-work.

Pour the warm water over the flour-fat mixture and stir with a fork until a rough dough forms. Turn out and knead for 2–3 minutes until smooth — flour tortilla dough should be worked less than bread dough. The goal is smooth, not elastic. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 30 minutes.

Divide the dough into 8–10 equal balls. On a lightly floured surface, roll each ball into a thin, roughly round shape about 20–22 cm in diameter. Roll from the center outward in all directions, rotating frequently. The ideal thickness is 1–2 mm — almost translucent. Rest each rolled tortilla under a cloth while you roll the others.

Heat a dry comal, cast-iron skillet, or heavy pan over medium-high to high heat until very hot. Cook each tortilla 45–60 seconds per side. The first side should develop golden-brown blisters. Flip when the surface loses its translucent, raw look and the first blisters appear. Stack finished tortillas in a clean cloth to trap steam and keep pliable.

recipes.name: Ligurian Focaccia
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine flour, salt, yeast, and warm water in a large bowl. Stir with a wooden spoon or dough whisk until no dry flour remains. The dough will be wet and sticky — this is correct. Do not add extra flour.

Drizzle half the olive oil over the dough. Perform a series of stretch-and-folds: wet your hand, grab one side of the dough, stretch it up and fold it over the center. Rotate the bowl 90 degrees and repeat. Do four folds per round, three rounds over 90 minutes (one round every 30 minutes).

Pour a generous pool of olive oil into a half-sheet pan. Transfer the dough into the pan and gently stretch it toward the edges. If it springs back, cover it and wait 15 minutes, then stretch again. Cover with plastic wrap and let it proof until doubled and filling most of the pan.

Drizzle the remaining olive oil over the surface and into any pools. Spread your fingers and press them firmly into the dough, all the way to the pan bottom, creating deep dimples across the entire surface. Scatter flaky salt. The oil will pool in the dimples — this is what makes focaccia focaccia.

Bake at 220 C (425 F) on the lower-middle rack for 22-28 minutes, until deeply golden on top and crisp on the bottom. Remove from the pan immediately to a wire rack to prevent the bottom from steaming.

recipes.name: Freekeh Pilaf with Caramelized Onions
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Large yellow onions, halved and thinly sliced
Toasted pine nuts or slivered almonds
Fine sea salt and black pepper

steps: Heat the fat in a wide, heavy skillet over medium-low heat. Add all the onions with a generous pinch of salt. Stir to coat, then leave mostly undisturbed, stirring every 3–4 minutes. After 10 minutes the onions will have wilted and turned translucent. After 25 minutes they will turn golden. After 40 minutes they will be deeply mahogany-brown, reduced to about a quarter of their original volume, and intensely sweet. This cannot be rushed — increase heat only at the very end if needed for a final deepening.

Add the freekeh to the pan with the caramelized onions (reserve half the onions for garnish). Stir the freekeh through the onions over medium-high heat. Add allspice and cinnamon. Toast, stirring constantly, for 3–4 minutes until the freekeh is warm throughout, smells lightly nutty, and a few grains begin to pop. This step deepens the grain's innate smokiness.

Pour the hot stock over the toasted freekeh. It will hiss and steam. Season with salt and pepper. Bring to a brisk boil, stir once, then reduce to the lowest possible simmer. Cover with a tight-fitting lid and cook for 35–40 minutes for whole freekeh (15–20 minutes for cracked). Do not lift the lid during cooking. After the cooking time, remove from heat and let it steam undisturbed, lid on, for 10 minutes.

Spoon the freekeh onto a large warm platter. Scatter the reserved caramelized onions over the top. Toast the pine nuts in a dry pan over medium heat until golden, then scatter over the onions. Serve immediately alongside labneh, a cucumber-tomato salad, or roasted vegetables. The freekeh holds its heat well and is equally good at room temperature.

recipes.name: French Bouillabaisse

ingredients.name: Mixed firm fish (rascasse, monkfish, conger eel), cut into chunks
Tender fish (red mullet, whiting), whole or halved
Saffron threads, steeped in 100ml warm water
Fresh thyme and bay leaf bouquet garni
Fine sea salt and black pepper

steps: In a large, wide pot (at least 6L), heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add the fennel, onion, and garlic. Sweat for 10 minutes until softened and fragrant. Add the tomatoes, orange peel, and bouquet garni. Cook over medium-high heat for 15 minutes until the tomatoes have broken down and the mixture is thick and fragrant. The oil should be visibly separated and shimmering at the edges.

Pour in the fish stock, saffron water, and pastis. Season generously with salt and pepper. Bring to a vigorous full rolling boil over high heat — the boil must be violent, not gentle. The aggressive boiling is what emulsifies the olive oil into the broth, turning it from a clear stock into the signature opaque, golden-orange broth of bouillabaisse. Boil hard for 20 minutes.

Reduce the boil to a vigorous simmer. Add the firm fish first (monkfish, conger, rascasse) and cook for 5 minutes. Add the tender fish next (mullet, whiting) and cook for 3–4 minutes more. Shellfish, if using, go in last minute. The fish should be just cooked through — opaque and just beginning to flake, not falling apart. Remove the bouquet garni. Do not stir — use a spoon to baste the fish with the broth instead.

Ladle the golden broth into large, warmed bowls. Arrange the fish pieces on top. Float the grilled croutons on the broth and spread each with a generous dollop of rouille. The rouille will dissolve slightly into the hot broth as it's eaten, enriching it further. Serve immediately with extra rouille and croutons on the side.

recipes.name: French Duck Confit
steps: Mix salt, thyme, smashed garlic, cracked pepper, and crumbled bay leaves together on a plate. Rub every surface of the duck legs with this mixture — get under the skin where possible, into every crevice. Lay in a single layer in a non-reactive dish. Cover and refrigerate overnight (12–18 hours, not longer or the cure will penetrate too deep and the meat will taste uniformly salty rather than seasoned at the surface). The cure will draw moisture from the skin and the bottom of the dish will be damp.

Rinse the cured duck legs under cold water and pat them absolutely dry with paper towels. Melt the duck fat in a deep, heavy pot or Dutch oven over low heat until fully liquid. Submerge the duck legs entirely in the fat — they must be covered. Maintain the fat temperature between 80–90°C (175–195°F). This is barely a simmer; occasional bubbles rising from the meat are correct. Cook for 2.5–3 hours until the meat pulls away from the drumstick bone with gentle pressure. Cool in the fat and refrigerate submerged for storage up to 1 month.

Remove the duck legs from the fat, scraping off excess. Place them skin-side down in a cold, dry, heavy skillet — no additional fat is needed; the duck carries more than enough. Turn heat to medium-high and let the skin render and crisp slowly as the pan heats, 8–10 minutes. Do not flip. The skin must go from pale and flabby to burnished mahogany and rigid. Flip for a final 2 minutes to warm the meat through. Serve immediately — the skin softens within minutes.

recipes.name: French Rolled Omelette
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Crack eggs into a bowl. Season with salt and white pepper. Beat with a fork until yolks and whites are fully unified — no streaks — but do not introduce air. The goal is a homogeneous liquid, not a foam.
Set an 8-inch nonstick or well-seasoned carbon-steel pan over medium-high heat. Add butter and swirl constantly. The butter will foam, then the foam will subside. Act before it colors.

Pour in the eggs. Immediately shake the pan with one hand while stirring rapidly with a fork or chopsticks held flat in the other. Pull the pan on and off the heat every few seconds. You are creating tiny, creamy curds, not large scrambled pieces.

Tilt the pan to a 45-degree angle, handle up. Let the omelette slide toward the far edge. Use the fork to fold the near third over the center, then invert the pan onto a warm plate so the omelette lands seam-side down.
Rub a small knob of cold butter across the surface for a glossy sheen. Scatter finely snipped chives along the top.

recipes.name: Provençal Ratatouille

ingredients.name: Red bell pepper, cut into 2cm pieces

steps: Toss the eggplant cubes with 1 teaspoon of salt in a colander. Set over a bowl and let sit for 30 minutes. The salt will draw excess moisture from the eggplant — you will see small beads of liquid form on the surface. After 30 minutes, pat thoroughly dry with paper towels. Dry eggplant roasts; wet eggplant steams. This step is the difference between silky, caramelized eggplant and spongy, pallid cubes.

In a large, heavy oven-safe pot or Dutch oven, heat 40ml of the olive oil over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 8 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the garlic and thyme and cook for 1 minute. Add the red pepper and cook for another 5 minutes until beginning to soften. This aromatic base will season the entire ratatouille from within.

Add the chopped tomatoes to the pot and cook for 5 minutes to break them down. Add the dried eggplant cubes and zucchini. Drizzle with the remaining 40ml of olive oil, season with salt and pepper. Stir gently to combine. The vegetables should be crowded but just fitting. Bring to a simmer, then transfer to a 160°C (320°F) oven, uncovered. Roast for 60–75 minutes, stirring gently once or twice, until all the vegetables are very soft, their edges are beginning to caramelize, and the liquid has reduced to a concentrated, oily sauce.

Remove from the oven and let the ratatouille rest for 10 minutes — it improves significantly as the flavors meld. Tear in the fresh basil and stir gently. Taste for seasoning. Ratatouille is excellent hot, at room temperature, or cold from the refrigerator. It improves the next day as the flavors continue to integrate.

recipes.name: Southern Buttermilk Fried Chicken

ingredients.name: Bone-in chicken pieces (thighs, drumsticks, breasts, wings)
Lard or peanut oil for frying (enough for 4 cm depth in skillet)

steps: Whisk 1 tsp of the salt and a good grinding of black pepper into the buttermilk. Submerge all the chicken pieces in the seasoned buttermilk, pressing them under the surface. Cover tightly and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. The acid in the buttermilk tenderises the surface of the meat and the moisture helps the dredge adhere in a thick, shaggy crust.

Whisk together the flour, cornstarch, paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, cayenne, remaining salt, black pepper, and baking powder in a wide, shallow bowl. The baking powder creates small CO2 bubbles during frying that puff and shatter the crust. Taste a pinch — it should be clearly, aggressively seasoned, because the chicken below is thick and needs the crust to carry the flavour.

Lift a piece of chicken out of the buttermilk, letting the excess drip back — but not shaking it bone-dry, you want a wet surface for the flour to grab. Press it firmly into the seasoned flour, turning and pressing several times so the dredge adheres in thick, uneven clusters. For the most shattering crust, drizzle a teaspoon of the excess buttermilk over the floured piece and press again — those wet spots create ragged, craggy bumps that fry into dramatic shards. Rest on a wire rack for 10 minutes before frying.

Heat the lard in a 12-inch cast-iron skillet to 175°C / 345°F. The fat should be 3–4 cm deep. Lower the chicken pieces in carefully, skin-side down, without crowding — fry in two batches if necessary. Maintain the oil at 160–170°C throughout (it will drop when you add the cold chicken; this is normal). Fry thighs and drumsticks 12–14 minutes per side, breasts 8–10 minutes per side, wings 6–8 minutes per side. Turn once, carefully, when the underside crust is deeply golden and releases freely.

Drain the fried pieces on a wire rack set over a baking sheet. Do not crowd them or stack them — each piece needs air circulation on all sides to stay crisp. Season immediately with a light pinch of fine sea salt while the crust is still glistening from the oil. Rest for at least 5 minutes before serving; the internal temperature will continue to rise and the juices will redistribute. The crust will remain shatteringly crisp on the rack for at least 15 minutes.

recipes.name: Italian Frittata
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Crack eggs into a wide bowl. Add milk or cream, Parmigiano, parsley, salt, and pepper. Whisk briskly for 30–40 seconds until completely uniform — no streaks of white, no unbroken yolk pockets. The batter should be one seamless pale yellow.

Heat olive oil in a 24 cm (10-inch) oven-safe skillet over medium heat. Add vegetables and cook, stirring occasionally, until just tender and any released moisture has evaporated — about 5–8 minutes. The pan should be dry; water in the pan steams the frittata instead of setting it. Season lightly.

Preheat the oven to 190 C (375 F). Pour the egg batter over the vegetables in the pan. Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook undisturbed — do not stir, do not cover — until the edges have set completely and turned matte, and the center still quivers like a barely-held jelly when the pan is gently nudged. This takes 5–7 minutes.

Transfer the skillet to the oven and bake for 8–12 minutes until the center is fully set and the top surface has developed scattered bronze spots. The frittata will puff slightly in the oven and then settle. Let it rest in the pan for 5 minutes before slicing — it continues cooking from residual heat and firms to a clean-cut texture.

recipes.name: Frumenty
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Whole wheat berries, cracked (bulgur or cracked wheat)

steps: Pick over the cracked wheat and rinse it under cold water until the runoff is mostly clear. Cover it generously with cold water — using about half the seething water — and leave it overnight, 8 to 12 hours, in a cool place. Medieval cooks did this to begin the long softening that makes the grain 'burst'; the cold soak hydrates the wheat to its center so it will swell and split rather than staying hard at the heart.

Put the drained wheat in a heavy pot with the rest of the water and the salt. Bring to a boil, then drop to the lowest steady simmer and cook gently, stirring now and again so it does not catch, for 45 to 60 minutes. This is the 'seething' the old recipes demand: cook until the grains split open and shed their starch into the liquid, turning the whole pot thick and glutinous. Top up with a little hot water if it tightens before the wheat is fully burst.

Crumble the saffron threads between your fingers and steep them in a spoonful of the warm milk for a few minutes until it stains a deep orange-gold. Stir this and the rest of the milk into the burst wheat over low heat. Let it barely simmer for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring, so the milk is drawn in and the whole pot turns silky and an even saffron yellow. Keep it well below a hard boil or the milk may catch and split.

Beat the egg yolks loose in a bowl. Off the boil, ladle a little of the hot pottage into the yolks while whisking hard to warm them gently, then pour the warmed yolks back into the pot, stirring constantly. Return it to the gentlest heat and cook, stirring without stop, for 2 to 3 minutes until it visibly thickens — never let it boil, or the yolks will scramble. Stir in the honey and the butter to finish, taste for salt, and serve hot beside venison, mutton, or a poached fish.

recipes.name: Ful Medames

ingredients.name: Dried small fava beans (Egyptian ful — the small brown ones, not the large broad beans)
Garlic cloves (raw, crushed to a paste with salt)
Fresh lemon juice (generous — ful should be bracingly lemony)
Chilli flakes or fresh green chilli, sliced (for serving)
Ripe tomato (diced small) and spring onion (sliced, for serving)

steps: Place the dried fava beans in a large bowl and cover with at least twice their volume of cold water. Allow to soak for a minimum of 8 hours, or overnight. The beans will approximately double in size. Drain and rinse thoroughly before cooking. If using tinned beans, skip this step entirely. The soaking removes oligosaccharides that cause digestive discomfort and reduces the cooking time from 3+ hours to a manageable 1–1.5 hours.

Place the drained soaked beans in a large saucepan. Cover generously with fresh cold water — at least 5cm above the bean level. Do not add salt yet (salt toughens bean skins during cooking). Bring to a boil, skim any grey foam that rises. Reduce to a steady simmer and cook for 1 to 1.5 hours, adding boiling water if the level drops below the beans. The beans are done when one can be smashed completely flat between two fingers with no firm centre remaining. Drain, reserving one cup of the cooking liquid.

In a large pan or heavy skillet, warm the olive oil over medium heat. Add the garlic paste and cumin and cook, stirring, for 60 seconds until fragrant. Add the cooked beans. Using a fork, potato masher, or the back of a ladle, roughly crush about half the beans — you want a mixture of completely mashed beans and intact whole ones. Add the lemon juice and salt. Add splashes of the reserved cooking liquid to loosen to your preferred consistency — some people like it thick as porridge, others spoonable like thick soup. Taste aggressively: it should be bold with lemon and cumin, salty, and earthy.

Ladle the hot ful into individual bowls or onto a large sharing plate. Drizzle heavily with fresh olive oil — don't be shy, this is the Egyptian way. Scatter the diced tomato, sliced spring onion, and chopped parsley directly on top. Add chilli flakes or fresh green chilli for those who want heat. Serve with warm flatbread for scooping. In Alexandria, a fried or hard-boiled egg on top is traditional. Ful is always eaten fresh and hot — it does not reheat well and the texture becomes gluey. Make only what you will eat.

recipes.name: Gado-Gado Peanut Sauce
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Bird's eye chili (2–4 chilies to taste), sliced

steps: If using whole roasted peanuts, pulse in a food processor or blender until you reach a coarse, chunky paste — not smooth peanut butter, but not whole peanuts either. You want irregular pieces from coarse sand to small pebble size. This textured paste will give the finished sauce its characteristic rustic body. If using natural peanut butter, skip this step.

Combine chilies, garlic, shallots, and galangal in a mortar or small blender. Pound or blend to a coarse paste. A mortar is traditional and gives a more fibrous, aromatic paste with better depth; a blender works fine if you are short on time. The paste should be uniformly pulped — no large chunks of garlic or shallot remaining.

Heat 2 tablespoons of neutral oil in a wok or saucepan over medium heat. Add the spice paste and stir-fry for 3–4 minutes until it darkens from pale pink-orange to a deeper rust-red and smells cooked and sweet rather than raw and sharp. Add the palm sugar and stir until melted and incorporated. The paste will begin to caramelise around the edges — this is correct. A properly fried spice base smells fragrant, slightly nutty, and deeply savoury.

Add the peanut paste to the fried spice base and stir to combine — the mixture will be very thick and dry at this point. Pour in coconut milk gradually, stirring constantly to incorporate the peanut and spice paste. Add tamarind paste, kecap manis, and salt. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium-low heat, stirring frequently to prevent the thick sauce from catching on the bottom. Simmer for 5–8 minutes until the sauce is thick enough to coat the back of a spoon heavily and the oil from the peanuts rises to the surface in golden droplets. Taste and adjust: more palm sugar if too sharp, more tamarind if too sweet, salt to lift the whole.

recipes.name: Galbi Marinade
steps: Grate the Asian pear on the coarse side of a box grater, capturing all the juice — those enzymes are the whole point. Grate the garlic and ginger on the fine side. Combine everything in a bowl and whisk until the sugar is fully dissolved. Do not blend this in a machine unless you want a very smooth marinade; the small pear and scallion fragments contribute texture that adheres to the meat and caramelizes on the grill. Taste the raw marinade: it should be strongly sweet, deeply salty, and faintly boozy from the mirin, with the pear's floral fruitiness clearly distinguishable beneath the soy. The sesame oil will sit on top; a quick whisk before pouring over the meat is all it needs. The marinade is intentionally bold — it must penetrate and season flanken-cut ribs that are over a centimeter thick.

Score the flanken-cut short ribs through to the bone at 2 cm intervals to allow the marinade deeper penetration. Place the ribs in a zip-lock bag or a deep tray and pour the marinade over, turning to coat every surface including between the bones. Press out the air and seal. Refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours; overnight (12–14 hours) produces the most tender, deeply flavored result. Do not exceed 24 hours — the pear's proteolytic enzymes will eventually break down the muscle fibers to a mushy, paste-like texture. If time is short, the enzymes in Asian pear are efficient enough that even 1 hour produces a meaningfully tenderized and flavored rib. Before grilling, remove the ribs from the refrigerator 30 minutes early to take the chill off; cold ribs contract when they hit heat.

Prepare a charcoal grill with a hot zone (you should be able to hold your hand 5 cm above the grate for no more than 2 seconds) or heat a cast-iron grill pan over maximum heat until it just begins to smoke. Shake excess marinade from the ribs — too much surface liquid will cause steaming and prevent caramelization. Lay the ribs across the grates in a single layer and do not move them for 2 minutes. The sugar in the marinade will caramelize quickly and create the characteristic dark, lacquered crust. Flip once and cook another 2 minutes. Flanken-cut galbi is thin and cooks through in 4–5 minutes total. Cut into individual rib pieces at the table with scissors — the traditional way to serve. Watch carefully during the last minute; the sugar makes these ribs prone to scorching.

recipes.name: Gambas al Ajillo

ingredients.name: Dried guindilla peppers or red chile

steps: Pour the olive oil into a cazuela, heavy skillet, or cast-iron pan. Set over the highest heat your stove allows. Wait patiently — the oil needs to be genuinely ripping hot, shimmering and almost smoking, before anything else goes in. A thermometer reads around 180 C (356 F). This extreme heat is not optional: it's what causes the prawns to sear rather than steam, and the garlic to perfume rather than burn.

Add the sliced garlic and whole dried chiles to the blazing oil in one confident movement. They will spit and sizzle violently — this is correct. Swirl the pan or use a wooden spoon to keep the garlic in constant motion. The window is narrow: you want the garlic golden at the edges, just slightly translucent at the center, with a nutty fragrance rising from the pan. About 30–45 seconds total.

Season the prawns lightly with salt, then add them to the pan in a single layer. Do not crowd — if your pan is small, work in two batches. The prawns must make contact with the hot oil, not with each other. Let them sear undisturbed for 60–90 seconds until the underside has turned coral-pink and opaque halfway up the flesh. The shells should be starting to char at the edges. Then flip each prawn.

Flip all prawns, then immediately pour in the dry sherry. The pan will roar and steam dramatically. The alcohol will flare briefly if you are on a gas stove — this is fine. Swirl the pan to dissolve the caramelized fond from the bottom and coat the prawns. Cook for 30 seconds more until the prawns are fully pink and the sherry has reduced to a glossy emulsion in the oil.

Off the heat, squeeze the lemon juice directly over the prawns and scatter the chopped parsley. Swirl the pan once more to combine. The acid from the lemon will cut through the richness of the oil and lift the entire dish. Transfer immediately to a warmed cazuela or serve directly from the pan — gambas al ajillo must arrive at the table still sizzling, with the garlicky oil pooled at the bottom for bread.

recipes.name: Garlic Butter Shrimp with Lemony Pea Rice

ingredients.name: Long-grain white rice, rinsed until the water runs mostly clear
Large shrimp (16–20 per lb), peeled and deveined, tails on or off

steps: Melt the butter in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Add the drained rice and stir 1–2 minutes until the grains turn opaque at the edges. Add the stock and 1/2 tsp kosher salt (less if your stock is salted), bring to a boil, then cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes. Without stirring, scatter the frozen peas over the rice, re-cover, and let stand off the heat for 10 minutes. Fold in the lemon zest and fluff with a fork.

While the rice rests, pat the shrimp very dry with paper towels and season with 1/2 tsp kosher salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a 12-inch (30 cm) skillet over high heat until just smoking. Add the shrimp in a single layer (work in two batches if needed) and sear without moving for 60–90 seconds, until pink and lightly browned underneath. Flip and cook 30 seconds more, then transfer to a plate — they will finish in the sauce.

Reduce the heat to medium-low. Add the butter to the skillet and, once it foams, add the sliced garlic and pepper flakes; cook, swirling, 60–90 seconds until the garlic is soft and pale gold. Add 2 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp water and swirl to form a loose sauce. Return the shrimp and any juices and toss for 1 minute until they are opaque throughout (145°F / 63°C at the thickest part).
Stir the parsley into the shrimp and taste the sauce; add more lemon juice or salt as needed. Divide the pea rice among plates and spoon the shrimp and every bit of garlic butter over the top.

recipes.name: Gâteau Basque
steps: Bring the milk to a simmer in a heavy saucepan with the vanilla pod and seeds. Meanwhile, whisk the egg yolks, caster sugar, and cornstarch together until pale and thick. When the milk steams, slowly pour it into the egg mixture while whisking constantly. Return everything to the saucepan over medium heat and whisk continuously until the cream thickens, bubbles, and holds a trail for 2 full minutes.

Pour the hot pastry cream into a flat, wide container. Press a sheet of cling film directly against the surface to prevent a skin from forming. Refrigerate until completely cold and set, at least 1 hour. Before using, beat briefly with a spatula to loosen it to a smooth, pipeable consistency.

Beat the room-temperature butter and caster sugar together in a stand mixer with the paddle attachment (or by hand) until pale, light, and noticeably increased in volume — about 4 minutes on medium speed. The mixture should look almost white and feel airy.

With the mixer running on medium, add the whole eggs one at a time, waiting until each is fully incorporated before the next. If the mixture begins to look curdled, add a spoonful of flour to stabilize it. The result should be a smooth, pale, glossy emulsion.

Sift together the flour, baking powder, and salt directly over the egg-butter mixture. Fold gently with a spatula — cut down through the center, fold up from the bottom, rotate the bowl and repeat. Stop the moment no dry flour is visible. Do not overmix — this is a short, crumbly pastry, not a developed dough.

Wrap both portions of dough in cling film, press into flat discs, and refrigerate for at least 1 hour. This resting period relaxes any gluten, firms the butter, and makes the dough workable without crumbling. Preheat the oven to 180°C (355°F) while the dough chills.

Press the larger dough portion into the base and up the sides of a buttered 22 cm tart tin. Spread the chilled pastry cream evenly over the base, leaving a 1 cm border. Roll or press the smaller dough portion into a disc to cover. Seal and crimp the edges firmly. Brush the top with beaten egg yolk and score a crosshatch pattern with a fork.

Bake at 180°C (355°F) for 35–40 minutes until deeply golden all over, with the crosshatch pattern clearly visible and the pastry sound hollow when tapped on top. Cool in the tin for 15 minutes, then unmold. Serve at room temperature — never hot, never cold.

recipes.name: Gazpacho Andaluz
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Ripe plum tomatoes, cored and roughly chopped
Green bell pepper, seeded and roughly chopped
Extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to finish

steps: Tear the stale bread into rough chunks and place in a small bowl. Pour the sherry vinegar over it, then add enough of the ice-cold water to barely submerge the bread. Press it under the liquid and leave it to soak for 10 minutes. The bread will swell, absorb the vinegar, and soften into a paste. This pre-soak ensures the vinegar is evenly distributed throughout the soup rather than sitting on top, and gives the bread time to hydrate so it emulsifies cleanly into the blended base. Squeeze the soaked bread gently before adding to the blender — you want saturated, not waterlogged.

Combine the chopped tomatoes, cucumber, bell pepper, and garlic in a high-speed blender with the squeezed soaked bread, olive oil, and salt. Blend on high for 90 seconds — the tomatoes will erupt into a frothy, vivid orange-red liquid. Taste and adjust salt. The initial blend will be warm from the motor friction and may look slightly grainy or frothy. This is normal. The key move here is blending the olive oil directly with the vegetables so it emulsifies into the tomato's natural water content — pour it in while the blender is running if your machine allows, which creates a smoother emulsion.

Set a fine-mesh strainer over a large bowl and pour the blended soup through in batches. Use a ladle or flexible spatula to press the solids and extract every drop of liquid — the tomato skins and fiber that remain in the strainer are what would make the final soup grainy. Work the back of the ladle in circular motions against the mesh. Discard the pressed solids. The strained soup will look dramatically cleaner, a deep ruby-orange, and silkier than before straining. Taste again and adjust salt and vinegar.

Cover the bowl tightly and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, preferably 3. The chill is not optional — gazpacho is a fundamentally cold dish and the flavors do not integrate until cold. As it chills, the olive oil emulsion will tighten, the acid will mellow, and the garlic will lose its raw sharpness and become part of the harmonic whole. Before serving, taste again: cold suppresses salt perception, so you will almost certainly need a touch more salt and vinegar at this stage. Serve in chilled bowls with a thread of olive oil, a few drops of extra sherry vinegar, and optional cucumber dice or chopped herbs on top.

recipes.name: Bavarian Brezel
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine flour, salt, yeast, and malt syrup. Add warm water and mix to a shaggy dough, then add softened butter. Knead by hand or stand mixer for 8–10 minutes until the dough is smooth, firm, and slightly tacky. Brezel dough is stiffer than bread dough — the low hydration (58%) creates the chew. Shape into a ball, oil lightly, cover, and let ferment at room temperature for 60 minutes until roughly doubled.

Divide the dough into 8 equal portions (about 90 g each). Working one at a time, roll each portion into a 60 cm rope that is thicker in the center and tapers at the ends. The center should be 2.5 cm thick; the ends, 5 mm. Cross the ends twice to form a twist, then fold the twist down onto the belly of the pretzel. Press the ends firmly to adhere. Place on parchment-lined trays. Chill uncovered in the refrigerator for 30 minutes — cold pretzels hold their shape better through the lye bath.

SAFETY: Wear rubber gloves and eye protection when handling lye solution. Prepare a 3% lye solution (30 g NaOH per liter cold water — add lye to water, never reverse). Dip each chilled pretzel for 30 seconds, turning once, then lift with a slotted spoon and drain briefly. Place on a rack set over a parchment-lined tray. Score each belly with a sharp blade or razor in a single slash, 5 mm deep. Scatter pretzel salt. Alternatively, use baked baking soda: dissolve 60 g baked baking soda in 1 liter water and dip for 1 minute — this produces a softer brown, not the dark mahogany of lye.

Bake in a preheated 220 C (425 F) oven with steam (add a pan of boiling water to the oven floor) for 14–18 minutes until deeply mahogany-brown with glossy, crackled crust. Do not open the oven in the first 8 minutes. The pretzels go from blond to amber to mahogany in a narrow window — watch from 12 minutes onward.

recipes.name: Ghormeh Sabzi
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: This step is the heart of ghormeh sabzi. Heat 8 parts of the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add ALL the herbs — parsley, fenugreek, cilantro, green onion — and fry, stirring constantly, for 20-30 minutes until they have turned very dark green, almost black, are completely dry, and smell nutty and deeply herbal rather than fresh and grassy. They will reduce to a fraction of their original volume. This is not a sauté — it is a long, patient frying that transforms raw herbs into something profound.

In a large, heavy pot, heat the remaining oil over medium-high heat. Add the diced onion and cook until golden-brown, about 10 minutes. Add the lamb pieces and turmeric, season generously with salt and pepper, and brown the lamb on all sides — 5-6 minutes per batch. Do not crowd the pot. The goal is a deep brown crust on the meat, not grey steaming.

Add the fried herb mixture (with all its oil) to the pot with the browned lamb. Add the pierced dried limes and the cooked kidney beans. Pour in enough water to barely cover — about 80 parts. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, reduce to a very low simmer, cover, and cook for 2.5-3 hours. The stew should barely move — a lazy bubble every 5-10 seconds. Check every 45 minutes and add splashes of water if it tightens too much.

Taste the stew carefully. The flavor should be deeply savory, bitter-herbal, and sour — the sourness is the defining characteristic. If it lacks sourness, squeeze a softened dried lime against the side of the pot to release its remaining juice. If it lacks depth, simmer uncovered for 10 minutes to concentrate. Adjust salt. Serve over Persian rice (tahdig if possible), with the dried limes placed on top as a garnish.

recipes.name: Ginger Chicken & Rice Soup

ingredients.name: Scallions, whites and greens separated, greens thinly sliced
Carrots, thinly sliced on the bias
Napa cabbage, cut into 2 cm ribbons
Toasted sesame oil, cilantro, and chili crisp

steps: Put chicken, cold water, ginger, scallion whites, garlic, and salt in a 6 litre pot. Bring slowly to a simmer over medium heat, skimming off the grey foam as it rises. Reduce to a bare simmer (occasional lazy bubbles) and cook 25–30 minutes, until the thighs read at least 165°F (74°C) and the meat is tender. Lift out the chicken to cool; strain out the ginger, scallion, and garlic, or leave the ginger in for more punch.

Bring the broth back to a simmer, add the rice and carrots, and cook 15–18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the rice is soft and just beginning to bloom open. Meanwhile, pull the chicken into bite-size shreds, discarding bones and cartilage.

Add the cabbage and shredded chicken and simmer 3–4 minutes until the cabbage is just tender. Season with fish sauce and white pepper, adding more salt if needed. Serve topped with scallion greens, a few drops of sesame oil, cilantro, and chili crisp. To freeze: the rice keeps drinking broth, so for best results freeze a portion before adding the rice, or thin with water on reheating. Cool in shallow containers, refrigerate within 2 hours, freeze up to 3 months, and reheat to 165°F (74°C).

recipes.name: Ginger-Scallion Pork Noodles with Bok Choy

ingredients.name: Fresh ginger, peeled and finely minced
Wheat noodles, dried (lo mein, ramen-style or thin udon)
Baby bok choy, quartered lengthwise and washed
Rice vinegar or Chinkiang black vinegar

steps: Put the scallions, ginger and salt in a heatproof bowl (metal or thick ceramic, with room to spare — it will bubble up). Heat the oil in a small saucepan over medium-high until it shimmers and reaches about 375°F (190°C), or until a scallion slice dropped in sizzles vigorously at once. Carefully pour the hot oil over the aromatics; stir. Let cool while you cook everything else.

Bring a large pot of unsalted water to a boil. Cook the noodles according to the package, adding the bok choy for the final 1 1/2 minutes. Scoop out 120 ml of the noodle water, then drain and rinse briefly under warm water to wash off surface starch so the noodles don't clump.

While the noodles cook, heat the oil in a 12-inch (30 cm) skillet or wok over medium-high heat. Add the pork, press it into an even layer and cook undisturbed 3–4 minutes until browned underneath, then break it into small crumbles and cook 2–3 minutes more until no pink remains and it reaches 160°F (71°C). Add the soy sauce, oyster sauce, sugar and vinegar and toss 1 minute until the liquid reduces to a glaze.

Add the noodles and bok choy to the skillet with half the ginger-scallion oil and 3–4 tbsp of the reserved noodle water. Toss over medium heat for 1 minute until everything is coated and glossy. Taste and add more soy or vinegar if needed. Divide among bowls and spoon the remaining ginger-scallion oil over the top, with chili crisp if you like.

recipes.name: Gnocchi al Burro e Salvia

ingredients.name: Floury potatoes, such as Russet or King Edward (about 700g before baking)

steps: Bake the unpeeled potatoes at 200°C (400°F) directly on the oven rack until completely tender — a skewer inserted meets no resistance, about 50 to 60 minutes. Baking, not boiling, is critical: boiling adds water to the potato, which forces you to add more flour for structure, and more flour means heavier gnocchi. While still steaming hot, halve the potatoes, scoop the flesh, and pass immediately through a potato ricer or fine-mesh drum sieve onto a clean, lightly floured surface. Spread the riced potato out and let the steam escape for 3 minutes.

Make a well in the centre of the riced potato. Add the egg yolk, salt, and about 100g of the flour. Using a bench scraper or your fingertips, work the flour into the potato with a cutting and folding motion — not kneading. Add more flour a tablespoon at a time only as needed. The dough is ready the moment it just comes together and no longer sticks to your hands. Overworking develops gluten and makes the gnocchi tough — the dough should feel pillowy and barely cohesive, almost impossibly soft.

Divide the dough into 6 portions. On a lightly floured surface, roll each portion into a rope about 1.5cm in diameter — roll from the centre outward with flat palms, applying even pressure. Cut into 2cm pieces with a bench scraper or sharp knife. For the classic ridged gnocchi, roll each piece down the back of a fork with your thumb, creating a slight curl and ridges that grip the sauce. Place on a floured baking sheet in a single layer. Cook within 30 minutes or freeze immediately.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil. Meanwhile, in a wide skillet, melt the butter over medium heat and continue cooking until the milk solids turn golden brown and the butter smells of toasted hazelnuts, about 3 to 4 minutes. Add sage leaves and fry until crisp and translucent, 30 to 45 seconds. Lower the heat to minimum. Drop gnocchi into boiling water in a single batch — they are ready about 30 seconds after they float to the surface. Remove with a spider directly into the brown butter pan, adding a splash of pasta water. Toss gently over medium heat for 30 seconds to coat, then serve immediately with grated Parmesan.

recipes.name: Gnocchi di Patate

ingredients.name: Floury potatoes (Russet or King Edward), unpeeled
Plain flour (all-purpose or 00), plus more for dusting
Unsalted butter and fresh sage leaves, for serving

steps: Preheat the oven to 200 C (400 F). Prick each potato several times with a fork and bake directly on the oven rack for 50–60 minutes until completely tender throughout and the skins have dried and crisped. This is not negotiable: baking the potatoes rather than boiling them keeps them dry. Boiled potatoes absorb water, and water-laden potato requires more flour to bind, making the gnocchi dense and tough. The goal is the driest, fluffiest potato interior possible.

Working as quickly as possible, halve the hot potatoes and scoop or press them through a potato ricer directly onto a large clean work surface or into a wide, shallow bowl — never a food processor, blender, or electric mixer, all of which develop the starch into glue. The potatoes must be riced while scorching hot: the heat drives off steam as they fall, drying them further. Spread the riced potato in a thin layer and let it steam-dry for 3–4 minutes. You should see wisps of steam rising from the pile. The more moisture that escapes now, the less flour you will need.

Make a well in the centre of the warm riced potato. Add the salt, egg yolk, and Parmigiano-Reggiano if using. Add about two-thirds of the flour. Using a bench scraper or your hands, incorporate everything with the lightest possible touch — a cutting and folding motion, never a kneading motion. Add flour in small increments from the remaining third only as needed for the dough to just barely hold together. Less flour is always better: the finished dough should look rough and just barely cohesive, not smooth and elastic. A smooth gnocchi dough has been overworked and will produce dense, chewy dumplings. Stop mixing the moment the dough holds together without crumbling.

Flour your work surface lightly. Divide the dough into 6–8 portions and roll each into a rope about 2 cm in diameter — use a light touch and no pressure. Cut each rope into 2 cm pieces. To shape: hold a fork in one hand, tines facing down. Press a gnocchi piece against the tines with your thumb and roll it down and off the fork in one smooth motion, creating the classic ridged shell. The ridge is not decorative — it dramatically increases the sauce-catching surface area. Alternatively, press lightly with your thumb to create a hollow. Place shaped gnocchi on a floured tray in a single layer without touching.

Bring a large pot of generously salted water to a rolling boil. Cook the gnocchi in batches — never crowd the pot, which drops the temperature and causes them to stick together. Lower them in gently. They will sink, then rise to the surface as they cook. Wait exactly 30 seconds after they rise before removing — that brief additional time sets the interior fully. Fish out with a spider or slotted spoon, letting them drain briefly. Meanwhile, melt the butter in a wide pan with the sage leaves until the butter begins to turn hazelnut-gold (beurre noisette). Toss the gnocchi in the brown butter for 30 seconds until coated and very lightly pan-seared. Serve immediately.

recipes.name: Potato Gnocchi

ingredients.name: Russet or Yukon Gold potatoes (floury variety)

steps: Preheat oven to 200 C (400 F). Scrub potatoes, prick all over with a fork, and place directly on the oven rack (not wrapped in foil — you want moisture to escape). Bake for 55–70 minutes until completely tender through the center when pierced with a skewer and the skin is papery and tight. Do not boil the potatoes — boiling adds water, which demands more flour, which makes heavy gnocchi.

While potatoes are still steaming hot, halve them and scoop the flesh directly through a ricer or food mill onto a clean board or baking sheet. Spread the riced potato in a thin layer and let the steam escape for 3–4 minutes. Do not mash with a masher — it crushes the cells and creates a gluey paste. Cool just until you can handle it, but no more.

Make a well in the riced potato. Add the beaten egg and salt into the well. Scatter the flour over the top. Using a bench scraper or your fingertips, cut and fold the mixture together — do not knead. Work until just combined: a shaggy dough forms and no dry flour remains. The moment you see a cohesive mass, stop. Over-working develops gluten and makes gnocchi tough.

Flour your work surface lightly. Tear off a golf-ball portion of dough and roll it into a rope about 1.5 cm in diameter, applying even pressure from the center outward. Cut the rope into 2 cm pillows with a bench scraper. Optional: roll each piece over a fork or gnocchi board, pressing gently with your thumb to create ridges that hold sauce. Place on a lightly floured baking sheet in a single layer.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a vigorous boil. Cook gnocchi in batches of 20–25 pieces. They are done the moment they bob to the surface and have stayed there for 30 seconds — no longer. Remove with a slotted spoon directly into a waiting skillet of browned butter over medium heat. Toss to coat and finish in the butter for 60 seconds until lightly golden.

recipes.name: Gochujang Glaze
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine all ingredients in a bowl or wide measuring cup. Whisk vigorously for 60-90 seconds until completely uniform — gochujang is thick and dense and does not dissolve easily, so sustained whisking is required. Work from the center outward, breaking up any pockets of paste as you go. The sesame oil will initially resist incorporation but will emulsify into the sauce as you whisk. The finished raw glaze should be smooth, uniform, and a deep brick-red throughout with no visible streaks of gochujang or unmixed paste.

Taste the glaze carefully and assess its four key axes: heat (from the gochujang and its fermented chile depth), sweetness (honey or sugar balancing the chile's aggression), saltiness (soy sauce carrying the savory base), and acid (rice vinegar cutting through the richness). The glaze should feel balanced but not timid — gochujang is an assertive ingredient and the glaze should announce its presence. Adjust incrementally: more gochujang for heat, more honey for sweetness, more soy for salt, more vinegar for brightness. The goal is a sauce where every note is present and none is harsh.

For use as a lacquering glaze (as opposed to a marinade or dipping sauce), pour the balanced glaze into a small saucepan and bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring constantly. Reduce for 3-5 minutes until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon with an even, slightly sticky film. Watch carefully — the sugars in the honey and gochujang will cause it to bubble aggressively and can scorch in seconds if left unattended on high heat. Use the reduced glaze brushed onto proteins or vegetables in the last few minutes of cooking, applying in two coats with a minute between each coat for the deepest lacquer.

recipes.name: Gougères
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Fine salt and pinch of white pepper

steps: Combine the water, butter, salt, and pepper in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Stir as the butter melts, then bring to a full rolling boil. Remove from heat and tip in all the flour in one addition. Stir vigorously with a wooden spoon until the mixture forms a smooth ball that pulls away cleanly from the sides of the pan. Return to medium-low heat and cook, stirring constantly, for 1–2 minutes until the paste dries slightly and a thin film forms on the pan bottom. This drying step is essential.

Beat the eggs lightly together. With the panade still warm, add the beaten egg in four additions, beating vigorously with a wooden spoon or electric mixer between each — the paste will look horrifyingly split and greasy at first; keep beating until it comes back together before adding more. After all eggs are incorporated and the paste is smooth and glossy, stir in three-quarters of the Gruyère and the nutmeg. The dough should fall from the spoon in a slow, heavy V.

Preheat the oven to 200°C (390°F). Line two baking sheets with parchment. Pipe or spoon walnut-sized rounds, about 3 cm in diameter, spacing them 4 cm apart. Wet a finger and smooth any peaks. Sprinkle the reserved Gruyère over the tops. Bake for 22–25 minutes until deep golden-brown and puffed. Do not open the oven in the first 15 minutes — the choux needs uninterrupted heat to set its structure. Gougères are done when they are deeply colored and feel light for their size.

recipes.name: Hungarian Goulash Paste
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Lard or beef tallow (or neutral oil)
Hot Hungarian paprika or smoked paprika

steps: Melt the lard or fat in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan (a cast-iron skillet is ideal) over medium-low heat. Add all the diced onions with a generous pinch of salt. Cook, stirring every 5-7 minutes, for 40-50 minutes total. The onions will go through stages: sweating and turning translucent at 10 minutes, then softening and reducing at 20 minutes, then beginning to caramelize and turn golden at 30 minutes. You want them at deep golden-amber — not dark brown — when the paprika goes in. Do not rush this step; increasing the heat to hurry the process causes bitterness.

Add the minced garlic, diced green bell pepper, and lightly crushed caraway seeds to the caramelized onions. Stir and cook for 3-4 minutes over medium heat until the garlic is fragrant and the bell pepper has softened slightly. The garlic should not brown — keep the heat moderate. Add the tomato paste, stir it into the mixture, and fry it for 2 minutes until it darkens to brick-red and smells caramelized.

CRITICAL STEP: Remove the pan from the heat entirely, or reduce to the absolute lowest setting. Add all the sweet and hot paprika at once. Stir it into the oil and onion mixture vigorously. The residual heat in the pan is enough — paprika burns in seconds if it hits a hot pan directly, turning bitter and irreversible. Stir continuously for 30-45 seconds until the paprika is fully incorporated and the mixture has turned a uniform, vivid brick-red. Return to the lowest possible heat.

Add the beef stock and salt to the paste. Stir to combine — the mixture will loosen into a thick paste-sauce. Simmer on very low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring frequently, until the stock has reduced and the paste has thickened back to a spreadable, jammy consistency that holds a mound on a spoon. Taste and adjust salt. The paste should be intensely savory, sweet, paprika-forward, and complex. Cool completely before storing — it keeps refrigerated for 2 weeks, or frozen for 3 months.

recipes.name: Gratin Dauphinois
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Floury potatoes (Russet or Maris Piper, peeled)
Garlic cloves (1 halved for rubbing, 2 minced)
Unsalted butter (for the dish and dotting)

steps: Peel the potatoes. Using a mandoline set to 2–3mm, slice each potato into uniform thin rounds. Do not rinse the sliced potato — the surface starch is what causes the cream to thicken and bind the gratin as it bakes. Place slices in a bowl as you work. The mandoline setting is not a suggestion: 4mm slices will still be firm in the center when the top is golden; 1mm slices will dissolve entirely.

In a wide saucepan, combine the cream, milk, minced garlic, salt, pepper, and a generous grating of nutmeg. Bring to a bare simmer over medium-low heat, stirring to dissolve the salt. Taste the cream — it should taste slightly overseasoned because the potato will absorb salt significantly. Do not boil. Remove from heat and set aside.

Preheat oven to 160°C (320°F). Rub a baking dish generously with the halved garlic clove, then butter it liberally. Layer potato slices evenly across the bottom, overlapping like scales. Season the layer lightly. Continue layering and seasoning until all the potato is used. Pour the hot cream mixture over the top — it should come about two-thirds up the depth of the potato. Dot with butter.

Bake at 160°C (320°F) for 60–75 minutes. For the first 45 minutes, do not open the oven — the potato is slowly absorbing the cream and the starch is thickening the matrix. At 45 minutes, increase heat to 190°C (375°F) and bake another 15–20 minutes until the top is deeply golden-brown and bubbling at the edges. Test doneness by inserting a thin knife into the center — it should slide through with zero resistance.

Allow the gratin to rest at room temperature for 15–20 minutes before serving. This rest period allows the cream matrix to firm up enough to slice cleanly. Serve in portions using a wide spatula, lifting from the bottom. The gratin reheats beautifully the next day — covered with foil at 160°C for 20 minutes.

recipes.name: Scandinavian Gravlax
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Coarse sea salt (not table salt, not iodised)
Fresh dill, large bunch, roughly torn

steps: Combine the coarse salt, sugar, and cracked white pepper in a small bowl. Stir together until evenly mixed. The ratio of salt to sugar should be 1:1 by weight — this is not negotiable. More salt produces a firmer, saltier cure; more sugar keeps the flesh softer but can make it cloying. Taste a pinch: it should be distinctly salty with a backing sweetness.

Lay a double sheet of cling film on a large tray. Scatter half the curing mixture in the centre in the shape of the fillet. Lay the salmon skin-side down on the cure. Drizzle the aquavit or vodka over the flesh if using. Press the remaining cure firmly onto every centimetre of the flesh side — the belly flaps and the thin tail end will cure faster than the thick centre, so use less cure there. Pile the dill in a thick, fragrant mass covering the entire flesh surface. Wrap the whole package tightly in the cling film, then again in a second layer.

Place the wrapped salmon on a rimmed tray in the refrigerator. Set a heavy weight directly on top — a cast iron pan, heavy books, or a brick. The weight presses the curing liquid back into the flesh rather than letting it pool below. After 24 hours, flip the entire package over. After 48 hours total, the gravlax is ready. The cure can safely stretch to 60 hours for a firmer, saltier result, or be stopped at 36 hours for a more delicate texture.

Scrape off all the dill and cure with the back of a knife and discard. Pat the flesh completely dry with paper towels. Place skin-side down. Using a long, thin, sharp knife (a carving knife or salmon slicer), angle the blade at 45 degrees and slice as thinly as possible — 2–3 mm at most — in long strokes, separating each slice from the skin. Work from the tail to the head. The slices should be almost translucent. Arrange overlapping on a cold plate and serve within 30 minutes of slicing.

recipes.name: Greek Baked Sea Bass (Lavraki Plaki)

ingredients.name: Fine sea salt and freshly ground black pepper

steps: Preheat the oven to 180°C (350°F). In a large roasting dish or oven-safe skillet, layer the potato slices across the bottom. Add the onion rings, tomato slices, and garlic over the top. Season generously with salt and pepper. Pour 60ml of olive oil and the white wine over the vegetables. Add the thyme sprigs. Bake for 25 minutes until the potatoes have begun to soften and the tomatoes are beginning to collapse. The preliminary bake ensures the potatoes are cooked through — they need more time than the fish.

Score the fish 3 times on each side. Season inside and out with salt and pepper. Stuff the cavity with parsley, lemon rounds, and a drizzle of olive oil. Lay the fish on top of the partially cooked vegetable bed. Drizzle the remaining olive oil over the fish. Arrange the remaining lemon rounds on top. Return to the oven for 30–35 minutes until the fish is cooked through. Spoon the pan juices over the fish twice during cooking.

Bring the entire roasting dish to the table — this is the way plaki is served. Scatter fresh parsley over the top. Each person takes a portion of fish and a spoonful of the vegetables and fragrant pan juices beneath. Serve with crusty bread to mop up the juices.

recipes.name: Galaktoboureko
steps: Combine the sugar, water, and lemon peel strip in a saucepan. Heat over medium, stirring only to dissolve the sugar. Once boiling, stop stirring and cook for 8-10 minutes until slightly syrupy. Remove the lemon peel, add the lemon juice, cook 1 minute more. Remove from heat and cool to room temperature. This syrup must be cold when it meets the hot pastry — make it first or at least 1 hour ahead.

Heat the milk in a large, heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium heat until just simmering. Whisk the semolina, sugar, and eggs together thoroughly in a bowl. Slowly pour a ladleful of the hot milk into the egg mixture while whisking constantly (tempering). Pour the tempered egg mixture back into the hot milk, whisking constantly. Cook over medium heat, whisking without stopping, until the mixture thickens dramatically — it should pull away from the sides of the pan and hold a shape when a spoon is drawn through it, about 8-10 minutes. Remove from heat, stir in butter and vanilla. Immediately cover the surface with plastic wrap touching the custard to prevent a skin.

Preheat oven to 180°C (350°F). Butter a 30x20cm baking pan generously. Layer 8-10 sheets of filo in the base, brushing each sheet generously with melted butter before adding the next — including the very first sheet on the pan bottom. Let the edges hang over the sides. Pour the warm custard over the filo base and spread evenly. Fold the overhanging filo edges over the custard. Layer the remaining 8-10 filo sheets on top, again brushing each layer generously with butter. Tuck the edges down into the sides of the pan. Brush the top layer very generously with remaining butter. Score the top layers (not all the way through to the custard) in diamond or square shapes with a sharp knife.

Bake at 180°C for 45-55 minutes until the top is deeply golden and the filo is crisp all over. The custard filling will have puffed slightly and the pastry will be blistered and golden at the scored edges.

This is the defining moment. The pastry must be smoking hot and the syrup must be completely cold. Pour the cold syrup evenly and slowly over the entire surface of the just-from-the-oven galaktoboureko. The pastry will hiss, steam, and splutter — this is correct. Pour along the score marks first, then over the entire surface. Use all the syrup. Allow to rest for at least 45 minutes before cutting — the syrup needs time to penetrate the layers and the custard needs time to set firmly enough to slice.

recipes.name: Gigantes Plaki

ingredients.name: Dried gigantes beans (giant white beans), soaked overnight

steps: Drain the soaked beans and rinse well. Cover with fresh cold water in a large pot by at least 5 cm. Bring to a boil, skim off any white foam that rises in the first 5 minutes. Reduce to a vigorous simmer and cook for 45 to 60 minutes until the beans are tender but still slightly firm at the center — they will finish in the oven. Drain and reserve.

Preheat oven to 180 C (350 F). In a large, wide oven-safe pan or skillet, heat half the olive oil over medium heat. Add onion, garlic, and celery. Cook, stirring, for 12 to 15 minutes until everything is very soft, sweet-smelling, and just beginning to turn golden at the edges. Do not rush this step.

Add the tomato paste to the soffritto and stir for 2 minutes until it darkens from bright red to rust-brown (this is pinçage — it mellows the acidity). Add the crushed tomatoes, sugar, salt, pepper, and water or stock. Stir to combine. Simmer for 10 minutes until slightly thickened.

Gently fold the parboiled beans into the tomato sauce in the pan. Drizzle the remaining olive oil over the top. Transfer to the preheated oven uncovered. Bake for 50 to 60 minutes, turning the beans once at the halfway point, until the sauce is thick and jammy and the top layer of beans has formed a slightly caramelized, darkened crust. Scatter fresh parsley over the top just before serving.

recipes.name: Greek Souvlaki
steps: Whisk together the olive oil, lemon juice, oregano, minced garlic, thyme, salt, and pepper in a bowl. The emulsion won't hold long but that's fine — it just needs to coat. Add the pork cubes and toss thoroughly. Transfer to a zip-lock bag or sealed container. Marinate in the refrigerator for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight (8–12 hours). The lemon juice will begin to denature the surface protein, which creates a better texture for charring. Beyond 24 hours the acid becomes aggressive and the texture suffers.

Thread the pork cubes onto metal skewers (or soaked wooden ones), 5–6 pieces per skewer, leaving a small gap between each cube. Heat the grill or grill pan to its highest setting — you want immediate searing, not slow cooking. Grill for 3–4 minutes per side (12–15 minutes total, turning every 3 minutes through all four faces). The goal is char on the exterior while the interior remains just cooked through and moist. Do not cover the grill — you want direct radiant heat, not the steaming effect of a closed lid.

Serve the skewers immediately with lemon wedges, warmed pita bread, tzatziki, sliced tomato, and red onion. In the Greek street food tradition, the pork can be slid off the skewer directly into the pita. Squeeze lemon generously at the table — the fresh acid is essential to balance the char.

recipes.name: Green Goddess Dressing
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Add the tarragon, parsley, chives, anchovy fillets, garlic, white wine vinegar, and lemon juice to a blender. Blend on high for 30–45 seconds until the herbs are completely pulverized and the mixture is smooth. The blend will be intensely green at this point — almost luminous — and the raw garlic and anchovies will have dissolved completely into the herb puree. Scrape down the sides once if needed.

Add the mayonnaise, sour cream, and salt to the blender with the herb mixture. Blend on high for 20–30 seconds until completely smooth and uniformly colored. The dairy will turn the intense herb green into a lighter, slightly more pastel sage-green. Taste immediately and adjust: more vinegar or lemon juice if it needs brightness, more salt if it tastes flat, more anchovy if the umami backbone is missing. The dressing should be pourable but thick — similar in consistency to a light ranch dressing.

Transfer the dressing to a sealed container and refrigerate for a minimum of 15 minutes before serving — ideally 30 minutes. The cold thickens the mayo-sour cream base slightly and allows the raw garlic to mellow and the fresh herbs to release more of their aromatic oils into the surrounding fat. The color will deepen slightly as it rests. Green Goddess can be refrigerated for up to 3 days; the herb flavors actually develop and intensify on day two.

recipes.name: Som Tam (Green Papaya Salad)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Green (unripe) papaya, peeled and shredded into matchsticks
Thai bird's eye chilies (2-5, adjust to tolerance)
Fish sauce (or soy sauce for vegan)
Dried shrimp (kung haeng) — optional for Isan style
Long beans or green beans, cut into 3cm pieces

steps: In a large clay or stone mortar, add chilies and garlic. Pound with the pestle until broken down into a coarse paste — not smooth, but no large chunks. The breaking of the cells releases volatile compounds that make the salad fragrant and permeating. A wooden salad bowl and spoon cannot replicate this; the mortar is not optional.

Add long beans and cherry tomatoes to the mortar. Use the pestle to bruise them — press and lightly pound the tomatoes until they release juice, and crack the beans open slightly. Then use a large spoon to toss everything together. The mortar technique simultaneously bruises and dresses — the vegetables should crack open, not disintegrate.

In a small bowl, combine lime juice, fish sauce, and palm sugar. Stir until sugar dissolves. Taste — it should be aggressively sour with a savory backbone and a subtle sweetness. This dressing ratio is a starting point; adjust to your preference before adding to the salad. In Thailand, som tam is adjusted to order at the mortar.

Add shredded papaya and dried shrimp to the mortar. Pour dressing over the top. Using both the pestle (lightly) and a large spoon, toss and bruise everything together for 1-2 minutes — simultaneously mixing and pressing to help the papaya absorb the dressing. Taste, adjust, and serve immediately alongside sticky rice.

recipes.name: Sauce Gribiche
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Lower eggs gently into boiling water and cook for exactly 11 minutes. Transfer immediately to an ice bath for 5 minutes — this stops carryover cooking and makes peeling easier. Peel under cold running water. Halve each egg and carefully lift the yolks out whole. Set the whites aside on a cutting board. The yolks should be fully set but still waxy in the center, not chalky or crumbly.

Press the egg yolks through a fine-mesh sieve into a bowl, or mash them very thoroughly with a fork until absolutely no lumps remain — any lump will create a grainy break-point in the emulsion. Add the Dijon mustard and white wine vinegar. Season with salt. Whisk vigorously until the mixture is smooth, thick, and completely homogeneous — it will look like a very stiff, pale-yellow paste.

Working exactly as for a mayonnaise: begin adding the neutral oil in a thin, steady trickle while whisking constantly. The first 30 ml is critical — add it drop by drop to establish the emulsion. Once the mixture turns thick and opaque and the whisk leaves furrow-marks, you can add the remaining oil in a thin, steady stream. Total whisking time is 3–4 minutes. Do not rush the oil addition.

Finely chop the reserved egg whites to a rough 5 mm dice — not a fine mince, you want texture. Using a rubber spatula, fold the chopped egg whites, capers, cornichon rounds, parsley, tarragon, and chervil into the emulsion base. Fold gently with a scooping motion from the bottom of the bowl — you want even distribution without deflating the sauce. Taste and correct: more vinegar if it needs lift, more salt if it tastes flat. Serve at room temperature within an hour of making.

recipes.name: Grilled Asparagus with Lemon and Parmesan

ingredients.name: Thick asparagus spears, woody ends snapped off

steps: Bend each asparagus spear gently near the base — it will snap naturally at the point where woody fibre gives way to tender stalk. Discard the woody ends (or use for stock). Toss the spears in olive oil until each one glistens. Season with salt. The asparagus must be dry before you add oil — any water will steam the grill grate and the spears will steam rather than char.

Place spears perpendicular to the grill grates on a very hot grill or ridged cast-iron grill pan (preheated to screaming hot). Grill without moving for 2–3 minutes until char marks develop, then roll 90 degrees and grill a further 2 minutes. The asparagus should show distinct char at the grill marks and the tips should be frizzled and blistered. Total cook time: 4–6 minutes for thick spears.

Arrange the hot spears on a serving plate. Squeeze lemon juice generously over all of them and zest the lemon directly over the top. Drape shaved parmesan ribbons over the spears while still hot so they soften slightly. Crack fresh black pepper over the top. The acid and salt of the lemon must be applied while the asparagus is still hot enough to absorb it.

recipes.name: Grilled Lamb Chops
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Lamb loin chops (2–3 cm thick, frenched)

steps: Combine the olive oil, smashed garlic, rosemary, thyme, lemon zest, and lemon juice in a shallow dish or zip-lock bag. Add the lamb chops and turn to coat every surface. The olive oil carries the aromatic compounds of the rosemary and garlic into the meat; the lemon juice tenderizes the surface proteins and brightens the finished flavor. Marinate at room temperature for 1–2 hours or refrigerated for up to 8 hours. If refrigerated, bring to room temperature for 30 minutes before grilling — cold meat seizes on contact with heat and cooks unevenly.

Prepare a very hot charcoal or gas grill — you want direct high heat that chars immediately on contact, not medium heat that dries. Wipe the excess marinade and herbs from the chops with paper towels (wet herbs and oil cause flare-ups and bitter char). Season generously with kosher salt on both sides immediately before grilling. Grill the chops 2–3 minutes per side for medium-rare — do not move them during each side. Use tongs to sear the fat cap along the edge for 1 minute. For 2 cm chops, total grill time is 5–7 minutes; for 3 cm, 7–9 minutes. Internal temperature should read 57–60°C / 135–140°F for medium-rare.

Transfer the chops to a rack set over a plate and tent loosely with foil — not sealed tight, which traps steam and softens the crust. Rest for 5 minutes per 2 cm of thickness. During resting, the muscle fibers relax and the juices redistribute from the center outward; cutting too early sends them flooding onto the board. The internal temperature will rise 2–3°C during rest from carryover cooking.

Arrange the chops on warmed plates, leaning against each other or upright so the charred faces and interior color are visible. Spoon the collected resting juices over them — do not waste a drop.
