Scatter torn fresh mint leaves over. Serve with grilled flatbread, tzatziki, or a simple salad of tomato and herbs.

recipes.name: Mediterranean Grilled Octopus
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Whole octopus, cleaned (mantle and beak removed)

steps: Place the cleaned octopus in a pot large enough to hold it comfortably. Add the white wine, bay leaves, celery, garlic, and peppercorns. Cover with cold water — start from cold; this allows the proteins to relax gradually rather than seizing in boiling water. Bring slowly to a simmer over medium heat, then reduce to the lowest possible setting: a barely trembling surface, not a boil. Cover with a tight lid. Cook for 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours depending on size. The collagen in the mantle needs a long, gentle poach to convert to gelatin; a boil will tighten and toughen the flesh irreversibly. Begin checking at 1 hour 30 minutes by piercing the thickest part of a tentacle with a thin knife.

Allow the octopus to cool completely in its poaching liquid. This resting period is not optional — the octopus reabsorbs moisture and the proteins fully relax as the temperature falls. Once at room temperature (about 45 minutes), transfer to a tray and pat the tentacles dry with paper towels. You can refrigerate at this point for up to 24 hours; resting overnight actually improves the texture for grilling, as the surface dries slightly and forms a better crust. If you wish, cut the head from the tentacles and split the tentacle cluster into individual pieces or pairs for easier grilling.

Heat a charcoal grill or gas grill to its absolute maximum, ideally 270 C (520 F) and above — cast-iron grill grates are preferred for maximum heat retention. Brush the octopus pieces generously with olive oil and season with flaky salt. Place on the hottest part of the grill. Do not move them for the first 2 minutes. You will hear aggressive sizzling and some flaring from the fat — this is correct. After 2 minutes, the tentacles in contact with the grill should be charred with defined grill marks; flip and repeat on the second side. Add the lemon halves to the grill cut-side down alongside. Total grill time: 4–6 minutes. You are not cooking the octopus — it is already cooked. You are creating char, crust, and smoke flavor.

Transfer the grilled octopus to a warm platter. Immediately dress while still sizzling-hot: drizzle generously with extra-virgin olive oil, squeeze the grilled lemon halves over everything (grilling concentrates and sweetens the juice), scatter the rinsed capers, and tear or roughly chop the flat-leaf parsley leaves over the top. Give the whole thing a final pinch of flaky salt. Eat at once — the contrast of smoky-charred crust against the tender, briny interior exists only for about 5 minutes before the crust softens.

recipes.name: Grilled Whole Branzino

ingredients.name: Whole branzino (European sea bass), cleaned and scaled, about 500g each
Lemon, half for juice, half sliced thin

steps: Using a sharp knife, make 3 diagonal cuts through the skin and flesh on each side of each fish — angled at 45 degrees toward the head, about 1 cm deep and 4 cm long, evenly spaced from the shoulder to the tail. These scores serve two purposes: they allow heat to penetrate the thickest parts of the fish more evenly, and they give the seasoning and cavity aromatics a path into the flesh. Pat the fish completely dry inside and out with paper towels — a dry fish grills, a wet fish steams.

Season the cavity of each fish generously with salt and a grind of pepper. Stuff each cavity with crushed garlic, thyme sprigs, a rosemary sprig, a few parsley sprigs, and 2–3 thin lemon slices. The herbs and lemon will perfume the fish from the inside as it cooks. Season the exterior — including into the score cuts — with salt, pepper, and a generous drizzle of olive oil. Use your hands to coat the entire outside surface, making sure oil reaches into every score.

Preheat a charcoal grill to high heat, or a gas grill to maximum (you need at least 280°C over the grate). Clean and oil the grate well — a clean, hot, oiled grate is the difference between fish that lifts off beautifully and fish that tears. Lay the fish on the grate at a 45-degree angle to the bars. Do not move the fish for 5–7 minutes. You will know it is ready to flip when the fish releases from the grate without sticking. Flip once using two wide spatulas, and cook the second side for 4–5 minutes.

Transfer the grilled fish to a warm platter and rest for 3 minutes before serving. This brief rest allows the residual heat to finish the very centre of the fish and allows the juices in the cavity to redistribute. Squeeze fresh lemon generously over the top — the acid brightens the smoky richness of the grilled skin. Present the fish whole at the table, and use a wide spatula and fork to fillet it tableside: lift the top fillet along the spine, then remove the backbone to reveal the bottom fillet.

recipes.name: Mediterranean Grilled Whole Fish

ingredients.name: Whole sea bass or sea bream (400–500 g each), scaled and gutted

steps: Pat fish dry inside and out. With a sharp knife, score each side of the fish with 3–4 diagonal cuts, slicing down to the bone. The cuts should be about 2 cm apart. Season the cavity generously with salt and pepper. Fill each cavity with alternating slices of lemon, garlic, and herb sprigs — pack it firmly. Rub the outside of both fish liberally with olive oil, pressing it into the score marks. Season the scored skin with coarse salt and pepper. Let rest at room temperature for 15 minutes before grilling.

Prepare a two-zone grill — one side very hot (direct coals or high flame), one side cooler (indirect). Clean the grate aggressively with a wire brush and oil it with a folded paper towel dipped in oil on tongs. Place fish on the hot zone at a 45-degree angle to the grates. Do not move them for 4–5 minutes. The skin will initially stick and then release on its own when the crust has formed. When the fish releases freely, rotate 90 degrees to create crosshatch marks. After 2 more minutes, flip once. Grill second side for 4–5 minutes. If the fish is browning too fast, move to the cooler zone.

Lift fish to a warm platter. Let rest 2 minutes — the interior temperature will equalize and carry-over cooking will finish the center gently. Squeeze lemon juice over the entire fish, letting it pool in the score marks and run into the cavity. Scatter torn parsley over the top. Serve whole at the table with lemon wedges. To serve: use two large spoons to lift the top fillet along the lateral line, then peel the backbone away to expose the bottom fillet.

recipes.name: Guajillo Enchilada Sauce
steps: Heat a dry comal or cast-iron skillet over medium-high heat until very hot. Working one at a time, press each guajillo and ancho chile flat on the dry surface with a spatula for 10 to 15 seconds per side. Guajillos have thin flesh and toast quickly — watch for the color to shift from flat brick-red to a deeper reddish-brown with a few blistered spots. You are listening as much as watching: a properly toasting chile makes a faint papery crackling sound as the moisture in the flesh volatilizes. The ancho is thicker and more forgiving — 15 seconds per side, until darkened and pliable. The instant you smell a clean, sweet dried-fruit and mild smoke aroma — like dark raisins warming on a stove — remove the chiles from the heat. Transfer immediately to a heatproof bowl and pour over 2.5 cups of very hot (not boiling) water. Weigh the chiles down with a small plate so they are fully submerged. Soak for 20 to 25 minutes. The water will turn a brilliant brick-red. Drain and reserve the soaking liquid.

On the same dry comal over high heat, char the tomato halves cut-side down until the surface is deeply blistered and black — do not move them while they char, 5 to 7 minutes. Flip and char the skin side for 2 to 3 more minutes. The tomatoes will collapse and their juices will caramelize on the pan. Char the onion quarters until their cut faces are deeply blackened, and char the unpeeled garlic cloves until their skins are black and the flesh inside is soft and golden. All this char is intentional — it provides the deep color and complex, rounded flavor that distinguishes a cooked enchilada sauce from a raw one. Remove from heat. Peel the garlic from its charred skins. Transfer everything, including all accumulated juices and any caramelized tomato solids, to the blender.

Combine the drained soaked chiles (use 3 tablespoons of the reserved soaking liquid), charred tomatoes, charred onion and garlic, stock, toasted cumin, dried oregano, vinegar, and salt in a blender. Blend on high for 2 full minutes until completely smooth. The sauce will be very thick and a vivid brick-red-orange. Strain through a medium-mesh sieve into a bowl, pressing with a spoon to extract all liquid. Taste the strained sauce: it should be bright, fruity, moderately spicy, and faintly tannic, with the charred vegetables providing a round, deep undertone. This blended, strained base is ready to fry in oil to deepen its flavor and round out its rawness.

Heat the lard or oil in a wide saucepan or skillet over medium-high heat until nearly smoking. Stand back and pour the blended guajillo sauce into the hot fat all at once — it will spatter aggressively and make a loud, sustained hissing sound as the moisture hits the hot fat. Stir immediately and cook, stirring frequently with a long-handled spoon, for 5 to 8 minutes. During this time the sauce will darken in color, thicken slightly, and the raw, sharp notes will transform into something deeper and more rounded. The fat will begin to separate at the edges — a ring of glossy red-tinted oil appearing at the perimeter of the sauce. This is the moment to stop: the sauce is ready when the fat separates and the aroma has shifted from raw chile to a deeper, more complex roasted smell. The finished sauce is ready to use as an enchilada sauce: dip rolled tortillas briefly in it, pour it over assembled enchiladas, or use it as a braising liquid for chicken or pork.

recipes.name: Gulab Jamun
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Neutral oil or ghee for deep-frying

steps: Combine the sugar and water in a wide saucepan over medium heat. Stir until the sugar dissolves, then stop stirring. Add the crushed cardamom pods. Bring to a boil and simmer for 5 to 7 minutes until the syrup is slightly thickened but still pourable — it should feel lightly sticky on a cold plate but not set. Add the rosewater and saffron off the heat and stir once. The syrup must stay warm (not hot, not cold) when the fried dumplings are added — warm syrup penetrates fastest. Keep it on the lowest heat possible or on a warm burner.

Sift the milk powder, flour, and baking soda together into a bowl. Rub the ghee into the dry ingredients with your fingertips until the mixture resembles very fine breadcrumbs with no visible fat pockets. Add the warm milk a little at a time, mixing gently with a spatula, until the dough just comes together into a soft, pliable mass that does not stick to the bowl. Do not over-knead — work it only until it is smooth. The dough should feel like firm playdough: soft enough to roll without cracking, stiff enough to hold a perfectly smooth ball. Rest for 5 minutes covered.

Divide the dough into equal balls — roll each between your palms with smooth, even pressure until the surface is perfectly crack-free and round. Heat the frying oil in a deep pan to 130°C to 140°C (265–285°F) — this is the critical variable. The low temperature allows the dumplings to cook through slowly before the exterior burns. Add the balls in batches and fry, stirring and turning gently and continuously with a slotted spoon, for 12 to 15 minutes until uniformly deep mahogany-brown all over. They should increase noticeably in size during frying as the baking soda expands. Transfer directly into the warm syrup immediately.

Slide the hot dumplings into the warm syrup while still sizzling. They should be fully submerged — tilt the pan to redistribute if needed. Turn the heat off entirely and cover the pan. Let them soak undisturbed for a minimum of 2 hours at room temperature. During this time the dumplings expand further, the syrup is drawn to the centre by osmosis, and the exterior softens from crackly to yielding and syrup-saturated. Serve warm or at room temperature. They keep in the syrup for 3 days and improve on the second day.

recipes.name: New Orleans Dark Roux
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Pour the oil into a heavy-bottomed cast iron skillet or Dutch oven. Heat over medium to medium-high until the oil is shimmering and a pinch of flour dropped in sizzles immediately and vigorously. The oil must be fully hot before the flour goes in — cold or warm oil causes the flour to absorb the fat unevenly and produces a lumpy roux that never smooths out.

Add the flour all at once to the hot oil and immediately begin whisking in quick, constant strokes covering the entire surface of the pan. Within 30 seconds the mixture will become smooth and uniform. This is your blond roux — the starting point. Continue whisking constantly over medium heat. There is no such thing as 'stirring too much' at this stage. If you stop, the bottom scorches.

Continue whisking constantly over medium to medium-high heat for the next 35–45 minutes. The roux will progress through a color spectrum: blond (5 min) → peanut butter (15 min) → milk chocolate brown (25 min) → dark chocolate (35 min) → near-black bittersweet (45 min). The heat is the enemy here — too high and it scorches before reaching the target color, too low and the process takes over an hour with less flavor development. If at any point you smell anything burnt, immediately slide the pot off the heat and whisk. A burnt roux cannot be salvaged.

Immediately add the Holy Trinity (roughly equal parts diced onion, celery, and bell pepper — typically 2 cups combined for this roux quantity) to the hot dark roux. The vegetables will hiss explosively and release steam that drops the roux temperature, stopping the cooking. Stir vigorously — the roux will seize around the vegetables briefly, then loosen as the vegetables release moisture. Cook the aromatics into the roux for 5–7 minutes until softened. This bloomed roux is the base into which stock is added for gumbo.

recipes.name: Gyoza — Pan-Fried Pork & Cabbage Dumplings
steps: Mince the napa cabbage very finely — each piece no larger than a sesame seed. Toss with the full measure of salt in a large bowl and massage it briefly. Let stand 10 minutes. The salt will pull an astonishing volume of water from the cabbage — you want to remove it, not cook with it. After 10 minutes, gather the cabbage in a clean cloth or your fist and squeeze with real force, twisting until almost no liquid drips. Do not skip this step. Wet cabbage will steam the dumpling from the inside during frying, preventing the bottom from crisping and causing the filling to become watery and loose. The squeezed cabbage should feel almost dry, reduced to roughly one-third its original volume.

Combine the squeezed cabbage with the ground pork, garlic paste, grated ginger, garlic chives, soy sauce, sesame oil, and white pepper in a large bowl. Mix using your hand (not a spoon) in one direction only — always clockwise or always counter-clockwise. This directional mixing aligns the proteins and builds a light binding structure that helps the filling stay cohesive when bitten. Mix for 90 seconds until the filling feels slightly sticky and holds its shape when pinched. Do not overwork or the pork fat will break and the filling will be greasy. Taste the raw filling — Japanese cooks taste it raw to calibrate seasoning. It should taste assertively seasoned, because the wrapper will dilute the flavors. Adjust soy sauce if needed.

Work with one wrapper at a time, keeping the others under a damp cloth. Place a wrapper on your non-dominant palm. Spoon 10–12 g of filling (roughly a leveled teaspoon) into the center — do not overfill. Dip your finger in water and wet the entire rim of the wrapper. Fold the wrapper in half to form a half-moon, pinching the center point closed with thumb and forefinger. Now pleat only the front side: starting from the center, push the front skin into three or four small folds toward the right, then repeat to the left. The back skin should remain smooth — this asymmetry is what creates the characteristic crescent and ensures the gyoza stands upright. Press each pleat firmly against the smooth back to seal. Place sealed side down on a parchment-lined tray. The base should be flat enough to sit without wobbling.

Heat a flat-bottomed non-stick or carbon-steel skillet over medium-high until a drop of water skips and evaporates instantly. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat. Working quickly, arrange the gyoza flat-side down in tight concentric rows or a single layer — they can touch. Fry undisturbed for 90 seconds until the bottoms are pale golden. Now pour in the water all at once: it will scream and steam violently. Immediately cover with a tight-fitting lid. The steam will cook the tops and fill the interior. Steam-fry 5–6 minutes until the water has entirely evaporated — you will hear the sizzle change from a wet hiss to a dry crackle. Remove the lid and fry 1–2 more minutes until the bottoms are deep amber and the skin pulls slightly away from the pan. Drizzle a few drops of sesame oil around the edge if desired. Invert onto a plate in one motion so the golden bases face up.

recipes.name: Halloumi Grain Bowls

ingredients.name: Halloumi (vegetarian rennet), cut into 1 cm slabs

steps: Bring the water to a boil with 2 teaspoons salt. Add the farro and boil like pasta for 20–25 minutes until tender but chewy. Drain well and spread on a tray for 5 minutes to steam off and cool slightly.
In a jar, combine 45 ml of the olive oil with the lemon juice, honey, garlic, oregano, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and plenty of pepper. Seal and shake hard for 15 seconds.
Toss the warm farro with two-thirds of the dressing and let it sit 5 minutes to absorb. Add the cucumber, tomatoes, red onion, olives, and herbs and toss again. Taste and adjust salt.

Pat the halloumi slabs very dry. Heat the remaining 15 ml olive oil in a nonstick skillet over medium-high heat. Add the halloumi in a single layer and cook 2–3 minutes per side, without moving, until deep golden. Serve within a few minutes — halloumi toughens as it cools.
Divide the farro salad among four bowls, top each with hot halloumi, and spoon over the remaining dressing.

recipes.name: Haricots Verts Amandine

ingredients.name: Haricots verts (French green beans), stem ends trimmed

steps: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Season it with salt until it tastes like mild sea water — about 15 g salt per litre. Drop the haricots verts in and cook uncovered for exactly 2–3 minutes: the goal is crisp-tender, never soft. Have a large bowl of ice water ready. Drain the beans and immediately plunge them into the ice bath.

In a wide sauté pan over medium heat, melt the butter and add the slivered almonds simultaneously. Swirl the pan frequently. The butter will foam, then the foam will subside as water evaporates. Watch carefully — the milk solids will begin to color to a toasty brown while the almonds toast alongside them. The moment the butter smells of hazelnuts and the almonds are golden, remove from heat.

Add the drained and thoroughly dried beans to the pan with the beurre noisette and almonds. Toss over medium-low heat for 1 minute until the beans are coated and reheated. Squeeze the lemon juice directly over the pan and toss once more. Season with white pepper and taste for salt. Serve immediately on a warmed plate.

recipes.name: Harira

ingredients.name: Ripe tomatoes, grated or canned crushed
Fresh coriander, chopped (stems and leaves separated)
Preserved lemon rind, white pith removed, minced
Cold water (for tedouira, whisked with flour)

steps: Set a large, heavy pot (at least 5 liters) over medium-high heat and add the olive oil. When the oil shimmers, add the lamb cubes in a single layer — do not crowd or the meat will steam rather than sear. Brown on two or three sides, about 3 minutes per side, developing a deep mahogany crust. Remove the browned lamb to a plate. In the same pot, reduce heat to medium and add the diced onion with a pinch of salt. Cook, scraping up the fond, for 5–7 minutes until the onion is soft and translucent. Add the coriander stems (reserve the leaves), cinnamon, ginger, turmeric, and black pepper directly to the onion. Stir and fry the spices for 60–90 seconds until they smell intensely fragrant and have dried out any remaining onion moisture. Return the seared lamb to the pot and stir to coat.

Pour the grated or crushed tomatoes over the spiced lamb and stir to combine, scraping up any fond from the base of the pot. Add the rinsed lentils and pour in the water or lamb stock. Bring to a vigorous boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady, gentle simmer — lid slightly ajar. Skim any grey foam that rises in the first ten minutes; this is coagulated blood protein from the lamb and you want it off the surface for a clean broth. Simmer for 45–50 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lentils have completely softened and begun to dissolve into the broth and the lamb is fully tender and yielding. The soup should have reduced and thickened slightly from the lentil starch.

In a small bowl, whisk the all-purpose flour with the cold water until completely smooth and lump-free — this is the tedouira, harira's traditional thickener and one of the things that makes it distinctly Moroccan rather than a generic lentil soup. Cold water is essential; hot water begins cooking the starch and creates lumps. Whisk vigorously, starting from the center and working outward, and tip the bowl to check the corners where dry flour hides. Let it stand 2 minutes, then whisk again — any remaining lumps will show up. A clean, perfectly smooth milky-white slurry is what you're after.

Add the chickpeas to the simmering soup and stir to incorporate. While the soup is at a steady simmer (not boiling), pour in the tedouira in a slow, steady stream while stirring constantly with a long spoon in wide circles. Pour slowly and stir continuously — this is the motion that prevents lumps. The soup will thicken noticeably within 2–3 minutes as the flour starch cooks out. Keep it at a gentle simmer for 5 more minutes to cook the flour completely; raw flour will make the soup taste starchy rather than silky. In the final minute, stir in the minced preserved lemon rind, chopped coriander leaves, and flat-leaf parsley. Taste and adjust salt. Serve immediately in deep bowls — harira waits for no one.

recipes.name: Sheet-Pan Harissa Chicken with Chickpeas and Cauliflower

ingredients.name: Chickpeas, canned, drained, rinsed and patted dry
Red onion, cut into 2 cm wedges
Fresh cilantro or parsley, roughly chopped

steps: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a rack in the upper-middle position. In a large bowl, stir together the harissa, 1 tbsp of the olive oil, the honey, garlic, cumin and 3/4 tsp kosher salt. Pat the chicken dry, add it to the bowl and turn to coat thoroughly. Let stand while you prepare the vegetables (10–15 minutes), or refrigerate up to 8 hours.
On a large rimmed sheet pan, toss the dried chickpeas, cauliflower and onion with the remaining 2 tbsp olive oil and 1/2 tsp kosher salt. Spread into an even layer.

Nestle the chicken thighs, smooth side up, among the vegetables, scraping any remaining marinade over them. Roast 22–28 minutes, stirring the vegetables around the chicken once halfway, until the chicken is charred in spots and registers 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part and the cauliflower is tender and browned.

Stir the yogurt with the lemon zest, 1 tbsp lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Squeeze the rest of the lemon over the hot pan and toss the vegetables in the spiced drippings. Scatter with the herbs and serve with the lemon yogurt spooned over or alongside.

recipes.name: Herb-Roasted Leg of Lamb
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Bone-in leg of lamb (2–2.5 kg, trimmed of excess fat)
Garlic cloves, peeled and cut into thin slivers
Dry white wine or water (for roasting pan)
Anchovy fillets in oil (optional, flavor deepener)

steps: Remove the lamb from the refrigerator 1 hour before roasting — a cold leg at the center will cook unevenly, leaving the outer layers overcooked while the center struggles to reach temperature. Using a narrow paring knife, cut 20–25 deep slits all over the leg, 3–4 cm deep, through the fat cap and into the muscle. Push a garlic sliver (and optionally half an anchovy fillet) deep into each slit so it is flush with the surface. Season the entire exterior aggressively with kosher salt and black pepper — a bone-in leg of lamb this size needs more seasoning than you expect, as only the outer layer is accessible to the salt.

Combine the Dijon mustard, rosemary, thyme, olive oil, lemon zest, and a pinch of salt in a bowl. Using a spatula or your hands, coat the entire surface of the lamb leg with this paste — it should be 2–3 mm thick and cover every surface except the cut end of the bone. The mustard acts as both flavor and adhesive, holding the herbs against the surface during roasting and forming the crust. Press the herbs firmly into the paste so they are embedded rather than loose on top.

Preheat the oven to 220°C / 425°F. Place the lamb on a rack in a roasting pan with the wine in the base of the pan. Start at high heat for 20 minutes to brown and set the crust. Reduce to 170°C / 340°F and continue roasting until an instant-read thermometer at the thickest part (not touching bone) reads 57°C / 135°F for medium-rare or 63°C / 145°F for medium, approximately 1 hour 20 minutes to 1 hour 45 minutes for a 2 kg leg. The thickest muscle at the hip end is the reference — the shank will be more cooked, which is fine. Baste with pan juices every 30 minutes. If the crust darkens too fast, tent with foil.

Rest the lamb uncovered on a cutting board for at least 20 minutes — a full 30 for a 2 kg leg. The internal temperature will rise 3–5°C during rest. During this time, deglaze the roasting pan with the remaining wine, scraping up all the golden fond and drippings to make a simple pan jus. To carve: hold the shank bone upright with a towel, run the knife along the bone to free the meat, then carve across the grain in 8–10 mm slices. The slices near the hip will be medium-rare; those near the shank will be more cooked, giving guests options.

recipes.name: Hokkaido Milk Bread
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Whisk the bread flour (6%) into the milk (30%) in a small saucepan. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a silicone spatula, until the mixture thickens to a paste and reaches 65 C (149 F) — about 3–4 minutes. You will see it transform from cloudy liquid to a thick, smooth, glossy paste that pulls away from the pan sides. Remove from heat, cover surface with cling film to prevent a skin, and cool to room temperature.

In a stand mixer bowl, combine flour, warmed milk, cream, sugar, salt, yeast, egg, and the cooled tangzhong. Mix on low with the dough hook for 3 minutes until a shaggy dough forms and no dry flour remains.

Increase mixer to medium. Knead 5 minutes until the dough is smooth. Add softened butter a tablespoon at a time, waiting for each piece to fully incorporate before adding the next. After all butter is in, continue kneading on medium-high for 8–10 minutes until the dough is extremely smooth, elastic, and passes a clean windowpane — a small piece stretched paper-thin between your fingers should be translucent without tearing.

Place dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise at 28 C (82 F) until doubled, about 1–1.5 hours. Enriched doughs rise slower than lean doughs — the fat and sugar both retard the yeast. Don't rush with excess heat, which can melt the butter and compromise the texture.

Divide dough into 3 equal portions. Roll each flat, fold in thirds like a letter, then roll up tightly into a log. Place the three logs side by side in a buttered 23x13 cm Pullman loaf tin (or standard loaf tin). Cover and final-proof until the dough crests 2 cm above the tin rim, about 45–60 minutes. Brush gently with egg wash (1 egg + 1 tbsp milk). Bake at 175 C (350 F) for 30–35 minutes until deeply golden and internal temperature reaches 93 C.

recipes.name: Hollandaise
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Water (or a splash of white-wine vinegar reduction)

steps: Set a heatproof bowl over a pan of barely simmering water — the bowl must not touch the water, and the water must steam, not boil. Add the yolks and the water (or vinegar reduction). Whisk constantly and vigorously, lifting the bowl off the heat every few seconds to control the temperature, until the yolks triple in volume and thicken to a pale, airy sabayon that holds a ribbon. This is the make-or-break stage: too much heat scrambles the yolks into sweet curds; too little and they never thicken enough to carry the butter.

Off the heat (or with the bowl resting on a damp towel for stability), begin adding the warm clarified butter in a thin, steady stream while whisking without pause. Start drop by drop until the emulsion takes and visibly thickens, then increase to a slow trickle. The butter must be warm, not hot — around 40-50 C / 105-120 F — and the sabayon warm too, so the fat stays fluid and droplets disperse evenly. Add butter faster than the yolks can absorb it, or let either component get cold, and the emulsion breaks into an oily, separated mess.

Whisk in the lemon juice a few drops at a time, tasting as you go — it brightens the sauce and loosens it slightly. Season with salt and a small pinch of cayenne. The lemon should lift and balance the richness without making the sauce taste sour; the cayenne is a background warmth you sense more than taste.

Hollandaise is a live, fragile emulsion that cannot be reheated. Hold it warm — not hot — in its bowl set over (not in) warm water around 50-60 C / 120-140 F, or in a warm spot near the stove, whisking occasionally. Use within an hour or two. Above roughly 65 C / 150 F the yolks scramble and the sauce breaks; let it go cold and the butter sets and separates.

recipes.name: Medovik Honey Cake
steps: In a bain-marie (heatproof bowl over simmering water), combine honey, sugar, and butter. Stir until melted and combined. Remove from heat briefly and whisk in the eggs quickly. Return to the bain-marie and whisk in the bicarbonate of soda — the mixture will foam dramatically and roughly triple in volume, turning pale and airy. Continue stirring over the heat for 5-7 minutes until the mixture deepens in colour to a rich amber.

Fold the flour into the warm honey mixture in two additions, stirring until a soft, sticky dough forms. Turn out onto a lightly floured surface. The dough will be warm and pliable. Divide into 8-10 equal balls, wrap in cling film, and rest for 20 minutes. The dough firms as it cools and becomes much easier to work with.

Roll each dough ball to a very thin circle (2 mm) directly on parchment paper — trace a 20 cm plate and trim to get precise rounds. Bake on the parchment at 180 C (350 F) for 5-7 minutes per layer. They bake very quickly — watch closely. The layers are done when they are uniformly golden and just firm to the touch. Cool completely on a rack.

Whisk the cold sour cream with the icing sugar and vanilla until just combined and slightly thickened. Do not overwhip — the frosting should be thick but still spreadable. Taste and adjust sweetness. Keep refrigerated until needed.

Spread a generous layer of sour cream frosting on each disc, stacking all layers. Apply frosting to the sides and top of the assembled cake. Crush one or two of the trimmed layer offcuts into fine crumbs and press onto the sides and top as decoration. Refrigerate for at least 8 hours — overnight is ideal. The magic is in this rest: the crisp layers absorb the cream and transform into something impossibly soft.

recipes.name: Honey Oat Sandwich Bread

ingredients.name: Rolled oats (old-fashioned), plus 10 g for topping

steps: In a large bowl (or stand mixer with a dough hook), stir the warm water and honey together, then add the flour, 80 g of the oats, and the yeast. Mix until a shaggy dough forms and rest 10 minutes so the oats and flour hydrate. Add the salt and butter and knead: 8–10 minutes by hand on an unfloured counter, or 6–7 minutes on medium-low in a mixer. The dough starts sticky but becomes smooth and elastic.
Place the dough in a lightly greased bowl, cover, and let rise in a warm spot (75–78°F / 24–26°C) for 60–75 minutes, until doubled in size.

Grease a 9 × 5 in (23 × 13 cm) loaf pan. Turn the dough out and press into a rectangle about 23 × 30 cm with a short side toward you. Roll it up tightly from the short end, pinching the seam at each turn, then pinch the final seam closed and tuck the ends under. Place seam-side down in the pan. Cover and let rise 40–50 minutes, until it crowns about 2.5 cm (1 in) above the rim. Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) during the last 20 minutes. Brush the top with milk and scatter with the reserved 10 g of oats.

Bake on the middle rack 35–40 minutes, until deep golden brown and an instant-read thermometer in the center of the loaf reads 195–200°F (90–93°C). Tent loosely with foil after 25 minutes if the top is browning too fast (honey browns quickly).
Turn the loaf out of the pan immediately and cool on a wire rack for at least 45 minutes (ideally 1 hour) before slicing with a serrated knife. The crumb is still setting as steam escapes.

recipes.name: Honeycomb Toffee (Cinder Toffee)
steps: Line a deep baking tray (at least 5 cm sides) with oiled parchment. Place the sugar, golden syrup, and water in a large, deep, heavy-bottomed saucepan — the pan must be at least 4x larger than the mixture, as it will expand violently when the baking soda is added. Stir over medium heat until the sugar dissolves completely. Once dissolved, stop stirring entirely — stirring will cause crystallization. Clip a candy thermometer to the side.

Boil the solution without stirring until it reaches 149–154 C (300–310 F) — the hard crack stage. Do not walk away. The temperature rises slowly at first and then accelerates dramatically above 130 C. At the target temperature, the caramel will be a deep amber — the color of very dark honey. Remove immediately from heat. Have the baking soda measured and ready in a small bowl before you start — you will have no time to measure it once the temperature is reached.

Working immediately and very quickly, whisk the fine salt and baking soda into the hot caramel. The mixture will react violently — expanding into a massive, hissing, volcanic foam of amber bubbles that rises from the pan. Stop whisking after 3–4 seconds (over-whisking deflates the bubbles) and immediately pour into the prepared tin. Do not spread it — let it flow and settle naturally, preserving the honeycomb structure. Do not touch or disturb it for 30–40 minutes until completely cold and set.

recipes.name: Hong Kong Egg Tarts (Dan Tat)
steps: In a bowl, rub the chilled lard into the icing sugar until it resembles fine breadcrumbs — or pulse briefly in a food processor. Add the egg yolk and cold water and mix until the dough just comes together into a smooth, pliable ball. Do not overwork: stop the moment no dry flour remains. Wrap in cling film and refrigerate for 30 minutes. The lard must stay cold to create the characteristic shatteringly flaky texture — butter-based pastry will be softer and more crumbly.

Whisk the eggs, milk, caster sugar, vanilla, and salt together in a bowl until the sugar is fully dissolved. Strain the mixture through a fine-mesh sieve twice — this removes any coagulated egg protein and air bubbles that would create a pocked, uneven surface on the baked custard. The strained custard should look perfectly smooth and slightly golden. Let it rest for 10 minutes so surface bubbles dissipate.

Preheat the oven to 200 C (390 F). Roll the chilled dough to 3 mm thickness on a lightly floured surface. Cut rounds and press into 8 cm tart moulds, pressing up the sides evenly and trimming any overhang. Prick the bases lightly with a fork. Fill each shell to 80% capacity with the custard mixture — the custard expands slightly when it sets. Bake on the middle rack for 18 to 22 minutes. For the first 10 minutes, do not open the oven door or the custard will sink. The tarts are done when the pastry is golden and the custard is just set — it should still have a very slight wobble in the centre when nudged.

recipes.name: Hong Shao Rou
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Pork belly, skin-on, cut into 4 cm cubes

steps: Place pork belly cubes in a cold pot and cover with cold water by 2 inches. Bring to a boil over high heat. As it heats, grey scum will rise to the surface — this is coagulated protein and blood. Skim and discard the scum as it appears. After reaching a full boil, blanch for 3 more minutes. Drain and rinse each piece under cold running water, rubbing with your fingers to remove any remaining scum. Pat dry with paper towels. This blanching step is non-negotiable — it removes impurities and prevents the final braising sauce from turning murky.

Heat a wok or heavy pot over medium-low heat. Add a small amount of oil, then the rock sugar crystals. Stir constantly with a spatula as the sugar melts — rock sugar melts unevenly and scorches quickly. As the sugar fully liquefies, it will shift from pale amber to a deep mahogany in about 2–3 minutes. Watch closely: too light and the braise lacks color and bitterness; too dark and it turns astringent. Once the color deepens to a dark amber and smells of burnt toffee, add the pork immediately.

Add the blanched, dried pork belly to the caramelized sugar and toss quickly to coat all surfaces. The hot caramel will seize and stick to the pork as it cools — work fast. Stir-fry over medium-high heat for 2–3 minutes until all surfaces are coated in the deep amber lacquer. The pork will spit and hiss intensely. This step creates the characteristic red-brown color of hong shao rou and seals the caramel into the meat's surface.

Add Shaoxing wine first — it will steam violently and deglaze the wok, lifting all the caramel. Then add dark soy, light soy, ginger slices, tied scallion knot, star anise, dried chili, and enough water or stock to just cover the pork. Bring to a boil, skim any remaining scum, then reduce to a very gentle simmer (barely bubbling). Cover and braise for 1 hour 30 minutes, turning pork every 30 minutes so all surfaces spend time submerged. The braise is done when a chopstick pierces the thickest part of the belly with no resistance.

Remove the ginger, scallion knot, star anise, and chili. Increase heat to medium-high and cook uncovered for 10–15 minutes, gently turning the pork every few minutes. The sauce will reduce by half and thicken into a glossy, lacquer-like glaze that coats the back of a spoon thickly. Continuously spoon the reducing sauce over the pork as it thickens. The final sauce should be glossy, deep mahogany-red, and cling heavily to each cube. If the sauce reduces too fast, add a splash of water.

recipes.name: Hoppin' John
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Smoked ham hock or thick-cut bacon

steps: The night before: rinse the dried black-eyed peas in cold water, picking out any stones or shriveled peas. Place in a large bowl and cover with cold water by at least 5 cm. Let soak at room temperature overnight, 8–12 hours. The peas will roughly double in volume. Drain and discard the soaking water. This step is not optional — soaking reduces the total cook time from 3 hours to under 90 minutes and ensures the peas cook evenly without their skins bursting before the interiors are done.

Place the drained peas and ham hock in a heavy pot or Dutch oven. Add the onion, smashed garlic, bay leaf, thyme, cayenne, and a generous pinch of salt. Cover with cold water by 5 cm. Bring to a boil, skimming any grey foam from the surface. Reduce to a gentle, steady simmer. Cook for 60–75 minutes, checking every 20 minutes and adding hot water to keep the peas just submerged. When the peas are completely tender, remove the ham hock and let it cool enough to handle. Pull all the meat from the bone in generous chunks and return it to the pot. Discard the skin and bone. Taste the broth — it should be deeply smoky, savory, and faintly spiced.

Bring the pot to a boil over medium-high heat. Stir in the rinsed rice and stir once to distribute evenly. Reduce to the lowest possible heat and cover tightly. Cook for 18–20 minutes without lifting the lid. The rice absorbs the smoky, pork-rich broth as it cooks — this is what makes Hoppin' John different from rice served alongside beans. Remove from heat and rest covered for 10 minutes. The rice should be fully cooked and the liquid completely absorbed. Fluff gently with a fork.

Taste the finished Hoppin' John one more time for salt, cayenne, and smokiness. Adjust as needed. Spoon into wide bowls and scatter a generous pinch of thinly sliced scallion over the top — the green is not just decoration but a fresh, sharp counterpoint to the deep, smoky richness of the peas and rice. Serve with hot-water cornbread, collard greens, and hot sauce on the table.

recipes.name: Huevos Rancheros

ingredients.name: Dried guajillo or ancho chili (stemmed, seeded)

steps: Heat a dry comal, cast-iron skillet, or flat griddle over high heat until very hot. Place the tomatoes, halved onion, and unpeeled garlic directly on the dry surface. Char them, turning occasionally, until the tomato skins blister and blacken in patches, the onion surfaces are dark brown, and the garlic is soft and fragrant — about 10 minutes total. Meanwhile, toast the dried chilies in the same dry pan for 30 seconds per side until they puff slightly and smell toasty but not burnt, then soak them in enough boiling water to cover for 10 minutes until pliable.

Peel the garlic. Add the charred tomatoes (with their juices), peeled garlic, browned onion pieces, and drained softened chilies to a blender. Blend until smooth — or leave slightly rough if you prefer a rustic texture. Season with salt. In a saucepan, heat one tablespoon of oil until shimmering, then pour the blended salsa in all at once — it will spit and splatter dramatically for 30 seconds. Fry the salsa, stirring, for 3–4 minutes until it darkens by a shade and the raw onion-garlic edge cooks out. The brief fry transforms blended ingredients into a cohesive sauce.

In a separate skillet, heat the remaining oil over medium-high heat. Pass each tortilla through the oil for 20–30 seconds per side — just long enough to warm through and pick up a few golden spots, but not enough to make them fully rigid. They should be pliable enough to fold but have a light crunch at the rim. Drain briefly on paper towels. Transfer to a warmed plate.

In the same skillet (or another), heat a film of oil over medium heat. Crack the eggs in carefully, keeping yolks intact. Fry sunny-side up: spoon hot oil over the whites to set the top edge, or cover with a lid for 1 minute to steam-set the whites without flipping. The whites should be fully set and opaque, with the yolk still completely liquid and bright orange-gold. Season with a pinch of salt.

Place the warm tortilla(s) on a plate. Slide the fried egg on top. Ladle the warm salsa generously over the egg white, leaving the yolk uncovered or just barely brushed so it remains visible and bright. Scatter crumbled cotija and fresh cilantro over the top. Serve with lime wedges on the side. Everything should arrive at the table hot — this is an assembly job that takes 30 seconds.

recipes.name: Hushpuppies
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Frying oil (peanut or vegetable), for deep frying

steps: Whisk together the cornmeal, flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt, and sugar in a large bowl until the leaveners are evenly distributed. This is important — baking powder and baking soda need to be spread evenly through the dry mix before the wet ingredients are added, or you will have uneven rising and pockets of chemical taste.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the buttermilk, egg, and grated onion (use the large holes of a box grater — grated onion releases more juice than diced and integrates more evenly). Pour the wet ingredients into the well in the dry mix and stir with a fork just until combined — 15–20 strokes maximum. Lumps are expected and correct. Overmixed hushpuppy batter develops too much gluten and produces tough, dense fritters instead of tender-crumbed ones. Rest the batter for 5 minutes before frying.

Pour at least 5–6 cm of oil into a heavy pot (cast iron Dutch oven ideal). Heat over medium-high to 185 C (365 F). Use a thermometer — temperature is the single most important variable in frying. Too cool and the hushpuppies absorb oil and are greasy and pale. Too hot and the outside burns before the inside cooks through.

Use two wet spoons or a small ice cream scoop to drop walnut-sized portions of batter into the oil, working in batches of 6–8 (overcrowding drops the oil temperature). The hushpuppies will sink briefly, begin to form a crust, and then roll themselves over as the leaveners create an uneven steam pocket — this self-rolling is the sign of a well-made batter. Fry 3–4 minutes total, turning once if they do not roll on their own, until deep golden-brown all over. Drain on a wire rack, not paper towels.

recipes.name: Imam Bayıldı
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Olive oil (use generously — this is the point)
Kosher salt, black pepper, and a pinch of sugar

steps: Peel the eggplants in alternating 2cm strips of skin and bare flesh — this striped pattern is traditional and helps the eggplant maintain its shape while still softening quickly. Make a deep lengthwise slit in each eggplant, not cutting all the way through. Salt the cut surfaces generously and the slits. Let rest in a colander for 30 minutes — the salt draws out the bitter liquid and also begins to relax the cell structure, reducing the spongy oil-absorption that makes eggplant dishes greasy when not pre-salted.

Heat half the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the onions very slowly for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they are completely soft and golden — they should be jammy and sweet with no raw bite. Add the garlic for the last 3 minutes. Add the tomatoes and cook for 10 more minutes until reduced to a thick, fragrant paste. Season with salt, pepper, and a pinch of sugar. Stir in the parsley. The filling should be very well-seasoned and richly flavored.

Rinse and dry the eggplants. Open the slits and fill generously with the onion-tomato mixture, pressing it in firmly. Arrange in a baking dish or wide pan that holds them snugly upright. Pour the remaining olive oil over and around the eggplants — do not be shy. Pour in 100ml of water. Cover tightly with foil and bake at 180°C (350°F) for 45–55 minutes until the eggplant walls are completely soft and translucent.

Imam bayıldı is traditionally served at room temperature or warm, never hot. Allow to cool for at least 30 minutes after baking. This resting is part of the recipe — the olive oil is reabsorbed as it cools, and the flavors concentrate and integrate. Serve directly from the baking dish, garnished with additional fresh parsley and a drizzle of olive oil. Accompany with crusty bread to catch the accumulated juices.

recipes.name: Garlic Naan
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: In a large bowl, whisk flour, salt, yeast, and baking powder together. Add yogurt, warm water, and oil. Mix until a rough dough forms, then knead by hand for 8 minutes until smooth and soft. The yogurt makes this dough notably more supple than plain water doughs. Aim for a consistency slightly softer than earlobe. Cover and rest for 1 hour until doubled.

Divide the dough into 6 equal balls (about 80 g each). On a lightly floured surface, roll each ball into a teardrop or oval shape about 20 cm long and 3 mm thick. Some lumpy irregularity is desirable — real tandoor naans are never perfectly uniform. If the dough springs back when rolling, let it rest 5 minutes then try again.

Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until it begins to smoke — at least 5 minutes of preheating. Place a naan directly on the dry pan. Cook 1–2 minutes until large bubbles form and the bottom has dark char spots. Flip and cook 30–60 seconds on the second side. While still hot, brush immediately with melted butter in which you have cooked the minced garlic until fragrant (30 seconds over medium). Scatter chopped coriander. Stack finished naans under a clean towel to keep soft.

recipes.name: Ethiopian Injera
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Ersho (teff fermentation culture, or 2 tbsp from a prior batch)
Neutral vegetable oil (to lightly oil mitad)

steps: Whisk together teff flour, warm water, and the ersho fermentation culture in a large ceramic or glass bowl until completely smooth with no lumps. The batter should be quite thin — thinner than pancake batter, closer to heavy cream in consistency. Cover the bowl loosely with a cloth (not airtight — the culture needs air) and leave at room temperature (22–26 C). The batter will ferment for 3 full days. Do not refrigerate.

Allow the batter to ferment at room temperature for 3 full days (72 hours). Stir once each morning. By day 2 you will see small bubbles forming at the surface and the batter will smell sour and slightly earthy. By day 3 the surface will be frothy, the color will have deepened, and the smell will be sharply acidic — the hallmark tang of authentic injera. A thin liquid (teff water) may separate to the top; stir it back in.

Stir the fermented batter well to reintegrate the separated layers. Add the fine salt and whisk to combine. Taste: the batter should be sharply sour with a pleasant earthiness from the teff. Season to balance, not neutralize — injera is supposed to be sour. If the batter seems very thick after fermentation (teff absorbs water over time), thin it with a small amount of room-temperature water until it pours freely.

Heat a 35–40 cm non-stick pan, cast-iron, or traditional clay mitad over medium heat. Lightly oil just the first injera — subsequent ones need no oil as the natural moisture of the batter prevents sticking. Pour a ladleful of batter in a quick spiral outward from the center (like a crêpe but do not tilt the pan — pour and let it spread). The batter should cover the pan in one pour. Immediately cover with a domed lid. Cook for 2–3 minutes until all the 'eyes' (the characteristic holes) have opened across the entire surface and the edges have lifted from the pan. Do not flip — injera is cooked on one side only. Slide out onto a clean cloth to cool. Stack cooled injeras — they will stick slightly and peel apart beautifully.

recipes.name: Irish Soda Bread
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Whole wheat flour (or half white, half wholemeal)
Cold unsalted butter, cubed (optional, for richness)

steps: Preheat the oven to 220°C (425°F). In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, baking soda, and salt until evenly combined. If using butter, rub it into the flour using your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs. Work quickly — you do not want the butter to melt from the heat of your hands. The dry mix should be aerated and loose.

Make a well in the center of the dry mix. Pour in all the cold buttermilk at once. Using a large fork or your hand held flat like a paddle, stir in large circular motions from the inside out — 15 to 20 strokes maximum. Stop as soon as the dough just comes together. It will be shaggy, rough, and slightly sticky — this is correct. Over-mixing develops gluten and toughens the crumb fatally. The reaction between the soda and buttermilk has already begun.

Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and shape quickly and gently into a round about 20cm in diameter and 5cm thick — use the minimum number of touches needed. Place on a parchment-lined baking tray. Using a sharp knife or blade, cut a deep cross into the top, nearly all the way through — this allows heat to penetrate the dense interior and is said traditionally to let the fairies out. Dust lightly with flour.

Bake at 220°C (425°F) for 20 minutes. Without opening the oven, reduce the temperature to 200°C (390°F) and bake for a further 20–25 minutes. To test doneness, lift the loaf and tap the base firmly with your knuckle — a fully baked soda bread sounds hollow, like an empty wooden box. If it sounds dense and dull, return to the oven for 5 more minutes base-side up. Cool on a wire rack for at least 20 minutes before cutting.

recipes.name: Isicia Omentata
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Dry white wine (Roman passum if you have it)
Stale bread soaked in wine (squeezed dry)

steps: In a dry pan over medium heat, toast the pine nuts until they turn pale gold and smell nutty, 2-3 minutes, shaking constantly. Tip them out, then briefly warm the cracked pepper, cumin and lovage seed in the residual heat just until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Crush the cooled pine nuts coarsely so they keep some bite.

In a wide bowl, combine the beef mince with the toasted pine nuts and spices, the wine-soaked bread, garum and wine. Work the mixture with your hands for about a minute until the garum is evenly distributed and the meat just begins to feel tacky and cohesive. Do not overwork it into a paste — you want a tender, open crumb, not a dense sausage.

Divide the forcemeat into 4-6 portions and shape each into a plump patty about 2 cm thick. Lay a piece of caul fat flat, set a patty in the centre, and fold the lacy membrane snugly around it, trimming any excess so it overlaps once on the underside. The caul will melt as it cooks, basting and crisping the surface.

Heat the olive oil in a heavy pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Lay the patties seam-side down and sear undisturbed for 3-4 minutes until a deep crust forms, then flip and cook the second side 3-4 minutes more, until the caul has rendered and crisped and the centre reaches a juicy 60-63°C / 140-145°F. Rest 5 minutes before serving with extra garum on the side.

recipes.name: Italian Acqua Pazza

ingredients.name: Whole fish (sea bream, snapper, or sea bass), cleaned

steps: In a wide, lidded skillet or shallow casserole, warm the olive oil over medium heat. Add the bruised garlic and peperoncino and cook gently for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the cherry tomatoes cut-side down and cook for 3 minutes until they begin to blister and collapse. Add the white wine and let it bubble for 1 minute. Add the water or fish stock and the capers. Season with salt. Bring to a vigorous simmer.

Score the fish 3 times on each side. Season inside and out. Lower the fish into the simmering broth. Cover the pan and cook over medium heat for 8–10 minutes per 500g of fish. Spoon the broth over the fish every 3 minutes. The fish is cooked when the score cuts have opened and the eye of the fish has turned white and opaque — this is the Neapolitan fisherman's traditional indicator of doneness.

Scatter torn fresh parsley leaves over the fish and drizzle a final thread of raw olive oil over the broth. Serve directly from the pan at the table. Provide good crusty bread for the broth — the acqua pazza (crazy water) is the real treasure: a light, herb-bright, tomato-scented essence that should be drunk from the bowl at the end.

recipes.name: Japanese Cotton Cheesecake
steps: Place cream cheese, butter, and milk in a large heatproof bowl set over a saucepan of barely simmering water (bain-marie). Whisk gently until the cream cheese has melted completely and the mixture is smooth, silky, and uniform — no lumps, no streaks. Remove from heat and cool to 40-45 C before adding yolks. If the mixture is too hot it will scramble the yolks.

Whisk the egg yolks into the cooled cream cheese base one at a time. Sift together the flour and cornflour and fold into the mixture in two additions until completely smooth with no lumps. Add vanilla. The batter should be thick but pourable — like thick pancake batter. Any lumps of flour will show as dense spots in the finished cake.

In a scrupulously clean bowl, whip cold egg whites with cream of tartar at medium speed until foamy. Add the caster sugar gradually while continuing to whip. Increase to medium-high and whip to firm peaks — the meringue should be stiff enough to hold a peak but still smooth and glossy, not dry or grainy. The critical point: do not over-whip. The meringue should be just firm, with a slight curl at the peak tip, not completely rigid.

Add the meringue to the yolk batter in three additions. The first addition: stir in roughly to lighten the batter without concern for preserving air. The second and third additions: fold with a wide rubber spatula, scooping from the base and folding over, rotating the bowl. Stop as soon as no white streaks remain. Pour into a parchment-lined 20 cm round tin. Tap the tin once on the counter to release large bubbles.

Wrap the base and sides of the tin tightly in two layers of foil. Place in a deep roasting tray and fill with boiling water to reach halfway up the tin sides (water bath / bain-marie baking). Bake at 160 C (320 F) for 55-65 minutes. The surface should be a deep amber-brown and the cake should tremble as a whole when the tin is gently shaken — not sloshing liquid, but a unified jiggle. Turn the oven off and leave the cake inside with the door ajar for 30 minutes before removing. Cool completely at room temperature before refrigerating overnight.

recipes.name: Japanese Curry
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Chicken thigh, bone-in or boneless (cut into large chunks)
Japanese curry roux blocks (S&B Golden Curry or similar)

steps: Heat oil in a large heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Pat chicken dry with paper towels and season generously with salt and pepper. Sear in a single layer, skin-side down if bone-in, for 3-4 minutes without moving until golden-brown. Flip and sear the other side for 2 minutes. Remove and set aside — chicken will not be cooked through at this point. The fond left in the pot is flavor gold.

Reduce heat to medium. Add onions to the same pot with the chicken fond. Cook, stirring regularly, for 12-15 minutes until the onions are deeply golden-brown and have reduced dramatically in volume. This extended caramelization of the onion is the secret to a rich, sweet Japanese curry base. Do not rush this step — pale, underdone onions produce a sharp, raw flavor that does not mellow in the sauce.

Add potato/sweet potato and carrot to the pot. Stir to coat in the caramelized onion. Return the seared chicken. Pour in water or stock, enough to just cover. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Skim any foam that rises. Simmer uncovered for 20-25 minutes until potatoes and carrots are completely tender when pierced with a skewer, and the chicken is cooked through. If using bone-in chicken, the meat should begin to pull away from the bone.

Break the curry roux blocks into the pot, distributing them evenly. Stir gently over low heat until the blocks have completely dissolved — about 3-5 minutes. Return to a very gentle simmer, stirring frequently, for 5 more minutes as the starch in the roux thickens the sauce. The curry should be glossy and coat a spoon thickly. Taste and adjust with a little extra soy sauce for saltiness, or grated apple for sweetness. Serve over short-grain white rice with fukujinzuke pickles and tonkatsu sauce on the side.

recipes.name: Kinpira Gobo (Braised Burdock and Carrot)
steps: Scrub the burdock root with a stiff brush under cold water — do not peel, the skin carries earthiness and nutrition. Cut into 5cm matchsticks (julienne), approximately 3–4mm square. As you cut, immediately transfer to a bowl of cold water with a splash of rice vinegar or lemon juice to prevent oxidation. Burdock discolors dramatically and quickly when exposed to air — within minutes it will turn from cream to dark brown. Drain and pat dry just before cooking.

Heat the sesame oil in a wok or medium skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chili flakes and stir for 10 seconds until fragrant. Add the drained, dried burdock matchsticks and the julienned carrot. Stir-fry over high heat for 3–4 minutes, tossing regularly, until the vegetables are beginning to pick up color and the burdock has softened slightly at the surface but is still firm at the center. The sesame oil should smell nutty and toasty.

Add the sake first — it will sizzle and reduce in 30 seconds. Add the mirin and soy sauce. Reduce heat to medium. Toss the vegetables in the glaze, then cook, stirring regularly, for 4–5 minutes until the liquid has reduced to a thin, glossy glaze that coats every strand. The burdock should be tender but with a slight, distinctive resistance at the core — kinpira is never soft. Taste for seasoning — it should be sweet, salty, and faintly earthy.

Transfer to a small serving dish or bowls. Scatter toasted sesame seeds generously over the top. Serve at room temperature as a banchan alongside rice. Kinpira gobo keeps refrigerated for 3–4 days and actually improves overnight as the glaze penetrates deeper into the burdock.

recipes.name: Japanese Milk Bread (Shokupan)
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Warm whole milk (38 C) for main dough

steps: Whisk the tangzhong flour with the cold milk in a small saucepan until completely smooth and lump-free. Place over medium-low heat and cook, stirring constantly with a silicone spatula, for 3–5 minutes until the mixture thickens into a thick, glossy, pudding-like paste and a thermometer reads 65 C (150 F). At this temperature the starch granules fully gelatinize, and in this gelatinized state they can absorb and lock in far more water than raw starch — this is the scientific reason shokupan stays softer longer than any other bread. Remove from the heat, press a sheet of plastic wrap directly onto the surface to prevent a skin forming, and cool to room temperature.

In a stand mixer bowl, combine the bread flour, sugar, salt, and instant yeast (keep salt and yeast on opposite sides of the bowl before mixing). Add the warm milk, egg, and cooled tangzhong. Using the dough hook, mix on low speed for 2 minutes until combined, then increase to medium for 5 minutes. The dough will be shaggy and sticky at first — resist adding extra flour. It will come together as the gluten develops and the tangzhong integrates. After 5 minutes it should begin to pull away from the bowl sides.

With the mixer running on medium, add the softened butter in small pieces, about 1 tablespoon at a time, waiting for each addition to be fully absorbed before adding the next. This will take 8–10 minutes of mixing in total after the butter is all in. The dough will go through an ugly phase — looking greasy and broken — before it comes back together into a silky, elastic ball that pulls completely clean from the bowl. Increase to medium-high for the final 2 minutes. The windowpane test should be very easy to pass: a small piece stretches to nearly translucent without tearing.

Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let it rise at room temperature (24–26 C) for 1 to 1.5 hours, until doubled in size. Because of the tangzhong and high butter content this dough rises more slowly than a lean dough. Punching it down once at the halfway point (45 minutes) helps develop a more even, fine crumb by redistributing the yeast and redistributing gas. After the full rise, chill the dough in the refrigerator for 20 minutes to firm it up, which makes the sticky dough much easier to divide and shape cleanly.

Divide the chilled dough into 4 equal pieces. Flatten each piece into a rectangle, fold the long sides in toward the center, and roll it into a tight cylinder. Place all 4 cylinders side by side in a greased 9x5 Pullman loaf pan (or a standard loaf pan), seam-side down. For a classic shokupan dome, leave the pan uncovered. For a flat-topped Pullman loaf, slide the lid on. Cover and proof at room temperature for 1 to 1.5 hours, until the dough crests 2 cm above the rim (dome) or fills the Pullman pan 90%.

Brush the proofed loaf with cream or milk for a shiny, deep golden crust. Bake at 180 C (355 F) for 30–35 minutes for a dome loaf, or 35–40 minutes with the Pullman lid on. The loaf is done when the top is a rich, even golden-brown (no pale doughy patches), the internal temperature reads 93–96 C (200–205 F), and the sides pull away from the pan. Remove from the pan immediately and cool completely on a wire rack for at least 1 hour before slicing. The crumb will be dense and gummy if cut hot — it continues to set as it cools.

recipes.name: Japanese Miso-Glazed Black Cod
steps: In a small saucepan, combine the mirin and sake. Bring to a boil over medium heat for 1 minute to cook off the alcohol. Reduce heat to low and whisk in the white miso and sugar until completely smooth. Cook, stirring, for 2–3 minutes until the mixture is glossy and thick. Remove from heat and cool completely to room temperature before using — adding hot marinade to the fish will begin cooking the exterior prematurely.

Coat each cod fillet generously on all sides with the cooled miso marinade. Place in a container, seal tightly, and refrigerate for 2–3 days (48–72 hours). The long marination is the signature of this preparation — the salt in the miso gently draws moisture from the fish while the sugars and umami compounds diffuse deep into the flesh. After marination, the fish will be notably firmer and more deeply flavored throughout.

Remove the cod fillets from the marinade and wipe off most (not all) of the miso with your fingers or a spatula. A thin layer should remain. Place skin-side down on a foil-lined, lightly oiled baking sheet. Broil at the oven's highest setting (230–260°C) for 8–10 minutes, watching constantly. The miso glaze will darken dramatically and some sections will look nearly burnt — this is the Maillard reaction and caramelization of the sugars, and it is the correct result. The fish is done when the glaze is deeply caramelized and the flesh flakes when a fork is pressed at the thickest point. Serve with pickled ginger and green onion.

recipes.name: Japanese Onigiri

ingredients.name: Fine sea salt (for hands and rice)

steps: Rinse the rice until the water runs nearly clear (5–6 rinses). Drain and let the rice sit dry in the pot for 10 minutes — this pre-resting firms the exterior. Add the measured water, cover tightly, and bring to a boil over high heat. As soon as you hear the boiling, reduce to the absolute lowest simmer and cook for 12 minutes. Remove from heat without lifting the lid and steam for 10 minutes. The rice is ready when you open the lid to a puff of steam with no visible water at the surface.

While the rice is still warm, turn it into a large flat bowl using a rice paddle. Sprinkle the salt evenly over the surface. Fold the rice using a cutting-and-folding motion (not stirring) to distribute the salt without crushing the grains. Fan or let cool to a temperature where you can comfortably handle it — just above body temperature, around 40°C.

Wet both palms with cold water and rub with a generous pinch of salt — this prevents sticking and adds flavor to the exterior. Take about 120g of warm rice and form a loose ball in one palm. Press a shallow indentation in the center and place your filling (umeboshi, tuna mayo, or salmon flakes) inside. Close the rice around the filling. Cup both hands into a V-shape and press firmly from the sides while rotating, forming a compact triangle with three flat faces and three ridges. Wrap the base with a strip of nori. Repeat for remaining rice and fillings.

recipes.name: Japanese Salmon Teriyaki
steps: Combine the soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small saucepan. Bring to a boil over medium heat and stir to dissolve the sugar. Simmer for 3–4 minutes until reduced by one-third and the glaze coats the back of a spoon with a thin sheen. Remove from heat. The glaze thickens further as it cools.

Pat the salmon fillets completely dry with kitchen paper — any moisture creates steam and prevents a crust. Score the skin 3 times diagonally to prevent curling. Heat the oil in a non-stick or cast-iron pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Place the salmon skin-side down and press firmly with a spatula for 10 seconds to prevent curling. Cook skin-side down for 4 minutes until the skin is deeply golden and crisp and the flesh has turned opaque 2/3 of the way up the sides. Flip once.

After flipping, cook the flesh side for 1 minute. Reduce heat to low. Pour the teriyaki glaze over and around the salmon. As it bubbles, spoon it over the top of the fillets repeatedly for 1–2 minutes. The glaze will reduce and lacquer the salmon in a shiny, mahogany coating. Remove from heat and spoon any remaining glaze over the top. Scatter green onion and sesame seeds. Rest 1 minute before serving.

recipes.name: Japanese Tonkatsu

ingredients.name: Pork loin chops, bone-in or boneless, 2cm thick

steps: Using a sharp knife, score the fat cap of each cutlet at 1cm intervals — this prevents the cutlet from curling in the oil. If using thick loin chops, use a meat mallet or rolling pin to pound to an even 1.5–2cm thickness between two sheets of plastic wrap. Season both sides generously with salt and white pepper. Let the cutlets rest at room temperature for 15 minutes — a cold cutlet will drop the oil temperature and result in greasy, not crisp, breading.

Set up a three-stage breading station: flour in a shallow dish, beaten egg in a second, panko in a third. Dredge each cutlet in flour, shaking off every trace of excess — too much flour makes a gluey paste under the egg. Dip in egg, letting the excess drip off, then press firmly into the panko on both sides, gently pressing the crumbs in with your palm to ensure adhesion. The coating should be thick and even, not patchy.

Heat the oil in a heavy pot or wok to 170°C (340°F). Test with a panko crumb — it should sink, immediately sizzle, and rise to the surface within 3 seconds. Lower the cutlet in slowly, away from you, and fry for 3 minutes per side without touching. At 170°C the crust sets before the interior overcooks. Raise the temperature to 180°C (355°F) for the final 30 seconds to flash-crisp the exterior to a deep golden color. Drain on a wire rack — not paper towels, which trap steam and soften the crust.

Using a sharp knife, slice the tonkatsu crosswise into 2cm strips — the goal is to preserve the crust while revealing the interior. Serve immediately with tonkatsu sauce drizzled over or alongside, finely shredded fresh cabbage, and steamed Japanese short-grain rice. The crust will begin to soften within 10 minutes, so timing is essential.

recipes.name: Japchae
steps: Julienne the beef into strips roughly 5 cm long and 3 mm thick, cutting against the grain. Combine 2 tablespoons of soy sauce, 1 tablespoon of sugar, 1 tablespoon of sesame oil, and all of the minced garlic in a bowl. Add the beef, toss thoroughly so every strip is coated, and let it sit at room temperature while you prep the other components — at least 15 minutes. The sugar draws out the beef's surface moisture and allows rapid caramelization in the pan. Do not salt additionally; the soy carries all the salinity the beef needs. The strips should smell deeply savory and faintly sweet, with the garlic softening and becoming aromatic as it sits.

Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Drop the dangmyeon noodles in without breaking them — they will soften and uncurl on their own. Cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent clumping. Taste a noodle: it should be fully translucent all the way through with a pleasantly chewy resistance — not gummy in the center, not mushy. Drain immediately and rinse under cold running water to stop cooking and remove excess starch. Shake the colander hard. While still warm, toss the noodles with 1 tablespoon of soy sauce and 1 teaspoon of sesame oil to season them and prevent them from sticking together. Use kitchen scissors to snip the noodles two or three times — this makes them far easier to toss and eat without losing their essential chew.

Work each vegetable separately — this is the labor of japchae and the source of its beauty. Heat a wok or wide skillet over high heat until it just begins to smoke. Add a teaspoon of neutral oil and stir-fry the carrot julienne for 90 seconds with a pinch of salt; it should still have a slight bite. Remove to a plate. Repeat with the bell pepper (60 seconds — it should stay vivid red), then the shiitake mushrooms (2 minutes, until their edges begin to brown and they smell deeply woody). For the spinach, blanch briefly in salted boiling water, drain, squeeze hard until almost dry, toss with a few drops of sesame oil and a pinch of salt. Cook the eggs as a thin jidan: beat yolks and whites separately if precision matters, cook as two thin omelets, let cool, slice into 5 cm strips. Each vegetable cooked alone retains its individual color, aroma, and texture — cooking them together muds both flavor and appearance.

Heat the wok over the highest flame your stove allows until it's visibly shimmering and beginning to smoke. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Spread the marinated beef in a single layer — do not crowd the pan or the meat will steam rather than sear. Cook undisturbed for 60–90 seconds until the bottom develops a dark caramelized crust from the sugar in the marinade. Toss and cook for another 30 seconds. The beef should be just cooked through — in a dish like japchae it should be tender, not stiff. The marinade sugar will char slightly in places, adding a pleasant bitterness that balances the sweetness of the sauce. Work in two batches if the pan is full; a crowded pan steams and the glaze turns into a puddle.

In the largest bowl or the wok itself, combine the seasoned noodles, all the cooked vegetables, and the beef. Drizzle over the remaining soy sauce, sugar, and sesame oil — taste as you go; japchae is meant to be distinctly sweet-savory, so be bold with both the sugar and the soy. Toss everything together gently but thoroughly with tongs or clean hands, lifting from the bottom to distribute everything evenly without breaking the noodles. Taste repeatedly and adjust: more sugar if it lacks warmth, more soy if it's flat, more sesame oil for richness and aroma. Transfer to a serving platter and arrange the egg jidan strips over the top. Scatter sesame seeds liberally. Japchae is excellent at room temperature and actually improves after resting 20 minutes — the noodles absorb the sauce and the flavors marry.

recipes.name: Jamaican Jerk Chicken

ingredients.name: Whole allspice berries, toasted and ground

steps: Combine all marinade ingredients in a blender or food processor. Blitz to a smooth, intensely aromatic paste. Taste it — it should be fiery, fragrant with allspice, and deeply savory. Adjust salt and lime. The color should be a deep olive-green flecked with red.

Using a sharp knife, score the chicken pieces to the bone — three deep parallel cuts per piece allows the paste to penetrate. Wearing gloves (scotch bonnet oil is serious), massage the jerk paste into every surface including under the skin where possible. Pack tightly into a zip-lock bag or sealed container. Refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours; overnight is ideal for full smoke-spice penetration.

Set up a two-zone grill: high direct heat on one side, indirect medium on the other. Start the chicken skin-side up on the indirect side, covered, for 25–30 minutes until internal temperature reaches 65°C. Then move to direct high heat, skin-side down, for 4–6 minutes to char and blister the exterior. Flip and char the flesh side for 2 minutes. The char is not a mistake — it is the point.

Rest the chicken on a wooden board, loosely tented with foil, for 8–10 minutes. The internal temperature will coast up 2–3°C. The juices, which have been driven to the center by the heat, redistribute through the meat. Do not cut early.

recipes.name: Jerusalem Artichoke Soup

ingredients.name: Truffle oil or hazelnut oil (for finishing)

steps: Preheat oven to 200 C (400 F). Cut the Jerusalem artichokes into roughly equal 3 cm pieces — no need to peel, the skin carries flavor. Toss on a baking sheet with the sliced shallots, unpeeled garlic cloves, olive oil, thyme sprigs, and a generous pinch of salt. Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, turning once, until the artichokes are golden-brown on the cut surfaces, completely tender, and the skins are slightly wrinkled.

While the artichokes roast, melt the butter in a large saucepan over medium-low heat. Let it foam and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until it smells faintly nutty — beurre noisette. This enriches the base of the soup.

Squeeze the roasted garlic from its skin into the blender. Add all the roasted artichokes, shallots, and the butter. Discard the thyme stems. Pour in enough warm stock to cover the solids. Blend on high speed for 2 to 3 minutes until completely smooth. Add more stock to reach a consistency between heavy cream and a thin porridge. Pass through a fine-mesh sieve for an exceptionally refined result.

Return the puree to a saucepan over low heat. Stir in the cream. Adjust consistency with additional stock if too thick. Season carefully with salt and white pepper. Do not boil after the cream is added. Ladle into warmed bowls. Finish each bowl with a thin drizzle of truffle or hazelnut oil, a scatter of snipped chives, and a few toasted crushed hazelnuts.

recipes.name: Party Jollof Rice
steps: Combine the canned tomatoes, red bell peppers, scotch bonnet, half the onion, garlic, and ginger in a blender. Blitz until completely smooth with no visible chunks — you want a liquid slurry, not a chunky salsa. The color will be a vivid brick-orange at this stage.
