Squeeze fresh lemon juice directly into each serving — about half a teaspoon per bowl — and serve immediately with crusty bread or flatbread alongside. The lemon must be added at serving, not to the pot, to preserve its brightness.

recipes.name: Libum
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: If your ricotta is loose and weeping, line a sieve with cheesecloth, spoon it in, and let it drain over a bowl for 20 to 30 minutes — or longer in the fridge — until it firms to the texture of soft, sliceable curd. Wet ricotta makes a batter that slumps and steams rather than bakes, so this step decides whether the libum holds a mound. Discard the whey.

Beat the drained ricotta hard with a wooden spoon until it loosens and turns creamy, then work in the egg until the batter is uniform and glossy. Add the salt, then fold in the spelt flour a little at a time — just until it disappears into a soft, thick, scoopable dough. Cato says to mix it 'bene' (well); beating the cheese smooth is what gives the baked libum its tender, even crumb. Stop the moment the flour is incorporated so the gluten stays slack.

Arrange the bay leaves on a baking sheet or in a shallow ovenproof dish, fanned so the cakes will rest directly on the leaves. Divide the batter into four and shape each into a round mound about three inches across and an inch high, setting one on each leaf. The bay's oils perfume the underside of the cake as it bakes and keep it from sticking — the leaf is flavor and parchment in one. Smooth the tops lightly so they bake evenly.

Bake at 375 F / 190 C. Cato directs the cake be cooked slowly under a hot earthenware cover — to mimic that 'sub testu' hearth, set an inverted metal bowl or a covered pot over the cakes for the first 15 minutes to trap gentle, even heat, then lift it off and bake 5 to 10 minutes more to color the tops. They are done when set through, puffed, and golden at the edges, 20 to 25 minutes total. The bay leaves will have browned and crisped beneath.

Warm the honey gently until it runs thin. Lift each libum from its bay leaf onto a serving plate while still warm, split or prick the top, and pour the warm honey over so it soaks into the cracks and pools around the base. Cato has the cakes served hot and drenched in honey — eat them straight away, when the curd is still soft and the honey sinks in. The toasted bay leaf can stay tucked beneath as a fragrant, edible-adjacent garnish.

recipes.name: Lion's Head Meatballs (Shi Zi Tou)

ingredients.name: Ground pork (30% fat — do not use lean)
Water chestnuts, fresh or canned, finely diced
Fresh ginger, grated to a pulp
Napa cabbage, outer leaves separated whole

steps: In a large mixing bowl, combine the ground pork, finely diced water chestnuts, beaten egg, cornstarch, grated ginger pulp (squeeze it through your fingers to include the juice, discard the fibrous residue), minced scallion white, light soy sauce, and Shaoxing wine. Like the wonton filling, mix vigorously in one consistent direction — always clockwise or always counter-clockwise — for 3–4 minutes until the mixture is completely homogeneous and has developed a slight stickiness. The directional mixing is not superstition: it aligns the myosin proteins in the pork into a coherent network that gives the cooked meatball its characteristic bouncy, springy bite rather than a crumbly texture. The water chestnuts provide crunch that contrasts beautifully with the soft surrounding meat — do not skip them. The mixture should be very soft and sticky — far softer than most Western meatball mixtures. Do not add breadcrumbs. The starch and egg are the only binders needed. Refrigerate for 30 minutes to firm up before shaping.

With wet hands, divide the mixture into 4–5 equal portions (each about 150 g). Roll each into a smooth, tight sphere — wet palms are essential because the mixture is very sticky. Work quickly and with light pressure: over-packing the sphere makes the interior dense rather than tender. Place on a wet plate as you go. Heat the oil in a wide, deep pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the meatballs gently, leaving space between each. Sear for 2–3 minutes on each major surface — they will not roll easily, so use a spoon to tilt and hold them against the hot surface. You are not trying to cook them through; you want a golden-brown crust on all surfaces that will hold the sphere together during the long braise and add depth of flavor to the finished dish. Do not attempt to flip them until the seared side releases naturally from the pot — a stuck meatball is an unseared meatball.

In the same pot, pour off most of the oil, leaving a thin film. Add the dark soy sauce and rock sugar to the residual fat and stir over medium heat until the sugar melts — about 1 minute. Add the Shaoxing wine and let it sizzle for 30 seconds. Add the stock and bring to a simmer. Taste and adjust seasoning — the braising liquid should be distinctly savory and subtly sweet. Lay the whole napa cabbage leaves across the bottom of the pot in a thick layer, then nestle the seared meatballs on top of the cabbage, which will act as a natural rack elevating them from the direct heat. Ladle the braising liquid over the meatballs. Cover the meatballs with more cabbage leaves. Cover the pot tightly. Braise over the lowest possible heat for 90 minutes. Turn the meatballs once at the 45-minute mark. The low, slow heat allows the collagen in the fatty pork to dissolve into gelatin, creating the interior texture that defines this dish. The cabbage simultaneously absorbs the braising liquid and releases its own sweetness into the pot.

recipes.name: Lobster Bisque
steps: Dispatch the lobsters humanely by placing them in the freezer for 20 minutes before splitting. Split the lobsters lengthwise with a sharp heavy knife, or use lobster tails and reserved shells. Heat the butter in a wide, heavy roasting pan or large dutch oven over high heat until foaming. Add the lobster shells and tail meat cut-side down. Roast over high heat, turning occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the shells turn a brilliant, uniform orange-red and the butter has taken on a coral tint from the shell pigments. Remove the tail meat when just cooked through and reserve for garnish.

Add the diced shallots, carrot, and celery to the pot of roasted shells. Cook over medium-high heat for 5 minutes, stirring, until the vegetables soften and begin to caramelize at the edges. Add the garlic and tomato paste. Stir the tomato paste constantly into the vegetables and shells for 2–3 minutes until it darkens from bright red to a deep, brick-red — this is pinçage, which removes the raw acidity and develops deep savory sweetness. The fond on the pan base will intensify.

Pour the cognac into the pot. On a gas stove, carefully tilt the pan to flame the cognac — the blue flame will extinguish within 10–15 seconds as the alcohol burns off. On induction or electric, simply allow the alcohol to bubble and evaporate for 2 minutes. Add the white wine and scrape up all the caramelized fond from the bottom of the pot with a wooden spoon — every bit of this fond is concentrated bisque flavor. Allow the wine to reduce by half before adding the stock.

Add the fish stock, tarragon sprigs, and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle, steady simmer. Cook uncovered for 25–30 minutes, allowing the shells to surrender all their flavor to the liquid. Skim any foam that rises to the surface during the first 5 minutes. The liquid will deepen in color and concentrate. Do not rush this step — this long simmer is what distinguishes a restaurant bisque from a shortcut approximation.

Remove the bay leaves. Transfer everything — shells included — to a high-powered blender in batches and blend on high for 60 seconds per batch. The shells will fragment and contribute starch, calcium, and color to the bisque. Pass the blended mixture through a fine-mesh sieve, pressing hard with the back of a ladle to extract every drop of liquid. Discard the shell fragments. Pass through the sieve a second time for an especially silky result.

Return the strained bisque to a clean saucepan. Add the heavy cream and bring to a gentle simmer. Reduce for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the bisque coats the back of a spoon and the flavor has further concentrated. Season carefully with salt, white pepper, and a discreet pinch of cayenne. Warm reserved lobster tail meat in the bisque for 60 seconds. Ladle into warmed bowls, place a piece of lobster meat in the center, and finish with fresh chervil or tarragon leaves and an optional drizzle of crème fraîche.

recipes.name: Lobster Thermidor
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Live lobster (about 600 g each, or cooked tail & claw meat)

steps: Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil. Plunge the lobsters in head-first and cook just until the shells turn bright scarlet and the meat is barely set — about 6 minutes for 600 g birds, no more. Lift them out and shock briefly in iced water to halt the cooking. Twist off the tails and claws, split the bodies lengthwise, and reserve the empty half-shells for serving.

Melt the butter in a wide sauté pan over medium-low heat. Add the minced shallots with a pinch of salt and sweat them gently, stirring, until soft, glassy and translucent without taking on any colour, about 4-5 minutes. This sweet, mellow base carries the whole sauce.

Pour in the cognac and, off the flame or with great care, ignite it to burn off the raw alcohol — let the flames die on their own. Add the white wine, raise the heat, and reduce the liquid by about two-thirds until it is syrupy and barely coats the pan floor, concentrating the shallot and brandy into a savoury glaze.

Pour in the cream and whisk in the Dijon mustard, a pinch of cayenne and white pepper. Simmer gently, stirring, until the sauce thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon, 4-6 minutes. Taste and season — it should be rich, faintly sharp with mustard, and warm with cayenne. Do not let it boil hard, or it may split.

Off the heat, whisk a spoonful of the hot sauce into the egg yolk to temper it, then stir the yolk back into the pan to enrich and bind — never let it boil now. Fold in the lobster meat and chopped tarragon, warming through for a minute. Spoon the mixture generously into the reserved half-shells set on a baking tray.

Scatter the grated Gruyère thickly over each filled shell. Slide under a hot grill (broiler) about 10 cm from the element and cook until the cheese melts, bubbles and blisters into golden-brown patches, 3-5 minutes. Watch constantly — it goes from pale to perfect to burnt in seconds. Serve at once, scalding hot, with lemon and crusty bread.

recipes.name: Lomo Saltado

ingredients.name: Beef sirloin or tenderloin, sliced 1cm thick against the grain
Yellow potatoes (Yukon Gold or similar), cut into thick fries
Red onion, cut into thick wedges (8 wedges per onion)
Ripe tomatoes, cut into thick wedges
Ají amarillo paste (or 1 fresh ají amarillo, seeded and sliced)
Fine sea salt and black pepper

steps: Heat about 4cm of vegetable oil in a large deep pot or wok to 175C / 350F. Test with a potato strip — it should sizzle immediately and vigorously. Fry the potato strips in batches, never crowding the oil, for 6–8 minutes per batch until cooked through and golden on the outside. Transfer to a wire rack set over paper towel and season immediately with salt while hot — the salt adheres to the hot potato surface. Do not cover; you want them to stay crisp. These potatoes will be added back to the wok at the end. This double-presence of fries and rice in a single dish is one of the things that makes lomo saltado uniquely Peruvian — the carb abundance is intentional and joyful.

While the potatoes fry, season the beef strips with ground cumin, salt, and black pepper. Toss to coat evenly. Let the beef sit at room temperature for 10 minutes — this isn't a long marinade but a short seasoning rest that lets the salt draw a small amount of moisture to the surface, which helps the meat sear faster and more evenly. Crucial point: the beef must be dry on the surface before it hits the wok. Pat it with paper towels if any moisture has pooled. Wet beef steams rather than sears, and the sear is everything in lomo saltado — it's what creates the signature smoky, charred edges that no amount of sauce can substitute.

Heat your wok or largest cast-iron skillet over the absolute highest heat your stove can produce for two full minutes. Add a thin film of vegetable oil and let it begin to smoke — this is the signal that you're at the right temperature. Add the beef strips in a single layer and leave them untouched for 60 seconds to develop a deep, dark sear. Toss once and sear for another 30 seconds. Remove the beef to a plate — you want it cooked to medium, not beyond. In the same screaming-hot wok (add a splash more oil if needed), add the red onion wedges and garlic. Toss constantly for 90 seconds — you want the onion to char slightly at the edges while staying crunchy at the core. Add the tomato wedges and ají amarillo paste, toss for 30 seconds, then return the beef. Pour the soy sauce and red wine vinegar directly into the center of the wok — they will spit, steam, and partially vaporize, creating the characteristic 'chifa smoke' of lomo saltado. Toss everything together vigorously for 60 seconds.

Add the fried potato strips to the wok and toss once with the stir-fried beef and vegetables — just once or twice; you want the potatoes to pick up the dark, glossy sauce without going soggy from excessive stirring. Scatter the fresh coriander over the top and toss again. Taste a piece of beef and a potato: the beef should be savory, slightly charred, warm-spiced from the cumin, with the sour brightness of vinegar; the potato should be crisp outside and carry a coating of the dark sauce. Serve immediately, piling directly alongside white rice. The potatoes should still have their crunch — lomo saltado waits for no one.

recipes.name: Loukoumades
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Neutral oil for frying (sunflower or rice bran)
Walnuts, lightly toasted and roughly crushed

steps: Combine the flour, instant yeast, salt, and sugar in a large bowl. Make a well in the center and pour in all of the warm water at once. Mix vigorously with a wooden spoon or your hand for 2–3 minutes until a completely smooth, thick, pourable batter forms — it should look like a very thick pancake batter or a soft porridge, not a kneadable dough. There should be no lumps. Cover the bowl tightly with clingfilm and leave in a warm place (28–30C) to ferment for 1 hour. The batter is ready when it has doubled in volume, is visibly bubbly throughout, and smells yeasty-sweet. Do not stir the proofed batter — you want to preserve the air bubbles that the yeast has worked to produce, as they are what make the loukoumades puff and become light inside.

Gently warm the honey in a small saucepan over very low heat, or in a heatproof bowl set over hot water, until it is pourable and fluid — around 40–50C. Do not boil it. Warm honey soaks into freshly fried loukoumades almost instantly, whereas cold honey sits on the surface and creates a thick, sticky coating that feels cloying. Set the warm honey, ground cinnamon, and roughly crushed toasted walnuts in small separate bowls next to the frying setup. The loukoumades must be dressed the instant they leave the oil, so everything needs to be in place before the first fritter hits the fat. Speed is the whole game at this stage.

Heat the frying oil in a wide, deep pot to 175–180C / 350–360F. Using two wet spoons or a small ice cream scoop dipped in water between batches, drop heaped tablespoon-sized portions of batter into the oil without crowding — 6–8 at a time is typical. The batter will immediately puff and begin rolling in the oil. Do not move them for the first 30 seconds. After they have set on the bottom, they will begin to rotate on their own as the steam inside expands and shifts their center of gravity — this self-rolling is the sign of properly fermented batter and correctly heated oil. Fry for 3–4 minutes total, turning once or twice with a slotted spoon to encourage even color, until they are a deep, uniform golden-amber. Remove with a slotted spoon, shaking off excess oil.

Transfer the hot loukoumades to a shallow bowl or plate. Immediately drizzle the warm honey generously over them — use more than you think you need, because the honey is partly absorbed by the hot dough. Dust liberally with ground cinnamon, then scatter the roughly crushed toasted walnuts over the top. The whole dressing process should take no more than 30 seconds per batch. Loukoumades must be eaten hot: the contrast between the crispy exterior and the steaming hollow interior is the defining characteristic of a great loukoumade, and within 5 minutes the exterior softens from the honey's moisture and the steam inside. At Greek festivals and street stalls, loukoumades are served in paper cones and eaten standing, immediately, without ceremony.

recipes.name: Ma Po Tofu

ingredients.name: Silken or soft tofu, cut into 2 cm cubes
Dried red chili flakes (er jing tiao or facing heaven chili)
Cornstarch mixed with 60 g cold water (slurry)

steps: Bring a pot of lightly salted water to a boil. Gently slide the tofu cubes in and blanch for 2 minutes. This firms the tofu slightly and removes any beany raw flavor. Drain carefully — the cubes are fragile. Leave to drain on a clean kitchen towel.

Heat oil in a wok over high heat until shimmering. Add ground pork and stir-fry, breaking up all clumps, until fully cooked and beginning to crisp at the edges — about 3 minutes. Push to the side. Add doubanjiang and fry in the oil for 1 minute until the oil turns red and the paste smells toasted. Add fermented black beans, garlic, ginger, and chili flakes. Fry together for 1 more minute.

Pour in the stock and soy sauce. Gently slide the tofu cubes into the sauce using a ladle or your hand — never stir vigorously. Shake the wok by the handle to distribute without breaking the tofu. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 3–4 minutes, occasionally tilting and swirling the wok rather than stirring.

Stir the cornstarch slurry to redistribute (it settles quickly). Drizzle it around the edges of the wok in three additions, gently shaking between each, allowing the sauce to thicken before adding more. The sauce should thicken to coat the tofu in a glossy, clingy layer — not thick like gravy, but substantial enough to cling.

Slide the ma po tofu from the wok into a serving bowl. Scatter freshly ground Sichuan peppercorn and green onion over the top. The Sichuan pepper must be added at the very end — it goes on top as a finishing element, not cooked into the sauce, to preserve its numbing, floral volatility. Serve immediately over steamed rice.

recipes.name: Maafe (West African Peanut Stew)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Bone-in lamb shoulder, cut into 5 cm pieces
Canned whole tomatoes, crushed by hand
Fresh scotch bonnet or habanero, whole

steps: Season lamb pieces generously with salt and pepper. Heat a neutral oil in a large, heavy pot over high heat until shimmering. Sear the lamb in batches — do not crowd the pot — for 3–4 minutes per side until deeply browned on at least two surfaces. Transfer to a plate. Browning is not merely aesthetic: it builds the Maillard flavor compounds that will give the stew its deep, roasted depth.

In the same pot over medium heat, add the diced onion and cook, scraping up the fond, for 5 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the crushed tomatoes and stir, scraping all the caramelized bits from the bottom — these dissolve into the sauce. Add the whole scotch bonnet pepper (leave whole and intact to control heat — puncturing it releases much more capsaicin). Pour in the stock and add the seared lamb back. Bring to a simmer.

Ladle a cup of the hot broth into a bowl and whisk the peanut butter into it until smooth — this tempers the peanut butter so it doesn't seize up when added to the pot. Pour the smooth peanut mixture back into the pot, stirring to fully incorporate. Add the sweet potato cubes. Simmer uncovered for 35–40 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes, until the lamb is pull-apart tender, the sweet potato is soft, and the sauce has thickened to a glossy, rich stew that coats the spoon.

Remove the whole scotch bonnet pepper before serving — discard it. Taste the stew and adjust salt, seasoning cube, and heat to your preference. If the stew is too thick, add a splash of stock. If too thin, simmer uncovered for 5 more minutes. The sauce should be thick enough to mound slightly on a serving spoon. Serve over white rice or with white bread, with the lamb and sweet potato prominently visible.

recipes.name: Baked Mac and Cheese
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Sharp cheddar, freshly grated (plus Gruyère optional)
Kosher salt, dry mustard, white pepper, nutmeg
Panko breadcrumbs toasted in butter (for topping)

steps: Bring a large pot of generously salted water to a rolling boil. Cook the macaroni for 2 minutes less than the package directions — it will finish cooking in the oven. The pasta should have a distinct white core when bitten. Drain but do not rinse — the surface starch helps the sauce cling. Toss with a small knob of butter immediately to prevent sticking.

In a heavy saucepan over medium heat, melt the butter until foaming. Add the flour all at once and stir constantly with a whisk for 2 minutes — this is the roux, and it must cook long enough to lose the raw flour taste. Gradually add the warm milk, a ladleful at a time, whisking vigorously after each addition until smooth before adding more. Once all the milk is incorporated, add mustard, nutmeg, salt, and white pepper. Cook, stirring, until the sauce thickens enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes.

Remove the béchamel from heat. Add the grated cheese in three additions, stirring between each until fully melted before adding more. The sauce must be off the heat — adding cheese to boiling sauce will cause the proteins to seize and become grainy. Stir gently in a figure-eight motion rather than vigorously, which can break the emulsion.

Preheat oven to 180°C. Fold the drained pasta into the cheese sauce until every piece is well coated. Pour into a buttered 23x33cm baking dish. Top evenly with the buttered panko breadcrumbs. Bake for 20–25 minutes until the breadcrumb topping is deep golden-brown and the edges are visibly bubbling.

Remove from the oven and rest for 5 minutes. This brief rest allows the sauce to tighten slightly so that portions hold their shape when scooped. Serve in generous portions, ensuring each scoop gets some of the golden crust from the top and the creamy pasta beneath.

recipes.name: French Macaron Shells (Italian Meringue Method)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Aged egg whites — divided: raw whites for tant-pour-tant, and whites for meringue
Caster sugar (for the Italian meringue syrup)

steps: Weigh the almond flour and icing sugar precisely — macarons are a baking formula, not a recipe, and a 5g deviation in a 300g batch will affect the outcome. Pulse them together in a food processor for 30 seconds to break up any clumps and homogenise the particle sizes. Sift through a fine-mesh sieve into a large bowl, discarding any coarse almond particles that won't pass through — these lumpy particles create bumps on the macaron surface. If your almond flour is coarser, re-process and sift again. The tant-pour-tant (equal-weight almond and sugar) should be completely smooth, dry, and fine, like very fine sand. Add the first portion of aged egg whites (approximately half the total egg whites) to the tant-pour-tant and mix with a spatula until you have a thick, paste-like batter. Cover and set aside.

Combine the caster sugar and water in a small, clean saucepan. Heat over medium-high heat without stirring — stirring encourages crystallisation. Fit a candy thermometer or use an instant-read thermometer. While the syrup heats, begin whipping the second portion of aged egg whites with the cream of tartar in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment, on medium speed. When the syrup reaches 115°C (239°F), increase the mixer to high speed. When the syrup reaches exactly 118–121°C (244–250°F, soft-ball stage), remove from heat immediately. With the mixer running on high, pour the hot syrup in a slow, thin, steady stream down the inside of the bowl — never directly onto the whisk, which will spin it into sugar threads on the bowl sides. The hot syrup cooks and stabilises the meringue as it is incorporated.

After incorporating all the syrup into the whipping whites, continue beating on high for 8–10 minutes until the meringue reaches firm, glossy peaks and the bowl feels just warm — not hot — to the touch. The Italian meringue should be bright white, very glossy, and hold stiff peaks that curl slightly at the tip. If you lift the whisk and turn it upside down, the peak should hold its shape without drooping. The meringue must cool to around 40°C before you fold it into the almond paste — too hot and it will melt the fat in the almond flour; too cold and it will stiffen and resist folding. The meringue can rest, covered, for up to 10 minutes while you prepare for the macaronage.

Add the Italian meringue to the almond paste in three additions, folding with a wide silicone spatula. The technique is called macaronage: use the flat of the spatula to smear the batter against the side of the bowl in a sweeping motion, rotating the bowl with your other hand. This deliberately deflates the meringue to achieve the correct ribbon consistency. The macaronage is complete when the batter falls from the spatula in a thick, continuous ribbon — draw the spatula through the batter and lift: it should flow back together in 10 seconds, erasing the trace completely. If the trace takes more than 15 seconds to disappear, continue folding. If the batter flows like liquid, you have gone too far. The correct batter moves slowly, like lava, and when a ribbon of it falls onto the surface it sinks back in 8–10 seconds. Most batches take 40–60 fold strokes total.

Pipe the batter onto parchment-lined baking sheets in 3.5 cm rounds, holding the piping bag perpendicular to the sheet at a height of 1 cm. After piping, firmly tap the baking sheet against the counter 5 times to release trapped air bubbles. Burst any bubbles with a toothpick. Let the piped rounds rest at room temperature for 30–60 minutes, until a dry skin forms on the surface — when you touch one lightly with the tip of a finger, it should not stick and should feel slightly tacky but firm. This skin is what forces the expanding air to push out through the bottom during baking, creating the characteristic ruffled feet. Bake at 150°C (300°F) in a convection oven (or 160°C / 320°F conventional) for 13–15 minutes. Rotate the pan at the 7-minute mark. The shells are done when they lift cleanly off the parchment with no resistance.

recipes.name: Macarons Parisiens
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Weigh the almond flour and icing sugar precisely — macaron ratios are unforgiving. Pulse them together in a food processor for 30 seconds to break up any lumps and create an ultra-fine, uniform tant-pour-tant. Pass the mixture through a fine-mesh sieve, discarding any coarse almond pieces that remain. Re-sift if needed — visible almond chunks will dome poorly and crack the surface. The goal is a powder as fine and uniform as commercial cake flour.

In a perfectly clean, fat-free bowl, begin whisking the aged egg whites with the cream of tartar at medium speed until foamy. Add the caster sugar in a thin, slow stream once soft peaks form, and continue whisking at medium-high until you reach stiff, glossy peaks. Aged whites (left uncovered in the fridge for 24–72 hours) have lower moisture and whip more stably. Crucially, do not over-whip — the meringue should be smooth and glossy, not dry and clumped. The finished meringue should hold a stiff, straight peak that does not curl.

Add all the tant-pour-tant to the stiff meringue at once. Begin the macaronage: using a flexible spatula, fold and press the batter against the side of the bowl in broad sweeping strokes, deflating the meringue deliberately. The goal is to knock out enough air so the batter flows smoothly but retains enough structure to hold piped rounds without spreading flat. Test frequently by lifting the spatula and letting batter fall — when it flows in a thick, slow, continuous ribbon and the ribbon settles back into the batter within 10 seconds, leaving a trace that smooths in 30 seconds, stop folding immediately. Over-folding is the most common failure.

Pipe the batter onto parchment- or silpat-lined baking sheets in rounds of about 3.5 cm, holding the piping bag perpendicular to the tray and releasing pressure before lifting. Bang the tray firmly on the counter three or four times to pop any surface bubbles. Leave the piped shells to rest uncovered at room temperature until they are dry and matt to the touch — they should not stick to a finger pressed very lightly. This skin formation is essential for foot development; in humid conditions this can take 45–90 minutes. Bake at 150 C / 300 F (fan-forced) for 13–15 minutes, rotating the tray halfway. Shells are done when they can be gently nudged off the parchment without sticking — they will still feel slightly soft at the top but firm at the base.

Bring the cream to a simmer and pour it over the finely chopped chocolate. Wait 60 seconds without stirring, then begin stirring from the center outward in small circles, gradually incorporating the chocolate until fully melted and smooth. Add the softened butter and stir to incorporate. The ganache should be glossy and fluid at this point. Allow to cool at room temperature until it reaches a pipeable consistency — about 1–2 hours, or accelerate by briefly chilling, stirring every 15 minutes.

Match shells in pairs by size. Pipe a mound of ganache onto the flat side of one shell — about 1 cm high, leaving a 3 mm border. Press the matching shell on top with a gentle twisting motion until the ganache reaches the edge. The filling should be clearly visible at the sandwiched seam. Refrigerate the assembled macarons for at least 24 hours before serving — this maturation period is non-negotiable: the moisture from the filling migrates into the shell, transforming it from crisp to the signature slight-chewy-outside, soft-inside texture.

recipes.name: French Macarons
steps: Pulse almond flour and icing sugar together in a food processor for 30 seconds to eliminate any lumps and evenly combine. Sift through a fine-mesh sieve. Discard any large almond pieces that won't pass. The mixture should feel like talc — if it clumps, your almond flour is too moist; spread it on a sheet tray and dry in a 100 C oven for 10 minutes.

Cook caster sugar and water in a small saucepan to 118 C (soft-ball stage), without stirring. Meanwhile, whip the aged egg whites with salt to soft peaks on medium speed. When the syrup hits 118 C, increase mixer to high and pour the syrup in a thin, steady stream down the bowl wall (not onto the whisk). Whip on high for 8-10 minutes until the bowl is no longer hot to the touch and the meringue is stiff and glossy.

Add the tant-pour-tant to the Italian meringue in two additions. Macaronage: using a wide rubber spatula, fold by pressing the batter flat against the side of the bowl, then scooping from the bottom and folding over. Work decisively — this is not a gentle fold. You are deliberately deflating the meringue to achieve the correct flow. Perform roughly 40-50 strokes. Stop when the batter flows from the spatula in a thick, continuous ribbon that disappears back into the bowl within 10 seconds.

Pipe 3.5 cm rounds onto silicone-mat-lined baking sheets, spacing 3 cm apart. Tap the sheet firmly on the counter 3-4 times to release large air bubbles. Let rest at room temperature for 30-45 minutes until the surface forms a dry skin — it should not stick to your fingertip. Bake one sheet at a time at 150 C (fan-forced) for 14-16 minutes. Shells are done when they slide cleanly off the mat with no resistance at the base.

Beat the softened butter alone for 3 minutes until very pale and fluffy. Add icing sugar in three additions, beating for 1 minute between each. The finished buttercream should be smooth, ivory, and stiff enough to hold a peak but soft enough to pipe easily. Add 1 tsp of vanilla or other flavouring, and a pinch of salt to balance.

Match shells by size into pairs. Pipe a generous, even disc of buttercream onto the flat side of one shell, leaving a 2 mm border. Sandwich with its pair and press gently until the filling reaches the edge. Refrigerate, uncovered, for 24 hours — this is the 'maturation' step. The moisture from the filling softens the shell interior to its characteristic chewy texture. Bring to room temperature for 20 minutes before serving.

recipes.name: Classic Madeleines
steps: Place the butter in a light-coloured saucepan over medium heat. It will melt, foam, subside, then foam a second time. At the second foam, swirl constantly and watch the milk solids on the bottom: they will turn from blonde to golden to hazelnut-brown (noisette). At the first scent of toasty hazelnuts, immediately pour the butter into a cold bowl to stop cooking. Cool to room temperature — it should be liquid but not warm.

In a large bowl, whisk together the eggs, caster sugar, and honey. Whisk vigorously — by hand for 3 to 4 minutes, or with an electric whisk on high for 2 minutes — until the mixture has roughly doubled in volume, turned pale ivory, and falls from the whisk in a thick ribbon that holds its shape on the surface for a few seconds before dissolving.

Sift the flour, baking powder, and salt directly over the ribbon mixture. Add the lemon zest and vanilla extract. Using a large spatula, fold gently with wide, sweeping, under-over strokes until just combined — no dry streaks, but don't over-mix. Finally, pour the cooled browned butter around the edge of the batter and fold it in the same way until fully incorporated. The batter will be smooth, glossy, and noticeably heavier.

Press cling film directly onto the surface of the batter and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or up to 24 hours. Meanwhile, butter the madeleine molds generously and dust with flour, tapping out the excess; refrigerate the prepared pan too. The cold shock when cold batter meets a hot oven creates the distinctive hump — do not skip this step.

Preheat the oven to 200°C (390°F) for at least 20 minutes. Fill the chilled, floured molds to three-quarters full. Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until the edges are deep golden and pulling away from the shell, the hump has risen fully and the peak is just set. Remove immediately and turn out onto a rack. Eat within 30 minutes — they are a different food after an hour.

recipes.name: Mafé (West African Groundnut Stew)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Canned whole tomatoes, crushed by hand
Dried chile flakes or scotch bonnet

steps: Pat the beef cubes completely dry with paper towels — moisture is the enemy of a good sear. Season aggressively with salt. Heat a heavy pot or Dutch oven over high heat until a drop of water evaporates on contact. Add oil and sear the beef in a single layer, without crowding, for 3–4 minutes per side until deeply browned on all surfaces. Work in batches. The goal is a dark mahogany crust on every face, not grey steaming.

In the same pot with the beef fond, add the diced onion and cook over medium heat, scraping up the fond constantly, for 8–10 minutes until deeply golden and translucent. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for another 2 minutes, stirring, until fragrant. The onion should be well beyond translucent — approaching golden-amber — before the liquids are added. This caramelization provides the sweet, savory undertone that balances the peanut butter.

Add the crushed tomatoes to the aromatics and cook 5 minutes, stirring, until the tomatoes darken and the oil separates at the edges — this is pinçage, even if the French don't claim this stew. Add the peanut butter and stir until fully dissolved into the tomato base. The paste will initially resist blending — press it against the hot pot wall and stir until smooth. Return the seared beef, add the stock and chile, bring to a boil, then reduce to the lowest simmer. Cook partially covered for 60 minutes.

Add the cubed sweet potato to the stew. Stir to submerge and coat in the peanut sauce. Continue simmering uncovered for 25–30 more minutes, until the sweet potato is fully tender and beginning to break down at the edges — those broken edges will thicken the stew further. Taste aggressively: mafé needs significant salt. Adjust with salt and chile. Serve over white rice or with thiéboudienne bread for soaking.

recipes.name: Malabi
steps: Measure out 100 ml of the cold milk into a small bowl. Add all the cornstarch and whisk vigorously until not a single lump remains — the mixture should look like thin white paint with no dry powder specks floating at the surface or clinging to the bowl. This slurry technique prevents the starch from seizing into lumps when it hits the hot liquid. The remaining 400 ml of milk goes into the saucepan.

Pour the remaining 400 ml of milk into a medium saucepan along with the cream and sugar. Warm over medium heat, stirring gently until the sugar dissolves. When the mixture is steaming and just below simmering, pour in the cornstarch slurry in a thin, steady stream while whisking continuously and vigorously. Do not stop whisking. The mixture will begin to thicken within 2–3 minutes. Continue whisking over medium-low heat until the first large, lazy bubbles break the surface — this activates the starch fully. Remove from heat immediately and whisk in rose water and orange blossom water. The residual fragrance is delicate; heat destroys it quickly, so add off the flame.

Pour the hot pudding into individual serving cups or glasses — about 120–150 ml per cup. If the surface has a skin forming, pass it through a fine sieve as you pour for a perfectly smooth top. Tap each cup gently on the counter to settle. Leave uncovered at room temperature for 15 minutes until the surface is no longer steaming, then cover with plastic wrap pressed directly onto the surface (to prevent a skin) and refrigerate for at least 2 hours. The pudding is best served cold — the rose water and orange blossom flavors bloom more clearly when chilled.

Combine sugar and water in a small saucepan over medium heat. Stir until the sugar dissolves then bring to a simmer for 3 minutes without stirring. Remove from heat and stir in rose water and pomegranate molasses or grenadine. The syrup should be a soft blush-pink or dusty rose color. Cool to room temperature — do not pour hot syrup over the cold pudding or it will melt the surface and create a watery pool. The contrast between the cold white pudding and the fragrant rose syrup is the entire point.

Just before serving, spoon 2–3 tablespoons of the room-temperature rose syrup over each chilled malabi cup, letting it pool at the surface edges and seep slightly down the sides. Scatter roughly chopped pistachios over the center — they provide the textural contrast that makes the dessert. Add a few dried rose petals and a pinch of desiccated coconut. Serve immediately while the pudding is still cold and the garnishes are fresh and crisp. Malabi does not wait well once garnished — the nuts soften in the syrup.

recipes.name: Manakeesh
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: In a large bowl, combine warm water, sugar, and yeast. Stir and let sit for 5 minutes if using active dry yeast (instant can go straight in with the flour). Add flour, salt, and olive oil. Mix with your hand or a wooden spoon until no dry flour remains and a shaggy, cohesive dough forms. The dough should be soft, slightly tacky, and pull together into one mass. Turn out onto an unfloured surface and knead for 6–8 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should not stick aggressively to the surface — a light tack is correct.

Form the dough into a smooth ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, and cover with a damp cloth or plastic wrap. Proof in a warm spot (28–32 C) for 45–60 minutes, until doubled in size. Street bakers in Beirut do a single warm rise at 40 C for 30 minutes; home bakers can also proof in a cold fridge overnight for a better flavour and a slower rise. The dough is ready when it looks puffy and jiggly and a finger poke leaves a slow-filling indent.

Combine za'atar spice blend and olive oil in a small bowl and stir into a thick, spreadable paste. The ratio should be roughly 3 parts za'atar to 2 parts oil — thick enough to coat a spoon and not run freely, but fluid enough to spread easily without tearing the dough. Taste the paste: it should be assertively herby, sour, and savory. Add more za'atar if it tastes only of oil; add more oil if it clumps dryly. Let the paste rest for 2 minutes for the herbs to hydrate slightly.

Preheat your oven to its maximum temperature — 250–270 C — with a baking stone or heavy baking sheet on the center rack for at least 30 minutes. Divide the proofed dough into equal balls (about 150 g each for individual portions). On a lightly floured surface, press and stretch each ball into a round disc 5–6 mm thick and roughly 20 cm in diameter. The edge should be slightly thicker than the center. Spoon 2–3 tablespoons of za'atar paste onto the center of each round and use the back of the spoon to spread it to within 1 cm of the edge in an even layer.

Slide the topped manakeesh onto the screaming-hot baking stone or preheated sheet. Bake at maximum oven heat for 6–8 minutes, until the edges are golden-brown and crisped, the za'atar paste is bubbling and fragrant, and the underside is golden-brown and pulls away from the surface with a crunch. The za'atar topping will darken noticeably — this is expected and correct. Serve immediately: manakeesh is a bread that must be eaten hot, folded in half like a soft taco, and consumed within minutes of baking.

recipes.name: Thai Mango Sticky Rice
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Glutinous (sweet) rice, soaked 2+ hours and drained
Palm sugar or light brown sugar
Ripe Ataulfo (honey) mangoes, peeled and sliced

steps: Cover the raw glutinous rice with cold water by at least 5 cm and soak for a minimum of 2 hours, ideally overnight. Drain completely through a fine-mesh sieve before steaming. Do not skip this step — soaking allows the rice to steam evenly all the way through without drying out.

Line a bamboo or metal steamer basket with damp cheesecloth or a banana leaf. Spread the drained rice in an even layer no more than 4 cm deep. Steam over briskly boiling water for 20–25 minutes, flipping the rice mass halfway through. The rice is done when the grains are translucent, sticky, and tender all the way through.

Combine the coconut milk, sugar, and salt in a small saucepan. Warm over medium-low heat, stirring, until the sugar and salt are fully dissolved. Do not boil — you want a warm, fluid cream, not a reduced sauce. Reserve 4 tablespoons of this liquid in a small bowl to use as the thin drizzle sauce for plating; keep the rest warm.

Transfer the hot steamed rice to a wide bowl. Pour the warm seasoned coconut cream (reserving the 4 tbsp set aside earlier) over the rice all at once. Fold gently with a wooden spoon or rice paddle — cut through the center and fold the sides over, rotating. Don't stir vigorously or the rice will turn gluey.

Cover the bowl tightly and rest for 15 minutes at room temperature. This allows the rice to fully absorb the coconut cream and the texture to stabilize — freshly dressed rice is too soft and wet to plate neatly.

Mound a generous portion of warm sticky rice onto a shallow plate or bowl. Arrange sliced mango alongside or fanning over the rice. Drizzle the reserved thin coconut sauce (the 4 tbsp set aside in step 3) over the rice and mango. Scatter sesame seeds over the top. Serve immediately.

recipes.name: Mantou (Chinese Steamed Buns)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: All-purpose flour or low-protein Chinese white flour (medium gluten)

steps: Dissolve the sugar in the warm milk, then add the yeast and let it bloom for 5 minutes until foamy. Combine with the flour and salt in a bowl. Bring together into a rough dough, then turn out and knead for 10-12 minutes by hand, or 6-8 minutes in a stand mixer with a dough hook, until perfectly smooth and elastic. Add the oil in the last 2 minutes of kneading. Unlike bread dough, mantou dough should be dry enough to handle without sticking — if it sticks, dust with flour, not water.

Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a damp cloth, and proof in a warm place (28-30 C) for 60 minutes, or until doubled in size. Do not rush this proof — a slow, even rise develops a more uniform, finely bubbled crumb than a fast one.

Turn the dough out onto a clean surface. Roll it into a flat rectangle about 1 cm thick. Roll it up tightly from one short end into a log — this lamination creates the layered internal structure. Cut the log into 6-8 equal oval portions. Place each bun cut-side up on a small square of parchment paper. Cover with a damp cloth and let rest for 25-30 minutes for the second proof.

Bring the steamer water to a rolling boil before placing the buns inside. Leave 3-4 cm space between each bun as they expand. Cover with a tight lid and steam over high heat for 12-15 minutes depending on size. Critical: do not lift the lid during steaming. When the time is up, turn off the heat and leave the lid on for 5 full minutes before opening — the rest prevents the sudden temperature drop that causes the surface to shrink and wrinkle.

recipes.name: Mantu
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine flour and salt, make a well, and pour in the warm water gradually, mixing with a fork until a shaggy dough forms. Turn onto a work surface and knead for 8-10 minutes until smooth, elastic, and not sticky. Mantu dough should be slightly stiffer than pasta dough — it needs to hold its pleats under the pressure of steaming. Form into a ball, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and rest for at least 45 minutes.

In a wide skillet, cook the diced onion in a small amount of oil over medium heat, stirring frequently, for 15-20 minutes until deeply caramelized and sweet — golden-brown, not pale. Add the ground beef, breaking it into fine crumbles, and cook until no pink remains. Add the spices and salt, stir for 2 minutes, then taste. The filling should be highly seasoned, as the dumpling dough dilutes the flavor. Spread on a plate to cool completely before filling.

Divide the rested dough into manageable portions. On a lightly floured surface, roll each portion as thin as possible — aim for 2mm, almost translucent. Cut into squares of 8-10cm. Mantu wrappers are slightly thicker than Chinese dumpling wrappers to withstand steaming, but thin enough to be delicate. Keep cut wrappers under a damp cloth.

Place a generous teaspoon of cooled filling in the center of each square — do not overfill or the pleats will split. The traditional mantu fold: bring all four corners up to meet at the top, then pinch the four seams shut, creating a 'four-petal' shape with a gathered top. Press the seams firmly so no steam can escape during cooking. Place formed mantu on a lightly oiled surface.

Stir together the yogurt, minced garlic, and a pinch of salt in a small saucepan. Warm very gently over the lowest possible heat, stirring constantly — yogurt must never boil or it will curdle. The goal is warmed through, not hot: 40-45 C (104-113 F). Taste and adjust salt. The sauce should be pourable and smooth.

Oil the steamer basket generously to prevent sticking. Place mantu with space between each — they expand as they steam. Steam over vigorously boiling water for 20-22 minutes until the wrappers are translucent and cooked through, not gummy. To serve: spread warmed garlic yogurt on the plate, arrange the steamed mantu on top, and finish with a drizzle of olive oil, a shower of dried mint, and optionally a spoonful of tomato-based chili oil. The mantu arrive at the table glistening.

recipes.name: Maple Bourbon Glaze
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Pure maple syrup (Grade A dark, robust taste)
Straight bourbon (100-proof preferred for flavor retention after cooking)
Fine sea salt and cracked black pepper

steps: Whisk together the maple syrup, bourbon, soy sauce, mustard, garlic, salt, and pepper in a small saucepan until fully combined and smooth. The mustard will need a few extra seconds of whisking to fully integrate. Taste the raw mixture — it will be intensely sweet with raw alcohol and sharp mustard. These edges will round significantly during cooking.

Bring the mixture to a boil over medium heat, stirring frequently. Once boiling, reduce to a steady simmer and cook for 8–12 minutes, stirring every 30 seconds, until the glaze has reduced by approximately half and coats the back of a spoon heavily. Watch carefully in the last 2 minutes — maple syrup glazes go from perfect to scorched very quickly. The alcohol will burn off in the first 2–3 minutes of simmering. Remove from heat when a finger drawn through the spoon coating holds a clean line for 5 seconds.

recipes.name: Mapo Tofu Sauce
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Scallions, white and green parts separated

steps: Place Sichuan peppercorns in a cold, dry wok or skillet. Heat over medium-low, shaking and stirring constantly. Toast until the peppercorns are fragrant — about 2–3 minutes. They should smell citrusy, floral, and slightly camphoraceous. Be careful: over-toasted Sichuan pepper turns bitter and loses the numbing hydroxy-alpha-sanshool compound that defines ma la. Immediately remove from the heat and grind coarsely in a mortar. The ground pepper should look like coarse black pepper.

Heat oil in a wok over medium heat. Add doubanjiang and stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until the oil turns deep red and the paste separates slightly. This step — frying the bean paste in oil — is called chao hong you ('frying red oil') and it is the flavor foundation of mapo tofu. Add minced garlic, ginger, and fermented black beans. Stir-fry for another 90 seconds until everything is aromatic and the raw garlic smell has mellowed. The paste will smell deeply savory, fermented, and slightly sharp.

Increase heat to high and add ground pork. Stir-fry briskly, breaking up any clumps, until the pork is fully cooked through and no pink remains — about 3 minutes. The pork should be in small, separate granules coated in the red chili paste, not large clumps. Each grain of pork should be individually seasoned by the doubanjiang. Once cooked, add the white parts of the scallions and stir for 30 seconds.

Add stock and soy sauce. Bring to a boil, stirring to incorporate all the stuck-on paste from the wok bottom. Reduce heat to a steady simmer and cook for 5 minutes to allow the flavors to meld. The sauce will be a rich, deep red. Taste and adjust salt with soy sauce. This is the moment to add silken tofu if serving as mapo tofu: add 400g silken tofu cut into 2.5 cm cubes, pushing them gently into the sauce with a spoon (never stirring or they will break). Simmer 3–4 minutes to heat the tofu through.

Give the cornstarch slurry a final stir (starch settles quickly). Pour in a slow, steady stream around the edges of the sauce, stirring gently. The sauce will thicken almost immediately. For tofu: use the back of a spoon to gently push the tofu, never stir. The sauce should be thick enough to coat tofu cubes and not pool excessively on the plate. Ladle into bowls. Finish with a generous shower of ground Sichuan peppercorns and the sliced green scallion tops. The pepper should be added last — heat destroys its numbing compounds.

recipes.name: Mapo Tofu

ingredients.name: Scallion, green parts only, thinly sliced

steps: Cut the tofu into 2cm cubes and place carefully in a bowl. Bring a pot of lightly salted water to a gentle boil. Slide the tofu cubes in and blanch for 2 minutes — do not stir aggressively, as silken tofu shatters easily. Drain with a spider or slotted spoon onto a plate lined with kitchen paper. This step firms the tofu surface slightly, seasons it from within, and removes any beany off-flavours — it is the difference between mapo tofu with clean, distinct cubes and a broken, murky mess.

Heat the oil in a wok or wide heavy pan over high heat until wisps of smoke appear. Add the ground pork and spread it into a thin layer. Let it sear undisturbed for 90 seconds until the bottom is golden and fat has rendered. Break it up and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3–4 more minutes until all pink is gone and the pork has rendered its fat and some pieces are golden and slightly crisp. Do not drain the fat — it carries the chili and fermented flavour into the sauce.

Add the doubanjiang to the wok and stir-fry with the pork for 2 minutes over high heat until the paste darkens from red to a deep rust-brown and the oil in the wok turns a vivid crimson — this is the hallmark of properly fried doubanjiang. Add the fermented black beans, garlic, and ginger; stir-fry for 1 more minute. Add the dried chili flakes. The wok should smell intensely of fermented chili, garlic, and caramelised pork — deeply savoury and slightly harsh in the raw stage, which will mellow once the stock goes in.

Pour the stock into the wok and scrape up any stuck bits from the bottom. Bring to a simmer, then gently slide in the blanched tofu cubes using a spatula. Add the soy sauce. Stir by gently rocking the wok and using a spatula to move the sauce — never stir through the tofu with a spoon or it will shatter. Simmer gently for 4–5 minutes so the tofu absorbs the sauce from the outside inward. The sauce will thin from the tofu's water — the cornstarch slurry in the next step will bring it back.

Give the cornstarch slurry a quick stir (it settles fast) and pour it around the edge of the wok in a slow, thin stream, gently rocking the wok as you add it. Cook for 30–60 seconds until the sauce thickens to a glossy, coating consistency that clings to the tofu. Remove from heat. Sprinkle the toasted, ground Sichuan peppercorn over the top — do not add it during cooking, or the numbing compounds will dissipate. Scatter the sliced scallion. Serve immediately over steamed rice. The ma (numbing) sensation builds over 30–60 seconds after eating.

recipes.name: Masoor Dal (Red Lentil Soup)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Tarka spices (mustard seeds, cumin seeds, dried red chili, turmeric)

steps: Combine rinsed lentils, tomatoes, ginger-garlic paste, and 2.5 parts water in a medium saucepan. Add a pinch of turmeric. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat, then reduce to a brisk simmer. Cook uncovered for 15–20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until lentils have completely dissolved into the tomatoes and the mixture is thick and smooth. The lentils will turn from orange-red to golden yellow as they cook.

In a small pan or ladle, heat mustard oil over high heat until it begins to smoke lightly (smoking point neutralizes mustard oil's harsh raw flavour). Add mustard seeds and wait for them to pop and splutter. Add cumin seeds — they will darken within 10 seconds. Add dried red chili and fry for 5 seconds. The entire tarka happens in under 30 seconds — have all spices measured and ready before heating the oil.

In the same dal pot, if including raw onion sauté it until golden in 1 tbsp oil, then combine with the dal. Pour the sizzling tarka directly over the surface of the dal in one decisive move. The oil will hit the dal with a dramatic hiss. Stir to incorporate. Add lemon juice, taste and adjust salt. The acidity brightens and lifts the entire dish — add it at the end, never during cooking.

recipes.name: Massaman Curry Paste
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Dried guajillo or dried red Thai chilies, seeded and soaked 20 min
Lemongrass stalks, white part only, thin-sliced
Galangal, fresh or frozen, peeled and rough-chopped
Shallots, halved and dry-roasted in a pan until charred outside
Garlic cloves, dry-roasted in shell until soft
Warm spice blend: cardamom pods (seeds only), cinnamon, cloves

steps: Place a dry skillet over medium heat. Add coriander seeds and toast, shaking frequently, for 2–3 minutes until they begin to pop and smell of warm citrus and earth. Add cumin seeds for the last 60 seconds — they toast faster and burn easily. In the final 30 seconds, add the cardamom seeds, a piece of cinnamon, and 2 cloves. Tip everything onto a cold plate immediately and let cool completely before grinding. A mortar and pestle or spice grinder will work; grind to a fine powder.

Place shallots (halved, skin on) and whole unpeeled garlic cloves in a dry skillet or directly over a gas flame. Cook over medium-high heat, turning occasionally, until the outsides are blackened in patches and the flesh inside is soft and caramelized — 8–12 minutes. Peel and discard the charred skins; the flesh underneath should be jammy and sweet with bitter edges. This char is essential: it builds the smoky depth characteristic of Thai curry pastes made by street vendors who hold aromatics over an open flame.

Drain the soaked chilies and squeeze out excess water. Tear into pieces and place in the mortar with the sliced lemongrass, galangal, and salt. Begin pounding with a rhythmic downward motion — not stirring, pounding. Rotate the pestle to ensure even pulverization. This will take 10–15 minutes of committed work. Add the fibrous materials first: the salt acts as an abrasive, the lemongrass and galangal must be completely broken down to fiber-free smoothness before anything else goes in. If using a food processor, pulse in bursts, scraping down frequently.

Add the peeled roasted shallots and garlic to the mortar and pound them into the paste until fully incorporated. Add the toasted shrimp paste and ground warm spices. Continue pounding until everything is unified — the paste will deepen from brick-red to a dark reddish-brown, almost mahogany, as the shrimp paste and spices integrate. Taste and adjust: it should be complex, fragrant, slightly sweet, earthy, with gentle heat that builds slowly. Store in a jar under a thin layer of oil in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks, or freeze in tablespoon portions.

recipes.name: Matcha Castella
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Warm the whole eggs (in their shells) in hot tap water for 5 minutes. Combine the warmed eggs, sugar, and honey in the bowl of a stand mixer (or use a hand mixer). Beat at high speed for 8-10 minutes until the mixture is very pale, tripled in volume, and holds a thick ribbon that dissolves back in about 10 seconds when the whisk is lifted. The warm eggs help dissolve the sugar and retain air. Do not rush this stage — the aerated egg foam is the only leavener in castella.

Sift the bread flour and matcha powder together twice to ensure even distribution. Sift one-third of the matcha-flour over the egg foam and fold with a large spatula in slow, sweeping movements from the bottom of the bowl — cut down the center, sweep along the bottom, fold up over the top. Rotate the bowl and repeat. Add the remaining flour in two more additions. Fold in the warm milk with the last addition. Stop as soon as no dry streaks remain — every additional fold deflates the foam.

Line a 21 x 10 cm loaf tin with baking paper (parchment), leaving overhang on all sides. Pour in the batter and gently tap the tin on the counter twice to release large air bubbles. Run a skewer through the batter in a figure-eight motion to break any visible bubble clusters. Bake at 160 C (320 F) for 50-60 minutes, rotating once at 30 minutes. The top should be a deep, dark brown — this is correct for castella, not a sign of overcooking. A skewer inserted in the center should come out clean.

Immediately upon removing from the oven, lift the castella out by the paper overhang and wrap the entire loaf tightly in plastic wrap while still hot. The steam trapped inside creates the characteristic moist, tight crumb of authentic castella. Place wrapped in the refrigerator for at least 1 hour (overnight is better). Slice into 2 cm rectangles with a wet knife, wiping the blade between cuts for clean edges.

recipes.name: No-Bake Matcha Cheesecake
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Hot water (just off the boil, for matcha paste)

steps: Crush the digestive biscuits in a food processor to a fine, even sand — no large chunks or sandy dust, a uniform medium crumb. Alternatively, seal them in a zip-lock bag and roll with a rolling pin. Stir in the melted butter until every crumb is evenly coated — the mixture should look like damp sand that just clumps when pressed. Tip into the base of a 20 cm (8 inch) springform tin lined with baking parchment. Use the flat base of a glass to press the crumbs into a compact, even, level layer. Refrigerate for 15 minutes to set the butter.

Submerge the gelatin sheets in cold water for 5–8 minutes until completely floppy and translucent. Lift them out and squeeze out the excess water — the gelatin should weigh almost nothing in your palm. Set aside. For powdered gelatin, sprinkle it over 2 tablespoons of cold water and leave it to absorb into a firm sponge before heating. Gelatin enables the no-bake filling to hold its shape while maintaining a creamy, barely-set texture rather than a rubbery one.

Sift the matcha powder into a small bowl — sifting is non-negotiable, as matcha clumps badly and will leave green specks in the filling if not dispersed. Add the hot water (about 70–80°C, just off the boil — not boiling, which degrades the vivid green and the delicate flavor). Using a small whisk or matcha chasen, whisk in tight 'M' or 'W' motions until the powder is fully dissolved into a smooth, vivid green paste with no lumps. Melt the squeezed gelatin in 2 tablespoons of warm cream in a small saucepan over very low heat, swirling until dissolved. Stir the gelatin into the matcha paste.

Beat the room-temperature cream cheese with the icing sugar and lemon juice until completely smooth and lump-free — 2 minutes with a hand mixer. Fold in the matcha-gelatin paste until evenly colored. In a cold bowl, whip the cold heavy cream to firm peaks. Fold the whipped cream into the matcha cream cheese mixture in three additions, from the bottom up, cutting and folding gently to retain the volume. The final filling should be airy, vivid green, and hold a soft peak.

Pour the filling over the chilled biscuit base and smooth the top with an offset spatula, spreading to the edges. Tap the tin gently on the counter twice to settle any air bubbles. Cover with cling film and refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours, or overnight — the gelatin needs time to set fully and the flavors to develop. Before serving, dust the surface lightly with sifted matcha powder through a fine-mesh sieve. Release the springform and cut with a hot, wiped knife for clean slices.

recipes.name: Matcha Ice Cream
steps: Sift the matcha powder into a wide, shallow bowl to break up any clumps — matcha is finely milled and prone to lumping. Add 3 tablespoons (about 45g) of the measured whole milk, warm but not hot (around 60 C). Using a bamboo chasen (matcha whisk) or a small balloon whisk, whisk the matcha and milk in rapid 'M'-and 'W'-shaped strokes until a smooth, lump-free paste forms. Add the remaining milk gradually, whisking to maintain smoothness. Matcha paste must be completely homogeneous before being added to the custard — a single undissolved lump will leave a bitter green streak in the finished ice cream.

In a medium heatproof bowl, whisk the egg yolks and caster sugar together vigorously for about 2 minutes until the mixture has turned pale, noticeably thickened, and falls from the whisk in a slow, wide ribbon. This is the ribbon stage — it indicates that enough air and emulsification have occurred to give the custard body. The yolks will be ready when they have doubled in volume, turned from deep orange to pale cream-yellow, and the ribbon holds on the surface for 3 seconds before sinking. This step also helps buffer the yolks against scrambling when the hot matcha milk is added.

Combine the matcha milk and remaining heavy cream in a medium saucepan. Heat over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the mixture just begins to steam and small bubbles appear at the edge — about 75 C. Do not boil. Slowly pour about one-third of the hot matcha cream into the yolk mixture while whisking constantly — this is tempering: gradually raising the egg temperature to prevent scrambling. Pour the tempered yolk mixture back into the saucepan with the remaining hot cream. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a silicone spatula in figure-eight patterns and scraping the bottom and corners, until the custard reaches 82 C and coats the back of a spoon cleanly. Add the pinch of salt. Immediately strain through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean bowl set over an ice bath.

Cool the custard base completely over the ice bath, stirring occasionally, then refrigerate for at least 2 hours or overnight until it is thoroughly chilled — around 4 C. Churn in an ice cream machine according to the manufacturer's instructions until the ice cream is the consistency of thick, scoopable soft-serve (about 20 to 25 minutes). Transfer to a chilled container, press parchment paper directly onto the surface to prevent ice crystal formation, and freeze for at least 3 hours before scooping. For a no-churn version: whip 200g of the heavy cream to medium peaks separately, fold into the chilled custard, and freeze in a loaf pan for 5 hours.

recipes.name: Mayonnaise
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Set a medium bowl on a damp folded towel so it cannot spin while you whisk one-handed. Add the egg yolk, mustard, vinegar, and salt and whisk for a full 30 seconds until the mixture is smooth, slightly paler, and slightly thickened. Everything must be at room temperature — a cold yolk emulsifies sluggishly and is far quicker to break. The mustard is not just flavor here: it is a second emulsifier that makes the sauce far more forgiving.

This is the whole game. Whisking constantly and hard, add the oil drop by drop for the first quarter of it — wait until each addition has fully disappeared before adding more. As the mixture thickens and lightens, you can relax to a thin, steady thread of oil, still whisking without pause. The base is grabbing oil droplets and locking them apart in a network; rush it and the network never forms. By the time the oil is in, you will have a thick, pale, jiggling mound.

Taste the emulsion — it will be flat and oily-rich and need brightening. Whisk in the lemon juice for acidity and lift, then adjust salt. If the mayonnaise is stiffer than you want, or looks dull and greasy, whisk in cold water a few drops at a time: it both loosens the sauce and re-tightens a slightly oily-looking emulsion, restoring the satin sheen. Chill at least an hour before serving; the flavors round out and it firms slightly.

recipes.name: Maza
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Barley grains (hulled, for roasting and grinding)

steps: Spread the hulled barley grains in a dry, heavy pan over medium heat and toast, shaking and stirring constantly, for 8 to 12 minutes. The grains darken from pale straw to a warm tan and throw off a popcorn-like, nutty aroma — this roasting (the ancient ?lphita process) is what gives maza its signature toasted flavor and was traditionally how the grain was prepared before milling. Let cool completely before grinding.

Grind the cooled roasted barley to a coarse meal in a mortar, hand mill, or pulse-grinder — aim for a texture between fine flour and cornmeal, with some grit left in. Ancient maza was deliberately coarse, not silky; that rustic body is part of its character. Sift out only the largest unbroken hulls.

Dissolve the salt (and honey, if using) in the warm water. Tip the barley meal into a bowl, add the olive oil and sesame, then pour in the liquid and work it together with your hands. Barley has almost no gluten, so this will never become a smooth elastic dough — instead knead just until it forms a cohesive, dense, slightly tacky mass that holds a shape. Press it together for a minute or two; over-working only dries it out. Let it rest 10 minutes so the meal fully hydrates.

Pat the dough into a flat round about 1.5 cm thick (or several small cakes) and bake on a hot stone or in a dry heavy skillet over medium heat, 6 to 9 minutes per side, until the surface is firm and freckled with golden-brown spots. Without leavening it stays dense and flat — a hearty griddle-cake rather than a fluffy loaf. Eat warm with olive oil and honey, or let it cool and pack it for the road as the ancients did.

recipes.name: Menemen

ingredients.name: Ripe tomatoes, cored and roughly chopped
Green sivri peppers or Italian frying peppers, sliced
Aleppo pepper (pul biber), or mild red pepper flakes

steps: Heat the butter and olive oil together in a wide, shallow pan — ideally a sahan (copper pan) or small cast-iron skillet, 22–24cm — over medium heat. If using onion, add it first and cook for 3–4 minutes until translucent. Add the sliced sivri peppers and cook, stirring occasionally, for 5–7 minutes until the peppers are completely soft, limp, and faintly blistered at the edges. The peppers should be almost sweet by this point — green pepper's bitterness cooks away with time. Season with a pinch of salt.

Add the roughly chopped tomatoes to the peppers, along with half the Aleppo pepper, the salt, and the black pepper. Stir to combine. Increase the heat to medium-high and cook, stirring occasionally and breaking up the tomato pieces with a wooden spoon, for 8–12 minutes until the tomatoes have completely collapsed and the mixture is thick, jammy, and reduced — the water has evaporated and the mixture is clinging to the pan rather than flowing freely. The sauce should be deeply coloured and fragrant.

Beat the eggs lightly in a bowl — just enough to break the yolks and roughly combine, leaving streaks of white visible (these streaks create a marbled effect in the finished dish). Pour the eggs directly over the tomato and pepper base. Using a silicone spatula, fold the eggs gently through the tomato base in slow, wide strokes — pull from the edges inward, letting the tomato base streak through the eggs. Alternatively, leave the eggs mostly whole for a different style: nest the eggs whole on top and cover with a lid for 3 minutes until the whites set but the yolks remain runny.

Remove the pan from the heat. Scatter the remaining Aleppo pepper generously over the top — it should look like a dusting of dark rust-red across the yellow-orange surface. Scatter the chopped parsley. Serve immediately in the pan — menemen is traditionally brought to the table in its cooking vessel with a stack of white bread alongside for tearing and scooping. Do not let it sit: the carry-over heat from the pan will continue cooking the eggs, and the difference between perfect and overcooked is measured in minutes.

recipes.name: Mexican Carnitas

ingredients.name: Pork shoulder (bone-in preferred), cut into 8cm chunks

steps: Place the pork chunks in a wide, heavy Dutch oven or deep skillet. Add the lard, orange juice, orange peel halves (squeezed side down), smashed garlic, bay leaves, oregano, cumin, and salt. Add just enough cold water to barely cover the pork — about 500ml. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook uncovered, maintaining a moderate simmer throughout. Do not cover — you want the liquid to evaporate. After 1 hour, add the condensed milk. Continue cooking for another 1.5–2 hours. As the water evaporates, the pork will transition from braising to frying in the rendered lard.

Once the liquid has evaporated and the pork is frying, begin turning the pieces every 2–3 minutes. The condensed milk will caramelize with the orange sugars, creating dark, lacquered spots. Break larger pieces apart with a spatula as you go. When the pork is a patchwork of deep golden and dark caramelized spots — or transfer to a foil-lined baking sheet and finish under the highest broiler for 5–7 minutes for extra shattering crispiness.

Taste the carnitas and adjust salt. Squeeze the remaining fresh orange juice over the hot meat — the acid will sizzle against the hot lard and brighten the flavor dramatically. Serve immediately on warm corn tortillas with diced white onion, fresh cilantro, salsa verde, and lime wedges. Carnitas are best within 30 minutes of cooking — the texture changes as they cool.

recipes.name: Esquites (Mexican Street Corn Salad)

ingredients.name: Fresh corn kernels (from 4 ears) or frozen

steps: Heat a wide, dry cast-iron skillet or heavy pan over the highest possible heat until you can hold your palm 5cm above the surface for only 1–2 seconds. Add the butter, let it foam and begin to brown, then add the corn kernels in a single, uncrowded layer — you may need to do this in two batches. Do not stir for 2 full minutes. Let the bottom layer of corn make hard contact with the hot pan and char. Then toss once and let it sit for another 90 seconds. The goal is visible black charring on some kernels with others remaining golden — a variety of char is more interesting than uniform browning.

While the corn is still hot, transfer to a bowl. Add the crema, mayonnaise, lime juice, chile powder, and sliced scallions. Toss immediately — the heat from the corn will warm the dressing and help it coat every kernel. Taste and adjust: more lime for brightness, more chile for heat, a pinch of salt if needed. The dressing should be creamy, tangy, and spicy — each bite should have all four elements simultaneously.

Transfer to cups or a serving bowl. Scatter the crumbled cotija generously over the top — it should look like a snow of salty cheese. Add the chopped cilantro. Finish with an extra dusting of chile powder on top for visual contrast and an additional hit of heat. Serve immediately — this is a hot dish and the textural contrast of the charred kernels diminishes as they cool.

recipes.name: Basbousa
steps: Combine the semolina, sugar, and baking powder in a large bowl. Add the yoghurt, melted butter, and rose water. Mix well with a spatula until fully combined — the batter will be thick and grainy, not smooth. Unlike a standard cake batter, it should hold its shape when mounded. Grease a 23x23cm baking pan. Spread the batter evenly with a wet spatula, pressing it into an even layer about 2cm thick. Let rest 15 minutes to allow the semolina to hydrate.

Preheat oven to 180°C (350°F). Score the rested batter into diamond or square shapes with a wet knife, cutting almost all the way through. Press a whole blanched almond into the center of each piece. Bake for 25-30 minutes until the top is golden and the edges are beginning to pull away from the pan. The surface should look slightly firm and dry.

Combine sugar and water in a small saucepan. Bring to a boil over medium heat, stirring only until the sugar dissolves. Once boiling, stop stirring and cook for 5-7 minutes until slightly thickened. Add the lemon juice and cook for 1 more minute (the acid prevents crystallization). Remove from heat and stir in the orange blossom water. The syrup should be ready just before the cake comes out of the oven — it must go hot onto hot.

Pour the hot syrup slowly and evenly over the hot basbousa in a thin, steady stream. Pour in the scored lines first, then over the whole surface. The cake will sizzle and absorb the syrup immediately. You should use all the syrup. Allow to rest at room temperature for at least 30 minutes until fully absorbed and the cake has cooled slightly. Cut along the score lines to serve. Basbousa improves after several hours as the flavors meld.

recipes.name: Mujaddara (Lentils and Rice with Crispy Onion)

ingredients.name: Large yellow onions, halved and thinly sliced

steps: Heat the olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan over medium-high heat. Add all the sliced onions — the pan will be very full. Cook, stirring every 3–4 minutes, for 35–45 minutes. The onions will shrink dramatically, releasing water first, then slowly browning as the water evaporates. In the last 10 minutes, increase heat to high and stir more frequently as the onions caramelize. The goal is deeply browned, almost crispy onions that are sweet and complex. Remove two-thirds of the onions and set aside as the topping. Leave one-third in the pan.

In the same pan with the remaining one-third of the caramelized onions, add the ground cumin, coriander, and allspice. Stir for 30 seconds. Add the rinsed lentils and the water. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook for 15 minutes until the lentils are partially tender but still have a slight bite — they are not done yet. Season generously with salt.

Add the rinsed basmati rice to the partially cooked lentils and stir to combine. Check the water level — there should be enough to just cover the mixture by 1cm. Add a splash more if needed. Bring to a boil, then cover tightly and reduce heat to the lowest setting. Cook for 15 minutes. Do not lift the lid. Remove from heat and let steam, covered, for 10 more minutes. Fluff with a fork. The lentils and rice should be cooked through and have absorbed all the liquid.

Plate the mujaddara in a wide, shallow bowl or deep plate. Pile the reserved caramelized onions on top — do not stir them in; the contrast of the soft, spiced rice-and-lentil base with the crispy, sweet onion crown is the dish. Serve with plain yogurt, a salad of chopped tomato and cucumber, and warm flatbread.

recipes.name: Pocket Pita Bread
