recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine flour, salt, yeast, and sugar. Add warm water and olive oil. Mix until a rough dough forms, then knead by hand for 8 minutes (or 6 minutes in a stand mixer on medium) until smooth and elastic. The dough should be soft but not sticky — it should clear the bowl sides cleanly. Divide into 8 balls (about 90 g each). Cover with a damp towel and rest 10 minutes, then place on a lightly oiled tray, cover, and proof for 1 hour at room temperature until puffy.

Place a baking stone or heavy inverted baking sheet in the oven and preheat to the maximum temperature (250–260 C / 480–500 F) for at least 45 minutes. On a lightly floured surface, roll each dough ball into a thin round 20–22 cm in diameter and about 3–4 mm thick. Even thickness is critical — thick spots won't puff. Transfer to a peel dusted with semolina or cornmeal, or a piece of parchment. Let the rolled pitas rest 5 minutes before baking.

Slide pitas directly onto the preheated stone or sheet pan. Bake for 3–4 minutes — do not open the oven. Watch through the oven glass: within 60–90 seconds the pita should begin to puff up into a balloon. Once fully inflated and lightly spotted with golden-brown, remove with tongs. Stack the hot pitas under a clean towel immediately — the steam inside softens the crust as they cool, creating the signature soft, pliable texture.

recipes.name: Middle Eastern Rice Pilaf with Vermicelli
steps: Rinse the rice in several changes of cold water until the water runs clear, releasing excess surface starch that would make the pilaf gluey. Cover with cold water and soak for 20 minutes. Drain thoroughly in a fine-mesh strainer and pat lightly dry — residual moisture will cause the butter to spatter.

Melt the butter in a heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium heat. Add the pine nuts and toss for 1–2 minutes until golden. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside — they burn quickly. Add the broken vermicelli to the remaining butter and toss constantly for 3–4 minutes until the noodles turn a deep amber-brown and smell of toasted hazelnuts. This is the defining character of the dish.

Add the drained rice to the toasted vermicelli and stir to coat in the butter for 1 minute. Pour in the hot broth, add salt and allspice. Stir once. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to the lowest simmer, cover tightly, and cook for 15 minutes. Remove from heat and steam, covered, for 10 minutes. Do not lift the lid during cooking or steaming.

Fluff the pilaf with a fork, turning gently from the bottom up. Mound onto a warmed serving platter. Scatter the reserved golden pine nuts over the top and finish with the chopped parsley. Serve immediately.

recipes.name: Misir Wot (Red Lentil Stew)

ingredients.name: Niter kibbeh or clarified spiced butter

steps: Place the finely minced onions in a heavy-bottomed pot with no oil over medium heat. Stir every 2–3 minutes for 20–25 minutes — the onions will first release water and steam in it, then dry out and begin to colour. The goal is a reduced, dark-tan, sweet-smelling onion base. This dry caramelization without fat is the traditional Ethiopian method (called 'dry frying' the onions) that gives misir wot its characteristic depth. The onions should shrink to about one-third of their starting volume and turn a warm golden-brown before any fat is added.

Add the niter kibbeh to the caramelized onions and stir until melted. Add the berbere, garlic, and ginger. Stir vigorously and cook over medium heat for 4–6 minutes, stirring constantly — the berbere will foam slightly as it hits the hot fat, then the fat will begin to separate at the edges as the spices cook. The mixture will become a very thick, dark, fragrant paste. The cooking of berbere in fat is non-negotiable: raw berbere tastes sharp and acrid; bloomed berbere tastes rounded, deep, and complex.

Add the rinsed red lentils to the spiced base and stir to coat them in the dark paste — they should turn a dark brick-red immediately. Add the water or stock and the salt. Stir to combine, scraping any stuck paste from the bottom. Bring to a boil over high heat, stirring occasionally. Reduce to a medium simmer, cover partially, and cook for 20–25 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes to prevent sticking. Red lentils cook quickly and dissolve completely — misir wot is not chunky; the lentils should entirely melt into the sauce to form a thick, uniform, porridge-like texture.

Add the lemon juice and stir through. Taste and adjust: more berbere for heat and depth, more salt for savory presence, more lemon for brightness. Let the stew rest for 5 minutes off the heat — it will thicken slightly as it sits. Serve on injera: spoon the misir wot in a mound on top of a large round of injera and allow it to spread and be absorbed. The injera tears into pieces that scoop the stew. Traditionally served alongside other wots on a single large shared plate.

recipes.name: Miso-Marinated Black Cod (Gindara Saikyo Yaki)

ingredients.name: Black cod (sablefish) fillets, skin-on, pin-bones removed

steps: Combine white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small saucepan over medium-low heat. Stir until the sugar dissolves and the mixture is smooth and slightly warmed (do not boil). Remove from heat and cool completely to room temperature. The marinade should be thick and spreadable, slightly thicker than heavy cream.

Pat the cod fillets completely dry with paper towels. Coat the flesh side generously with marinade, pressing it into the fish surface. A thin layer on the skin side is fine. Place in a zip-lock bag or container, making sure each piece is well-coated. Refrigerate for 2–3 days (72 hours for the full effect). The longer the marination, the deeper the flavor penetration and the more dramatic the miso lacquer during cooking.

Remove fillets from the marinade and gently scrape off the excess with a spoon or your fingers — do not rinse. Excess miso will burn, not caramelize. Place skin-side down on a foil-lined baking sheet lightly oiled. Broil 15–18 cm from the element for 8–12 minutes, watching constantly. The miso should caramelize to a deep golden-mahogany — not burnt, not pale.

Transfer each fillet carefully — they are extremely delicate — to a warm plate using a wide spatula. Add a small pile of sliced pickled ginger beside the fish. Grate a tiny amount of yuzu or lemon zest over the top. Serve immediately with steamed rice and a simple cucumber vinegar salad to cut the richness.

recipes.name: Miso-Butter Salmon with Roasted Green Beans

ingredients.name: Salmon fillets, skin-on, about 150 g each

steps: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a rack in the upper-middle position. In a small bowl, mash the miso, softened butter, honey and grated garlic with a fork until completely smooth and uniform.
On a rimmed sheet pan, toss the green beans with the oil and 1/2 tsp kosher salt and spread them out. Roast for 8 minutes to give them a head start.

Pat the salmon dry. Push the beans to the edges of the pan and lay the fillets skin-side down in the center. Spread the miso butter thickly over the tops and sides of the fillets. Roast 9–12 minutes, depending on thickness, until the salmon flakes easily and is opaque at the center or reads 145°F (63°C) in the thickest part. If the tops are pale, switch to the broiler for the final 1–2 minutes, watching constantly — miso burns quickly.

Drizzle the rice vinegar over the green beans and toss them in the melted miso butter on the pan. Plate the salmon with the beans, spoon over any remaining pan juices, and scatter with scallions and sesame seeds. Serve with steamed rice if you like.

recipes.name: Miso-Glazed Black Cod

ingredients.name: Black cod fillets (sablefish), skin-on, pinbones removed
Fine sea salt (for patting fish dry)

steps: Combine sake, mirin, and sugar in a small saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 2-3 minutes, stirring, until the sugar dissolves and the alcohol cooks off — the raw boozy smell will mellow to a soft, sweet aroma. Do not boil vigorously. Remove from heat and allow to cool to room temperature completely before adding the miso.

Add the white miso to the cooled sake-mirin base and whisk vigorously until the paste is completely dissolved and the mixture is uniformly smooth and creamy. There should be no lumps of miso visible. The finished marinade is sweet-salty, intensely savory, and pale ivory in color. Cool completely before use.

Pat the cod fillets completely dry with paper towels, then lightly salt both sides and let them sit 10 minutes. The salt draws out surface moisture that would dilute the marinade. Wipe the salt and any exuded moisture away. Spread the miso marinade generously over all surfaces of each fillet, working it gently into the flesh. Place in a sealed container or zip-lock bag, pressing out air, and refrigerate for a minimum of 24 hours — 48-72 hours is ideal and transforms the fish.

Preheat the broiler to maximum heat with the rack 10-12 cm (4-5 inches) from the element. Wipe away excess marinade from each fillet with your fingers — too thick a layer burns before the fish cooks through. Place fillets skin-side down on a foil-lined tray. Broil for 8-12 minutes, watching constantly. The glaze will bubble, caramelize, and turn a deep amber-to-mahogany in patches. The fish is done when it is opaque throughout and flakes easily with a fork at the thickest point.

Serve immediately on warmed plates. The fish needs nothing beyond itself, though a small mound of pickled ginger and a few stems of blanched broccolini complete the plate. If the fillet sticks to the foil, slide a thin spatula between skin and foil — the skin sometimes adheres. Serve skin-side down and eat the caramelized glaze first — it is the crown of the dish.

recipes.name: Miso-Glazed Black Cod

ingredients.name: Black cod (sablefish) fillets, skin-on, 150–180 g each

steps: Combine mirin and sake in a small saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 2 minutes to burn off the alcohol — this prevents the marinade from tasting raw and sharp on the finished fish. Remove from heat. Whisk in the white miso paste until completely smooth with no lumps. Whisk in the sugar until dissolved. The marinade should be thick, silky, and uniformly tan-gold. Cool to room temperature before using.

Pat the cod fillets completely dry — any surface moisture will dilute the marinade and prevent even coating. Coat each fillet generously on all sides with the cooled miso marinade. The coating should be visible and substantial, about 3–4 mm thick. Place in a non-reactive container (not aluminum — the miso acid will react), cover, and refrigerate. Marinate for a minimum of 2 days; 3 days is the traditional preparation. The miso enzymes will deeply penetrate the fish, converting some proteins and creating the characteristic silky texture.

Preheat the broiler to maximum heat. Very gently wipe each fillet with your fingers or a dry paper towel to remove the bulk of the miso marinade — leave a thin, even coating behind. Excess marinade will burn black under the broiler before the fish cooks through. Brush a broiler-safe pan with a thin film of neutral oil. Place fillets skin-side down. Broil 10–15 cm from the heat element for 5–7 minutes, watching constantly. The miso sugar will caramelize rapidly. You are looking for a lacquered, deep amber glaze with some dark caramelized spots — not charred black.

Transfer the fillets immediately from the pan to warmed serving plates using a thin fish spatula — black cod is fragile at this point and will break apart if manhandled. The skin, having rendered its fat, should release easily from the pan. Serve immediately with steamed Japanese rice, pickled ginger, and a simple dashi broth alongside. No garnish is needed — the lacquered surface is the presentation.

recipes.name: Nasu Dengaku

ingredients.name: Scallion, thinly sliced on the bias

steps: Halve the eggplants lengthwise. Using a sharp paring knife, score the cut face in a deep crosshatch pattern — cut about two-thirds into the flesh at 1 cm intervals in both directions without piercing the skin. This scoring is critical: it allows heat to penetrate and sesame oil to seep into the flesh, preventing steam from splitting the skin and dramatically shortening the roasting time. Press the cut face lightly to open the grid slightly.

Brush the scored cut face generously with sesame oil, working the oil into the crosshatch cuts with the brush. Flip and brush a thin layer over the skin side as well. The sesame oil serves double duty: it prevents sticking and imparts a deep, nutty fragrance that suffuses the flesh during roasting. Line a baking tray with foil and place eggplant halves cut-side down.

Roast cut-side down in a 220°C (425°F) oven for 12–15 minutes, until the flesh is completely tender when pierced with a chopstick or skewer and the cut faces have taken on a light gold color from contact with the tray. This initial roasting collapses the air pockets in the spongy eggplant flesh and drives out moisture, which concentrates the flavor and creates the right base for the glaze to adhere to. Do not rush this step — underdone eggplant will have a bitter, spongy bite.

While the eggplant roasts, combine white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small saucepan over very low heat. Whisk constantly as the mixture warms — the goal is just to dissolve the sugar and bring everything into a smooth, homogeneous paste, not to cook it. The glaze should be warm, fluid, and spreadable, the consistency of thick yogurt. Remove from heat as soon as it is smooth. Taste: it should be deeply savory, sweetly balanced, and intensely fragrant.

Flip the roasted eggplant halves so the cut face is now up. Spoon the dengaku glaze generously over each half, spreading it to the edges with the back of the spoon. The layer should be thick enough to be opaque — roughly 3–4mm — so it caramelizes and chars slightly rather than burning off thin. Do not be timid: a thick, generous glaze is what makes this dish.

Broil the glazed eggplant halves under a hot broiler (or salamander) for 3–5 minutes, watching constantly. The glaze should bubble, then caramelize to deep amber-brown with slightly charred edges and spots — this Maillard browning and mild caramelization is the defining character of dengaku. Remove from the broiler and let rest for 1 minute on the tray. Transfer to serving plates, scatter toasted sesame seeds generously, and finish with sliced scallion. Serve immediately while the eggplant is still trembling-soft and the glaze is warm.

recipes.name: Miso-Glazed Salmon
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Whisk together the white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar until fully smooth and the sugar has dissolved. The marinade should be a pale caramel paste that flows like thick honey. Taste it: it should be intensely savory and sweet, with the faint sting of alcohol — the sake and mirin will carry the volatile top notes away as the fish broils, leaving the miso caramelized and fragrant.

Season the salmon lightly with salt, then coat each fillet on all sides with the miso marinade. Place in a shallow dish or zip-lock bag, making sure the marinade contacts every surface. Refrigerate for at least 1 hour and up to 24 hours — the longer the rest, the deeper the savory penetration and the more intense the caramelized crust. Wipe off the excess marinade before broiling; any thick layer will burn before the fish cooks.

Position an oven rack about 15 cm from the broiler element and preheat the broiler to maximum. Line a baking sheet with foil and lightly oil it. Wipe the excess marinade from the salmon, place skin-side down, and broil 8–12 minutes depending on thickness — no flipping needed. Watch continuously: the miso sugars move from golden to burnt in under a minute at this heat. The skin should crisp and the glaze should bubble, bronze, and develop dark caramelized spots at the edges.

Slide the fillets onto warm plates using a thin spatula. The skin may stick to the foil — use the spatula to separate it cleanly. Scatter thinly sliced scallion greens over the top. Serve immediately with steamed short-grain rice and a small mound of pickled ginger or a wedge of sudachi if available.

recipes.name: Miso-Roasted Sweet Potato

ingredients.name: Japanese sweet potatoes (Satsumaimo) or orange-flesh sweet potatoes
Thinly sliced spring onion (green part only)

steps: Preheat the oven to 180 C (355 F). Place the whole, unpeeled sweet potatoes directly on the oven rack with a foil-lined tray below to catch drips. Roast for 55–75 minutes depending on size (a chopstick pressed into the thickest part should meet no resistance). The skin will blister and deflate; a dark, caramelised syrup will drip from the ends.

While the potatoes roast, combine the softened butter, white miso, and mirin in a small bowl. Stir vigorously until completely smooth and homogenous. The mixture will be a pale amber paste. Set aside at room temperature.

Split each sweet potato lengthwise with a sharp knife — but not quite all the way through. Press the two ends toward each other to open up the split and create a cavity. Spoon or pipe a generous amount of the miso butter into the cavity. Finish under the grill (broiler) at high heat for 3–4 minutes until the glaze is bubbling and caramelised. Scatter flaky salt, sesame seeds, and spring onion.

recipes.name: Strawberry Daifuku Mochi
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Tsubuan or koshian (sweet red bean paste)

steps: Divide the anko (bean paste) into portions — approximately 25g per daifuku. Flatten each portion into a disc in your palm. Place a hulled strawberry point-down in the center and wrap the anko up around it, pinching to seal at the base of the strawberry. The strawberry tip should just be visible or barely covered. Refrigerate wrapped strawberries for 15 minutes to firm.

Whisk shiratamako, sugar, and water together in a microwave-safe bowl until smooth with no lumps. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and microwave on high for 2 minutes. Remove, stir thoroughly with a wet spatula, then microwave for a further 1 minute. Stir again — the mochi should be fully translucent with no white, opaque patches. If white patches remain, microwave in 30-second bursts, stirring each time. Alternatively, steam in a covered steamer for 20 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Dust a work surface generously with katakuriko. Turn the hot mochi out onto the dusted surface — it will be extremely sticky and very hot, so work quickly. Dust the top and your hands. Divide into equal portions (approximately 40g each) using a dusted dough cutter or scissors. Stretch each portion into a disc about 10 cm wide. Place an anko-wrapped strawberry in the center, point-down. Gather the mochi edges up and over, pinching firmly to seal at the base. Pinch point downward. Dust the finished daifuku with more katakuriko to prevent sticking.

recipes.name: Japanese Basic Mochi
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine the glutinous rice flour and sugar in a microwave-safe bowl. Add the water gradually while stirring with a spatula until completely smooth and lump-free. The batter will be thin — like very thick cream — and should pour off the spatula in a slow, even sheet. Pass it through a fine strainer if any lumps remain. Cover loosely with microwave-safe plastic wrap or a damp paper towel.

Microwave the covered batter on HIGH for 2 minutes. Remove, uncover, and stir vigorously — the outer edge will have cooked to a translucent, rubbery mass while the centre remains white and liquid. Stir to combine them, re-cover, and microwave again for 1 to 2 minutes until the entire mass is translucent, pulling away from the bowl sides, and glistening. Stir well between each burst. The dough should look uniformly glossy and slightly translucent, not chalky or opaque. Total microwave time: 4 to 6 minutes in 1-2 minute bursts.

Dust a clean work surface generously with cornstarch. Turn the hot mochi out onto the surface and dust the top as well. Let it cool for 5 to 10 minutes — it should be warm but comfortable to handle. Do not let it cool completely: cold mochi becomes stiff and tears when portioned. Divide into 8 equal pieces using a bench scraper or a knife dusted with cornstarch. Flatten each piece into a round disc about 8 cm in diameter, working quickly.

Roll a tablespoon-sized ball of anko between your palms to a smooth sphere and place it at the centre of each mochi disc. Gather the edges of the mochi up around the filling and pinch firmly together at the top, rotating and pleating as you go, until the seam is completely sealed with no filling visible. Pinch the seam tightly — a loose seam opens during handling. Turn seam-side down and roll gently between cupped palms to smooth the surface. Roll in kinako to coat. Arrange seam-side down on a tray. Eat at room temperature on the day they are made.

recipes.name: Oaxacan Mole Negro
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Dried mulato chilies, stems and most seeds removed
Dried pasilla negro chilies, stems and most seeds removed
Dried ancho chilies, stems and most seeds removed
Dried chihuacle negro chilies, stems removed
Ripe plantain, peeled and sliced thick
Dark chocolate (70% cacao minimum), roughly chopped
Day-old corn tortilla, torn into pieces

steps: Heat a dry comal or heavy skillet over medium-high. Working in batches, toast each chili variety: press them flat against the hot surface for 15–20 seconds per side until they blister, puff, and release a deep, smoky fragrance — not the acrid scent of burning. Immediately submerge toasted chilies in a bowl of very hot water and weigh them down with a plate; soak 25–30 minutes until fully soft. In the same dry pan, toast cumin seeds until fragrant (30 seconds), then cinnamon, peppercorns, sesame seeds, pumpkin seeds, and torn tortilla pieces separately, each until golden and aromatic. Toast the reserved chili seeds if you want more heat (optional). Keep all toasted dry components together.

Place tomato halves, quartered onion, and unpeeled garlic directly on the same dry comal over high heat. Char them without moving: you want dramatic blackening on at least one side — this char is structural flavor, not a mistake. Turn once and char the other side. Garlic is done when its papery skin is blackened and the cloves feel soft inside when pressed. In a small pan with a splash of lard or oil, fry plantain slices over medium heat until deeply caramelized and bronze on both sides (3–4 min per side). Add raisins to the pan in the last minute and fry until they puff. Peel the garlic; do not peel the onion char.

Drain the soaked chilies, reserving the soaking liquid (but use sparingly — it can be very bitter). Working in batches in a blender: combine soaked chilies, charred tomatoes and onion, peeled charred garlic, toasted spices, sesame seeds, pumpkin seeds, tortilla pieces, fried plantain, and raisins. Add warm broth as needed (not chili soaking liquid) to get the blades moving — typically 3–4 ladles per batch. Blend each batch for at least 2 full minutes until completely smooth. Pass through a medium sieve if you want a very refined texture; leave it as-is for a more rustic, textured mole.

Heat the lard in a large, heavy-bottomed pot (preferably clay or enameled cast iron) over high heat until it begins to smoke lightly. Pour the mole paste in all at once — it will spit violently, so stand back and have a lid ready. Fry the paste, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, for 10–15 minutes until it darkens another shade, thickens, and the fat separates visibly at the edges. This frying step is what transforms a blended mixture into a true mole. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add warm broth one ladle at a time, stirring well after each addition. Add dried thyme, oregano, and salt. Simmer gently for at least 1 hour, skimming any fat that rises. Add the chopped chocolate in the final 5 minutes, stirring until fully melted. Taste and adjust salt.

recipes.name: Moqueca Baiana

ingredients.name: Firm white fish fillets (e.g. sea bass or cod), 4 cm chunks
Red and green bell peppers, thinly sliced
Fresh cilantro, stems and leaves separated

steps: Toss fish chunks with lime juice, a pinch of salt, and minced garlic (half the garlic). Cover and refrigerate for 20-30 minutes. The acid will begin to set the exterior proteins, helping the fish hold together in the stew without falling apart.

Heat dendê oil in a heavy clay pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add onion and cook 5 minutes until soft and turning golden. Add remaining garlic and bell peppers and cook 3 more minutes. The dendê oil will turn the whole base a vivid orange — this is correct and beautiful.

Add tomatoes and cilantro stems to the sofrito. Cook 5 minutes until tomatoes begin to dissolve. Pour in coconut milk and stir. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat. Season well with salt and taste — the broth should be rich, sweet from coconut, and slightly acidic from the tomato.

Nestle the marinated fish gently into the simmering broth in a single layer. Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 8-12 minutes, depending on thickness. Do not stir — use the lid to baste. The fish is done when it flakes easily at the thickest point and is opaque throughout. Scatter cilantro leaves over the top and serve straight from the clay pot.

recipes.name: Moqueca de Peixe

ingredients.name: Thick white fish fillets (cod, sea bass, or grouper)
White onion, sliced into thin rounds
Red and green bell peppers, sliced into thin strips
Malagueta chillies or scotch bonnet, finely sliced

steps: Cut the fish fillets into large portions (approximately 150 g each). In a bowl, combine with the lime juice, half the garlic, and salt. Toss gently to coat. Marinate for 20–30 minutes in the refrigerator. The lime juice will begin to denature the surface proteins, giving the fish a slightly opaque look and a more flavourful surface.

In a heavy clay pot (ideal) or wide, heavy-bottomed pan, pour the dendê oil. Layer the onion rounds across the base, then the tomato rounds, then the pepper strips, then the chilli. This layered approach is traditional — the vegetables cook in sequence from the heat of the oil below.

Lay the marinated fish pieces on top of the layered vegetables. Pour the coconut milk over everything — it should nearly submerge the fish. Cover tightly and cook over medium heat for 15–20 minutes, without stirring, until the fish is just cooked through and the coconut milk has combined with the vegetable juices and palm oil to create a brilliant orange-red broth. Add most of the coriander in the final 2 minutes. Taste and adjust salt.

recipes.name: Moroccan Chermoula Baked Fish

ingredients.name: Whole sea bream or sea bass (1–1.2kg), cleaned and scored

steps: Combine all chermoula ingredients in a food processor or pound in a large mortar. Process until a thick, bright-green paste forms — it should have body and cling to a spoon, not be a smooth liquid. Taste: it should be intensely herby, sour from the preserved lemon, and earthy-warm from the cumin. A traditional chermoula made in a mortar will have more texture; a processor gives a smoother result. Both are correct.

Score the fish deeply on both sides — 4–5 diagonal cuts per side, down to the bone. This is essential for two reasons: it allows the chermoula to penetrate deep into the flesh, and it prevents the skin from buckling in the oven. Rub two-thirds of the chermoula aggressively into every surface of the fish: inside the body cavity, into every score cut, and over the skin. Marinate for at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to 4 hours in the refrigerator.

Place the fish on a lightly oiled baking sheet or in a tagine. Spoon the reserved chermoula over the top. Bake at 200°C (400°F) for 20–25 minutes depending on thickness (10 minutes per 2.5cm of thickness at the widest point). The fish is done when the score cuts have opened and the flesh inside is white and opaque, and the skin is lightly blistered. Rest 5 minutes before serving. Garnish with lemon wedges and fresh cilantro.

recipes.name: Moroccan Couscous with Seven Vegetables
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Place the lamb or chicken pieces in the bottom of a couscoussier or large pot with a steamer basket. Add the quartered onion, tomatoes, ras el hanout, and salt. Cover with cold water by 3 cm. Bring to a boil, skimming any foam, then reduce to a vigorous simmer. The broth should bubble steadily — it will cook the meat and serve simultaneously as the steaming liquid for the couscous. Simmer for 30 minutes before adding vegetables.

Put the dry couscous in a large bowl. Sprinkle lightly with cold salted water (about one-quarter the volume of the couscous), working it in with your fingers to moisten every grain without clumping. Rake the grains apart with your fingers until they are separate and loose. Transfer to the steamer basket or couscoussier top, spreading evenly. Set over the simmering broth without sealing the seam — the steam should rise through the grains freely. Steam uncovered for 15–20 minutes until the grains are swollen and show visible steam passing through them.

Turn the steamed couscous into a large wide bowl or tray. Working quickly with your hands (or two large forks), break apart every clump — rake, separate, and aerate the grains until they are completely loose. Add the butter in small pieces and work it in thoroughly, coating every grain. Sprinkle with a little more salted water if the grains seem dry, then rake apart again. This breaking step is what separates fluffy couscous from gummy couscous — do not rush it.

Add the carrots to the simmering broth first — they need the most time. After 10 minutes add the zucchini and chickpeas. Simultaneously, return the buttered couscous to the steamer and steam for a final 15–20 minutes. All elements should finish together: the couscous perfectly fluffy, the vegetables tender but not falling apart, the broth deeply flavored. To serve, mound the couscous in a wide, deep serving dish. Create a well in the center and pile the meat and vegetables into it. Ladle some broth over everything. Serve the remaining broth in a separate bowl for people to add at the table.

recipes.name: Khobz — Moroccan Round Loaf
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: In a large bowl, whisk together flour, semolina, salt, and yeast. Make a well in the center and pour in warm water and olive oil. Mix with your hand or a wooden spoon until no dry flour remains. The dough will be slightly rough — semolina takes time to hydrate. Turn out and knead by hand for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Semolina gives the dough a sandy texture initially; keep kneading until it becomes cohesive.

Divide the dough into 2 equal portions (about 350 g each). On an unfloured surface, roll each piece into a smooth ball by pushing it against the counter in a tight circular motion. Flatten each ball gently with your palm into a round disc about 18–20 cm in diameter and 2.5 cm thick. Do not use a rolling pin — hand-shaping keeps air in the loaf. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Wet the surface lightly with a brush dipped in water and press sesame seeds generously across the top.

Cover the loaves loosely with a clean kitchen towel and proof at room temperature until noticeably puffy and the edges have risen, about 45–60 minutes. The loaves won't double dramatically — Moroccan khobz is intentionally denser than European breads. Use the poke test: press a floured fingertip 1 cm into the dough. It should spring back slowly but not fully.

Preheat the oven to 220 C (425 F) with a baking stone or inverted sheet pan on the middle rack. Slide the parchment directly onto the hot surface. Bake for 18–22 minutes until the crust is a rich golden-brown and the loaves sound hollow when tapped on the bottom. Cool on a wire rack for at least 15 minutes before tearing.

recipes.name: Moroccan Lamb Tagine
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder, bone-in, cut into 5cm chunks
Saffron threads (bloomed in 2 tbsp warm water)
Preserved lemon (rind only, rinsed and sliced)
Fresh cilantro and toasted almond slivers

steps: In a large bowl, toss the lamb chunks with the grated onion, ras el hanout, ground ginger, and bloomed saffron water. Mix thoroughly to coat every surface. The onion will begin to break down from the salt in the spices and coat the lamb in a fragrant, slightly wet paste. Cover and marinate for at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to 24 hours refrigerated. The longer the marinate, the deeper the spice penetration into the meat.

Heat olive oil in a tagine base or heavy Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Remove the marinated lamb from the bowl, scraping off excess onion paste (set it aside — it goes in next). Sear the lamb in batches, without crowding, for 3–4 minutes per side until deeply browned. The spice coating will caramelize and form an aromatic mahogany crust. Do not rush this step — proper browning provides the structural complexity the long braise builds upon.

Add the reserved onion paste to the pan and cook over medium heat for 5 minutes until softened. Return the seared lamb and any resting juices. Add the apricots, preserved lemon rind, and stock — the liquid should reach halfway up the lamb pieces, not submerge them. Bring to a simmer, then cover tightly (use foil under the lid for a better seal) and reduce heat to the lowest possible simmer. Cook for 1 hour 45 minutes to 2 hours, checking every 30 minutes and turning the meat once, until the lamb is falling off the bone and the sauce has reduced to a richly flavored, slightly syrupy consistency.

Taste the sauce and adjust — it should be complex, sweet-sour-savory, with the preserved lemon providing background brightness. If too sweet, add a squeeze of fresh lemon. If too thin, simmer uncovered on medium for 5–10 minutes with the lid off. Scatter fresh cilantro and toasted almond slivers over the surface just before serving. Serve in the tagine or Dutch oven directly at the table with couscous, flatbread, and harissa on the side.

recipes.name: Moroccan Cumin-Spiced Roasted Carrots with Harissa
steps: Preheat the oven to 200°C (400°F). In a large bowl, toss the halved carrots with olive oil, cumin, coriander, smoked paprika, cinnamon, salt, and pepper. Make sure every surface is coated in oil and spice. Arrange cut-side down on a large baking sheet in a single layer with space between each carrot — crowding causes steaming rather than roasting. Roast for 25–30 minutes until the cut sides are deeply caramelized and the edges show char spots.

Whisk together the harissa paste and honey into a smooth, rust-red glaze. Flip the partially roasted carrots cut-side up. Using a pastry brush or spoon, coat the cut side of each carrot generously with the harissa-honey glaze. Return to the oven for 8–10 more minutes until the glaze is bubbling, caramelized at the edges, and sticky. The sugar in the honey and the natural sugars in the carrots should reach deep caramelization — dark, almost jewel-like.

Transfer the glazed carrots to a serving plate, glaze-side up. Scatter the toasted pumpkin seeds over the carrots. Tear or roughly chop the fresh cilantro and scatter it over. A final drizzle of good olive oil finishes the dish. Serve warm or at room temperature — these are excellent both ways. At room temperature the glaze sets slightly and becomes almost candy-like in texture.

recipes.name: Moros y Cristianos
steps: Drain and rinse the soaked black beans and place in a large pot. Cover with cold water by 8 cm. Add the bay leaves. Bring to a boil over high heat, skimming any grey foam that rises to the surface in the first 10 minutes. Reduce to a gentle simmer and cook for 45-60 minutes until the beans are fully tender but still hold their shape. The cooking liquid will turn a deep, dramatic purple-black — this liquid is liquid gold; it is what turns the rice. Do not add salt until the beans are cooked — salting before tenderness toughens the skin.

In a wide, heavy-bottomed pot (large enough to hold the finished dish), heat the olive oil over medium heat until shimmering. Add the onion and green pepper and cook, stirring regularly, for 6-8 minutes until completely soft, translucent, and beginning to turn golden. Add the garlic and cook for 1 more minute. Add the ground cumin and oregano and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant — you will smell the spices bloom immediately. This sofrito is the flavor backbone of the dish.

Add the cooked beans and exactly 375 ml of their cooking liquid to the sofrito pot, reserving any remaining liquid. Stir to combine. Add salt and pepper. Taste the liquid — it should be assertively seasoned, slightly saltier than you want the finished dish, because the rice will absorb and dilute it significantly. Bring to a rolling boil over high heat.

Rinse the rice until the water runs nearly clear and drain well. Add the rice to the boiling bean base and stir once, firmly, to distribute the rice and submerge any floating grains. Reduce heat to the absolute lowest setting and cover tightly. Cook for 20 minutes without lifting the lid — the rice will absorb the bean liquid and turn the characteristic deep purple-grey that gives the dish its visual identity.

After 20 minutes, lift the lid briefly and check for steam holes on the surface — the telltale craters that signal the liquid has been fully absorbed and the rice is cooked. Remove from heat and rest, covered, for 10 minutes. Fluff gently with a fork, folding from the bottom up. Taste and adjust salt. Just before serving, drizzle the white wine vinegar over the dish and fold in gently — this sharp acid note brightens the deep, earthy flavor and is the traditional finishing touch that ties the dish together.

recipes.name: Moules Marinière
steps: Scrub each mussel under cold running water with a stiff brush to remove any barnacles and grit. Pull off the beard (the fibrous string protruding from the seam) by gripping it and pulling sharply toward the hinge end — pulling the other way tears the mussel. Tap any open mussel sharply on the counter: if it does not close within 10 seconds, discard it — it is dead. Discard any with cracked or broken shells. The mussels should smell purely of the ocean — clean, briny, and cool.

In a large, wide pot with a tight-fitting lid, melt half the butter over medium heat. Add the shallots, garlic, and bay leaf. Cook gently for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until the shallots are completely soft and translucent — they should not color at all. This short, gentle sweat is the flavor base and the moisture from the mussels will build on it. Season with pepper — no salt yet; the mussels will season the broth.

Raise the heat to high. Pour in the wine — it will spit and steam instantly. Let it boil hard for 1 minute to drive off the raw alcohol. Tip in all the cleaned mussels at once. Clamp the lid on tightly and cook on high heat for 3–4 minutes, shaking the pot vigorously once or twice by gripping the handles and swirling it in a circle. Open the lid after 3 minutes — nearly all mussels should be open. Cook another minute if needed. Discard any that remain closed after 5 minutes.

Remove the pot from heat. Add the remaining cold butter and swirl the pot to melt it into the broth — do not stir, just swirl, which emulsifies the butter into a slightly creamy, glossy broth. Add the parsley and give one final swirl. Taste the broth and adjust for pepper — the mussels will have seasoned it with salt. Divide into warmed deep bowls, making sure the broth is ladled over each portion generously. Serve immediately with crusty bread or frites.

recipes.name: Moules Marinières
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Crusty baguette or sourdough, to serve

steps: Tip the mussels into a colander under cold running water. Discard any with cracked or broken shells. Hold each open-shelled mussel and tap it firmly on the edge of the sink — a live mussel will clench shut within 30 seconds. Discard any that stay open. Grip any visible beards (the fibrous tuft protruding from the seam) between your fingers and rip firmly toward the hinge to pull them free. Scrub off any remaining barnacles with a stiff brush. Keep the sorted mussels in the colander at room temperature; do not submerge them in fresh water.

Set a large, wide, heavy-based pot over medium heat — it must be big enough to hold all the mussels with room to spare. Melt the butter until foaming. Add the shallots and garlic. Sweat gently, stirring often, for 3–4 minutes until completely soft, glassy, and sweet-smelling. Do not let them colour at all — any browning will push the final broth bitter.

Pour in the white wine and add the cracked black pepper. Raise the heat to high and bring to a vigorous rolling boil. Let it boil for 1 minute to drive off the harsh raw-alcohol edge. The liquid should reduce very slightly and smell like a clean, refined court-bouillon — bright and winey but not sharp.

Tip all the sorted mussels into the boiling broth in one go. Clamp the lid on immediately and cook over maximum heat for 3–4 minutes. Shake the pot vigorously by the handles once or twice during cooking to redistribute the mussels so every shell gets direct steam contact. Lift the lid and inspect: every shell must be open. Any mussel still clamped shut after 6 minutes of total cooking must be discarded — they were dead before they went in.

Ladle the mussels and every drop of fragrant broth into deep, warmed bowls. Scatter a generous fistful of roughly chopped parsley over each bowl. Serve instantly with a basket of crusty bread for mopping. The entire pot should reach the table within 90 seconds of leaving the heat — mussels are the most time-sensitive dish in French bistro cooking.

recipes.name: Moussaka

ingredients.name: Fine sea salt and black pepper

steps: Salt the eggplant slices liberally on both sides and let them sit in a colander for 20 minutes to draw out moisture — the collected liquid will be visibly briny. Pat every slice completely dry with paper towels. Heat a generous pour of olive oil in a wide heavy skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Fry the eggplant in batches without crowding, 2–3 minutes per side, until deep golden-brown on both faces. The oil will be absorbed rapidly at first and then released again as the flesh collapses — this is the moment to flip. Drain on a paper-towel-lined tray. The slices must be properly golden, not pale: their caramelized surface is what holds the layers of the moussaka together.

In the same pan with a thin film of fresh oil, cook the onion over medium heat until softened and translucent, 8 minutes. Add garlic and cook one minute more. Add the lamb mince and cook, breaking it up with a wooden spoon, until no pink remains and the meat has taken on a light brown crust in places. Pour in the wine and scrape up any stuck bits — it will hiss and reduce to almost nothing in 2 minutes. Add the crushed tomatoes, cinnamon, allspice and bay leaves. Season generously with salt and pepper. Simmer uncovered on medium-low for 25–30 minutes until the sauce is thick, glossy and almost dry — moisture is the enemy of a clean-slicing moussaka. Remove bay leaves.

Melt the butter in a heavy saucepan over medium-low heat. Whisk in the flour and cook, stirring constantly, for 2 minutes until the roux smells of warm biscuit. Pour in the warm milk in a thin stream, whisking hard, adding it gradually to prevent lumps. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook 8–10 minutes, whisking often, until thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Remove from the heat and let it cool for 5 minutes — you must cool it slightly or the eggs will scramble. Whisk in the beaten eggs, nutmeg and half the grated cheese vigorously. Season with salt and pepper. The result is richer, eggier and more custard-like than a plain béchamel — it will set in the oven like a savory flan.

Preheat the oven to 180°C / 350°F. Lightly oil a deep 30×22cm baking dish. Layer half the fried eggplant across the base in overlapping shingles. Spread the entire lamb sauce evenly over the eggplant, pressing it flat. Layer the remaining eggplant over the meat sauce in the same overlapping pattern. Pour the béchamel over the top, spreading it to the edges with a spatula — it should form an even layer at least 1.5cm thick, enough to set properly. Scatter the remaining grated cheese over the surface. Bake for 45–50 minutes until the top is a deep, even golden-brown and the edges are bubbling. Rest for at least 20 minutes before cutting — the internal structure needs time to set.

recipes.name: Msemen (Moroccan Laminated Flatbread)
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Vegetable oil (for oiling hands and surface)

steps: Combine both flours, salt, and yeast. Add the warm water and mix until a dough forms. Knead by hand for 10–12 minutes until the dough is smooth, supple, and only slightly tacky. The semolina gives it a faintly grainy feel that will mellow as it rests. Divide the dough into 8 equal balls (about 80–90g each). Oil your hands and each ball generously. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 30–45 minutes until the dough relaxes and becomes very extensible.

On a lightly oiled surface, use oiled hands and fingertips to stretch a dough ball into a very thin rectangle — almost translucent. Spread a thin smear of softened butter across the entire surface with your fingers. Sprinkle a pinch of coarse semolina over the butter — this is what creates the separate layers. Fold one third of the rectangle toward the center, then fold the other third over (letter fold), making a long strip. Fold the strip into thirds again to create a square. Press gently. Repeat for all balls. Rest 10 minutes.

Heat a dry cast iron griddle or heavy skillet over medium-low heat. Do not oil the pan — the butter within the dough will render and fry the bread from the inside. Cook each square for 3–4 minutes per side, pressing gently with a flat spatula, until each side is a mottled golden-brown with darker patches where the layers are thickest. The interior will puff slightly as steam builds between the layers. Serve immediately — msemen becomes leathery as it cools.

recipes.name: Mujadara
steps: Heat two-thirds of the olive oil in a wide, heavy skillet over medium heat. Add all sliced onions with a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring every 3–4 minutes, for 35–45 minutes total — patience here is not optional. The onions will reduce dramatically: first they release water and become translucent (15 min), then they will start to color (25 min), then darken and concentrate into a rich mahogany sweetness (35–45 min). Do not rush with high heat — the sugars must caramelize slowly.

In a separate small saucepan, heat remaining olive oil over medium-high. Add shallot rings — the oil should sizzle immediately. Fry, stirring often, for 8–10 minutes until rings are deeply golden and just beginning to darken. They will crisp as they cool, so remove them when still slightly flexible. Drain on paper towels. They turn crispy within 2 minutes of draining.

In the same caramelized-onion pot (with the onions still in it minus the reserved portion), add lentils and cover with water or stock. Add cumin and allspice. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 15 minutes until lentils are about two-thirds cooked — still with a slight firmness. Season with salt at this point.

Stir in the rinsed rice. Ensure there is enough liquid to cook the rice — about 1.5 cm above the surface of the lentil-rice mixture. Bring back to a boil, then cover tightly with a lid and cook over very low heat for 15 minutes. Remove from heat, keep covered, and steam for 5 more minutes. Fluff gently with a fork. The lentils and rice should be cohesive but not mushy.

recipes.name: Mujaddara
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Pick over the lentils and rinse under cold water. Place in a pot and cover with cold water by 5 cm. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook 15–20 minutes until the lentils are just barely tender — they should still hold their shape and have a faint toothsomeness at the center. Do not fully cook them here; they will finish cooking with the rice. Drain, reserving the cooking liquid. Measure the liquid and top up with water to have 2 cups of liquid per cup of rice.

While the lentils cook, warm the olive oil in a wide, heavy pan over medium-low heat. Add all the sliced onions with a generous pinch of salt and stir to coat with oil. Cook, stirring every few minutes, for 30–40 minutes total. Do not raise the heat to rush them — the goal is slow, even browning, not scorching. In the first 15 minutes they will steam and wilt. Between 15 and 25 minutes they will begin to turn golden. Between 25 and 40 minutes they will deepen to a rich mahogany-brown, almost jammy, with a sweetness that is intensely concentrated. Reserve the oil in the pan.

Return the par-cooked lentils to the pot along with half the caramelized onions (the other half is reserved for topping). Rinse the rice and add it to the pot. Pour in the reserved cooking liquid — the lentil water adds body and earthy depth. Add cumin, cinnamon, allspice, salt, and pepper. Bring to a boil, stir once, then reduce to the lowest possible heat. Cover tightly and cook for 15–18 minutes without lifting the lid. Turn off the heat and let the pot steam, still covered, for another 10 minutes.

Spoon the cooked rice and lentils onto a wide serving platter and pile the reserved caramelized onions and all their oil generously over the top. The contrast between the pale grain base and the dark, glossy onion crown is the visual signature of mujaddara. Serve immediately with cold plain yogurt alongside — the cool, tangy yogurt is not optional, it is the counterpoint that makes the dish.

recipes.name: Mushroom Barley Risotto

ingredients.name: Parmesan-style hard cheese (vegetarian rennet), finely grated

steps: Heat 30 ml of the oil in a wide, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer (in two batches if crowded) and leave undisturbed 4 minutes. Stir, then cook 4–6 minutes more until the released water has evaporated and the mushrooms are deeply browned. Add the thyme, soy sauce, and a pinch of pepper, toss 30 seconds, then transfer to a bowl. Leave the pot unwashed.

Lower the heat to medium and add the remaining 15 ml oil to the same pot. Cook the shallots 3–4 minutes until soft, add the garlic for 30 seconds, then add the barley. Stir 2–3 minutes so the grains toast and pick up the mushroom fond.

Add the wine and stir until almost fully absorbed, about 2 minutes. Add the hot stock one ladle (about 180 ml) at a time, stirring often and adding more when the pot looks nearly dry. Keep at a lively simmer. Barley takes 35–40 minutes — longer than rice — and won't get quite as creamy, so stir well to release its starch. Season with salt halfway through.

Off the heat, add the cold butter and grated cheese and beat vigorously with a wooden spoon for 30 seconds until glossy. Fold in two-thirds of the mushrooms. Rest 1 minute, loosen with a little stock if needed, then serve topped with the remaining mushrooms, parsley, and black pepper.

recipes.name: Mushroom Bourguignon
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Mixed mushrooms (cremini, shiitake, king oyster), roughly torn
Burgundy or other dry red wine
Fresh thyme sprigs and bay leaves
Fine sea salt and black pepper

steps: Heat olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over high heat until shimmering. Add mushrooms in a single layer — work in batches if needed. Season with salt and do not stir for 2 minutes. Allow the mushrooms to release their moisture and then re-absorb it, developing a deep mahogany sear on each cut face.

In the same pot over medium heat, add shallots. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 6–8 minutes until softened and golden at the edges. The shallots should be translucent throughout but still hold their shape. Scrape up any remaining fond with a wooden spoon as the shallots release their liquid.

Pour the red wine into the pot with the shallots and add the thyme and bay leaves. Raise heat to medium-high and bring to a boil. Reduce the wine by half, about 8–10 minutes. This cooks off alcohol, concentrates fruit, and allows the tannins to mellow before the mushrooms rejoin.

Return the seared mushrooms to the pot, pour in the vegetable stock, and stir to combine. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover partially and cook for 40–45 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes. The liquid should maintain a slow, lazy bubble throughout — aggressive boiling will toughen the mushrooms.

recipes.name: Risotto ai Funghi
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Dried porcini mushrooms (soaked in 500 ml warm water)
Fresh mixed mushrooms (porcini, cremini, chanterelle — sliced)
Warm mushroom and porcini soaking stock (from above + water)
Unsalted butter (divided: half for soffritto, half for mantecatura)

steps: Melt half the butter with the olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan over high heat. When foaming subsides, add the fresh mushrooms in a single layer — do not crowd them or they will steam and grey rather than roast. Cook without stirring for 2 to 3 minutes until deeply golden on the bottom, then toss and cook 2 more minutes. Add the garlic and thyme, toss 30 seconds, season with salt and pepper. Remove from the pan to a bowl and reserve. The mushrooms will go back in at the finish.

In the same pan, melt the remaining butter over medium heat. Add the shallots and sweat gently for 4 to 5 minutes until soft and translucent — no browning. Add the dry Carnaroli rice and stir continuously for 1 to 2 minutes until every grain turns translucent and picks up a faint nutty smell. This tostatura seals the outside of the grain, slowing starch release for a creamy-yet-al-dente finish. Add the white wine all at once and stir until completely absorbed.

Begin adding the warm mushroom stock — including the strained porcini soaking liquid — one ladle at a time. After each addition, stir constantly until the stock is almost fully absorbed before adding the next ladle. The starches released from the Carnaroli grains need this constant agitation to build the surrounding creamy matrix. This process takes 16 to 18 minutes over steady medium heat. Taste after 14 minutes — the rice should be just approaching al dente. Season with salt as you go. Keep the stock warm in a separate pan; cold stock shocks the rice and breaks the rhythm.

Pull the pan completely off the heat. Add the reserved sautéed mushrooms and fold them through. Then add the cold butter (cubed) and the Parmigiano all at once. Stir vigorously in a circular motion — this is the mantecatura, the moment where the fat from the cold butter emulsifies with the starchy cooking liquid to create the glossy, creamy sauce. Season to taste. The risotto should flow on the plate like a wave — not stand in a pile, not pour like soup. This is all'onda and it requires the risotto to be slightly looser than you think, because it sets on the plate.

recipes.name: Mushroom Stroganoff

ingredients.name: Mixed mushrooms (cremini, shiitake, porcini), thickly sliced
Egg noodles or tagliatelle, cooked to serve
Fine sea salt and black pepper

steps: This is the most important step and the most commonly botched. Heat a wide, heavy skillet — cast iron ideal — over high heat until it smokes. Add half the butter. When the foam subsides and the butter begins to brown, add the mushrooms in a single layer. Do NOT stir. Do not add all the mushrooms at once if they crowd the pan — do them in two or three batches. Let them sit and sear, undisturbed, for 2–3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms on the underside, then turn them. Initially the mushrooms release a large amount of liquid; this is normal. Stay on high heat and let that liquid evaporate completely. The sound in the pan changes from a steam-hiss to a sizzle when the moisture is gone — that is your cue. The mushrooms should be deeply browned, about 70% reduced in volume, their edges slightly crisped. Season with salt and pepper and transfer to a plate.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add the remaining butter to the same pan — the brown fond on the base will immediately begin to release into the butter, darkening it beautifully. Add the shallots and thyme and cook, stirring regularly, for 5–6 minutes until the shallots are soft and golden. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute more. Pour in the brandy — step back as it may flame briefly if the pan is hot enough. Scrape the base of the pan vigorously as the brandy reduces to almost nothing in about 1 minute. Pour in the stock and return the seared mushrooms to the pan. Simmer for 5 minutes until the stock has reduced by about half and the liquid is slightly thickened and glossy.

Reduce the heat to the absolute lowest setting — sour cream must never boil or it will split and curdle into grainy, broken lumps. Add the Dijon mustard to the pan and stir through. Spoon in the sour cream and fold it gently through the sauce in slow, wide strokes. Let it warm through for 1–2 minutes, barely simmering — the surface should shiver gently but never bubble actively. The sauce will turn from brown to a warm, pale buff colour as the cream is incorporated. Taste and adjust salt and pepper carefully — the reduction will have concentrated the saltiness already. The finished sauce should be creamy, tangy from the sour cream, warmly savory from the mushrooms, and bright from the mustard.

Add the cooked, drained egg noodles directly into the pan with the sauce and toss to coat every strand. If the sauce is too thick to coat the noodles freely, add a splash of pasta cooking water to loosen — it emulsifies beautifully with the cream. Divide into warm bowls and shower generously with freshly chopped flat-leaf parsley. Serve with nothing more than a grinding of black pepper and a simple green salad. The noodles should be enrobed, not drowning; each strand should carry a visible, creamy coating.

recipes.name: Naan
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Whisk the instant yeast and sugar into the warm milk and let it sit a minute. In a large bowl, combine the flour and salt, then make a well and add the yeast-milk, the yogurt, and the oil. Mix with a spoon, then your hand, until no dry flour remains and a rough, sticky mass comes together. The yogurt's acidity and the milk sugars are what give naan its tang and its quick-browning crust, so don't substitute them away lightly.

Knead on a lightly oiled surface for 8 to 10 minutes (or 5 minutes in a stand mixer with the dough hook) until the dough turns smooth, supple, and elastic. Resist adding much flour — keep your hands and the bench lightly oiled instead, so the dough stays soft. You are building just enough gluten for the bread to puff and tear into chew without going tough.

Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and leave somewhere warm to rise until roughly doubled — about 1 to 2 hours depending on your kitchen. A full, slow rise deepens flavour, so don't rush it with too much heat. When risen, gently deflate, divide into 6 to 8 equal pieces, round each into a ball, and rest them covered for another 15 minutes so the gluten relaxes and the dough rolls out without fighting back.

Set a heavy cast-iron skillet or tawa over high heat for a full 5 minutes until it is smoking-hot — this is your stand-in for the tandoor. Meanwhile, on a lightly floured surface, roll or stretch each ball into a teardrop or oval about 5 to 6 inches long and a generous 3 to 4 millimetres thick, leaving it slightly thicker than a tortilla. Don't roll it paper-thin; naan needs body to puff. Brush the top lightly with water just before it hits the pan — the moisture helps it grip and steam.

Lay the naan wet-side-down onto the dry, smoking pan. Within a minute it will balloon up with steam and the underside will char in dark spots — cover with a lid for 30 seconds to trap heat and encourage the puff. When the top is bubbling and the bottom is blistered black-and-gold, flip and cook the second side 30 to 60 seconds until spotted too. For an even more tandoor-like char, hold the puffed naan with tongs directly over an open gas flame for a few seconds. Keep finished breads wrapped in a towel to stay soft.

Warm the ghee or melted butter with the minced garlic just until fragrant — don't brown the garlic. The moment each naan comes off the heat, brush it generously with the garlic-ghee so it soaks into the hot, open crumb, then scatter with chopped coriander. Serve immediately, stacked and wrapped in a clean towel to hold their softness and steam.

recipes.name: Nasi Goreng

ingredients.name: Day-old cooked jasmine rice, cold and separated
Regular soy sauce or kecap asin
Sambal oelek or fresh red chili, sliced
Fried shallots, cucumber slices, spring onion, and/or fried egg for serving

steps: Break up the cold day-old rice with your fingers or a fork until no clumps remain — every grain should be individual and dry. Cold, separated grains fry; fresh warm rice steams and turns to paste. If using solid terasi (shrimp paste), break off the required amount and toast it briefly: wrap in foil and hold over a low gas flame for 1 minute per side, or dry-fry in a small pan until fragrant and slightly crumbly. The toasting kills any fishy rawness and converts the paste into a powerfully savory, nutty compound. Crumble the toasted terasi into a small dish. Have all other ingredients measured and within arm's reach — nasi goreng moves fast.

Heat a wok or large cast-iron skillet over the highest flame you have until a drop of water vaporizes instantly on contact — this takes 2–3 minutes. Add the oil; it should ripple and shimmer immediately. Add the sliced shallots and stir-fry for 60 seconds until translucent and beginning to colour. Add the minced garlic and crumbled terasi, pressing the terasi against the hot wok with the spatula to break it up. Stir-fry for 30 seconds — the kitchen will fill with a powerful, savory, slightly funky aroma that quickly becomes complex and toasted. Add the sambal and toss for 15 seconds. The wok should be smoking lightly.

Push the aromatics to one side of the wok. Crack both eggs into the empty space. Leave them to set for 10–15 seconds without touching — the yolk should just begin to set at the edges. Then scramble them roughly with the spatula, breaking up into large, irregular curds. Before the egg is fully set and while it still looks slightly wet and shiny, push the aromatics back over the eggs and fold everything together. Partially-set egg integrates into the rice better than fully-cooked scrambled egg, which clumps separately.

Add the separated rice to the wok in two additions, tossing vigorously after each — use a spatula and a rapid scooping-and-flipping motion. Pour in the kecap manis and regular soy sauce over the rice (not the aromatics directly, which can burn) and toss continuously for 2–3 minutes. Every grain should be coated in the dark, mahogany-brown glaze. The rice may crackle and pop as individual grains toast against the wok surface — this is the wok hei you want. Taste and adjust with soy or kecap manis. Plate immediately.

Plate the nasi goreng immediately — it does not wait well. Top with a fried egg (sunny-side up, the yolk runny), crispy fried shallots scattered over the top, sliced cucumber alongside, and spring onion. The fried egg's yolk, broken at the table, acts as a sauce for the rice. The fried shallots add a final crunch and sweetness that the recipe sorely needs after all that heat. A few slices of cucumber cut through the richness. Serve with extra sambal on the side for those who want more heat.

recipes.name: Nasi Lemak
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Dried red chilies, soaked and blended

steps: Combine rinsed rice, coconut milk, pandan leaves, and salt in a heavy saucepan. Add enough water so the total liquid sits exactly 1.5 cm above the rice surface. Bring to a boil over medium heat, stir once, then immediately reduce to the lowest possible heat, cover tightly, and cook for 12 minutes. Remove from heat and steam, undisturbed, for 10 more minutes. Remove pandan before serving.

Heat oil in a wok until shimmering (about 175 C). Add dried anchovies in a single layer and fry, stirring constantly, for 3–5 minutes until deep golden and crunchy throughout. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper. They will continue to crisp as they cool. In the same oil, fry peanuts for 2 minutes until golden. Drain separately.

In the same wok (add oil if needed), fry blended shallots and chili paste over medium heat, stirring constantly, for 12–15 minutes. The paste will sputter, darken, and shrink dramatically. Add palm sugar and continue to cook, scraping the bottom, for 5 more minutes until the sambal is very dark brick-red, glossy, and the oil has separated back to the surface. Season with salt and a small squeeze of tamarind if available.

Mound coconut rice in the centre of a banana leaf or plate. Add a generous spoonful of sambal alongside. Scatter fried anchovies and roasted peanuts over and around. Classic accompaniments include half a hard-boiled egg and sliced cucumber. Serve immediately — the contrast of hot rice, room-temperature sambal, and crunchy toppings is the point.

recipes.name: Nasu Dengaku
steps: Preheat oven to 200°C (400°F). Halve the eggplants lengthwise. Using a sharp knife, score the cut flesh in a deep crosshatch pattern — cuts about 1.5 cm apart and 1 cm deep — without piercing the skin. Brush the scored flesh generously with sesame oil. Place cut-side down on a lined baking tray and roast for 15–18 minutes until the flesh is completely soft and the skin has begun to wrinkle.

Whisk together the white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small bowl until completely smooth and glossy. The glaze should be thick enough to mound on a spoon — if it seems too stiff, add a teaspoon of mirin. If it runs freely, the miso may be very wet; a brief stir over low heat will tighten it.

Flip the roasted eggplant halves cut-side up. Using a spoon or pastry brush, spread the dengaku glaze generously and evenly across each cut surface, covering the entire flesh and working it into the scored crosshatch. Place under a hot broiler (or return to top rack at 230°C) for 3–5 minutes, watching closely, until the glaze darkens to a deep mahogany brown and bubbles vigorously at the edges. Garnish immediately with sesame seeds and scallion.

recipes.name: Nduja Butter
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, softened to room temperature

steps: The butter must be genuinely soft — not cold and hard, and not starting to melt. Leave it at room temperature for at least 45–60 minutes before beginning, or until it dents easily under gentle finger pressure. Beat the softened butter in a bowl with a wooden spoon or hand mixer on medium speed for 2–3 minutes until it turns pale ivory, increases in volume, and becomes noticeably lighter and fluffier in texture. This step aerates the butter and creates the foundation for a silky compound that melts smoothly rather than breaking into greasy pools.

Add the nduja to the whipped butter. At room temperature, nduja is soft and spreadable — it will cream into the butter easily. Beat on medium speed until the nduja is completely incorporated and no red-orange streaks remain. The nduja's fat and spice oils will dye the butter a warm terracotta-orange color throughout. The mixture will smell intensely of pork fat, fermented meat, and Calabrian chili — a very direct, animal aroma. This step should take no more than 90 seconds of active beating.

Add the chives, lemon zest, black pepper, and salt to the nduja butter base. Fold in gently with a rubber spatula — do not beat, which would bruise the chives and turn them dark. Three or four broad folds are enough to distribute them evenly. Lay a large sheet of plastic wrap on the counter. Spoon the butter along one edge and use the wrap to roll it into a compact log about 5 cm in diameter. Twist the ends firmly to compress and shape the log. Refrigerate for at least 45 minutes until very firm, or freeze for up to 2 months. Slice into rounds directly from the refrigerator.

recipes.name: Nduja Tomato Sauce

ingredients.name: Burrata or fresh mozzarella to serve (optional)

steps: Heat olive oil in a heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium heat. Add garlic and cook for 90 seconds until pale golden. Add nduja in one piece. Using a wooden spoon, press and break it up as it heats — within 2–3 minutes it will melt into the oil completely, releasing vivid orange-red fat and transforming the olive oil into a blazing, chili-scented emulsion.

Add canned tomatoes to the pan, crushing them with your hand as you pour. Stir to incorporate the nduja emulsion into the tomatoes — the sauce will instantly turn a deep, vivid red-orange. Season lightly with salt (remember nduja is already salty). Simmer uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally and crushing any remaining tomato chunks. The sauce should reduce and thicken visibly.

Remove from heat. Tear basil leaves and stir through the sauce. Taste and adjust salt. Toss immediately with cooked rigatoni, paccheri, or calamarata (tube pastas that trap the spicy sauce inside). Add a spoonful of pasta water if needed to emulsify. Serve with torn burrata draped over the top, which cools the heat and adds rich contrast.

recipes.name: Neapolitan Pizza Dough
steps: Stir yeast into cool water (18–20 °C / 65–68 °F) until no granules float on the surface.
Add flour to the slurry. Stir with a wooden spoon until no dry flour remains.
Cover and let the dough rest 20–30 minutes at room temperature. The flour will fully hydrate and gluten will begin organizing on its own.
Sprinkle salt across the surface. Pinch and fold until it disappears into the dough.

Perform stretch-and-folds at 30-minute intervals: lift one side, stretch up, fold over. Rotate. Repeat across four rounds (about 2 hours total), then let the dough relax 15–20 minutes before the bulk rise.
Cover. Let rise at cool room temperature (18–20 °C / 65–68 °F) for 8–12 hours — or 4–6 hours at a warm 24–26 °C / 75–79 °F — until the dough has roughly doubled and is jiggly when nudged.

Divide into equal portions (about 250–280 g each for a 30 cm pizza). Tuck each into a tight ball under cupped hands, sealing the seam underneath, then cover and proof 4–6 hours at room temperature (or cold-proof in the fridge 24–48 hours, returning the balls to room temperature about 2 hours before stretching) until puffy and relaxed.

recipes.name: New England Clam Chowder
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Chopped clams, canned or fresh (with liquor reserved)
Salt pork or thick-cut bacon, diced
Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and diced 1cm
Kosher salt, white pepper, and fresh thyme

steps: Place the diced salt pork in a cold, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven and set over medium-low heat. Cook slowly, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the fat has fully rendered and the pork bits are golden and crispy. Starting cold ensures maximum fat extraction. Remove the crispy pork bits with a slotted spoon and reserve.

Add the diced onion to the rendered fat over medium heat and cook, stirring occasionally, for 5–7 minutes until soft and translucent but not browned. Sprinkle the flour over the onions and stir continuously for 1–2 minutes, coating every piece of onion. This blonde roux is the chowder's body — it must cook enough to lose its raw flour taste but must not take on any color.

Pour the reserved clam liquor plus enough water or clam juice to cover the potatoes by 2cm into the pot while whisking to prevent lumps. Add the diced potatoes. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 12–15 minutes until the potatoes are tender but still holding their shape. Do not boil vigorously — aggressive boiling will cause the potatoes to break apart and make the chowder muddy.

Reduce heat to low. Stir in the heavy cream and the chopped clams. Heat gently for 3–5 minutes until warmed through. Do not boil after adding the cream — it will break and curdle. The clams only need to be warmed, never cooked; if they were raw they would toughen severely at this stage. Taste and adjust salt and white pepper.

Ladle the chowder into warm bowls. Top with the reserved crispy pork bits and a crack of black pepper. Optionally drizzle with a few drops of heavy cream in a spiral. Serve with oyster crackers or crusty bread on the side. The chowder thickens considerably as it cools — serve while hot.

recipes.name: New York Bagels
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Everything bagel seasoning or sesame/poppy seeds

steps: Combine flour, salt, yeast, and malt syrup. Add cold water (cold water slows fermentation and improves texture). Mix until a very stiff, dry-looking dough forms — bagel dough is noticeably stiffer than any other bread dough, with only 55% hydration. Knead vigorously for 12–15 minutes by hand (or 10 minutes on medium in a stand mixer) until the dough is satiny smooth and extremely tight. Divide into 8 portions (about 110 g each).

Shape each portion into a tight ball, then use the thumb-through method: press both thumbs through the center of the ball and stretch the ring to 8–9 cm diameter with a 3 cm hole (the hole shrinks during proofing and baking). Alternatively, roll each ball into a 25 cm rope and join the ends with a 3 cm overlap, pressing firmly and rolling the seam against the work surface to seal. Place on parchment-lined trays dusted with cornmeal or semolina. Refrigerate uncovered overnight (12–16 hours).

Remove bagels from refrigerator. Float test: drop one bagel in cold water — it should float within 10 seconds. If it sinks, let the batch proof at room temperature for 30 more minutes. Bring a wide pot of water to a rolling boil. Add barley malt syrup. Boil bagels 2–3 at a time for 60 seconds per side (softer) or 90 seconds per side (chewier, more authentic). Remove with a spider or slotted spoon, drain, then immediately press the wet top into seeds or seasoning.

Bake on a parchment-lined tray (or preheated baking stone) at 230 C (450 F) for 18–22 minutes until deeply golden-brown with no pale patches. Rotate the tray at 10 minutes. The bagels will darken significantly in the final 3 minutes. Cool on a wire rack for at least 15 minutes before cutting — the crumb is still setting.

recipes.name: New York Cheesecake
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Graham crackers, crushed to fine crumbs

steps: Combine the graham cracker crumbs and melted butter in a bowl and mix until the crumbs are evenly moistened — they should look like wet sand and hold together when squeezed. Press firmly into the bottom of a 23cm springform pan using the flat bottom of a measuring cup. Press firmly and evenly — including 2–3cm up the sides. Bake at 175°C for 8–10 minutes until just set. Cool completely before filling.

All ingredients must be at room temperature — cold cream cheese will not beat smooth and will leave lumps that never fully incorporate. Beat the cream cheese with a stand mixer paddle (not whisk) on medium speed until completely smooth and creamy, about 2 minutes. Scrape the bowl and beater thoroughly. Add the sugar and beat for 2 more minutes. Scrape again. Beat in the vanilla and salt. The goal is smooth — not airy. High-speed beating incorporates air that causes cracking.

With the mixer on low speed, add the eggs one at a time, beating only until each is just incorporated before adding the next — no more. Overmixing after adding eggs develops the batter and adds air. Finally, add the sour cream and mix on low just until combined. Scrape the bowl one final time and fold gently by hand with a spatula. The finished batter should be smooth, thick, and flow slowly.

Preheat oven to 160°C. Wrap the outside of the springform pan tightly in two layers of heavy foil (to prevent water ingress). Pour the batter into the cooled crust. Set the pan in a larger roasting pan and pour boiling water into the roasting pan to come halfway up the sides of the springform. Bake for 60–70 minutes until the edges are set and the center 10cm jiggles as a single mass. Turn off oven, crack door 5cm, and leave for 1 hour.

Remove from the water bath after the oven rest. Run a thin knife around the inside edge of the springform to release the cheesecake (this prevents cracking as it shrinks). Cool at room temperature for 2 hours. Refrigerate uncovered for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. Remove the springform ring only when the cheesecake is fully cold. Slice with a hot, dry knife for clean cuts.

recipes.name: Nibitashi
steps: Bring a large pot of unsalted water to a rolling boil. Submerge the spinach stems first for 15 seconds, then push the leaves under and blanch for 30–45 seconds total. The water must be at a full rolling boil throughout — a weak boil steams instead of blanches and the color suffers. Transfer immediately to a bowl of ice water and leave for 1 full minute.

Combine dashi, soy sauce, and mirin in a small saucepan. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat. Taste — the broth should taste pleasantly salty and lightly sweet, slightly more assertive than you want the finished dish to be, because the greens will dilute it. Simmer for 2 minutes to cook off the raw mirin alcohol.

Add the squeezed blanched greens to the simmering broth. Gently submerge them and simmer for just 60 seconds — this opens the cell walls slightly to allow the broth to enter. Remove from heat and let the greens steep in the broth, off the heat, for 15 minutes as the liquid cools. Lift the greens out, squeeze gently again to remove excess broth, and cut into 4 cm lengths. Arrange in small mounds in serving bowls. Spoon a small amount of the steeping liquid over each portion and top with bonito flakes.

recipes.name: Okonomiyaki

ingredients.name: Kewpie mayonnaise + aonori (green seaweed flakes) + katsuobushi for topping
