Remove from heat and immediately add both paprikas. Stir vigorously for 30 seconds; the residual heat will bloom the spices without burning them. Burning paprika is irreversible and produces a sharp, acrid bitterness.

Add the crushed tomatoes, sherry vinegar, salt, and sugar to the saucepan. Stir to combine with the bloomed paprika base. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, then reduce to low. Cook uncovered for 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce has thickened to a loose paste that mounds slightly on a spoon and no longer tastes raw.

For a restaurant-smooth sauce, carefully transfer the warm sauce to a blender and blend on high for 60 seconds until completely smooth. Alternatively, use an immersion blender directly in the pan. This is optional — the sauce is excellent either chunky or smooth — but the smooth version clings better to fried potatoes.

For the aioli layer: stir the mayonnaise with a small additional minced garlic clove and the fresh lemon juice until smooth. Taste — it should be sharp with garlic, bright with lemon, and creamy. This is a shortcut aioli; for the full version, emulsify from egg yolk. Refrigerate until service.

recipes.name: Patatas Bravas
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Floury potatoes (Maris Piper or Russet), peeled and cut into 3 cm chunks
Olive oil or sunflower oil for frying
Ripe tomatoes, roughly chopped (or canned whole plum tomatoes)
Olive oil for the brava sauce

steps: Place the potato chunks in a large pot and cover generously with cold salted water. Bring to a boil over high heat and cook for 12–15 minutes until the potatoes are just cooked through but not falling apart — a skewer should slide in with slight resistance at the center. Drain in a colander and shake the colander vigorously 5–6 times to rough up the edges. This roughing-up shatters the exterior starch into jagged, uneven points that will turn into the craggy, shattery crust that defines great bravas. Spread the roughed-up potatoes in a single layer on a rack and let them steam-dry for at least 10 minutes. The drier the surface, the more ferocious the crust in the fry.

Heat the olive oil for the sauce in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook for 1–2 minutes until pale gold. Add both paprikas and stir for 30 seconds — the paprika blooms almost immediately, turning the oil a vivid red-orange. Add the chopped tomatoes and a pinch of salt and cook, stirring occasionally, for 15–20 minutes until the tomatoes have broken down completely and the sauce has thickened and darkened. Add the sherry vinegar, stir to combine, and taste. The sauce should be bold, smoky, and hot — not just mildly spiced but genuinely brava (brave, ferocious). Blend until smooth with a stick blender or pass through a sieve. Keep warm.

Heat the frying oil in a wide, heavy pan to 150C / 300F. Add the potato chunks in batches and fry for 4–5 minutes until they have a pale, set exterior but no color — this is the first fry, which drives out any remaining surface moisture and begins to build the interior structure. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel. Raise the oil temperature to 190C / 375F. Return the potatoes in smaller batches and fry for 3–4 minutes until they turn deep gold, with a craggy, puffed, irregular crust. Remove and drain immediately. Season with flakes of sea salt the moment they leave the oil while the surface is still wet with fat — the salt will stick. Do not pile the finished potatoes — they lose their crust in seconds against each other's steam.

Arrange the fried potatoes in a shallow dish or cazuela in a single loose layer. Spoon the warm brava sauce generously over the top — not a thin drizzle but a proper coating, enough that every potato gets touched. The sauce should puddle slightly in the gaps between the potatoes. Serve immediately. Bravas should always arrive at the table hot — the window between perfect and soggy is narrow. If serving with aioli (traditional in some regions), drizzle it over the sauce in thin lines or zigzags. The dual-sauce version (bravas with both brava and aioli) is called bravas 'ali-oli' and is a common Madrid tapas bar offering.

recipes.name: Pâte à Choux
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Whole eggs, lightly beaten, room temperature
ingredients.measure: 1 parts by weight of egg to flour

steps: Combine the water, cubed butter, salt, and sugar in a medium heavy-bottomed saucepan. Place over medium heat and bring to a full, rolling boil. The objective here is to melt the butter completely before the water boils — if the water boils first and begins to evaporate before the butter is melted, the fat-to-water ratio of the dough is compromised and the choux will be unpredictable. Watch carefully: as the butter melts you will see the water turn from clear to a slightly milky white emulsion. As it approaches the boil, the emulsion will foam up. The moment it reaches a full boil, proceed immediately to the next step — every extra second of boiling evaporates water and changes the dough's consistency.

Remove the pan from the heat and add all the sifted flour in one go. Beat immediately and vigorously with a wooden spoon — this is urgent. The hot butter-water must hydrate every flour particle in the first few seconds, and the starch must gelatinise instantly in the residual heat. Beat until no dry flour remains, then return the pan to medium heat. Cook the panade (the dough ball), stirring and pressing constantly, for 2–3 minutes. You are driving off moisture — the panade is ready when it pulls away completely from the sides of the pan, forms a cohesive ball in the center, and leaves a thin, dry film on the bottom of the pan. This film is the sign that enough water has evaporated. The dough will be very stiff and non-sticky at this point.

This is the most nuanced step in choux. Allow the panade to cool for 5 minutes (so it does not cook the eggs on contact), then begin adding the beaten eggs gradually — a tablespoon at a time for the first few additions, beating vigorously between each addition. The dough will at first look broken and curdled as the egg tries to separate from the fat in the panade. Keep beating — it will come back together. Do not add all the egg at once. The total egg needed varies with the exact water content of your panade, the protein content of your flour, and the ambient humidity. Stop adding egg when the dough reaches the correct consistency: when you lift the spatula and allow the dough to fall, it should drop in a slow, heavy 'V' shape that bends but does not break — the beak should be 2–3 cm long before it drops. Test by pulling the spatula through the dough: it should form a smooth channel that slowly closes.

Pipe the choux onto parchment-lined baking sheets: for profiteroles, make 3 cm rounds spaced 4 cm apart; for éclairs, pipe 10 cm lines. Dampen your fingertip and smooth any peaks. Bake at 200°C (390°F) for 10 minutes without opening the oven — the initial blast of heat causes rapid steam expansion that puffs the shells. Then reduce to 180°C (356°F) and bake for a further 15–20 minutes until the shells are deep golden-brown all over, not just on top. The shells must be fully coloured before you open the oven: a pale shell will collapse when it meets the cool air. In the final 5 minutes, crack the oven door open 5 cm to allow steam to escape and the shells to dry completely inside. Transfer to a wire rack and pierce each shell with a skewer at the base to vent remaining steam.

recipes.name: Pâte Brisée (Shortcrust Tart Pastry)
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Place the flour and salt in a large bowl (or food processor). Add the cold butter cubes. Rub the butter into the flour with your fingertips, lifting and dropping the mixture from a height to aerate it, until the mixture resembles coarse, damp sand with no individual butter pieces larger than a pea. Work quickly — if your hands are warm, press the bowl against a cold surface. Alternatively, pulse in a food processor 8–10 times.

Beat together the egg yolk and ice-cold water in a small bowl. Make a well in the flour-butter mixture and pour in the egg-water. Using a fork or a pastry cutter, bring the dough together with minimal mixing — use a chopping and stirring motion, not kneading. The dough will look shaggy and barely coherent. As soon as it comes together when you squeeze a handful in your fist, stop. Turn out onto a lightly floured surface and press together into a flat disc. Do not knead.

Wrap the disc tightly in cling film and refrigerate for at least 45 minutes, or up to 3 days. This rest allows the gluten to relax (so it does not shrink when baked) and the butter to firm up again (so it stays in distinct layers). Remove from the fridge 5–10 minutes before rolling if very hard.

Roll the rested dough on a lightly floured surface to 3–4 mm thickness. Line a 23 cm tart tin, pressing gently into the corners. Trim the edge and prick the base lightly with a fork. Freeze for 15 minutes. Line with parchment and fill with baking beans or rice. Blind bake at 180 C for 15–18 minutes, remove beans, brush the base with a little beaten egg, and return for 5–8 minutes until the base is dry and golden. The egg wash seals the pastry against wet fillings.

recipes.name: Patina de Piris
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Garum / liquamen (fish sauce, a few drops)

steps: Peel and core the pears and cut them into rough chunks. Simmer them gently with the honey and a splash of water in a covered pan until completely tender and translucent, 12-15 minutes. The honey draws out their juice and seasons the flesh from within. Drain off most of the loose liquid so the finished custard will set.

Tip the drained pears into a mortar (or food processor) and pound to a smooth purée. Crack the pepper and grind the cumin fresh, then work them through the warm fruit. Apicius is emphatic about pepper here — it should be present, a gentle prickle that lifts the sweetness rather than a sting. Let the purée cool to just warm before adding the eggs.

Beat the eggs until smooth and stir them steadily into the warm pear purée so they thicken it without scrambling. Add just a few drops of garum — enough to deepen and round the flavour, not to taste of fish. Taste: it should read sweet first, then savoury, with a peppery warmth underneath. Whisk to a loose, pourable batter.

Brush a shallow baking dish with olive oil and pour in the batter. Bake at 170°C / 340°F until the patina is just set with the faintest wobble at the centre, 30-35 minutes (a water bath gives the silkiest set). Crack a little more pepper over the top. Cool until barely warm — it firms as it rests — and serve in soft spoonfuls.

recipes.name: Pavlova

ingredients.name: Egg whites (room temperature, no trace of yolk)
White wine vinegar or lemon juice

steps: Ensure the mixing bowl, whisk, and all utensils are completely clean, dry, and free of any trace of fat — even a drop of egg yolk or a smear of butter will prevent the whites from whipping. Wipe everything with a cut lemon half and dry thoroughly. Beat the room-temperature egg whites on medium speed until they form soft peaks that droop at the tip when the whisk is lifted. Begin adding the caster sugar one tablespoon at a time — this slow addition is non-negotiable. After each addition, beat for 30 seconds before adding more. The process takes 10–12 minutes total, and the patience is what creates a stable, dense meringue rather than a brittle shell.

Sprinkle the cornstarch and vanilla extract over the meringue and pour in the vinegar. Fold with a large metal spoon or rubber spatula using exactly three or four large, sweeping motions from the bottom of the bowl up and over the top. Do not stir or beat. This technique is intentionally under-mixed — a few unincorporated streaks are perfectly fine. The cornstarch and vinegar work together with the egg proteins to create the marshmallow interior: the starch gelatinizes and the acid keeps the proteins tender, preventing the meringue from setting entirely solid.

Draw a 22cm circle on a sheet of parchment paper (trace a dinner plate), flip the parchment so the pencil is face-down, and place on a baking sheet. Spoon the meringue onto the circle in a mounded pile. Using the back of a spoon, shape it into a disc with slightly raised sides and a shallow indent in the center — the well is where the cream and fruit will pool. Bake at 140°C (285°F) for 1 hour and 15 minutes. Turn the oven off completely and leave the pavlova inside with the door closed for at least 2 hours — overnight is ideal. Do not open the oven during this time.

Just before serving — not hours ahead — beat the cold heavy whipping cream and vanilla extract in a chilled bowl until the cream reaches medium-firm peaks. The cream should hold its shape when the bowl is tilted but still have a slight jiggle at the top of the peaks. Stop before the cream becomes stiff or grainy. The target is a cream that billows generously rather than standing in rigid blocks — it will settle slightly on the meringue, which is the correct look.

Transfer the cooled pavlova shell to a serving plate. Pile the whipped cream into the center well in generous, billowing mounds, allowing it to spread naturally toward the raised edges without spilling over. Arrange the strawberry halves and kiwi slices first, then scatter the blueberries and finally spoon the passionfruit pulp over everything — the golden, seedy pulp running down over the cream and fruit is the signature finish. Serve immediately or within 30 minutes — the pavlova softens quickly once topped.

recipes.name: Peach Melba
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Icing sugar (for the sauce, to taste)

steps: Combine the water and caster sugar in a saucepan just wide enough to hold the peaches snugly. Scrape in the vanilla seeds and drop in the pod, add the strip of lemon peel and a squeeze of the juice, and warm over medium heat, stirring, until the sugar fully dissolves. Bring to a gentle simmer so the syrup is clear and fragrant before the fruit goes in.

Lower the whole peaches into the barely-simmering syrup, cover with a round of parchment to keep them submerged, and poach gently for 12-18 minutes depending on ripeness, turning once. They are done when a paring knife slides into the flesh with no resistance. Lift them out, and once cool enough to handle, slip off the skins — they should peel away in sheets. Halve and stone them, then chill the peaches in their syrup.

Blitz the raspberries with the icing sugar and a few drops of lemon juice to a smooth purée — no cooking, to keep the colour vivid and the flavour fresh. Pass it through a fine sieve, pressing hard to extract every drop and leaving the seeds behind. Taste and adjust the sugar so the sauce is sweet but still bright with acidity. Chill until cold.

Chill your coupes or shallow glasses. Set a generous scoop of cold vanilla ice cream in the base of each, arrange two peach halves cut-side down over the top, then spoon the cold melba sauce over the fruit so it bleeds down over the ice cream. Scatter with toasted flaked almonds and serve at once, before the ice cream begins to soften.

recipes.name: Peanut Sauce
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Thai red curry paste (krueng gaeng phed)
Coconut cream (thick, top of the can)

steps: Dry-roast the raw peanuts in a heavy pan over medium-low heat, shaking constantly, 8 to 12 minutes, until golden and fragrant with dark freckling. Let them cool completely — they crisp as they cool. Pound in a granite mortar (or pulse in a processor) to a coarse rubble: about two-thirds gritty meal and one-third pea-sized pieces. You want texture, not peanut butter; over-grinding releases oil and turns the sauce pasty and flat.

Put the thick coconut cream alone in a wide pan over medium heat and let it bubble and reduce, stirring, 4 to 6 minutes, until it 'cracks' — the cream splits and a slick of clear oil pools at the edges. Stir in the red curry paste and fry it in that coconut oil, pressing and turning, 3 to 5 minutes, until the raw garlic-and-galangal smell cooks off and the oil glows red and aromatic. This frying of the paste (pad prik gaeng) is what builds depth; skip it and the sauce tastes flat and dusty.

Stir the pounded peanuts into the fried paste so every grain is coated in the red oil, then pour in the coconut milk (or water). Bring to a gentle simmer and cook 8 to 12 minutes, stirring often as the peanuts drink the liquid and thicken the sauce. It will go from loose to luxuriously thick; thin with a splash more coconut milk or water whenever it gets too tight to fall off the spoon. The peanut starch and oil now carry the chili heat and give the sauce its body.

Off a vigorous simmer, stir in the tamarind, palm sugar, and fish sauce. Let it melt together for a minute, then taste and tune: it should hit sweet first, then salty and sour close behind, with the chili heat blooming at the back. Adjust in small amounts — palm sugar to round, tamarind to brighten, fish sauce to deepen — until no single note dominates. Loosen to a thick-but-pourable dipping consistency. Spoon into a bowl, scatter the reserved chopped peanuts over the top, and serve warm with grilled satay.

recipes.name: Pear Ginger Crisp

ingredients.name: Pears, ripe but firm, peeled, cored, cut into 2 cm chunks
Fresh ginger, peeled and finely grated
Unsalted butter, cold, cut into 1 cm cubes

steps: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) with a rack in the middle. In a large bowl, toss the pears with the lemon juice, 50 g brown sugar, cornstarch, fresh ginger, and crystallized ginger until the cornstarch disappears. Spread evenly in a 9 × 9 in (23 × 23 cm) or 2 qt (2 l) baking dish.

Stir the flour, oats, 100 g brown sugar, cinnamon, and salt together in a bowl. Add the cold butter cubes and rub them in with your fingertips (or a pastry cutter) until the butter is in pea-sized pieces and the mixture holds together in clumps when squeezed, 3–4 minutes. Chill 10 minutes if the butter feels soft.

Scatter the topping evenly over the pears, leaving it in clumps rather than pressing it down. Set the dish on a foil-lined sheet pan to catch drips. Bake 45–55 minutes, until the topping is deep golden brown and the filling is bubbling thickly at the edges — a knife should slide into the pears with no resistance. Tent with foil if the topping browns before the filling bubbles.
Cool on a rack for at least 20 minutes so the juices thicken as they cool. Serve warm with vanilla ice cream or lightly sweetened whipped cream.

recipes.name: Pecan Pie Filling
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Spread the pecan halves on a dry sheet pan in a single layer. Roast at 175 C (350 F) for 8–10 minutes, stirring once halfway through. You are not just toasting for color — you are driving off moisture so the nuts stay crisp through a long bake inside a wet custard.

In a large bowl, whisk together the dark corn syrup, brown sugar, melted (not hot) butter, salt, and vanilla until the sugar has partially dissolved and the mixture is uniform in color. The butter must be cooled to below 50 C or it will begin to cook the eggs when they are added. Rub a drop between your fingers — you should not feel undissolved sugar crystals, though some is acceptable at this stage.

Add the eggs one at a time, whisking each in fully before adding the next. Do not beat aggressively — you are incorporating eggs, not building foam. Excess air creates a soufflé-like filling that puffs and cracks dramatically in the oven. Whisk gently, just until each egg is fully absorbed and the mixture is homogeneous.

Arrange the toasted pecan halves in concentric circles in an unbaked 9-inch pie shell, flat side down, covering the entire bottom. Pour the filling batter gently over them — the pecans will float up and redistribute. Do not try to hold them in place; they will self-arrange as they bake. Fill to within 1 cm of the crust rim.

Bake at 175 C (350 F) on the lower-middle rack for 50–60 minutes. Shield the crust edge with foil or a pie shield after the first 20 minutes. The custard sets from the outside inward — the edges will firm up while the center still appears liquid. Do not overbake waiting for the center to set firm in the oven; it will finish cooking off-heat.

recipes.name: Peking Duck
steps: Mix five-spice and salt. Remove the neck and giblets. Dry the duck cavity thoroughly with paper towels. Rub the five-spice-salt mixture inside the cavity. Stuff the cavity with ginger and spring onion. Truss the opening with a skewer. Using a bicycle pump or air compressor nozzle inserted under the skin at the neck opening, inflate the skin away from the breast — this separates subcutaneous fat from flesh, the key to shatteringly crisp skin.

Hold the duck over a large pot or wok by its trussed neck. Ladle boiling water slowly and evenly over the entire skin surface for 2–3 minutes — the skin will tighten and turn opaque white. This opens the pores and tightens the protein matrix, allowing better lacquer adhesion and a crisper final skin.

Warm the maltose in a small pan over very low heat until it just flows. Stir in the Shaoxing wine and soy sauce to make a lacquer. Brush a thin, even coat over the entire duck skin. Hang the duck in a cool, airy spot (or in front of a fan) and repeat the lacquering every 4 hours for a total of 3–4 coats over 24 hours. The skin must be fully dry between coats. This is non-negotiable — moisture trapped under the lacquer steams the skin during roasting instead of crisping it.

Preheat oven to 220 C (430 F). Place the duck breast-side down on a wire rack set over a deep tray with 2 cm of water beneath (to catch dripping fat and prevent smoking). Roast 25 minutes. Flip to breast-side up, increase to 240 C (465 F), and roast a further 20–25 minutes until the skin is shatteringly crisp and deeply lacquered.

recipes.name: Peperonata
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Mixed sweet bell peppers (red, yellow, orange — halved, seeded, cut into 1cm strips)

steps: Heat olive oil in a wide, heavy pot or deep skillet over medium-low heat. Add sliced onion and garlic. Season with a pinch of salt. Cook very gently, stirring occasionally, for 15 minutes until the onion is completely soft, sweet, and golden — not browned, just deeply cooked. Peperonata is a slow recipe; do not rush this step.

Add all the pepper strips to the pot. Season with salt. Stir to coat in the oil and onion. Cover with a lid and cook over medium-low heat for 20 minutes, lifting the lid and stirring every 5 minutes. The peppers will release a great deal of liquid — this is correct. The steam and pepper juice create the braising liquid.

Add the chopped tomatoes. Stir to combine. Remove the lid and cook over medium-low heat for 20–25 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes, until the tomatoes have completely collapsed, the liquid has reduced to a thick, jammy, glossy sauce that just coats the peppers, and the whole pot is a unified, glistening compote. The peppers should be completely tender and silky.

Off the heat, add a small splash of red wine vinegar if using — it lifts and brightens the sweetness. Taste and adjust salt. Tear fresh basil and stir through. Serve warm, at room temperature, or cold. Peperonata is extraordinarily versatile: use it as a side dish, bruschetta topping, pasta sauce, pizza base, or accompaniment to grilled meats and fish.

recipes.name: Peri-Peri Chicken
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Blend the chilies, garlic, lemon juice and zest, smoked paprika, oregano, olive oil, and salt in a blender or food processor until smooth. The sauce should be a vivid red-orange. Taste carefully — it should be very hot, punchy with acid, and deeply savory. Adjust salt and lemon to balance. For a milder result, remove seeds before blending. For maximum heat, use the whole chili including seeds.

Score the chicken skin in a crosshatch pattern with a sharp knife — 4–5 cuts per side, slicing through the skin to the flesh. This allows the marinade to penetrate deeply. Rub the peri-peri sauce all over the chicken: under the skin where possible, into all scoring lines, into the cavity. Reserve about 3 tablespoons of the marinade for basting during grilling. Place the chicken in a container, cover, and refrigerate for a minimum of 2 hours or overnight.

Prepare a two-zone grill: direct high heat on one side, indirect medium heat on the other. Start the chicken skin-side up on the indirect side and cook with the lid closed for 35–40 minutes, basting every 10 minutes with the reserved marinade. The lower, slower indirect heat allows the interior to cook through before the exterior burns. When the internal temperature reaches 68 °C in the thickest part of the thigh, move the chicken to direct heat skin-side down for 5–8 minutes to lacquer and char the skin.

Rest the chicken breast-side down on a cutting board for 10 minutes — resting breast-side down keeps the breast meat basted in its own juices. Carve and serve with Portuguese rolls, chips, and a simple salad. Drizzle any resting juices over the carved meat. The heat from peri-peri builds slowly — warn guests that the full effect arrives 30 seconds after the first bite.

recipes.name: Pernil (Puerto Rican Slow-Roasted Pork Shoulder)

ingredients.name: Bone-in pork shoulder (picnic or Boston butt), skin-on
Fresh cilantro with stems, roughly chopped

steps: Using a pilón (mortar and pestle) or food processor, pound the garlic, oregano, salt, pepper, and cumin to a rough paste. Add vinegar and olive oil and mix to a thick, pungent adobo. Stir in the sazón and cilantro. The paste should be thick enough to press into incisions without falling out.

Score the skin in a crosshatch pattern, cutting through skin and fat but not meat. Using a thin, sharp knife, make 20–30 deep incisions all over the meat (under and around the skin flap) and push a generous amount of adobo into each with your finger. Rub remaining adobo all over the meat. Rub coarse salt all over the skin only. Place in a roasting pan, skin-side up, uncovered, in the refrigerator for 24–36 hours.

Place pork skin-side up on a rack in a deep roasting pan. Add 2 cups of water to the pan bottom. Cover tightly with foil. Roast at 160 C (325 F) for 5–6 hours (approximately 1.5 hours per kilogram). The pork is done when an instant-read thermometer reads 90 C (195 F) at the thickest part — this temperature ensures all collagen has converted to gelatin.

Remove the foil and increase oven to 230 C (450 F). Roast uncovered for 30–45 minutes, watching constantly, until the skin bubbles and shatters into golden cuerito (crackling). Rotate the pan every 10 minutes. The skin should go from pale and steamed to blistered and golden — listen for the crackling, popping sound.

Rest uncovered for 15 minutes. Carve by pulling the meat in large chunks with two forks — pernil should not be sliced, it should be pulled. Keep the cuerito intact and break it into pieces separately, distributing equitably. Serve with arroz con gandules and tostones.

recipes.name: Persian Rice with Tahdig
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Neutral oil or clarified butter (for pot)

steps: Rinse the basmati in cold water, changing the water 4-5 times until it runs clear. Cover the rinsed rice with cold water, add 1 tsp of salt per cup of rice, and soak for at least 30 minutes — ideally 1-2 hours. The soaking whitens the grains, separates them during cooking, and cuts the final steam time.

Bring a large pot of generously salted water (as salty as pasta water) to a rolling boil. Drain the soaked rice and add to the boiling water. Parboil for exactly 5-7 minutes, stirring once. Test frequently from minute 5: the rice should be cooked on the outside but still have a distinct chalky white line at the very center when bitten. Drain immediately through a fine colander and rinse with cold water to stop cooking.

Heat the oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot (nonstick or well-seasoned) over medium-high heat until shimmering. Whisk the yogurt with a ladleful (about 15 parts) of the drained parboiled rice and the bloomed saffron water. Spread this yogurt-rice mixture across the bottom of the hot pot in an even layer — this forms the tahdig. Mound the remaining parboiled rice over the top in a pyramid, keeping it away from the pot sides. Drizzle the remaining saffron water over the top. Wrap the lid tightly in a clean kitchen towel (to absorb steam) and place on the pot. Cook over medium-high heat for 10 minutes to set the crust, then reduce to the lowest possible heat.

After 45-55 total minutes of steaming, remove the lid. Scoop out the fluffy upper rice onto a serving platter and scatter the saffron-stained grains and barberries over the top for color. Now the moment of truth: place a large flat platter over the mouth of the pot and invert in one decisive motion. The tahdig should release as a single, golden disc — crackling and glossy. If it sticks, return to low heat for 2 more minutes.

recipes.name: Persian Chelo Rice with Tahdig

ingredients.name: Fine sea salt (for soaking and parboiling)

steps: Rinse the basmati in cold water until the water runs clear — at least 5-6 rinses. Soak in cold water with 1 tablespoon of salt for 30 minutes minimum (up to 4 hours). The soaking hydrates the grain, which allows it to elongate dramatically during steaming. Drain and rinse once more.

Bring a large pot of heavily salted water to a rolling boil (should taste like seawater). Add the drained rice. Parboil uncovered for exactly 5-7 minutes, stirring gently once. A grain is ready when it has elongated and is tender at the outside but still has a firm, white core when bitten — like pasta 2 minutes before al dente. Drain immediately into a sieve and rinse with cold water to stop cooking. The rice is only half done at this point.

Melt the butter in a heavy-bottomed non-stick pot over medium-high. Layer sliced potato in a single even layer on the bottom. Mound the parboiled rice on top in a gentle pyramid — do not press it. Drizzle the bloomed saffron over the top third. Wrap the pot lid in a clean cloth to absorb condensation, place on tight. Cook on medium-high for 3 minutes, then reduce to the lowest possible heat. Steam for 35-45 minutes. To serve: invert the entire pot onto a serving platter so the golden tahdig comes out on top.

recipes.name: Persian Saffron Rice (Chelow)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Saffron threads, bloomed in 3 tbsp hot water
Lavash bread or thin flatbread (optional tahdig base)

steps: Rinse the basmati rice in several changes of cold water until the water runs clear — this removes surface starch that would make the cooked grains clump. Add salt to cold water (about 1 tablespoon per 2 cups rice) and soak the rinsed rice for 30–60 minutes, up to overnight in the refrigerator. Soaking allows the grain to begin absorbing water, which ensures it cooks evenly all the way through during the rapid parboil and prevents the exterior from overcooking before the center is done.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a vigorous boil — the water should taste pleasantly salty, like pasta water. Add the drained soaked rice and cook, stirring occasionally, for exactly 5–7 minutes. The rice is ready to drain when each grain has grown significantly in length and is just tender at the exterior but still has a firm, white, chalky core when bitten. The center should still have a snap. Drain immediately in a fine colander and rinse briefly with cool water to stop cooking.

In a wide, heavy-bottomed pot with a tight-fitting lid, heat the oil over medium heat. If using lavash, place a single layer over the oiled pot bottom, pressing to the edges. If using potato, layer thin slices over the base. Add 2 large spoonfuls of parboiled rice and spread to cover the lavash. Mound the remaining parboiled rice in a cone shape over the top — do not press or pack it. Create 5–6 holes down through the rice mound with the handle of a wooden spoon to allow steam to rise from below. Wrap the pot lid tightly in a clean kitchen cloth (this absorbs steam and prevents condensation dripping back onto the rice).

After 5 minutes on medium-high, reduce to absolute minimum heat (use a heat diffuser if available). Steam for 45 minutes. While the rice steams, bloom the saffron in hot water for 5 minutes, then mix with 2 tablespoons of melted butter. At the 45-minute mark, remove the lid and drizzle the saffron butter over 3–4 spoonfuls of rice in a separate bowl — stir to coat, then return this golden-orange rice to the top of the pot as a garnish. Replace lid for 5 more minutes. To serve: invert the pot onto a large round platter in one decisive motion. The tahdig should release with a satisfying thud.

recipes.name: Persian Tahdig (Crispy Rice)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Rinse the rice in cold water until the water runs clear — this removes excess surface starch that would otherwise glue the grains together. Soak in cold, lightly salted water for 30 minutes minimum, 2 hours ideally. Drain. Bring a large pot of heavily salted water (it should taste like the sea) to a vigorous boil. Add the soaked, drained rice and parboil for exactly 6–7 minutes, stirring gently once. The rice is done when the outside is fully cooked but the center still has a small chalky core — bite a grain to check. Drain immediately in a colander and rinse briefly with lukewarm water to stop the cooking.

In a heavy-bottomed, non-stick pot (24–26cm diameter), heat the oil over medium heat until shimmering. For a plain crust: add 2–3 tablespoons of water to the oil and let it sizzle, then immediately pile in all the parboiled rice, mounding it slightly in the center. Do not press or compact it — use a spoon handle to poke 5–6 holes down through the rice to allow steam to travel upward. For a potato tahdig (beloved variation): place thin potato slices in the oiled pan in a single overlapping layer before adding the rice. Scatter the cubed butter over the top of the mounded rice.

Wrap the pot lid tightly in a clean kitchen towel, securing the corners at the top so they do not hang near the burner. Place the lid on the pot — the towel absorbs condensation that would otherwise drip back down and make the rice wet. Set heat to medium-high for 3 minutes to start building the crust, then reduce to the absolute lowest simmer your burner offers. Cook undisturbed for 40–45 minutes. Do not lift the lid. The golden crust develops from below through even, gentle heat — disturbing this process resets it.

The unmolding is the theater of tahdig. Place a large serving platter on top of the pot. With one decisive, confident motion, flip the entire pot over onto the platter — like unmolding a cake. If the tahdig releases cleanly, you will hear it land in one piece. If it sticks, place the pot back on the cold sink bottom for 30 more seconds, then try again. Alternatively, serve family-style by first spooning the fluffy top rice onto the platter, then carefully lifting the crust in one piece to place on top, golden-side up.

recipes.name: Persillade
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Flat-leaf parsley, leaves and tender stems

steps: Peel the garlic cloves and mince them very finely with a sharp knife. Scatter the salt over the minced garlic on the cutting board. Using the flat side of the chef's knife, smear the garlic and salt across the board in long, forward strokes, then scrape it back with the blade and repeat — alternating between chopping and smearing. After 2–3 minutes of this motion, you have a smooth, sticky garlic paste. The salt abrades the garlic, releasing its juice and breaking down the cell walls to give a milder, more integrated flavor than raw chunks.

Pile the parsley leaves on the garlic paste on the cutting board. Chop together with a rocking motion, folding the mixture back toward the center as the parsley spreads outward. The goal is integration, not obliteration: you want the garlic paste fully coated in parsley oil and the parsley finely minced, but not reduced to a wet green mash. Keep chopping and folding until the mixture is uniform, fragrant, and vivid green. If using olive oil, drizzle it over the finished persillade and fold through — this both preserves the color and makes the persillade easier to scatter.

recipes.name: Peruvian Ceviche with Leche de Tigre

ingredients.name: Red onion, thinly sliced into half-moons
Fresh cilantro, leaves and thin stems
Choclo corn kernels (or corn on the cob)

steps: Ensure the fish is as cold as possible — partially freeze for 20 minutes if needed for cleaner cuts. Cut into 2cm cubes against the grain of the flesh. Uniformity matters: irregular pieces cure at different rates, leaving some over-cured and chalky while others are still raw. Place immediately in a chilled ceramic or glass bowl.

Season the fish cubes with salt and toss to coat. Add the garlic, ginger, and ají amarillo paste. Pour the lime juice over all — there should be enough to fully submerge the fish. Toss gently. The acid cure begins immediately: for Peruvian ceviche, the ideal cure time is just 3–5 minutes for a tender, barely-cooked interior. Taste at 3 minutes — the fish should be white on the exterior but still slightly translucent at the very center.

Add the sliced red onion and half the cilantro to the ceviche and toss once. Taste and adjust salt and ají amarillo level. Serve immediately in chilled bowls — pour the full leche de tigre over and around the fish. Arrange the choclo corn and sliced camote on the side. Scatter remaining cilantro over. The leche de tigre is not a by-product — it is the whole point. Serve with a spoon.

recipes.name: Picarones

ingredients.name: Orange-flesh sweet potato, cooked and mashed
Chancaca (raw cane sugar block) or dark muscovado sugar

steps: Ensure the sweet potato and squash mashes are cooled to lukewarm — warm enough to activate the yeast, cool enough not to kill it (38°C / 100°F is ideal). Combine the mashes in a large bowl. Dissolve the yeast in 3 tablespoons of warm water with a pinch of the sugar and leave 5 minutes until foamy. Add the foamy yeast, remaining sugar, salt, and anise seeds to the mash. Add the flour gradually, mixing to form a soft, slightly sticky dough. It will be softer and stickier than bread dough due to the vegetable moisture — do not add too much flour.

Cover the bowl with plastic wrap or a damp cloth. Leave in a warm place (25-28°C / 77-82°F) for 1-2 hours until the dough has roughly doubled in volume and looks airy and loose. The dough will also become even stickier as the yeast activates — this is normal. The anise aroma will become more pronounced.

Break or chop the chancaca into pieces. Combine with water, cinnamon stick, cloves, and orange peel in a saucepan. Heat over medium, stirring to dissolve the sugar. Once dissolved, bring to a gentle boil and cook for 10-12 minutes until syrupy and fragrant. Strain out the spices and peel. Keep warm. The syrup should be dark, spiced, and thick enough to drizzle.

Heat the oil to 175°C (345°F) in a deep, wide pan. Wet your hands thoroughly. Grab a golf ball-sized portion of dough, poke a hole through the center with your finger, and stretch into a ring shape (about 10cm diameter) directly over the hot oil. Drop it in. Fry in batches of 3-4, turning once after 2-3 minutes, until both sides are deep golden-brown. Total frying time is 4-5 minutes per batch. The dough will expand in the oil. Drain on paper towels.

recipes.name: Pesto alla Genovese
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Genovese basil leaves (small, young, picked from the tips)
Garlic clove, peeled and green germ removed
Coarse sea salt (acts as the abrasive in the mortar)
Ligurian extra-virgin olive oil (mild, fruity, low-bitter)

steps: Drop the peeled, de-germed garlic and the coarse salt together into a marble mortar. Crush with a circular grinding motion of the wooden pestle — not a pounding hammer — until the garlic dissolves into a smooth, wet paste. The salt crystals do double duty: they shred the garlic's cells and draw out its moisture, so a little goes a long way and the harsh raw bite is tamed before any basil ever touches it.

Add the pine nuts to the garlic paste and grind them down with the same patient circular motion. They are soft and oily, so they break quickly into a thick, sandy cream that loosens the garlic and rounds out its sharpness. Work until you have a cohesive, buttery base with no whole nuts left — this fat-rich layer is what will carry and protect the basil's color in the next step.

Add the basil a generous handful at a time, pressing and rolling the leaves up the sides of the mortar with the pestle rather than smashing them flat. The goal is to bruise and tear the leaf cells so they weep their oils — a rotating, wall-scraping motion does this without overheating. Add more basil only as the previous handful breaks down. Work fairly briskly; the longer the cut basil is exposed to air and friction heat, the faster it oxidizes from electric green toward muddy olive.

Stir the two grated cheeses into the basil paste; they thicken it into a dense, clay-like mass. Now switch to a spoon or the pestle and work in the olive oil in a slow thread, beating it into the paste a little at a time the way you would mount a sauce, until the pesto turns glossy, loose, and pourable but still coarse. Taste: it should be lush, salty from the cheese, and almost too intense on its own — it is meant to be cut by hot starchy pasta water at the moment of saucing. Use within a few hours, the surface filmed with a little extra oil to seal it from the air.

recipes.name: Pierogi Dough
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Mound the flour on a clean work surface and make a wide well in the center. Add the egg yolks, sour cream, warm water, and salt to the well. Beat the wet ingredients gently with a fork, then gradually incorporate the flour from the inner walls of the well, stirring in a widening spiral. When the mixture becomes too thick to stir, begin kneading with your hands — flour from the edges inward, pressing and folding. The dough will come together into a rough, slightly sticky mass.

Knead the dough on a lightly floured surface for 5-8 minutes using a push-fold-turn rhythm: push the heel of your hand forward, fold the dough back over itself, rotate a quarter turn, repeat. The dough transforms from rough and lumpy to smooth and supple. It should not require much flour — add only enough to prevent sticking. Once smooth, wrap tightly in plastic wrap and rest at room temperature for 30 minutes. This rest is essential: it relaxes the gluten so the dough can be rolled paper-thin without springing back.

Divide the rested dough into two halves (keep one half covered while working the other). On a lightly floured surface, roll with a rolling pin from the center outward, turning the sheet a quarter turn after every 3-4 passes. The goal is a uniform sheet 2mm thick — thin enough to be almost translucent when held up to light, but not so thin it tears. Cut circles with a 7-8 cm round cutter or an upturned glass. Re-roll scraps once.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil. Work in batches — no more than 8-10 pierogi at a time to prevent sticking and temperature drops. Lower the pierogi gently with a slotted spoon. They will sink to the bottom, then float up as they cook. Once they float, cook for a further 2-3 minutes for a total of 4-5 minutes from entry. Remove with a slotted spoon, drain, and toss immediately with melted butter to prevent sticking.

recipes.name: Pierogi
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine the flour and a pinch of salt in a bowl. Add warm water gradually, mixing with a fork until shaggy. Turn out and knead by hand for 8–10 minutes until the dough is completely smooth, supple, and slightly tacky but not sticky. The dough should have the elasticity of an earlobe. Wrap tightly in cling film and rest for 30 minutes at room temperature — resting is non-negotiable, as it relaxes the gluten so the dough can be rolled paper-thin.

Sauté half the diced onion in butter until golden, then set aside to cool. In a bowl, combine the riced potatoes, farmer's cheese, and sautéed onion. Season aggressively with salt and white pepper — the filling will be encased in unseasoned dough, so it must carry all the flavor. Mix until just combined; do not overwork or the potato becomes gluey. Taste and adjust salt until the filling tastes pleasantly salty on its own.

On a lightly floured surface, roll the rested dough to 2–3mm thickness — thin enough to see the shadow of your hand through it. Cut circles using a 8–9cm cutter or glass. Place a generous teaspoon of filling in the center of each circle. Fold the dough over the filling and press the edges firmly together, crimping with a fork or a tight finger-pinch. Sealed edges must be completely airtight — any opening will burst during boiling.

Bring a large pot of heavily salted water to a rolling boil. Add pierogi in batches — do not crowd. They will sink, then float to the surface after 2 minutes. After they float, cook 2 minutes more for a total of 4–5 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon. For the classic finish, melt butter in a wide pan over medium heat, add the remaining diced onion and cook until golden. Toss the boiled pierogi in the browned butter for 2 minutes until lightly crisped on one side.

recipes.name: Bacalà al Pil-Pil
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Desalted salt cod (bacalao), skin-on fillets, soaked 48 hr in cold water
Dried guindilla chili peppers (or dried cayenne)
Fine sea salt (taste before adding — the cod carries salt)

steps: If not already desalted, submerge the salt cod in a large bowl of cold water in the refrigerator. Change the water every 8–12 hours for 48 hours. The fish is ready when a small piece tastes pleasantly salty rather than overwhelming. After desalting, remove the fillets from the water and pat them completely dry on multiple layers of paper towel, then leave them uncovered on a rack at room temperature for 20 minutes. This drying step is critical: surface moisture is the enemy of the emulsion — it will cause the gelatin to dilute into water rather than binding with the oil. Run your fingers over the skin; the fillets should feel dry and faintly tacky, not wet.

In a wide, shallow clay cazuela or heavy skillet, combine the olive oil, sliced garlic, and dried chilis over the lowest possible heat. When the garlic begins to sizzle gently (about 2 minutes), nestle the cod fillets in skin-side up. The oil should never bubble aggressively — it should hover around 60–70C / 140–160F, which is well below a fry. Cook for 12–15 minutes, periodically tilting the pan to baste the fish with the warm oil. You will begin to see small white droplets forming at the edges of the fillets — this is the gelatin leaching from the fish into the oil. This is the raw material for the emulsion. When the fish is just cooked through and beginning to flake, gently remove the fillets with a slotted spatula onto a warm plate. Reserve every drop of the oil with its garlic and gelatin droplets.

This is the defining technique of the dish. With the reserved warm oil still in the pan over the lowest heat, begin moving the pan in slow, continuous circles — tilting it forward, sideways, backward, in a hypnotic, patient swirl. Do not stir, do not whisk. Just swing the pan. As you do this, the gelatin droplets begin to bind with the olive oil, and after 5–10 minutes a pale, creamy emulsion starts forming at the edges of the pan and slowly spreading to the center. The sauce goes from oily to ivory-white and slightly thickened, like a very loose aioli. If at any point it looks like it's about to split — the oil separates from the white mass — add a teaspoon of cold water and slow down the swirl. Taste and adjust salt very carefully. A pil-pil sauce that holds is one of the great quiet miracles of the kitchen.

Gently lower the reserved cod fillets back into the emulsified sauce, skin-side up, and tilt the pan to baste them with the sauce. The residual heat of the sauce will warm the fish through without further cooking. Taste the sauce carefully and add a pinch of salt only if needed — the fish and oil will have already contributed significant salt. To serve, bring the cazuela directly to the table. Tear crusty bread and drag it through the ivory sauce. The dish should be served warm, not hot — pil-pil breaks at temperatures above 80C, so never return it to a burner at this stage.

recipes.name: Butter Pilaf
steps: Rinse the rice under cold running water, swirling with your hand, until the water runs nearly clear — this removes excess surface starch that would cause the grains to clump. Transfer to a bowl and cover with cold water. Soak for 30 minutes. This hydrates the outer layers of the grain so they can expand uniformly under steam without the center remaining chalky. Drain thoroughly before cooking.

Melt the butter in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot with a tight-fitting lid over medium heat until it foams and then settles — this is clarified butter temperature, ideal for frying. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring often, for 5-6 minutes until completely soft and just beginning to turn golden at the edges. Add the carrot julienne and cumin seeds and cook for 3 more minutes until the carrot softens slightly. The pot should smell of warm butter, sweet onion, and earthy cumin.

Add the drained rice to the pot with the aromatics and stir to coat every grain in the butter. Spread the rice in an even layer and cook over medium heat, stirring frequently, for 2-3 minutes. The grains will turn from opaque white to a slightly translucent, glassy appearance, and the pot will smell of warm, toasted grain — like popcorn but delicate. This toasting step coats each grain in fat, which keeps them separate during steaming.

Pour the hot stock over the toasted rice — it will hiss and steam immediately. Add salt and black pepper. If using, nestle the whole unpeeled head of garlic into the center of the rice, cut side down (it perfumes the steam without making the pilaf garlicky). Stir once to distribute everything. Bring to a full boil over high heat, then immediately reduce to the absolute lowest setting. Cover tightly with the lid and cook for 15 minutes without lifting the lid once.

Remove the pot from heat and let it rest, completely undisturbed with the lid on, for 10 minutes. This is not optional — it is the moment the steam redistributes through the grains, equalizing moisture and ensuring even texture. After 10 minutes, remove the lid and the garlic head (if used). Using a fork or the handle of a wooden spoon, gently fluff the rice from the bottom up with light, lifting motions — never press down or stir aggressively, which would crush the grains.

recipes.name: Pineapple Upside-Down Cake
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, softened (for the sponge batter)

steps: Preheat oven to 175°C (350°F). Place a 24cm oven-safe skillet or round cake tin directly on the stovetop over medium heat. Add the butter and let it melt. Add the dark brown sugar and stir briefly to combine, then leave undisturbed for 2 minutes until it bubbles and darkens slightly. The caramel does not need to be fully made at this point — it will finish in the oven — but the butter and sugar should be melted and fragrant. Remove from heat.

Lay the pineapple rings over the hot caramel in the pan, fitting them snugly — one in the centre and as many as will fit around the edge without overlapping. Press them gently into the caramel. If using canned pineapple, pat the rings thoroughly dry first — excess juice will water down the caramel and prevent the fruit from browning properly. Place a maraschino cherry or dried cherry in the centre of each ring if desired.

In a bowl, beat the softened butter and caster sugar together with an electric mixer for 3 minutes until pale and fluffy. Add the eggs one at a time, beating well after each addition. Sift in the flour and baking powder and fold until just combined — a few turns with a spatula rather than vigorous beating. The batter should be smooth, thick, and fall from the spatula in slow ribbons. A small splash of milk or pineapple juice from the tin can loosen it to the right consistency.

Pour the batter carefully over the pineapple arrangement, spreading gently to the edges to cover everything evenly without disturbing the fruit arrangement. Bake at 175°C for 30–35 minutes until the sponge is deep golden and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean. Remove from the oven and rest for 5 minutes — not longer. Run a knife around the edge, place a large serving plate on top, and invert decisively in one motion. Lift the pan straight up. Any caramel clinging to the pan can be scraped off and poured over the top.

recipes.name: Pistou
steps: In a mortar, pound the garlic cloves with the coarse salt until a completely smooth, white paste forms. The salt crystals act as an abrasive and draw out the moisture from the garlic. This step is crucial — any remaining garlic chunks will make the sauce harsh and unpleasant. If using a food processor instead, mince the garlic as fine as possible before proceeding.

Add basil leaves to the mortar in two or three batches. Pound and grind with a circular pressing motion — not sharp strikes — until each batch is completely incorporated before adding the next. The goal is to bruise and crush the cells to release the oils, not to create friction heat. If using a food processor, pulse briefly in short bursts — blending too long heats the basil and turns it black.

Stream in olive oil a little at a time, stirring and pressing the paste against the sides of the mortar to incorporate. The sauce will loosen and become glossy as the oil emulsifies with the water content of the basil. Add a small squeeze of lemon juice if using. The consistency should be thick enough to coat a spoon but fluid enough to pour. Use immediately — pistou begins to oxidize and lose its vivid color within 30 minutes.

recipes.name: Greek Pita Bread
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine flour, instant yeast, and salt in a large bowl. Add warm water and olive oil. Mix with a wooden spoon until no dry flour remains, then use your hand to bring it into a rough ball. The dough should be moderately soft and slightly sticky — noticeably softer than pizza dough but not as wet as focaccia. Turn out onto a lightly floured surface.

Knead for 8 minutes on a lightly floured surface using a push-fold-rotate motion. The dough will transform: from sticky and rough to smooth, elastic, and barely tacky. After 8 minutes it should pass the basic stretch test — pull a small piece and stretch it a few inches without it tearing immediately. Shape into a ball, lightly oil the surface, and place in a clean bowl.

Cover the bowl with a damp towel or plastic wrap. Let rise at room temperature (22–25 C) for 60–75 minutes until doubled. While the dough rises, place a heavy baking stone or inverted cast-iron pan on the top rack of the oven. Preheat the oven to its maximum temperature — 260 C (500 F) or higher — at least 30 minutes before baking. A screaming-hot surface is essential for pita to puff.

Punch down the dough and divide into 8 equal portions (about 70 g each). On a lightly floured surface, roll each portion into a smooth ball. Cover and rest 10 minutes so the gluten relaxes. Then roll each ball with a rolling pin into a round 18–20 cm across and about 4–5 mm thick. Do not roll too thin — a pita that is too thin won't form a proper pocket. Place on a sheet of parchment and rest 15 minutes before baking.

Working in batches of 2–3 (however many fit on your baking stone), use a peel or the back of a flat baking sheet to slide pita rounds directly onto the screaming-hot stone. Bake for 3–4 minutes — no more. You will see the pita begin to puff dramatically about 60–90 seconds in, inflating into a dome. Once fully puffed and barely pale gold on top, remove. Do not over-bake — the goal is a soft, pliable pita, not a crisp one. Wrap immediately in a clean towel to keep soft.

recipes.name: Polenta
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Pour the water into a heavy-bottomed pot — copper or thick-clad steel holds heat best and resists scorching. Add the salt and bring to a bare simmer over medium heat. The water should be hot and lazily steaming, with small bubbles trembling at the edges, NOT at a rolling boil. A violent boil flings cornmeal everywhere and seizes it into lumps.

Stir the simmering water into a slow whirlpool with a whisk. While it spins, add the cornmeal in a thin, steady rain from your fist — never dump it. Whisk constantly as you pour so each grain disperses before the next lands. Once all the cornmeal is in, switch to a sturdy wooden spoon. The mixture will look loose and milky, like thin cream.

Drop the heat to its lowest setting so the polenta blips rather than boils — a thick bubble should heave up and burst every few seconds, like a slow mud pot. Cook 35-45 minutes, stirring every few minutes with the wooden spoon, scraping the bottom and corners to prevent scorching. The polenta is done when the grains have lost all grittiness and the mass pulls cleanly away from the sides of the pot as you stir.

Off the heat, beat in the cold butter and grated Parmigiano, stirring vigorously until both melt into a glossy, unified cream. For a soft, spoonable polenta, loosen with the warm milk until it slumps slowly off the spoon. Taste and adjust salt. Serve at once in warm, shallow bowls — polenta stiffens fast as it cools.

recipes.name: Pollo a la Brasa (Peruvian Rotisserie Chicken)

ingredients.name: Garlic cloves, minced to a paste
Aji panca paste (or dried aji panca, rehydrated)
Fresh jalapeño or aji amarillo (for aji verde)

steps: Whisk together soy sauce, garlic paste, cumin, aji panca paste, smoked paprika, lime juice, salt, pepper, oregano, and oil until uniform. The mixture should be thick, dark, and deeply aromatic — the soy and aji panca together create the characteristic mahogany color of pollo a la brasa.

Dry the chicken thoroughly inside and out. Using your fingers, carefully separate the skin from the breast and thigh meat and push half the marinade directly under the skin, massaging it over the meat. Rub remaining marinade all over the exterior and inside the cavity. Place in a large zip-lock bag or covered dish. Refrigerate 12–24 hours, turning once.

Place chicken breast-side up on a rack in a roasting pan (or on a rotisserie spit). Roast at 200 C (400 F) for 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes. Every 20 minutes, baste with pan drippings. Rotate the pan if using a regular oven. The chicken is done when the thigh joint reads 82 C (180 F) and the skin is deeply burnished. Rest 10 minutes before carving.

Blend mint, cilantro, jalapeño, mayonnaise, and lime juice in a blender until completely smooth and vivid green. Season with salt. The sauce should be bright, herby, creamy, and slightly spicy — the essential accompaniment to cut the richness of the chicken.

Carve the rested chicken: separate the legs, split the breast, cut the wings. Arrange on a warm platter skin-side up so the burnished skin remains visible. Serve the aji verde in a bowl alongside, with fried yuca or papas fritas and a simple salad.

recipes.name: Pollo en Adobo

ingredients.name: Dried ancho chiles (stems and seeds removed)
Dried guajillo chiles (stems and seeds removed)

steps: Heat a dry comal or heavy skillet over medium heat until very hot. Toast the stemmed, seeded ancho and guajillo chile pieces in batches by pressing them flat against the hot surface for 10-15 seconds per side — you will see them puff slightly, change color, and release an intoxicating smoky-sweet fragrance. Do not scorch them black: a toasted chile smells of raisin, chocolate, and dried fruit; a burnt chile smells of acrid carbon and will make your sauce bitter. Once toasted, transfer immediately to a bowl and cover with boiling water. Soak for 20-30 minutes until completely soft and pliable.

Drain the rehydrated chiles, reserving 120 ml of the soaking liquid (it has flavor but can be bitter — taste before using). Place the chiles in a blender with the quartered onion, garlic, apple cider vinegar, toasted cumin, oregano, cinnamon, and cloves. Add 60 ml of the soaking water and 60 ml fresh water. Blitz to a completely smooth, thick paste, 2-3 minutes on high. The finished adobo should be the color of dark brick, intensely aromatic, slightly sour from the vinegar, and thick enough to coat a spoon. Pass through a fine-mesh strainer if desired for a smoother texture.

Heat the lard in a large, heavy pot (Dutch oven) over high heat until smoking. Working in batches, sear the salted chicken pieces skin-side down for 4-5 minutes without moving until deeply browned. Turn and sear the other side for 2 minutes. Remove and set aside. Reduce heat to medium. Add the adobo paste to the hot fat — it will splatter furiously. Stand back, then stir constantly for 3-4 minutes, frying the paste in the fat. This step, called freír el adobo, transforms the raw chile paste into a deep, complex sauce: the color darkens, the sharp raw smell mellow to something round and toasted, and the fat begins to bleed out visibly — the Mexican equivalent of bhunao.

Return all the seared chicken pieces to the pot with the fried adobo paste. Pour in the chicken stock and stir to combine — the liquid should come about halfway up the chicken. Bring to a simmer, cover the pot, and cook over low heat for 45-60 minutes until the chicken is completely tender at the bone. The adobo will penetrate every surface of the chicken. A fork inserted at the thigh joint should meet no resistance and the meat should want to pull from the bone.

Remove the lid and increase heat to medium-high. Cook uncovered for 10-15 minutes, turning the chicken pieces frequently and spooning sauce over them. The adobo will reduce and glaze: each piece of chicken becomes lacquered in a thick, glossy, brick-red coating. The sauce should be thick enough that it coats the back of a spoon and holds for a moment. Taste and adjust salt. Serve over rice or with warm tortillas, with pickled jalapeños and sliced white onion alongside.

recipes.name: Porchetta

ingredients.name: Skin-on pork belly, deboned, butterflied flat
Fresh fennel fronds or wild fennel
Fennel seeds, toasted and coarsely ground

steps: The night before: lay the pork belly skin-side down. Score the flesh side in a crosshatch pattern about 5 mm deep (this is where the filling will cling). Season the flesh generously with salt — use about half the total salt. Flip the belly and score the skin with a sharp knife in parallel lines about 1 cm apart, cutting only through the skin and just into the fat — do not cut into the flesh. Salt the skin lightly, rub in, and refrigerate uncovered overnight. Dry skin is the key to crackling.

Roughly chop rosemary, fennel fronds, and garlic together on a cutting board until finely minced. Transfer to a bowl. Add ground fennel seeds, black pepper, and olive oil. Stir into a fragrant, moist paste. Taste — it should be aggressively herby and garlicky. This is the soul of the porchetta.

Spread the herb paste evenly over the entire scored flesh side, pressing it into the crosshatch cuts. Roll the belly tightly from one short end, keeping the tension even, ensuring the roll is tight with no air pockets. Tie with kitchen twine at 3 cm intervals — tight enough that the roll holds a drum-like firmness. Rub remaining salt all over the skin. Refrigerate uncovered for at least 2 hours, or overnight if possible.

Take porchetta from the fridge 1 hour before roasting. Preheat oven to 230 C (450 F). Place porchetta on a wire rack over a roasting pan, seam-side down. Roast at 230 C for 30 minutes — this blast of heat begins the crackling. Reduce heat to 160 C (325 F) and roast for 2 to 2.5 more hours until internal temperature reaches 70 C (158 F) at the center.

Rest the porchetta on a wire rack (not a cutting board) uncovered for 20–30 minutes. Resting lets the juices redistribute through the fat and flesh. Do not tent with foil — steam will soften the crackling you worked so hard for. Slice with a sharp, serrated bread knife using a sawing motion — a chef's knife will crack and shatter the crackling rather than cut through it cleanly.

recipes.name: Hong Shao Rou (Red-Braised Pork Belly)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Pork belly (skin-on), cut in 4 cm cubes

steps: Place pork belly cubes in a cold pot, cover with cold water. Bring to a boil over high heat and blanch for 5 minutes, skimming the grey foam vigorously. Drain and rinse each piece under cold running water to remove all grey protein residue. Pat completely dry with paper towels. This step is essential for a clean, clear braising sauce with no off-flavors.

In a wide, heavy pot or wok, heat the neutral oil over medium heat. Add the rock sugar and cook, stirring gently, until it melts and turns a deep amber color — like old whiskey. This takes about 4–6 minutes. Do not walk away. The caramel transitions from clear to pale gold to amber to dark amber very quickly.

Add the pork belly to the hot caramel and toss to coat (stand back — it will spit). Add Shaoxing wine, dark and light soy sauces, star anise, cassia, ginger, and scallion knot. Pour in enough water to just barely cover. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a very low simmer. Cover and braise for 1.5–2 hours, turning the pork every 30 minutes.

Uncover the pot and increase heat to medium-high. Baste the pork continuously with the braising liquid as it reduces and concentrates. Cook for 10–15 minutes, turning the pork gently, until the sauce is thick, glossy, and sticky — it should coat each pork cube in a shiny, lacquered shell. Remove the whole spices, ginger, and scallion knot.

recipes.name: Chashu Pork Belly
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Lay the pork belly skin-side down on a clean board. Roll it tightly from one short end into a compact cylinder, keeping the roll as even in diameter as possible. Tie at 2 cm intervals with butcher's twine — snug but not so tight that it cuts into the fat. The tight roll ensures even slices for ramen, and the twine holds the shape through the braise. If the belly is very thick or the skin tough, score the skin lightly at 1 cm intervals before rolling to help it render and soften evenly.

Heat the oil in a heavy pan or Dutch oven over high heat until shimmering. Place the rolled belly in the pan and sear, turning every 2 to 3 minutes with tongs, until every surface including the two flat ends is golden-brown. This takes about 10 to 12 minutes total. The skin side will sputter and contract energetically — use a splatter screen if needed. The Maillard crust built here contributes the roasted, caramelized notes that distinguish chashu from a simple braised pork roll.

Remove the seared roll to a plate. Deglaze the hot pan with the sake, scraping all the fond from the bottom. Add the soy sauce, mirin, sugar, water, scallion stalks, and ginger slices. Stir to dissolve the sugar. Return the roll to the pan — the braising liquid should come about halfway up the roll. Bring to a bare simmer, then cover with a tight-fitting lid or a cartouche of parchment paper. Cook over the lowest heat that maintains a gentle simmer, turning the roll every 30 minutes so all sides have equal time submerged, for 2 to 2.5 hours total.

Allow the chashu to cool in the braising liquid to room temperature, then transfer the roll (still in its braising liquid) to the refrigerator and chill overnight, or at minimum 4 hours. Chilling accomplishes two things: the fat solidifies, making clean slicing possible (warm chashu is too soft to slice neatly), and the roll continues to absorb the braising liquid as it cools, deepening the flavor penetration. The chilled braising liquid will set to a dark, jiggly gel — reserve it as a tare or glaze for other applications.

To serve, cut the twine with scissors and slice the chilled roll into rounds of 8 to 12 mm thickness. For ramen service, heat a small non-stick or cast-iron pan over medium-high heat until it just begins to smoke. Lay the chashu slices in without oil — they carry enough rendered fat from the braise. Sear for 45 to 60 seconds per side until the edges caramelize and char at the points and the surface takes on a glorious, lacquered char. Alternatively, brush the slices with a little of the gelled braising liquid and briefly torch them or place under a very hot broiler for 60 seconds to lacquer and caramelize the surface.

recipes.name: Pork Belly Confit

ingredients.name: Rendered pork fat or duck fat

steps: Mix together the salt, sugar, lightly crushed garlic, thyme, bay leaves, cracked peppercorns, and juniper berries in a small bowl. Score the skin of the pork belly in a crosshatch pattern with a sharp knife or Stanley blade — cuts 1 cm apart, through the skin and just into the fat layer but not reaching the meat. This scoring promotes even crackling later. Rub the cure mixture thoroughly over every surface of the belly, working it into the score cuts and pressing the aromatics firmly into the flesh. Place skin-side up on a wire rack set over a tray, cover loosely with cling wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8-12 hours).

Preheat the oven to 90°C (195°F). Melt the pork fat in a deep roasting dish or Dutch oven large enough to hold the belly. Place the belly skin-side down, pour in enough warm fat to completely submerge it — the fat should cover the belly by at least 1 cm. Place a piece of parchment over the surface and then the lid or tight foil. Transfer to the oven and cook for 6-8 hours. Do not rush this with higher heat. At 90°C, the collagen in the connective tissue and skin gradually converts to gelatin without ever forcing the fat to fry — the distinction between confit and poaching in fat.

Line a small baking dish or loaf tin with cling wrap, leaving an overhang on all sides. Lift the belly from the fat and place it skin-side down in the lined tin. Fold the cling wrap over the top. Place another baking sheet directly on the cling wrap and weigh it down with heavy cans — at least 2 kg of weight. Refrigerate for a minimum of 6 hours, ideally overnight. The pressing compacts the belly into a uniform slab for clean portioning and forces the fat and gelatin to redistribute evenly throughout.

Portion the pressed belly into individual serving pieces (typically 5-6 cm squares). Place a heavy oven-safe skillet — cast iron ideal — over medium-low heat. Do not add fat; the belly itself will render immediately. Place the portions skin-side down, pressing firmly with a spatula. Cook over medium-low heat for 12-18 minutes without moving — patience here is essential. The fat will slowly render and the skin will progressively crisp and turn translucent amber. It should crackle like glass underfoot when tapped with a spoon. Flip for the final 2 minutes to lightly colour the meat side.

recipes.name: Chashu Pork Belly

ingredients.name: Scallions, roughly cut in 5 cm sections

steps: Lay the pork belly flat, skin-side down. Starting from the shorter end, roll the belly tightly into a compact cylinder, trapping as many fat-to-meat layers as possible within the roll. Tie at 2–3 cm intervals with butcher's twine, pulling each loop firmly so the roll holds its circular cross-section during cooking. A loose roll will unravel and produce uneven slices. The goal is a tight, even cylinder that will hold its shape through 3 hours of braising.

Heat a Dutch oven or heavy pot over medium-high heat with no oil — the belly's own exterior fat will render immediately. Place the roll in and sear, turning with tongs every 90 seconds, until all sides are evenly golden-brown, including the flat cut ends. This sear builds the Maillard flavor base that enriches the braising liquid and creates the lacquered exterior. Total searing time: 8–10 minutes.

Pour the sake into the hot pot and bring to a boil, scraping up the fond from the bottom. Add soy sauce, mirin, sugar, water, scallion, and ginger. Return the pork roll to the pot — the liquid should come about two-thirds of the way up the roll. Bring to a very gentle simmer (90°C, barely bubbling — large bubbles will cause the roll to turn tough and the skin to contract unevenly). Cover and braise for 2.5–3 hours, turning the roll every 45 minutes so all sides spend time submerged. The liquid will reduce and deepen.

The key: refrigerate the chashu roll in its braising liquid overnight before slicing. Cold fat and gelatin give the roll structural integrity — room-temperature chashu collapses under the knife. Remove from the liquid (reserve the liquid: it becomes your tare for ramen). Remove all twine. Using a very sharp, thin-bladed knife, slice rounds 1.5–2 cm thick in a single confident stroke — no sawing. For ramen, sear each cold slice in a screaming-hot dry pan for 30 seconds per side to reheat and caramelize the glaze before placing in the bowl.

recipes.name: Pork Carnitas

ingredients.name: Pork shoulder (boston butt, cut into large 6cm chunks)
Orange (1 large — halved, juice squeezed, shells reserved)
Mexican cinnamon stick (canela, one small piece)

steps: Pat the pork chunks thoroughly dry with paper towels — surface moisture is the enemy of both rendering and browning. Toss generously with the salt until every surface carries a visible, even coating. Leave at room temperature for 20 minutes while you gather the aromatics. The salt draws the barest trace of moisture to the surface, then the surface dries: this tack helps the lard cling and the seasonings penetrate.

Nestle the pork chunks in a single layer in a heavy wide pot or Dutch oven. Add the lard, then squeeze the orange juice over the top and drop in the spent orange shell halves. Tuck in the onion, garlic, bay leaves, and cinnamon stick. Add just enough cold water to come level with the top of the meat — the water will cook off first, and when it does, the lard takes over. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered on the lowest heat, never letting it boil, for 1.5 to 2 hours. The water gradually evaporates over the first hour; the pork then quietly poaches in clear lard for the second hour until fork-tender.

Once the water is fully gone and the pork sits in clear lard, raise the heat to medium-high. If using condensed milk, drizzle it in now and stir — the trace of dairy sugar accelerates browning in the authentic Michoacán way. Cook, turning the pieces only every 3 to 4 minutes, until deeply browned and crisp at all the exposed edges and high points. The fat will bubble vigorously around the pieces. Resist the urge to stir constantly — extended contact between meat and hot metal is what builds the crust. Total frying time 8 to 15 minutes.

Transfer the carnitas to a large cutting board and let them rest 5 minutes. The resting is important — the residual heat finishes any remaining pink interior, and the crust sets rather than steaming back soft. Using two forks or your fingers, roughly pull and chop each piece into a mix of large crispy shards and tender shreds. Spoon a tablespoon of the warm reserved lard back over the top to gloss them. Taste and season with a pinch of flaky salt and a squeeze of fresh lime. Serve immediately on warm corn tortillas with white onion, cilantro, lime, and your salsa of choice.

recipes.name: Seared Pork Chops with Apples, Cabbage and Mustard Pan Sauce

ingredients.name: Bone-in pork rib chops, about 2.5 cm (1 inch) thick
Firm, tart-sweet apples (such as Honeycrisp or Pink Lady), cored and cut into 1 cm wedges
Green cabbage, cored and thinly sliced

steps: Pat the chops dry. If there is a thick fat cap, slash it every 2–3 cm to keep the chops from curling. Season generously on all sides with about 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt total and pepper. Let stand at room temperature 10–15 minutes while you slice the apples, cabbage and shallot.

Heat the oil in a 12-inch (30 cm) heavy skillet (cast iron or stainless) over medium-high heat until it just smokes. Lay the chops in, pressing lightly so they make full contact, and sear without moving 4–5 minutes until deeply browned. Flip, reduce the heat to medium, and cook 3–5 minutes more, turning once more if needed, until an instant-read thermometer inserted near (not touching) the bone reads 140°F (60°C). Stand the chops on their fat edges for the last minute to render it. Transfer to a plate and rest 5 minutes; carryover heat brings them to the USDA-safe 145°F (63°C).

Pour off all but about 1 tbsp fat from the skillet. Over medium-high heat, add the apple wedges in a single layer and cook 2 minutes per side until caramelized at the edges. Add the shallot, cabbage and a pinch of salt and cook, tossing, 4–5 minutes until the cabbage is wilted and browned in spots but still has some bite.

Pour in the cider and stock, add the thyme sprigs, and scrape up the browned bits. Boil 4–5 minutes until reduced by about half. Reduce the heat to low, stir in the mustard and the resting juices from the chops, then swirl in the cold butter a piece at a time until glossy. Stir in the cider vinegar, discard the thyme stems, and season. Return the chops to the pan for 30 seconds to warm, spooning sauce over them, and serve over the apples and cabbage.

recipes.name: Wiener Schnitzel

ingredients.name: Eggs, lightly beaten with a fork (not whisked)

steps: Place a cutlet between two sheets of plastic wrap or inside a zip-lock bag. Using a meat mallet or the bottom of a heavy pan, pound the meat to an even 3mm thickness with firm, outward strokes — starting from the center and sweeping toward the edges to stretch rather than tear the meat.
