The salt draws moisture out slowly and creates a sealed, even-temperature cooking environment, concentrating sugars far more than conventional roasting.

Roast in a preheated 190 C (375 F) oven for 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours. The salt will partially harden into a crust. To test for doneness, push a thin metal skewer through the salt into the largest beet — it should pass through with no resistance, like pushing into room-temperature butter. Small beets take 80 minutes; very large ones may need 2 hours 15 minutes.

Crack the salt crust with a spoon and remove the beets. The skin will peel off in large pieces using just your fingers and a paper towel (wear gloves if you don't want to stain your hands deep red for a day). Slice, quarter, or serve whole. Dress immediately with olive oil and a few drops of red wine vinegar or balsamic to add brightness to the concentrated sweetness.

recipes.name: Roasted Cauliflower with Tahini Lentils

ingredients.name: Cauliflower, cut into 4 cm florets (1 large head)
Garlic, 1 smashed whole and 1 finely grated
Lemon juice (about 1.5 lemons), plus zest of 1

steps: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Toss the florets with 45 ml of the oil, the cumin, paprika, and 1 teaspoon salt. Spread on a large sheet pan with cut sides down and space between pieces. Roast 25–30 minutes, flipping once at 15 minutes, until tender and well charred at the edges.

While the cauliflower roasts, put the lentils, bay leaf, and the smashed garlic clove in a saucepan with the water. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer and cook 20–25 minutes until tender but holding their shape. Salt the water in the last 5 minutes. Drain, discard the bay and garlic.

Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice, the grated garlic clove, and a pinch of salt. It will seize and thicken — keep going. Add the ice water a tablespoon at a time, whisking until it lightens to a smooth, pourable sauce.

Toss the warm lentils with half the tahini sauce, the remaining 15 ml olive oil, the lemon zest, and half the parsley. Season with salt. Spread on a platter, top with the roasted cauliflower, drizzle over the remaining tahini, and finish with almonds and the rest of the parsley.

recipes.name: Whole Roasted Cauliflower
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Whole cauliflower head (leaves trimmed, stem cut flat)
Flaky sea salt and black pepper (to finish)
Chopped parsley and toasted pine nuts

steps: Bring a large, deep pot of water to a rolling boil and season it aggressively with the kosher salt and the juice of half the lemon — it should taste like seawater. Lower the trimmed whole head in stem-side down, cover, and simmer 8 to 12 minutes. This seasons the cauliflower to its core and softens the dense stem so it cooks through before the surface scorches in the oven. Lift it out carefully with two slotted spoons or a spider and set it stem-down on a rack to drain and steam-dry completely.

Whisk the olive oil with the garlic paste, cumin, and smoked paprika into a loose, rust-colored slurry. Set the drained head in an oven-proof skillet or on a lined sheet and massage the spiced oil over every surface, working it down into the crevices between florets and over the cut stem. Be generous — the oil is both the seasoning and the frying medium that crisps the crown.

Roast in a hot oven at 220C / 425F for 30 to 40 minutes, basting once or twice with the oil that collects in the pan. The Maillard browning turns the surface curds deeply golden and concentrates the sugars into a nutty, almost popcorn sweetness. The head is done when the crown is bronzed and crackly and a skewer slides through the center without resistance.

Transfer the rested head to a warm platter. Squeeze over the juice of the remaining lemon half, scatter with flaky salt and a few grinds of black pepper, then shower with chopped parsley and toasted pine nuts. Bring it whole to the table and carve into thick wedges from the crown down through the tender stem, spooning the spiced pan oil over each portion.

recipes.name: Roasted Root Vegetables
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Fresh thyme sprigs and bay leaves
Flaky sea salt and black pepper

steps: Peel all vegetables. Cut into pieces of approximately equal size and similar surface area so they roast at the same rate — this is the single most important prep step. Parsnips halved lengthwise; carrots halved or quartered depending on size; beetroot into 6–8 wedges. Toss in a large bowl with the oil, coating every surface — do not season with salt yet, as salt draws moisture and creates steam in the early roasting stage.

Preheat the oven to 220°C (430°F) with a large, heavy roasting tray inside. The preheated tray is essential — vegetables placed in a cold tray steam rather than roast. Spread the vegetables in a single layer with the cut sides down, with space between each piece — touching vegetables steam each other. Scatter thyme and bay leaves throughout. Roast for 25 minutes without opening the oven.

Turn each piece over to expose an unbrowned side. Season now with flaky sea salt and black pepper. Drizzle honey or maple syrup over the pieces in the tray. Return to the oven for 15–20 more minutes until everything is tender, deeply caramelized, and the honey has darkened and concentrated. The sugar in the glaze accelerates the Maillard reaction on the freshly exposed surfaces.

recipes.name: Roasted Tomato & Garlic Soup

ingredients.name: Yellow onions, cut into thick wedges
Red bell pepper, seeded and quartered
Sugar (only if the tomatoes are sharp)

steps: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Divide tomatoes (cut-side up), onion, pepper, and garlic between two rimmed sheet pans, drizzle with oil, sprinkle with the salt, and tuck in thyme sprigs. Roast 45–55 minutes, rotating the pans halfway, until the tomatoes are slumped and blackened in spots and the garlic is soft.

Squeeze the garlic from its skins and discard the skins and thyme stems. Scrape everything into a 5 litre pot, pour a little of the stock onto the hot pans to loosen the stuck juices, and add it all with the remaining stock and the basil. Simmer 10 minutes to marry the flavors.

Blend until smooth with an immersion blender (or in batches in a vented blender). For a silkier soup, press through a sieve to remove skins. Stir in vinegar, then taste: add a pinch of sugar only if it's sharp, and adjust salt. Stir in cream and warm gently without boiling. To freeze: freeze before adding cream (dairy can separate) — cool quickly, refrigerate within 2 hours, freeze up to 4 months, then add cream after reheating.

recipes.name: Rösti
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Peel the potatoes. Grate them on the coarse side of a box grater into a large bowl. Working quickly (grated potato oxidizes and discolors), gather handfuls of the grated potato and squeeze them as hard as you can over the sink. Remove as much starch-water as possible — this is critical for crispness. If the potato releases a bluish-purple liquid, it contains excess starch: squeeze more. Season the dry-ish grated potato with salt and pepper and toss to distribute evenly.

Heat a 24–26cm cast-iron or heavy non-stick pan over medium heat. Add the clarified butter and swirl to coat. When the butter is hot and shimmering but not smoking, add all the grated potato at once. Immediately use a wide spatula to press the potato into a firm, even disc, extending it to the pan edges. Do not touch it again. Cook on medium-low heat for 10–12 minutes. The goal is a deep golden-brown crust built slowly from even, patient heat.

To flip: invert a large plate over the pan and, in one confident motion, flip both together so the rösti drops onto the plate crust-side up. Add the remaining clarified butter to the pan. Slide the rösti back in, uncooked side down. Increase heat to medium. Cook 8–10 minutes until the second side is equally golden and crisp.

Slide the finished rösti onto a wooden board. Season lightly with additional flaky salt. Rest for 2 minutes before cutting into wedges — this allows the interior steam to redistribute and the crust to firm completely. Serve immediately. Classic accompaniments are fried eggs, smoked salmon, applesauce, or alpine cheese.

recipes.name: Romesco Sauce

ingredients.name: Day-old sourdough bread, crusts removed (use GF bread to keep GF)

steps: Char the bell peppers directly over a gas flame or under a screaming-hot broiler, turning with tongs until completely blackened on all sides — this takes 10–15 minutes. Place in a sealed bag or covered bowl for 15 minutes to steam. Peel off the charred skin (a little residue adds flavor), remove the seeds and core. Wrap the garlic cloves unpeeled in foil with a drizzle of oil and roast at 200 C for 20 minutes until completely soft. Squeeze from skins.

In a dry skillet over medium heat, toast the almonds for 4–6 minutes, tossing frequently, until golden-brown and fragrant. Set aside. In the same pan with a splash of oil, fry the torn bread pieces until golden and crisp on all sides, 3–4 minutes. The toasted bread is the thickener — it emulsifies the sauce and gives it body.

In a food processor or blender, pulse the almonds and toasted bread first until coarsely ground. Add the roasted peppers, garlic, sun-dried tomatoes, smoked paprika, cayenne, sherry vinegar, and salt. Process until a rough, textured paste forms. With the motor running, drizzle in the olive oil to emulsify. Process to your preferred consistency — classic romesco is chunky, not smooth. Taste and adjust: more vinegar for acidity, more paprika for smoke, more oil for richness. The sauce should taste bold enough to be slightly overwhelming on its own.

recipes.name: Romesco
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Day-old country bread (fried in olive oil)

steps: Roast the bell peppers over a flame or under a hot broiler until the skins blacken and blister all over, then steam them in a covered bowl for 10 minutes and slip off the skins; discard stems and seeds. Roast the whole tomatoes the same way until collapsed and charred. Meanwhile, stem and seed the ñora chiles, cover with hot water, and soak 20 minutes until soft; scrape the softened flesh from the skins with a spoon and discard the papery skins.

Toast the blanched almonds in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking constantly, until golden and fragrant, 4–6 minutes; tip out and reserve. In the same pan, warm a third of the olive oil and fry the bread slice and whole garlic cloves until both are deep golden and the garlic is soft, about 3 minutes per side. The bread will thicken the sauce; the fried garlic gives mellow sweetness without raw bite.

Traditionally done in a large mortar: pound the toasted almonds, fried garlic, and a pinch of salt to a coarse meal, then work in the fried bread, the ñora flesh, the roasted peppers, and the charred tomato, pounding until you have a thick, textured paste. A food processor works too — pulse the nuts and bread first, then add the rest and pulse, keeping some grit. You want texture, not a smooth purée.

With the mortar or processor running, drizzle in the remaining olive oil in a slow stream so it emulsifies into the paste, thickening it to a loose, glossy sauce. Sharpen with the sherry vinegar, then taste and adjust salt and vinegar — romesco should taste sweet, nutty, and faintly smoky with a bright acidic lift. Let it rest 30 minutes before serving so the flavors marry.

recipes.name: Malaysian Roti Canai
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine flour, salt, and sugar in a large bowl. In a measuring jug, mix warm water, beaten egg, and half the ghee. Pour the wet ingredients into the flour and mix with your hand in circular strokes until a shaggy dough forms. The dough will be soft, slightly sticky, and richer than a standard bread dough thanks to the egg and ghee. Do not add extra flour. Knead briefly in the bowl until it just comes together — about 2 minutes.

Knead the dough on a lightly oiled surface (not floured — oil keeps it extensible) for 10 minutes by hand. Use a push-pull-fold motion. The goal is to develop just enough gluten for the dough to stretch paper-thin without tearing, while remaining soft and supple — not a tight, elastic bread dough. Toward the end of kneading, the dough will become notably smoother and almost silky.

Divide the dough into 8 equal balls (roughly 80 g each). Coat each ball generously in ghee, turning it until completely slicked. Arrange in a single layer on an oiled tray, ensuring the balls are not touching. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and rest at room temperature for at least 3 hours, or refrigerate overnight. The gluten relaxes completely during this rest, making it possible to stretch each ball to an almost see-through thinness without tearing. Do not skip or shorten this step.

Oil your tawa or work surface lightly. Place one ball and begin pressing it out flat with oiled fingers. Then use the back of your hand and a slapping motion to stretch it outward — rotate constantly, slap from underneath, let gravity thin it. Work until the dough is nearly paper-thin and you can see the surface below through it (roughly 45–50 cm diameter). Smear a thin film of ghee across the entire surface. Fold in from two opposite sides like a letter, then fold again to create a square packet. Coil the square into a tight snail. Let all 8 coils rest 5 minutes before flattening. Press each coil down firmly with your palm into a flat round, 15–18 cm diameter.

Heat a tawa or flat cast-iron pan over medium-high heat until very hot. Add a generous spoonful of ghee — it should shimmer instantly. Place a shaped roti round on the pan. Cook 1.5–2 minutes until the bottom is golden-brown and the roti has puffed in places. Flip, add another dab of ghee, and cook 1–2 minutes more. Immediately remove from heat and 'scrunch' the roti with both hands (like clapping it accordion-style) to separate the layers and release steam. This is the signature move — it turns a flat disc into a pillowy, flaky cloud.

recipes.name: Rum Baba

ingredients.name: Vanilla pod or 1 tsp vanilla extract

steps: In a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine flour, sugar, salt, and instant yeast. Add the warm milk and then the eggs one at a time with the mixer running on medium. Beat for 8–10 minutes until the batter is smooth, shiny, and elastic, pulling cleanly away from the bowl sides. The mixture is wetter than a bread dough — closer to a thick batter.

With the mixer running on medium-low, add the very soft butter one tablespoon at a time. Wait until each addition is fully incorporated before adding the next — this takes patience, about 15 minutes total. The batter will loosen dramatically at first, then tighten into a smooth, glossy, enriched dough that pulls cleanly from the bowl.

Cover the bowl and let the dough proof at room temperature until doubled, 45–60 minutes. Then butter individual baba molds (or a muffin tin) generously. Fill each mold halfway with batter using a piping bag or spoon. Let proof again until the dough crests just above the rim, 20–30 minutes.

Bake at 190°C (375°F) for 18–22 minutes until deeply golden on top and pulling away from the mold sides. A skewer inserted in the center should come out clean. Turn onto a rack immediately and let cool for 15 minutes before soaking — they must be warm but not hot.

Combine water, caster sugar, honey, and the vanilla pod in a wide, shallow saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring until the sugar and honey dissolve completely. Simmer 2 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in the rum. Keep the syrup warm — it must be hot when the babas are soaked.

Place the warm babas into the wide pan of warm syrup (having added the rum to the syrup base). Spoon syrup over continuously, turning the babas, for 2–3 minutes until each one has absorbed the maximum syrup it can hold. A fully soaked baba should feel waterlogged and heavy, and syrup should run from it when pressed gently.

Combine the very cold heavy cream with a small amount of sugar and vanilla extract (if using extract rather than pod) in a chilled bowl. Whip to soft, billowing peaks — Chantilly for baba should be cloud-light, not stiff or butter-like.

Place each soaked baba on a shallow plate. Spoon or pipe a generous dome of Chantilly cream directly on top. Drizzle any remaining warm rum syrup around the base. Serve immediately while the baba is warm and the cream is cold — the contrast is essential.

recipes.name: Scandinavian Rye Bread
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Cracked rye or rye berries (soaked 12 hr)

steps: Cover the cracked rye berries or whole rye berries with cold water and leave to soak for 12 hours or overnight. They will absorb a significant amount of water and soften considerably. Drain before using. This soaker adds texture, moisture, and a nutty chew to the finished loaf — unsoaked grains would be unpleasantly hard and would steal hydration from the dough itself during baking.

Combine all the flours, the rye starter, remaining water (adjust for grain moisture), salt, and molasses in a large bowl. Mix vigorously with a wooden spoon or dough scraper — rye dough contains almost no gluten and behaves more like thick batter than bread dough. No kneading is needed or useful: rye proteins do not form gluten strands. Fold in the drained soaker, sunflower seeds, and caraway seeds until evenly distributed. The dough will be very sticky and stiff-heavy — it should hold its shape when scooped but not stretch. Cover and ferment at room temperature 8–12 hours.

Transfer the dough to a well-oiled 9 × 5-inch loaf tin. Dip your hands or a spatula in water and smooth the top into an even dome — rye dough cannot be shaped in the traditional sense; the tin does all the work. Sprinkle a few extra sunflower seeds or caraway on the surface. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and proof at room temperature until the dome crowns about 1 cm above the tin rim and cracks appear in the surface, 2–4 hours. Rye dough will not achieve the dramatic rise of wheat bread — a 20–30% increase is ideal. Preheat the oven to 425°F / 220°C.

Bake at 425°F / 220°C for 15 minutes, then reduce to 375°F / 190°C and bake a further 45–55 minutes. The internal temperature should reach 205°F / 96°C. The loaf will shrink slightly from the tin sides when done. Turn out and cool completely on a wire rack — at least 8 hours, preferably 24 hours — before slicing. The crumb is gummy and unset when hot; slicing too soon produces a sticky, undercooked interior regardless of the actual bake level. The loaf's interior continues to set as it cools.

recipes.name: Saag Aloo

ingredients.name: Waxy potatoes (Desiree or Charlotte), cut into 3 cm cubes

steps: Place the cubed potatoes in a saucepan of cold salted water. Bring to a boil and cook for 8–10 minutes until just tender — a skewer meets slight resistance at the center. Drain and allow the steam to escape for 2 minutes so the surface dries slightly.

Heat the ghee in a wide, heavy pan over high heat until shimmering and a mustard seed dropped in skips and pops. Add the mustard seeds — cover immediately and let them pop for 30 seconds. Reduce heat to medium, add cumin seeds and let sizzle for 15 seconds. Add onion and cook, stirring, until deep golden and beginning to crisp at the edges, 10–12 minutes. Add ginger, garlic, green chili, and turmeric; cook 2 minutes until the raw smell disappears.

Add the spinach in large handfuls to the pan, stirring between each addition until each batch wilts before adding the next. Once all spinach is wilted (about 3 minutes), transfer half of it to a blender or use a hand blender to blitz it to a smooth, vivid-green purée — leave the other half whole for texture. Return the purée to the pan. Add the parboiled potatoes, garam masala, and salt. Stir gently to coat, then simmer on low heat for 5 minutes so the potatoes absorb the sauce. Taste and adjust salt.

recipes.name: Saag Paneer

ingredients.name: Fresh spinach (palak), washed, tough stems removed

steps: Bring a large pot of unsalted water to a fierce rolling boil. Add all the spinach at once — it will seem like an enormous volume, but it collapses dramatically. Push the spinach below the surface and cook for exactly 2 minutes: no more, or it will lose its vivid green color and turn a muddy army-green. Immediately drain and plunge into a bowl of ice-cold water, holding for 1 full minute to arrest all cooking. Lift the spinach from the cold water and squeeze firmly with both hands to remove as much liquid as possible — excess water will thin the final sauce. Transfer to a blender and blitz until completely smooth, about 2 minutes, adding just 2–3 tablespoons of the blanching water if the blade struggles. The puree should be electric green and pourable.

Heat the ghee in a wide, heavy pan over medium-high heat. When it shimmers, add the cumin seeds and let them crackle and darken for 20 seconds. Add the onion and cook, stirring frequently, for 10–12 minutes until it is deeply golden and caramelized at the edges — do not rush this step; the sweetness of properly browned onion forms the flavor backbone of the entire dish. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for 2 more minutes until the raw smell vanishes and the mixture turns a pale golden paste. Add the ground coriander, cumin, chili powder, and turmeric; stir constantly for 90 seconds, toasting the ground spices in the fat without letting them scorch. The masala is ready when the fat separates visibly around the edges of the spice mixture — an old cook's signal called 'bhunoing' that the rawness has been driven off.

Pour the spinach puree into the hot masala base — it will sputter and steam dramatically. Stir to combine thoroughly and reduce the heat to medium-low. Simmer uncovered for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the saag has darkened slightly from its electric green to a richer forest green and has thickened to the consistency of a pourable sauce. Season with salt. Stir in the garam masala and swirl in the cream or yogurt — the dairy tempers the sharpness and adds body. If using yogurt, lower the heat to minimum before adding to prevent curdling. The sauce should now taste fully seasoned, warmly spiced, and rich without heaviness.

In a separate small pan, heat 1 tablespoon of ghee over medium-high heat. Add the paneer cubes in a single layer — they should sizzle immediately on contact with the fat. Let them sit undisturbed for 90 seconds until the bottom face is golden, then flip each cube and repeat on the adjacent side. You are only browning the surface — the interior of paneer does not need cooking, only the exterior needs color and a slight crust to help it hold its shape in the sauce. Work in batches if your pan is small. Drain on a paper towel.

Gently fold the golden paneer cubes into the hot saag sauce, being careful not to break the cubes. Turn the heat to low and let the paneer warm through in the sauce for 3–4 minutes — this allows the cheese to absorb the spiced sauce at the surface while remaining firm at the center. Do not boil the sauce after adding paneer, as high heat will make it rubbery. Taste the final dish for salt. Serve with a final swirl of cream or a small knob of butter over the top, accompanied by hot naan, paratha, or steamed basmati.

recipes.name: Chelow ba Tahdig

ingredients.name: Fine salt (for soaking and parboiling water)

steps: Place the basmati rice in a large bowl. Dissolve 15 g of salt in 1 liter of cold water and pour over the rice — the water should be as salty as the sea; this salting firms the grain structure and prevents the rice from becoming mushy in later steps. Soak for a minimum of 30 minutes and ideally 1 hour. Soaking allows the grain to hydrate slowly and evenly so the parboiling step can cook the outside while the center remains firm. Drain and rinse gently with cold water.

Crush the saffron threads between fingertips or in a small mortar to a fine powder — whole threads release color and flavor incompletely. Place the saffron powder in a small glass or cup. Pour 60 ml of water that is just off the boil (not violently boiling — around 90°C) over the saffron. Stir once and cover the cup. Let steep for a minimum of 15 minutes. The water will turn a deep, glowing amber-orange and smell of hay, honey, and something metallic and floral. This bloomed saffron is used in two places: mixed into the tahdig, and drizzled over the finished rice.

Bring a large pot of water to a vigorous rolling boil — use at least 2 liters of water for 400 g of rice; Persian rice demands space to move freely. Add the remaining salt (10 g). Add the drained rice and stir gently once. Boil uncovered for exactly 5-7 minutes. Test the rice by removing a grain and biting it in half: the outside should be fully cooked and soft, but a small white line should still be visible at the center — the grain is two-thirds cooked. This is the parboil stage. Drain immediately and run cold water over the rice for 15 seconds to stop cooking.

Pour the oil into a wide, heavy-bottomed pot (non-stick or well-seasoned) and heat over medium heat. In a bowl, mix 3 large spoonfuls of parboiled rice with the yogurt, half the saffron water, and turmeric if using — this is the tahdig mixture. Spread it in a thin, even layer across the bottom of the hot oil. Listen: it should sizzle gently. Now pile the remaining rice on top in a pyramid shape — do not press down. Make 5-6 holes through the mound with the handle of a spoon to allow steam to circulate. Drizzle a thin stream of oil or melted butter over the pyramid.

Wrap the pot lid tightly in a clean kitchen towel — the cloth absorbs condensation and prevents water droplets from falling back onto the rice, which would make it wet rather than fluffy. Place the lid on tightly. Cook over medium heat for 5 minutes (this starts the tahdig crisping), then reduce to the lowest possible heat and cook for 40-45 minutes without lifting the lid. To unmold: place the pot on a cold, damp cloth or a pot holder for 2 minutes — the thermal shock helps release the tahdig. Remove the lid, place a large flat platter firmly over the pot, and flip in one confident movement. The tahdig should slide out golden and intact onto the platter. Drizzle the remaining saffron water over the white rice.

recipes.name: Salsa Roja Tatemada
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Serrano chilies (whole, with seeds for heat)

steps: Heat a dry comal, cast-iron skillet, or griddle over high heat until it is very hot — a drop of water should evaporate instantly. Place the whole tomatoes, serrano chilies, onion wedges, and unpeeled garlic directly on the dry surface. Do not add oil. Leave undisturbed for 3-4 minutes per side until deeply blackened in places. The tomatoes will collapse and weep juice; the onion and garlic skins will char and blacken. Turn each piece once, and char the second side equally. This is not burning — it is tatemado, the technique of charring aromatics to build depth.

Peel the charred garlic cloves. Transfer all the charred vegetables and any juices on the comal (scrape them in — that char is flavor) to a blender or food processor. Add salt. Pulse in short bursts — do not puree — until you reach a chunky, coarse texture with distinct bits of tomato and chili still visible. Add cilantro and pulse once more. Taste and adjust salt. The salsa should be bold, smoky, and chunky.

recipes.name: Salsa Roja
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Dried guajillo chilies (stems and seeds removed)
White onion, cut into thick wedges

steps: Heat a dry comal or heavy cast-iron skillet over high heat until it starts to smoke. Place the tomato halves cut-side down, onion wedges, and unpeeled garlic directly on the dry surface. Do not add oil. Char everything: tomatoes should develop patches of true black on the cut face and the skins should blister and split; onion wedges should char at the edges and soften through; garlic should darken in the peel and feel soft when squeezed. Turn everything once or twice and remove as it reaches the right level of char. The garlic will take about 6-8 minutes, the tomatoes 5-7, the onion 8-10.

On the same hot comal, toast the dried guajillo and árbol chilies. Press each chili flat for 10-15 seconds per side using a spatula — you want them to puff slightly, release a toasted chili fragrance, and develop a few darker spots. Do not char them as heavily as the tomatoes; the goal is to wake up their earthy, fruit-dried flavors and soften them slightly. Once toasted, immediately soak in just-boiled water for 10 minutes to rehydrate before blending. Drain and use as is — no need to strain the soaking liquid away unless it is very bitter.

Peel the garlic from its charred skins. Add the charred tomatoes (with their skins and any charred bits), onion, garlic, drained chilies, and dried oregano to a blender. Blend at high speed for 30-60 seconds — not too long. A great salsa roja has texture: visible flecks of chili skin, small tomato seed pockets, a slightly coarse consistency. Season with salt and add lime juice. Taste: it should be smoky, deep, and earthy with a bright acid finish and present but not overwhelming heat.

Heat the oil in a saucepan over medium-high until shimmering. Carefully pour in the blended salsa — it will spit and hiss violently. Stir and fry, letting the salsa sizzle in the hot oil for 3-5 minutes, stirring frequently. This brief frying — called 'freír la salsa' — deepens the color, concentrates the flavor, and integrates the raw edges. The salsa will darken slightly, reduce a little, and develop a more unified, round flavor. Taste again for salt and lime.

recipes.name: Salsa Verde Cruda
steps: Remove the papery husks from the tomatillos and rinse them under cold water, rubbing off the sticky, slightly waxy coating on their skin. This coating is mildly bitter and slightly acidic — removing it ensures the salsa doesn't carry an unwanted soapy note. Quarter them. Taste a small piece raw: the tomatillo should taste bracingly sour with a fruity, apple-like undertone. If they taste flat, they are under-ripe; very ripe tomatillos are better for cooked salsa.

Combine the tomatillos, jalapeño, onion, garlic, cilantro, lime juice, and salt in a blender. Pulse 8 to 12 times — do not blend continuously. The texture should remain slightly chunky, not pureed. Cruda means raw and it means textured. Taste after the first few pulses and adjust: more jalapeño for heat, more lime for brightness, more cilantro for green flavor. The salsa will seem thin but will thicken as it rests.

recipes.name: Italian Salsa Verde
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Place the garlic cloves in a mortar with the salt. Pound in a circular motion, scraping down the walls periodically, until you have a smooth, sticky, slightly translucent paste with no visible garlic chunks remaining. The salt acts as an abrasive — use it generously from the start. This takes about 2 minutes of sustained work. If using a knife instead: mince the garlic fine, then use the flat of the blade to smear it across the board, scraping and repeating until it forms a paste.

Add the anchovy fillets to the garlic paste and pound until they completely dissolve into the base — the anchovies should vanish, leaving no visible flesh, only a deeper savory color and scent. Add the capers and pound until they are crushed but retain some rough texture: you want fragments, not obliteration. Add the Dijon mustard and stir it through with the pestle. Taste: it should be intensely savory, salty, and punchy.

Stack the parsley leaves and chop them very finely with a sharp chef's knife — do not use a food processor, which bruises the parsley and turns it grey within minutes. Aim for a near-mince. Add the chopped parsley to the mortar paste and fold together with the pestle. Loosen with red wine vinegar and olive oil, adding each in alternating small additions while tasting after each — the oil brings body and rounds the flavors; the vinegar keeps it alive. The final consistency should be spoonable and flowing, not stiff like a paste and not watery like a dressing.

recipes.name: Salsa Verde (Tomatillo)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Position an oven rack 4 inches beneath the broiler and set it to high. Arrange the tomatillos, whole jalapeños, onion quarters, and unpeeled garlic cloves on a foil-lined baking sheet in a single layer. Broil for 8-10 minutes, rotating the pan once, until the tomatillos are blackened and blistered in spots, softened and collapsing, and the jalapeño skins are charred. Flip everything once at the halfway mark. The garlic should be soft inside its skin.

Squeeze the roasted garlic from its papery skins directly into a blender. Add the charred tomatillos and their accumulated juices, the jalapeños (seeds and all for full heat, or deseed for milder), and the onion. Pulse 4-5 times to break it down, then add the cilantro, lime juice, and salt. Blend to your preferred texture — a few more pulses for rustic and chunky, a 20-second blitz for a pourable sauce.

Taste the salsa and season in layers: add salt first until the tomatillo flavor snaps into focus, then add lime juice in small increments to amplify the brightness without pushing it into sourness. A good salsa verde should taste bright and tangy, with the heat arriving at the back of the palate. Let it rest at room temperature for 10 minutes before serving — the flavors knit together as it sits.

recipes.name: Salt and Pepper Shrimp

ingredients.name: Fresh red chillies, thinly sliced (optional but traditional)

steps: Pat the shrimp completely dry with kitchen paper — any surface moisture will cause the oil to spit violently and prevent the shell from crisping. Toss in the cornstarch to coat very lightly — just enough for a barely-there dusting, not a thick batter. Mix in half the salt, white pepper, and the five-spice.

Heat the oil in a wok over the highest possible heat to 190 C (375 F). Fry the shrimp in batches — 8–10 at a time — for exactly 60–75 seconds. The shells will sizzle aggressively and turn bright orange-red. Remove with a spider and drain on a rack. Do not over-fry — the shrimp continue cooking from residual heat.

Pour off most of the frying oil, leaving about 1 tablespoon in the wok. Return to high heat. Add the garlic, most of the spring onion, and sliced chilli. Stir-fry for 30 seconds until the garlic is golden and fragrant. Add the fried shrimp back to the wok and toss furiously for 30 seconds to coat with the aromatic mixture. Season with remaining salt and white pepper. Drizzle with sesame oil and toss once more. Serve immediately, garnished with remaining spring onion.

recipes.name: Salt and Pepper Squid
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Fresh squid tubes and tentacles, cleaned
Neutral oil for deep-frying (peanut or sunflower)
Long red chili and green chili, thinly sliced

steps: Open the squid tubes and score the inside surface in a crosshatch pattern at 5mm intervals — this gives the starch something to grip and helps the squid curl dramatically in the oil. Cut into 4cm pieces. Keep tentacles whole. Dry everything very thoroughly with paper towels.

Combine potato starch, salt, white pepper, and Sichuan pepper in a bowl. Add the dried squid and toss to coat completely. Shake off excess in a sieve — you want a thin, even coating that barely obscures the squid, not a heavy cloak.

Heat oil to 200 C (390 F) in a wok or deep pan — higher than most frying, because squid is wet. Fry in small batches for exactly 90 seconds. The squid will curl and the coating will set. Do not stir for the first 30 seconds so the crust can form. Remove to a rack — immediately.

Pour off most of the frying oil, leaving a thin slick. Over high flame, add garlic, chili, and spring onion. Stir-fry for 20–30 seconds until fragrant and the garlic is barely golden. Add the fried squid back and toss furiously for 15 seconds — just enough to perfume the crust without steaming it soft.

recipes.name: Salt-Baked Branzino

ingredients.name: Whole branzino (European sea bass), gutted and scaled

steps: Preheat the oven to 190°C (375°F). In a large bowl, combine the coarse sea salt with the egg whites. Mix firmly with your hands until every grain of salt is coated and the mixture resembles wet sand — it should clump when squeezed and hold an impression of your fist. This is the mortar that will seal the fish. If it crumbles and won't hold a shape, add a fourth egg white.

Check the fish cavity is clean and dry. Season the interior lightly with a pinch of salt. Lay the lemon rounds in a shingle pattern along the cavity floor. Pack the fennel fronds, thyme, and parsley in on top of the lemon — the cavity should be visibly full. The herbs will steam inside the crust and perfume the flesh from the inside out without penetrating it externally at all.

Spread a third of the salt mixture onto a rimmed baking sheet in the exact shape and size of the fish, about 1.5 cm thick. Lay the stuffed branzino on top. Pack the remaining salt mixture firmly over the top and sides of the fish, pressing and smoothing it into a solid, even casing at least 1.5 cm thick at every point. Pay special attention to the head and tail — cracks there will let steam escape and dry the flesh. The fish should be completely invisible under the crust. Smooth the surface with wet palms.

Bake at 190°C (375°F) for 25–30 minutes for a 600g fish. The timing scales with fish weight: add 5 minutes per additional 200g. The crust will harden to a rigid, chalky shell and may develop faint ivory-to-beige colouring on top. It will not brown dramatically — the visual cues here are all about the crust hardening. A probe thermometer inserted through the crust should read 58–60°C at the thickest part of the fish. If you do not have a probe, use the timing as your guide.

Bring the baking sheet to the table. Using the back of a heavy spoon or a small mallet, crack the crust firmly along the spine of the fish. It will fracture in large shards — peel these away and discard. Carefully lift the top fillet free, then remove the spine in one piece. The bottom fillet sits on the lower salt bed — slide a spatula underneath to lift it clean. Serve the fillets on warmed plates with a generous pour of extra-virgin olive oil and the lemon slices from inside the cavity.

recipes.name: Salt-Baked Sea Bass

ingredients.name: Whole sea bass, cleaned and scaled (about 700g)
Coarse sea salt (not fine — it must be granular)
Fresh ginger, peeled, sliced into coins
Scallions (spring onions), tied in a loose knot

steps: Preheat the oven to 200°C (390°F) with a rack in the centre position. Pat the sea bass completely dry — inside the cavity and all over the outside — with multiple changes of paper towels. Dryness is critical: any moisture on the fish surface will steam inside the salt crust rather than allowing the fish to cook in the dry residual heat of the crust. Inspect the fish for any remaining scales by running a finger from tail to head — any that remain will prevent the crust from sealing properly and can embed in the fish.

Lay the ginger slices in an overlapping layer along the length of the cavity floor. Place the knotted scallions on top of the ginger, and tuck the cilantro sprigs around them. Drizzle the Shaoxing wine into the cavity — it will perfume the fish as it steams. Close the cavity by pressing the sides of the fish together gently. The aromatics inside do not season the flesh directly; they create a fragrant steam environment that perfumes the fish from within.

Mix the coarse sea salt and lightly beaten egg whites together with your hands until the mixture resembles wet sand that holds its shape when squeezed — it should clump, not crumble. Spread a 1.5cm bed of the salt mixture on a baking tray or oven-proof dish. Lay the stuffed fish on the bed. Pack the remaining salt mixture over and around the entire fish, pressing firmly to build a uniform crust 2cm thick on all sides. Seal any gaps, especially around the tail and head. Bake at 200°C for 25–30 minutes (about 20 minutes per 500g of fish weight, plus 5 minutes for the crust).

At the table, present the salt-crusted dish. Using the back of a heavy spoon or small hammer, crack the crust along the spine with a few firm blows. Lift off the large pieces of crust — the fish skin will often come away with the top crust, revealing bright, pearlescent white flesh beneath. Brush away any salt granules clinging to the flesh with a pastry brush. The fish will not taste salty — the salt crust seasons it only from the outside through the skin, not into the flesh.

Working quickly so the fish does not cool, drizzle the soy sauce evenly over the exposed flesh, followed by the toasted sesame oil — the sesame oil should sizzle faintly as it hits the hot fish. Serve directly from the dish with steamed white jasmine rice and a simple stir-fried green vegetable. Use a tablespoon to scoop portions of the flesh off the spine, keeping the segments as large and intact as possible — this fish deserves to be eaten in generous, moist chunks, not shredded.

recipes.name: Brandade de Morue

ingredients.name: Whole milk, warmed to hand temperature

steps: Place the salt cod skin-side up in a large bowl or deep baking dish and cover with cold water. Refrigerate for 24 hours, changing the water at least 3 times — every 6–8 hours is ideal. The water will turn white and cloudy each time, carrying away the curing salt. After the final soak, taste a thin flake from the thickest part: it should taste pleasantly salty, like a well-seasoned fish, not briny or harsh. If it is still harsh, soak 2 more hours.

Place the desalted cod in a wide pan and cover with fresh cold water. Add the thyme. Bring slowly to a bare simmer — tiny bubbles rising at the edges, the water trembling but not boiling. Poach for 10–12 minutes. Do not boil: boiling at this stage firms the protein into a tough, rubbery slab and breaks the fine flakes. The cod is done when it flakes easily along its natural seams when prodded with a fork. Lift out, discard the poaching water, and let it cool enough to handle.

Remove all skin and bones from the cod — run your fingers carefully through the flakes to find every pin bone. Place the cod and raw garlic in a mortar and pound to a paste, or pulse in a food processor. The goal is to break the fish down into a fine, cohesive mass that will absorb the oil and milk. Do not process to a completely smooth paste yet — a slightly grainy, textured base is correct at this stage. The garlic should be fully incorporated and invisible.

With the cod paste in the mortar or a bowl set over gentle heat (or in a stand mixer with paddle), begin adding the warm olive oil in a thin, slow stream, working it in constantly — exactly like making a mayonnaise. When half the oil is incorporated, add a tablespoon of warm milk. Alternate oil and milk until both are fully incorporated. The brandade will transform from a dense paste to a smooth, fluffy, ivory-white emulsion that is light enough to scoop but rich enough to mound. Season with white pepper and lemon juice. Taste: it should be salty, rich, faintly fishy, and deeply satisfying.

recipes.name: Salt-Crusted Whole Fish

ingredients.name: Whole sea bass or sea bream (600-800 g), gutted and scaled

steps: Whisk egg whites to a light foam — no stiff peaks, just broken and fluid. Pour over coarse salt and work with your hands until the mixture resembles wet sand. It should clump when squeezed and hold the shape of your fist. If it won't clump, add water a tablespoon at a time.

Preheat oven to 220 C (425 F). Spread a 1.5 cm layer of salt paste on a baking sheet to form the bed. Stuff the fish cavity with thyme, lemon rounds, and garlic. Lay the fish on the salt bed. Pack remaining salt paste firmly over the entire fish, including head and tail, sealing all seams. Press to compact.

Roast for 25-30 minutes for a 700 g fish. The crust will set and begin to show faint golden spots on its highest points. An instant-read thermometer inserted through the crust into the thickest part of the fish should read 55-60 C (130-140 F). The fish steams inside its own armor.

At the table, crack the crust with the back of a heavy spoon or a small mallet, following the line of the fish's spine. Lift away the top half of the crust in large pieces — it comes off in satisfying slabs. Brush away any salt crystals with a pastry brush. Peel back the skin and serve the fillets with olive oil and lemon wedges. The flesh will be luminous, juicy, and perfectly seasoned.

recipes.name: Saltimbocca alla Romana

ingredients.name: Veal escalopes (noce or fesa), 150 g each
Dry white wine (Frascati or Pinot Grigio)

steps: Place each veal escalope between two sheets of plastic wrap. Using the flat face of a meat mallet or the bottom of a heavy pan, pound with firm, even strokes from the center outward — not vertical blows that tear the meat, but angled slides that stretch the fibers. Target 5–6 mm thickness, roughly even across the whole escalope. Season lightly with white pepper only — the prosciutto will provide all the salt needed.

Lay 2–3 sage leaves flat on the top (smooth) side of each escalope. Drape one or two slices of prosciutto over to cover the sage and the entire escalope surface — the ham must extend slightly beyond the meat edges. Secure with one or two wooden toothpicks pierced at an angle through ham, sage, and meat. Season the underside (veal side) very lightly with salt only. Dust the veal side in flour and pat off all excess — you want a gossamer coating, not a thick crust.

Heat a large stainless or carbon steel pan over medium-high heat. Add butter and let it foam and subside — when the first wisps of color appear in the butter, it is ready. Place escalopes prosciutto-side down. Press them flat with a spatula for the first 10 seconds to ensure full contact. Cook prosciutto-side for 2–3 minutes until the ham crackles and has rendered its fat into the butter. Flip and cook the veal side for just 60–90 seconds — veal is lean and overcooks in moments.

Remove the escalopes to a warm plate. Over high heat, pour the wine into the still-hot pan and immediately scrape up the browned bits from the base — these are the flavor. Let the wine reduce by half, about 90 seconds of vigorous bubbling. Remove from heat, add a cold knob of butter, and swirl constantly until the sauce becomes glossy and emulsified. Pour over the escalopes immediately. The dish is best eaten within 3 minutes of plating.

recipes.name: Samosa Filling

ingredients.name: Waxy potatoes (Yukon Gold or similar), boiled whole and peeled
Green peas (fresh shelled or frozen, thawed)
Coriander seeds, lightly crushed in a mortar
Green chilies (serrano or Thai), finely minced
Fresh cilantro leaves and tender stems, finely chopped

steps: Cover the whole, unpeeled potatoes with cold water in a pot. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer and cook until a thin knife slides through the center with zero resistance — about 20–25 minutes depending on size. Do not rush with high heat or the skins will split and the potatoes will absorb too much water. Drain and immediately peel while hot — the skins slip off easily and the potato flesh sheds moisture better when peeled warm. Spread the peeled potatoes on a tray and leave them uncovered for 5 minutes to steam-dry. Then roughly crush them with a fork or your hands into a mix of small chunks and larger broken pieces. Do not mash smooth — the filling needs texture. Some pieces of potato 1–2 cm across are desirable.

Heat the oil or ghee in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Add the cumin seeds and crushed coriander seeds together — they should sizzle immediately and begin crackling. Let them bloom for about 30–40 seconds until the cumin turns a deep chestnut brown. Do not stop here — add the minced ginger and green chili and stir for 1 minute until the raw ginger smell softens to a sweet, fragrant note. Add the ground coriander, amchur, garam masala, and turmeric. Stir constantly for 60 seconds, scraping the bottom — the ground spices will form a thick, fragrant paste in the fat. This step, called the tadka or bhuna, is critical: the oil carries fat-soluble spice compounds directly into the potato and peas at the moment of contact. If your spice paste smells warm and rounded, with no raw edge, it is ready.

Add the frozen or fresh peas directly to the spiced fat in the pan. Stir and cook for 2 minutes — the peas will warm through and absorb the spiced oil. Add the crushed potatoes all at once and fold everything together using a wide spatula or wooden spoon, working from the bottom of the pan and turning the mixture over itself. You want to evenly coat every piece of potato and pea in the spice blend without turning the mixture into a smooth mash — the filling should retain texture, with visible pieces of potato and peas throughout. Season with salt and stir. Off the heat, fold in the fresh cilantro. Taste: the filling should be intensely flavored — boldly salty, bright with amchur's sour note, and warmly spiced throughout. It needs to be seasoned aggressively because the pastry shell will dilute the intensity. Allow the filling to cool completely before enclosing in pastry — warm filling will steam the pastry and make it soggy.

recipes.name: Samosa with Aloo Filling

ingredients.name: Waxy potatoes (boiled, cooled, and roughly mashed)
Fine sea salt (for both pastry and filling)
Neutral oil for deep frying (sunflower or vegetable)

steps: Combine flour and half the salt in a bowl. Rub the ghee or shortening into the flour with your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs and no large fat lumps remain — this is the critical step for a flaky, layered crust. Drizzle in ice-cold water a tablespoon at a time, mixing with a fork after each addition, until the dough just comes together without being sticky. It should feel firmer than a bread dough — this tight, stiff dough is what gives samosas their snap. Knead very briefly — 1 minute only — then wrap tightly and rest for 30 minutes at room temperature.

Heat 2 tablespoons of the frying oil in a skillet over medium heat. Bloom the cumin seeds for 30 seconds until they crackle and darken. Add the green chili and ginger, fry for 1 minute. Add the mashed potatoes and peas and fold gently to combine, trying to keep some potato texture — do not turn it into baby food. Add amchur, garam masala, and the remaining salt. Mix and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until the filling is fragrant and slightly dry. Taste: it should be assertively seasoned, sour from the amchur, and warming with spice. The filling must be fully cool before wrapping — warm filling creates steam inside the samosa and makes the pastry soggy.

Divide the rested dough into 10 to 12 equal balls. Roll each ball on a lightly floured surface into an oval roughly 15 cm × 8 cm, 2–3 mm thick — thinner than you think you need. Cut each oval in half across the long axis, giving two D-shaped pieces. Fold each D into a cone: moisten one straight edge with water, overlap the two straight edges by 5 mm, and press firmly to seal. Fill the cone two-thirds full with cooled filling — do not overfill. Moisten the open top edge with water and press firmly to seal into a triangle. Press each seam between your fingers and then press lightly against the work surface to create the flat, pyramid shape. Set on a lightly oiled tray. The sealed edges must be completely watertight — test by gently squeezing each samosa over the sink.

Heat the frying oil in a deep, heavy pot to 160°C (325°F) — lower than you expect. Samosas must fry slowly to develop the characteristic blistered crust: high heat seals the outside before the inside cooks through and the pastry has no time to develop its flaky layers. Lower 3 to 4 samosas at a time into the oil and fry, turning every 2 minutes, for 10 to 12 minutes total until they are an even deep amber-gold on all faces. Raise the temperature to 175°C (350°F) for the final 2 minutes to crisp the exterior. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain upright in a rack or colander, not lying flat — this preserves the crust on all sides.

recipes.name: Potato & Pea Samosas
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Vegetable shortening or ghee (for rubbing into flour)
Russet potatoes, boiled and roughly mashed
Filling spice blend (cumin seeds, coriander, amchur, garam masala, green chili, ginger)

steps: Combine flour, fat, salt, and 1 tsp ajwain (carom seeds) if available. Rub the fat into the flour with your fingertips for 3–4 minutes until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs with no loose flour remaining — this is the critical step for flakiness. Add ice-cold water 1 tbsp at a time (about 6–8 tbsp total) until the dough just comes together. It should be firm, stiff, and not sticky. Knead for 2 minutes, then rest covered for 20 minutes.

Heat 1 tbsp oil in a pan over medium-high heat. Add cumin seeds and let them splutter 10 seconds. Add green chili and fresh ginger, cook 30 seconds. Add roughly mashed potato and peas, then all remaining ground spices. Cook for 3–4 minutes, folding rather than stirring to keep some potato texture. Add amchur (dried mango powder) or lemon juice for tartness and salt to taste. Spread on a plate and cool completely before using.

Divide the rested dough into equal portions and roll each into a thin oval about 18–20cm long and 10cm wide. Cut in half to make two semicircles. Form a cone by folding the straight edge over and sealing with a little water. Fill the cone with 2 tbsp of filling — do not overfill. Pinch the open edge closed firmly, pressing the seam flat. The sealed edge must be completely airtight or the samosa will burst during frying.

Heat oil to 160–170°C (325°F) — lower than standard frying temperature. Slide samosas in gently, 3–4 at a time. Fry slowly for 12–15 minutes, turning occasionally, until deep golden. The low temperature slowly renders and crisps the pastry all the way through without burning the exterior before the interior heats. Drain on a wire rack, not paper towels — steam must escape from all sides to keep the crust crisp.

recipes.name: Satay Peanut Sauce

ingredients.name: Roasted peanut butter, natural (no added sugar)
Thai red curry paste (store-bought or homemade)
Roasted peanuts, roughly crushed, for topping

steps: Pour the coconut milk into a small saucepan over medium heat. When it begins to steam and show the first signs of simmering at the edges, add the red curry paste. Whisk constantly to break up the paste and disperse it evenly through the coconut milk. Continue to cook over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring regularly. You are not just dissolving the paste — you are cooking out the raw edge of its dried chilies and spices, blooming them in the coconut fat the way you would bloom spices in oil. The mixture will shift from bright orange-red (raw paste) to a deeper, richer terracotta-orange as the paste cooks. The aroma will change from sharp and raw to roasted and complex. This bloom step is what separates a cooked satay sauce from a merely mixed one.

Add the peanut butter to the simmering curry coconut mixture. Whisk vigorously to incorporate — the peanut butter will resist at first, then suddenly combine into a thick, uniform sauce. Add the palm sugar, tamarind paste, fish sauce, and salt. Stir constantly over medium-low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until the sugar dissolves and all elements are fully integrated. The sauce will thicken as it heats — adjust consistency with small additions of warm water if it becomes too thick to pour easily. The finished sauce should flow off a spoon in a heavy, slow ribbon. Taste and balance: if too thick and sweet, add a teaspoon more tamarind; if too sharp, add a pinch more palm sugar; if flat, a few more drops of fish sauce. The balance to aim for is rich-sweet-slightly-sour-deeply-savory.

Transfer the warm peanut sauce to a serving bowl or pour it into a small clay pot for table presentation. Scatter the roughly crushed roasted peanuts over the surface — they should be chunky enough to provide texture but not so large they fall off a dipped item. Add a small pinch of dried chili flakes for color and a visual hint of heat. Serve warm alongside grilled chicken or pork satay skewers, fresh cucumber rounds, and the traditional Thai ajad (pickled cucumber relish). The sauce can be made up to 3 days ahead and refrigerated — it will thicken on cooling but returns to the correct consistency when gently reheated with a splash of water or coconut milk.

recipes.name: Satay Sauce
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Lemongrass stalks (white and pale-green part only), sliced
Galangal (fresh or frozen), peeled and roughly chopped
Dried red chiles (stemmed and seeded), or 1 tsp sambal oelek
Palm sugar or packed brown sugar
Tamarind paste (from a block, dissolved in warm water)

steps: Combine the shallots, garlic, lemongrass, galangal, and dried chiles in a blender or food processor. Add a tablespoon of water and blend until you have a rough paste, scraping down the sides as needed. The lemongrass is fibrous and the galangal is woody — blend for at least 2 minutes at high speed, pausing to scrape the sides, until the paste is as smooth as the blender will allow. Some texture is acceptable and even desirable, but the lemongrass in particular must be finely broken down or it will remain fibrous and unpleasant in the finished sauce. A high-powered blender will give a smoother result; a food processor gives a rougher but excellent paste.

Heat 2 tablespoons of neutral oil or coconut oil in a wok or wide saucepan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the blended aromatics paste and the torn kaffir lime leaves and fry, stirring constantly, until the raw smell of garlic and shallot has cooked out and the paste is fragrant, drier, and deeper in color — 5-8 minutes. Crucially, cook until you can see the oil beginning to separate and collect at the edges of the paste — this is called pecah minyak (oil breaking) in Indonesian and Malay cooking, and it signals that the water in the aromatics has fully evaporated and the paste is truly fried, not merely stewed. This step transforms the raw sharp aromatics into a mellow, complex base.

If using whole roasted peanuts, pulse them in a food processor to a rough, crumbly texture — about the size of coarse breadcrumbs, not a paste. Add the ground peanuts to the fried aromatics paste and stir to coat them in the fragrant oil. Pour in the coconut milk and water, stirring to combine everything into a thick, rough soup. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring frequently, and cook for 10-12 minutes until the sauce is thick, glossy, and the peanuts have absorbed the coconut milk and swelled slightly. The sauce should coat a spoon in a heavy, flowing layer — much thicker than pourable cream.

Add the palm sugar, fish sauce, tamarind paste, and lime juice to the simmering sauce. Stir to dissolve the palm sugar completely and simmer 2-3 minutes more to integrate everything. Now taste carefully and balance the sauce along four axes: savory-salty (fish sauce), sweet (palm sugar), sour-tamarind (tamarind and lime), and heat (chile). The sauce should be rich and deeply savory first, with the sweetness present but not candy-like, the sourness brightening rather than dominating, and the chile an undercurrent of warmth. Adjust each element incrementally — a satay sauce that tastes sweet and peanut-buttery without complexity is incomplete; one that tastes only fishy has the fish sauce ratio wrong.

recipes.name: Sauce Tomate (Classical French)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Dice the salt pork small and set it in a heavy-bottomed pot over low-medium heat (or simply melt the butter). Let it render slowly without browning, drawing the fat out clear and the scraps to a pale gold. You want a film of clean fat coating the pot, not a fry.

Add the finely cut mirepoix and the garlic to the fat. Sweat over low-medium heat, stirring often, until the onion turns translucent and the whole pot softens and goes silent of its raw bite. Do not let it color — this is a foundation, not a fond.

Add the chopped tomatoes (crush canned ones by hand) and the pinch of sugar to correct their acidity. Raise the heat to a lively simmer and cook down, stirring as it thickens, until the watery tomato has collapsed into a thick, jammy base and the bright raw smell turns deep and sweet.

Pour in the white stock, tuck in the bouquet garni, and season lightly with salt (go easy if you used salt pork). Bring to the barest simmer and hold it there, partially covered, for an hour and a half or more, skimming the fat and scum that gather at the surface. The sauce should ripple, never boil.

Discard the bouquet garni and the pork scraps. Pass the sauce through a food mill or push it through a fine sieve with a ladle, working the solids until only dry skins and fibre remain behind. Return it to the heat, taste, and adjust salt and the pinch of sugar to balance the acidity into a smooth, velvety sauce.

recipes.name: Rhineland Sauerbraten

ingredients.name: Beef bottom round or top round (about 1.5 kg, tied)
Gingersnap cookies (Lebkuchen or ginger snaps), crumbled

steps: Do not heat the marinade — a cold marinade is traditional for sauerbraten. Combine the red wine vinegar, red wine, water, onion, celery, carrot, bay leaves, juniper berries, cloves, peppercorns, sugar, and salt in a large non-reactive bowl or pot (glass, ceramic, or stainless steel — never aluminium or cast iron at this stage). Stir until the salt and sugar dissolve. Submerge the beef completely, pressing it down. Cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate for 3–4 days, turning the meat once per day so all sides marinate evenly.

Remove the beef from the marinade and pat it completely dry with paper towels — moisture is the enemy of a good sear. Strain and reserve all the marinade liquid. Heat the lard or oil in a heavy Dutch oven or braising pot over high heat until just beginning to smoke. Sear the beef on all sides, including the ends, for 3–4 minutes per side without moving it. You are building deep brown crust for colour and flavour — the Maillard crust will dissolve into the braising liquid and become the backbone of the sauce.

Return the seared beef to the pot. Pour the strained marinade over it — the liquid should come at least halfway up the sides of the meat. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, then cover with a tight lid and reduce to the lowest possible heat (or transfer to a 160°C oven). Braise for 2.5–3 hours, turning the beef every 45 minutes. The meat is done when a carving fork slides in and out without resistance, and the fibres are beginning to separate when pressed.

Remove the beef and keep warm under foil. Pour all the braising liquid through a fine strainer into a wide saucepan — discard the spent aromatics. Bring the liquid to a vigorous boil and reduce by one-third, about 10 minutes. Crumble in the gingersnaps and whisk over medium heat until they dissolve completely and the sauce thickens noticeably to a coating consistency. Taste for balance — it should be sweet, sour, warm with spice, and deeply savoury. If it is too tart, add another crumbled gingersnap. Off the heat, stir in the sour cream if using, and reheat gently without boiling.

recipes.name: Shanghai Scallion Oil Noodles (Cong You Ban Mian)

ingredients.name: Fresh thin Shanghai noodles (or dried lo mein)

steps: Combine the scallion pieces and neutral oil in a cold small saucepan or wok — starting in cold oil is critical. If you add scallions to already-hot oil they will fry hard and fast, browning too quickly before they have time to release their aromatics into the oil. Place over the lowest heat you can manage and cook for 30–40 minutes. The first 15 minutes will see very little activity — the oil will warm slowly and the scallions will begin to soften and wilt. From 15–25 minutes, the scallions will begin to shrink dramatically and you will see the first signs of browning at the green tips. From 25–40 minutes, the scallions will caramelize progressively from the tips down toward the white roots, going from golden to amber to a deep reddish-brown. The goal is that the scallions go almost fully dark — sweet-bitter, crispy shards — while the oil turns a deep golden-amber and smells like nothing else: sweet, savory, deeply caramelized allium. Stir every 5 minutes, more frequently in the last 10. When the scallion pieces are uniformly dark golden-brown and crispy, remove from heat.

In a large mixing bowl that will also serve as your tossing bowl for the noodles, combine the warm scallion oil (about 3 tablespoons per serving), light soy sauce, dark soy sauce, and sugar. Stir together with a spoon or chopsticks until the sugar is fully dissolved. The sauce will be a dark, glossy, highly aromatic liquid — the dark soy provides color and depth, the light soy provides salinity and brightness. Taste it: it should be very salty and intensely sweet-savory, because it will dilute dramatically when tossed with the starchy noodles. The ratio of scallion oil to soy sauce is important: too much oil and the noodles are greasy; too much soy and they are one-dimensionally salty. Adjust to your preference — more dark soy for a deeper color and molasses-sweet flavor, more light soy for a brighter, saltier result.

Cook the noodles in a large pot of vigorously boiling, lightly salted water until just done — fresh Shanghai noodles take 2–3 minutes, dried lo mein 4–5 minutes, thin spaghetti 7–8 minutes. Drain well, shaking the colander hard. Transfer immediately to the bowl of scallion sauce while the noodles are still very hot — the heat helps the sauce coat every strand. Toss vigorously and quickly with chopsticks or tongs, lifting and folding the noodles continuously for 60–90 seconds until every strand is evenly coated in the dark, glossy sauce. The hot noodles will absorb the soy quickly, so work fast. Taste and adjust: more soy for salt, more oil for richness, a few drops of scallion oil for aroma. Transfer to a serving plate or bowl and scatter a generous amount of the reserved crispy scallion pieces over the top. Serve immediately — scallion oil noodles are a dish of the moment, and the texture deteriorates rapidly.

recipes.name: Scallion Pancake (Cong You Bing)
steps: Place flour in a large bowl and make a well in the center. Pour the boiling water directly into the well and immediately stir with chopsticks or a fork in a circular motion from the center outward — the boiling water partially cooks (gelatinizes) the starch, producing a tender, slightly translucent dough. After stirring for 1 minute, add the cold water and continue mixing until a rough ball forms. The combination of hot and cold water produces a dough that is simultaneously soft (from the hot water gelatinization) and elastic (from the cold water activating remaining gluten). The dough will look shaggy at first — this is correct.

Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 5-7 minutes until the surface becomes very smooth. Hot-water doughs knead faster than cold-water doughs because the heat has already done structural work — do not over-knead or the dough becomes tough. The finished dough should be smooth as a pearl, non-sticky, and extremely pliable — more so than bread dough, closer to fresh pasta. Divide into 4 equal portions, cover with a damp cloth, and rest for 20-30 minutes.

Working one portion at a time on a lightly floured surface, roll each piece into a thin rectangle approximately 30 x 20 cm (12 x 8 inches). Brush generously with sesame oil, leaving a 1 cm border. Scatter a quarter of the scallions evenly across the surface and season with salt and five-spice if using. Starting from the long edge closest to you, roll the rectangle tightly into a log — exactly as you'd roll a jelly roll. Then coil the log on itself into a tight spiral, tucking the tail end underneath, and press down gently to seal the coil. Let the coiled discs rest 10 minutes before flattening. Use a rolling pin to flatten each coil to about 6 mm thickness — the layered spiral compresses without losing its laminated structure.

Heat a wide, heavy skillet (cast iron or carbon steel preferred) over medium-high heat until smoking. Add 1 tablespoon of neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place a pancake in the pan and cook for 2-3 minutes until the bottom is deeply golden brown with some darker spots. Flip, add another small splash of oil to the pan, and press the pancake gently but firmly with a wide spatula for 5 seconds to ensure even contact. Cook another 2-3 minutes. Flip again, pressing once more, and cook a final minute if needed. The total cooking time is 5-7 minutes — enough to cook the interior layers through while building a shattering crust. Drain briefly on a rack (not paper towels, which steam and soften the crust).

recipes.name: Scallion Pancakes (Cong You Bing)

ingredients.name: Neutral oil for frying (vegetable or rapeseed)

steps: Place the flour in a bowl and pour in the boiling water all at once. Immediately stir with a chopstick or wooden spoon in circular motions until the water is absorbed and the mixture looks like a shaggy, steaming mass. The boiling water partially cooks the starch — this gelatinisation is what makes the dough pliable and the pancake chewy rather than biscuity. Once cool enough to handle (about 2 minutes), knead briefly in the bowl until a smooth dough forms — about 3 minutes. It should feel soft and slightly tacky.

Divide the rested dough into 4 equal pieces. On a lightly oiled surface (not floured), roll each piece into a thin rectangle about 3 mm thick. Brush generously with sesame oil to within 5 mm of the edges. Scatter salt and sliced scallion evenly across the surface, pressing lightly so they adhere. Now roll the rectangle into a tight log from the long edge, like a Swiss roll. Then coil the log into a tight snail shape and press it flat with your palm. Re-roll the coiled disc to about 5 mm thick. This double-rolling is the technique that creates the layered structure.

Heat a heavy skillet or cast iron pan over medium heat. Add enough neutral oil to coat the bottom with a 2 mm layer. When the oil shimmers, add one pancake. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes on the first side without moving it — the underside should be golden and crisping. Flip and press lightly with a spatula to encourage even contact with the pan. Cook the second side for 2 minutes. The pancake is done when both sides are deep golden-brown with dark, crispy edges and you can hear it crackling and hissing in the oil.

recipes.name: Seared Scallops with Pea Purée and Pancetta
steps: Melt 20 g of the butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the diced shallot and garlic with a pinch of salt and sweat gently for 3–4 minutes until completely soft and translucent — no color at all. Add the frozen peas and double cream, bring to a simmer, and cook for 3 minutes until the peas are just tender and brilliant green. Transfer everything to a blender, add the mint leaves, and blend on high until completely smooth. Pass through a fine sieve if you want restaurant-level silkiness. Season with salt, white pepper, and a small squeeze of lemon. Keep warm.

Place the diced pancetta in a cold dry frying pan and set over medium heat. As the fat renders slowly, the pancetta will crisp evenly without burning. Cook for 5–7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the dice are deeply golden and crispy and the surrounding fat has fully rendered out. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel. Reserve the rendered fat in the pan — this will be used to sear the scallops.

Pat the scallops completely dry with paper towel — this is the single most important step. Any surface moisture will steam rather than sear. Season both flat faces with salt and white pepper. Add the neutral oil to the pancetta-fat pan and heat over the highest possible heat until the oil just begins to smoke. Place scallops flat-side down in the pan, one by one, and do not touch them for exactly 90 seconds to 2 minutes. The sear must be uninterrupted. They are ready to flip when they release easily from the pan — not when the timer says so.

The moment the scallops are flipped, add the remaining cold butter to the pan in two pieces. It will melt and foam immediately in the residual heat. Tilt the pan and use a spoon to continuously baste the scallops with the foaming butter for 30–45 seconds. Add a tiny squeeze of lemon. Remove scallops the moment the second side shows a pale gold — the center should still feel yielding. Rest on a warm plate for 30 seconds while you arrange the components.

Working quickly, spoon a swoosh of warm pea purée across each plate using the back of a warm spoon. Arrange three scallops per plate on and around the purée, seared-side facing up to display the crust. Scatter the crispy pancetta dice over and around the scallops. Finish with a small cluster of pea shoots or watercress placed in the center, dressed with a tiny drizzle of olive oil. The three elements must arrive together: any one of them cold ruins the dish.

recipes.name: Schiacciata
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Extra-virgin olive oil, plus generous amount for pan and top
Flaky sea salt (Maldon or Fiore di Sale)

steps: Combine the flour, instant yeast, and fine salt in a large bowl, keeping the salt and yeast on opposite sides of the bowl initially. Pour in the warm water and olive oil. Mix with a dough scraper or your hand until no dry flour remains — the dough will be moderately sticky, softer than a bread dough but not as wet as focaccia. It should pull away from the sides of the bowl. Do not add more flour. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.

Perform three sets of stretch-and-fold over 60 minutes, one set every 20 minutes. For each set: wet your hand, grab the dough at one side of the bowl, stretch it firmly upward as far as it will reach without tearing, then fold it over the center. Rotate the bowl 90 degrees and repeat until you have completed four folds. After three sets, the dough should be noticeably smoother, more cohesive, and beginning to show bubbles beneath the surface. Cover and let bulk ferment at room temperature for another 30 minutes until puffy.

Pour a very generous amount of olive oil onto a half-sheet pan or rimmed baking tray — at least 4-5 tablespoons. Schiacciata is an olive oil bread and should practically float in it. Transfer the dough to the pan and use your fingertips to begin pressing and stretching it toward the edges. If the dough springs back firmly, cover and wait 10-15 minutes, then try again. The dough should eventually be pressed quite flat — roughly 1.5 cm thick throughout. Cover with plastic wrap and proof at room temperature for 30-45 minutes until noticeably puffy and slightly domed.

Using all ten fingers held flat, press the dough firmly and repeatedly across its entire surface, pushing all the way through to the pan. The dough should be pressed quite flat — flatter than focaccia. This is the 'schiacciata' — the crushing. Drizzle another generous pour of olive oil across the entire surface, letting it pool in the dimples. Scatter the flaky salt and rosemary leaves if using. The salt goes on now, not after baking.

Bake at 230 C (450 F) on the lowest rack for 15-20 minutes. Schiacciata bakes hotter and faster than focaccia because it is thinner. Watch carefully after 12 minutes. The edges should be deep brown and very crisp; the center should be golden. Remove from the pan immediately to a wire rack — do not let it cool in the pan or the bottom will steam and soften. Cool for 5 minutes before cutting. Schiacciata is best eaten within 1 hour of baking, while the contrast between the crisp exterior and the moist, oily crumb is still at its peak.

recipes.name: Scotch Egg
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Black pepper, white pepper, mace blend

steps: Lower eggs gently into a pot of vigorously boiling water. Cook exactly 6 minutes 30 seconds for a jammy, coral yolk. Transfer immediately to an ice bath and chill for 10 minutes — this stops the carry-over cook that turns yolks grey. Peel carefully under cold running water, keeping the white intact. Pat dry with paper towels.

Mix sausage meat with salt and spice blend until evenly seasoned. Fry a small patty in a dry pan and taste — the sausage should be boldly seasoned, as the egg and breadcrumbs will dilute its flavor. Adjust. Divide the meat into equal portions — one per egg. Flatten each portion into a thin, even disc on a sheet of cling film.

Dust each boiled egg lightly with flour — this helps the sausage grip. Lay a flattened sausage disc on cling film and center the egg on top. Use the film to lift and wrap the sausage around the egg, sealing it with wet hands and pinching any seams closed. Roll in flour, dip in beaten egg, then coat thoroughly in panko, pressing to adhere. Rest in the fridge for 20 minutes.

Heat oil to 170 C (338 F) in a deep, heavy pot. Lower Scotch eggs in carefully — do not crowd the pot. Fry for 7–8 minutes, turning every 2 minutes for even color, until the crumb is a deep, even mahogany and the sausage reaches 70 C (158 F) internal. Drain on a rack, not paper towels. Rest 5 minutes before cutting.

recipes.name: Scotch Eggs
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Eggs, for the centres (large, very fresh)
Good-quality pork sausage meat (or sausages, skinned)
Dijon mustard, fine salt, and black pepper
Fresh sage and thyme, finely chopped together
Eggs, beaten for the coating (2 eggs)

steps: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Gently lower the eggs on a spoon — do not drop them or the shells will crack. Boil for exactly 6 minutes for a runny-firm yolk that will hold together during frying. Transfer immediately to an ice bath — a bowl of water with as much ice as you can spare — and leave for 5 full minutes. The cold stops the carry-over cooking that would ruin the yolk. Peel carefully under cold running water, starting from the wide air-pocket end. The whites will be very delicate.

Combine the sausage meat, mustard, chopped herbs, nutmeg, and a generous seasoning of salt and pepper in a bowl.
