Taste the dressed tabouli and adjust. The correct seasoning for tabouli is different from most dishes: the lemon must be the loudest note — if you are hesitant, add more. The olive oil should be present but should not make the salad heavy. The allspice and cinnamon are subtle warmth, not detectable as distinct spices. Salt should make everything pop without being perceptible on its own. Let the tabouli rest at room temperature for 15 minutes before serving — this brief rest allows the salt to draw a small amount of moisture from the herbs, which mingles with the dressing and creates the finished sauce.

recipes.name: Tacos Al Pastor

ingredients.name: Pork shoulder, sliced 5 mm thin across the grain
White wine vinegar or apple cider vinegar

steps: Toast dried chilies on a dry comal or skillet over medium heat for 15–20 seconds per side, until blistered and fragrant. Transfer to a bowl, cover with boiling water, and soak 20 minutes until fully softened. Drain, reserving 100 g of soaking liquid.

Blend the drained chilies with achiote paste, onion, garlic, cumin, oregano, pineapple juice, vinegar, salt, and 80 g of chili soaking liquid until completely smooth. Pass through a medium strainer. The marinade should be vivid crimson, completely smooth, and smell of toasted chili, earthy achiote, and bright pineapple acid.

Toss the thin pork slices with all the marinade in a large bowl, ensuring every surface is coated. Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, ideally overnight. The pineapple juice enzymes (bromelain) tenderize the meat — but more than 12 hours can make the texture mealy in thin slices.

Home method: Layer marinated pork slices in a cast iron skillet or on a baking sheet, overlapping slightly. Tuck pineapple rounds between and on top. Roast at 200 C (400 F) for 30 minutes, then broil for 5–8 minutes until the top edges char and caramelize. Alternative: build a vertical stack of pork slices on a skewer, interspersed with pineapple, and roast under the broiler, rotating every 5 minutes for 20–25 minutes total.

Slice or chop the roasted pork into small, irregular pieces, including the charred edges. Warm corn tortillas directly over a gas flame or dry comal until lightly charred and pliable. Double the tortillas (Mexican taqueria style). Pile pork on tortillas, top with diced onion, cilantro, and a square of pineapple. Serve with lime wedges and salsa.

recipes.name: Baja Fish Tacos

ingredients.name: Firm white fish fillets (mahi-mahi, cod, or halibut), skinless
Neutral oil for deep-frying (vegetable or sunflower)

steps: Whisk minced chipotles in adobo into the crema until fully combined. Start with half the chipotle and taste — it should be smoky, creamy, and moderately spicy. The heat blooms after a minute of contact, so taste again before adding more. Transfer to a squeeze bottle or small bowl. Refrigerate until ready to use.

Whisk flour, baking powder, salt, cumin, and paprika together in a wide bowl. Make a well in the center and pour in the ice-cold beer all at once. Whisk just until combined — lumps are welcome, overworking builds gluten and the batter will be tough. The batter should be the consistency of thin pancake batter. Keep the batter cold; set the bowl over ice if your kitchen is warm.

Heat oil in a deep, heavy pot to 185°C (365°F). Cut fish into strips about 2.5 cm × 8 cm. Pat completely dry. Working in batches of 4–5 strips, dip each piece in batter, let excess drip for 2 seconds, then lower gently into the oil. Fry for 3–4 minutes, turning once, until the batter is deep golden and the fish floats freely. Drain on a wire rack over a sheet pan — never on paper towel, which steams the crust soft.

Warm tortillas directly on a gas flame or dry hot griddle until pliable and slightly charred at the edges. Double them up (traditional Baja style prevents sogginess). Layer: a pinch of raw cabbage, 2–3 strips of hot fish, a drizzle of chipotle crema, a scattering of cilantro, and a stripe of salsa or pickled jalapeños. Finish with a hard squeeze of lime. Eat immediately — the crust on the fish is a living, dying thing that begins to soften the moment it is dressed.

recipes.name: Lamb, Chickpea and Apricot Tagine
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Bone-in lamb shoulder, cut into 7cm pieces
Saffron threads, bloomed in 2 tbsp hot water
Fresh cilantro and flat-leaf parsley, chopped
Fine sea salt and black pepper

steps: Combine the lamb pieces with ras el hanout, garlic, salt, and pepper in a bowl. Massage the spice blend into every surface. Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or overnight. The ras el hanout is a pre-made blend of up to 30 spices; a good one will include ginger, cinnamon, coriander, cumin, and rose petals. The marinated lamb should be deeply fragrant and the spices should have begun to hydrate against the meat's surface.

In the base of a tagine or a heavy Dutch oven, heat the olive oil over medium-high heat. Sear the lamb pieces on all sides, working in batches, until deeply golden-brown. Do not rush and do not crowd the pot. The spiced crust needs 3–4 minutes on each surface to develop. Set the seared lamb aside. In the remaining fat and fond, add the diced onion and cook over medium heat for 10 minutes until soft and golden.

Return the seared lamb and softened onion to the tagine base. Add the apricots, drained chickpeas, preserved lemon, and the bloomed saffron with its soaking liquid. Add just enough water to come halfway up the lamb — about 200ml. Place the conical tagine lid on, or cover the Dutch oven tightly. Cook over the lowest possible flame (use a flame diffuser if available) for 1.5–2 hours. Do not lift the lid for the first 60 minutes.

Adjust seasoning with salt, pepper, and additional lemon juice or preserved lemon if needed. Scatter the chopped cilantro and parsley over the tagine in a thick, fragrant layer. Serve directly at the table in the tagine pot, accompanied by warm Moroccan bread (khobz) or couscous to absorb the sauce. The meat should be so tender it is served with a spoon, not a knife.

recipes.name: Lamb Tagine with Prunes and Almonds

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder (cut into 5 cm chunks, bone-in pieces preferred)
White onion (grated on a box grater)
Saffron threads (steeped in 3 tbsp warm water)
Blanched almonds (toasted in a dry pan until golden)
Fine sea salt and black pepper

steps: Pat the lamb pieces dry with paper towels and season generously with salt and pepper. Heat the olive oil in a heavy tagine base or wide Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Sear the lamb in batches, leaving space between pieces, for 2–3 minutes per side until deeply golden-brown. The lamb fat renders beautifully and smells of lanolin and sweetness — do not crowd or you will steam instead of sear. Remove and rest on a plate, retaining all the fat in the pot.

Lower the heat to medium. Add the grated onion to the pot — it will splutter and release a great deal of moisture immediately. Cook, stirring often and scraping the fond loose, for 8–10 minutes until the onion has softened completely and the moisture has largely evaporated. Add the garlic, ginger, ras el hanout, cumin, cinnamon, and turmeric. Stir continuously for 2 minutes until the spices are fragrant and coat everything evenly in a deep terracotta paste. The kitchen should smell complex, warm, and almost floral.

Pour in the warm stock and the saffron with its steeping water, stirring to combine with the spice base. Return the seared lamb to the pot and nestle the pieces so they sit in a single layer, mostly submerged. Bring to a gentle simmer, then cover and cook over low heat (or in a 160°C / 325°F oven) for 1 hour 30 minutes, turning the lamb once halfway through.

Add the prunes and drizzle in the honey. Stir gently so as not to break up the now-tender lamb pieces. Remove the lid and raise the heat to medium. Simmer uncovered for 20–25 minutes, basting the meat occasionally, until the sauce has reduced to a thick, glossy, mahogany-coloured glaze that coats the back of a spoon heavily. The prunes will have partially dissolved into the sauce, adding body and sweetness. Taste and correct the seasoning with salt.

Scatter the toasted almonds over the surface of the tagine and finish with a generous handful of roughly chopped cilantro. Serve directly from the tagine base or transfer to a wide serving dish. The contrast of the crunchy almonds against the silky sauce and soft lamb, and the brightness of the fresh herb against the dark, sweet glaze, is what makes the dish complete. Serve with couscous, warmed flatbread, or rice to absorb the sauce.

recipes.name: Lamb Tagine with Preserved Lemon

ingredients.name: Bone-in lamb shoulder, cut into 2-inch pieces
Yellow onion, grated on a box grater
Saffron threads, bloomed in 2 tbsp warm water
Preserved lemon, rind only, finely chopped

steps: Combine all ground spices in a large bowl. Add the grated onion, minced garlic, and lamb pieces. Toss until every surface of the lamb is coated in the wet spice paste. The grated onion provides moisture that helps the spices penetrate. Marinate at room temperature for 30 minutes or refrigerate for up to 12 hours.

Heat olive oil in the tagine base or a wide, heavy Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Brown the lamb in uncrowded batches — do not rush this step. Turn every 2-3 minutes to build a crust on at least two sides of each piece. The spice coating will stick and darken — this Maillard reaction is the foundation of the braise's depth. Reserve the onion paste from the bowl.

Return all lamb to the pot. Add the bloomed saffron with its soaking water, stock, and preserved lemon rind. The liquid should come only halfway up the lamb — this is a braise, not a stew. Place the conical tagine lid on (or use a tight-fitting Dutch oven lid). Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce to the lowest possible flame. Braise for 2 to 2.5 hours, turning the lamb once at the 1-hour mark.

Add the olives to the tagine and cook uncovered over medium heat for 15 minutes to concentrate the sauce and infuse the olive brine into the braise. Taste and adjust salt — the preserved lemon and olives contribute significant sodium. Remove from heat. Scatter fresh cilantro and parsley across the top. Serve in the tagine with khobz (Moroccan bread) or couscous.

recipes.name: Tahini Sauce
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Garlic clove, grated to a paste

steps: Open the tahini jar and stir it thoroughly from the bottom up before measuring — tahini separates in storage, and you need a fully recombined paste, not the dry paste at the bottom with the separated oil on top. Transfer the required amount to a mixing bowl. The tahini at this point should be a uniform, thick, peanut-butter-brown paste with a strong sesame aroma. If the tahini is very stiff or cold, the sauce will be harder to whisk smooth — room temperature tahini works best.

Add the lemon juice all at once to the tahini and whisk immediately. The mixture will seize dramatically — it will thicken and seize into a stiff, pale, crumbly-looking mass. This is expected and not a failure. It is the same reaction as seizing chocolate: the acid is disrupting the fat emulsion and binding the solids. Add the grated garlic paste, salt, and cumin (if using) and whisk them into the seized mass. The mixture will look broken and unappetizing — resist the urge to add anything else yet.

Add the ice-cold water one tablespoon at a time, whisking vigorously after each addition. With each addition the sauce will first appear to loosen further before pulling back together — this is normal. Continue until the sauce is smooth, silky, and falls off the whisk in a slow, unbroken ribbon. The sauce should be noticeably pale — an almost off-white cream color — significantly lighter than the raw tahini. Taste and adjust: more lemon for brightness, more water for a looser consistency, more salt to bring everything forward.

recipes.name: Tamago Kake Gohan (TKG)

ingredients.name: Freshly cooked Japanese short-grain rice (very hot)

steps: Crack the egg and separate the yolk from the white into two small bowls. Beat the white alone with chopsticks for 30 seconds until it forms a loose, slightly frothy foam — this is the secret TKG technique. The beaten white will coat the rice grains individually, giving the final dish an airy, creamy texture rather than a slimy one. The yolk is added last, raw, as a finish.

Mound the very hot rice into a bowl. Immediately pour the beaten egg white over the rice and stir rapidly with chopsticks in small circles for 20–30 seconds — the heat of the rice gently sets the white into a silky coating on every grain. Add soy sauce and stir to distribute. The rice should look glossy and uniform, not wet.

Make a small well in the center of the rice and nestle the raw yolk into it. Scatter green onion over the top. Serve immediately — the yolk is left whole for the eater to break at the table, releasing a rich, uncooked stream through the already-seasoned rice. Eat within 2 minutes; the carryover heat will continue to set the yolk if left too long.

recipes.name: Tamagoyaki
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Dashi stock (ichiban dashi or hondashi dissolved in water)

steps: Crack the eggs into a spouted bowl or large measuring jug. Add the dashi, soy sauce, mirin, and sugar. Using a pair of hashi (chopsticks) or a fork held flat, cut through the eggs with a slicing motion rather than beating — the goal is a fully combined, streak-free mixture with no visible strings of egg white, but minimal air bubbles. Foam in the mixture will create unsightly holes in the finished roll. Pour the mixture through a fine-mesh sieve to remove any chalazae and remaining lumps. The mixture should be pale golden, uniform, and still.

Heat a rectangular tamagoyaki pan (or a small non-stick skillet) over medium heat. Dip a folded piece of kitchen paper into the oil and wipe the pan in an even, thin coat — no pooling oil. Pour in roughly one-third of the egg mixture, tilting the pan to coat the entire surface in a thin, even layer. Wait for the surface to turn from glossy-wet to barely set and just matte — still slightly moist at the centre but no longer fluid. Using hashi or a flat spatula, begin rolling the omelette from the far end toward you in 3 or 4 short folds, pressing each fold gently but firmly. Push the completed roll to the far end of the pan.

Wipe the exposed pan surface with oiled kitchen paper and pour in another third of the egg mixture, lifting the existing roll slightly to let raw egg flow underneath it. Wait for the new layer to reach that same barely-set, just-matte surface state. Roll the entire log back over the new layer — the new egg adheres to the log and builds another layer. Push the growing roll back to the far end. Repeat with the final third of the egg mixture. Each layer should be thin, even, and barely cooked before rolling so the roll stays tender throughout.

Roll the hot tamagoyaki in a clean bamboo sushi mat or a sheet of cling film, squeezing gently but firmly into a tight rectangular log. Fold in the ends of the mat and press to square off the corners. Let it rest for 3–5 minutes — the steam inside continues cooking and the shape sets. Slice into 2–3 cm rounds to reveal the spiral cross-section inside. Serve immediately or at room temperature.

recipes.name: Tamale Masa
recipes.note: Quantities are percentages by weight of the main ingredient (the one at 100%). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Masa harina (Maseca or fine-ground nixtamal corn flour)

steps: In a large bowl, combine the masa harina with the warm stock. Stir with a wooden spoon or your hands until no dry flour remains and a rough, slightly stiff dough has formed. The masa should feel like thick modeling clay — cohesive but not yet smooth. Cover the bowl with plastic wrap or a damp cloth and let the masa rest for 20 minutes. This rest allows the nixtamalized corn flour to fully absorb the liquid, swell the starches, and lose the raw, powdery texture that straight-mixed masa can have.

In a stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment (or using a hand mixer), beat the room-temperature lard on medium-high for 3–4 minutes until it turns white, fluffy, and nearly doubles in volume. Add the baking powder, salt, and optional bouillon and beat another minute to incorporate. The lard should look and feel like thick whipped cream — light, airy, and pale. This aeration step is critical: the air beaten into the fat is what ultimately makes tamale masa light and tender, not heavy and dense.

With the mixer running on medium, add the hydrated masa to the whipped lard in four additions, beating for 2 minutes between each addition. The mixture will look rough and broken at first — keep going. After all the masa is added, beat the combined dough on medium-high for 5–8 minutes, adding the remaining stock a tablespoon at a time if the dough seems too stiff. The finished masa should be smooth, fluffy, and light. Perform the float test: pinch off a small ball and drop it into a cup of cold water. If it floats, the masa is ready. If it sinks, keep beating and aerating.

Cover the beaten masa tightly with plastic wrap pressed directly against its surface to prevent drying. Rest at room temperature for 30 minutes before spreading onto soaked corn husks. This resting period allows the masa to relax, the starches to fully hydrate, and the flavors to mellow. While the masa rests, soak your corn husks in warm water for at least 30 minutes until fully pliable. When ready to use, wipe each husk dry and spread the masa into a thin, even rectangle — approximately 3mm thick — leaving a border at the top and sides. Fill, fold, and steam upright for 60–75 minutes until the masa pulls cleanly away from the husk.

recipes.name: Tamales de Pollo con Salsa Verde

ingredients.name: Masa harina (corn dough flour, Maseca brand)
Serrano or jalapeño chiles (2–3, roughly chopped)
White onion (half for braise, half for salsa verde)
Dried corn husks (30–35 husks, soaked in hot water 1 hour)

steps: Combine the chicken thighs, halved tomatillos, chopped chiles, half the onion (roughly sliced), and garlic in a pot with enough water to just cover (about 400g). Bring to a boil and simmer for 35–40 minutes until the chicken is completely cooked through and pulling from the bone. Remove the chicken pieces and let cool enough to handle. Shred the meat, discarding the bones and skin. Return the braising liquid and cooked vegetables to a blender and blend until smooth — this is your salsa verde filling sauce. Return the shredded chicken to the sauce and season assertively with salt. The filling should taste boldly seasoned — it will mellow inside the masa.

Beat the soft lard in a stand mixer with the paddle on high for 3–4 minutes until it is very pale, fluffy, and has roughly doubled in volume. With the mixer on medium, add the masa harina and baking powder alternating with the warm chicken broth in 4 additions, scraping down between each addition. Beat the salt in at the end. The finished masa should be light, spreadable, and very smooth — like thick hummus or a slightly stiff whipped cream. Test by dropping a small ball into a glass of cold water: if it floats, the lard is sufficiently aerated and the masa will be light. If it sinks, beat 2 more minutes.

Lay a softened corn husk with the wider end facing you. Spread about 60g of masa in a thin, even rectangle (15x10 cm) on the upper two-thirds of the husk, leaving the bottom third and a 2cm border on the sides bare. Place 2 tablespoons of filling in a line down the center of the masa. Fold one side of the husk over the filling so the masa meets and encloses the filling, then fold the other side over, and fold the bare bottom of the husk up to seal. Stand the tamales upright in a steamer basket, open end up. If needed, use extra torn husk strips to tie them closed.

Place the assembled tamales upright and packed tightly together in a steamer pot — they support each other. Add water to just below the steamer basket. Bring to a rolling boil over high heat, then reduce to maintain a vigorous steam. Cover tightly and steam for 75–90 minutes, checking the water level every 30 minutes and adding boiling water as needed. The tamales are done when the masa pulls cleanly and completely away from the corn husk without sticking. Let rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving — they firm and set during the rest.

recipes.name: Tamarind-Braised Oxtail

ingredients.name: Scotch bonnet or habanero pepper, whole
Fine sea salt and black pepper

steps: Season the oxtail pieces generously with salt and black pepper on all sides. Heat the oil in a large, heavy Dutch oven over high heat until just smoking. Working in small batches of 3-4 pieces maximum, sear the oxtail undisturbed for 4-5 minutes per side until they develop a deep mahogany-brown crust. The collagen-rich exterior of oxtail takes patience — it will stick initially and release cleanly when the crust has formed. Between batches, pour off excess rendered fat if it accumulates more than 3-4 mm deep, but do not scrape the fond. This brown fond is the foundation of the entire dish.

Reduce heat to medium. Add the diced onion to the pot and cook in the residual fat and fond for 8-10 minutes until softened and golden, scraping up the fond as the onion releases moisture. Add the garlic, scallions, scotch bonnet (kept whole — do not pierce it unless you want intense heat throughout), thyme, and allspice. Cook 2 minutes until fragrant. Add the browning sauce and soy sauce and stir — these will sizzle dramatically and lift the remaining fond from the pot. Add the tamarind paste and brown sugar, stirring until the sugar dissolves into a dark, glossy, sweet-sour glaze coating the aromatics.

Return all the seared oxtail pieces to the pot, pressing them down into the glossy base. Pour over enough stock to come two-thirds up the meat — the oxtail should be mostly but not completely submerged. Bring to a simmer, then cover tightly and cook over very low heat or in a 150°C (300°F) oven for 2.5-3 hours. The oxtail is done when the meat is trembling-tender and beginning to pull away from the bone at the ends. Do not rush with higher heat — oxtail collagen converts to gelatin at a low, sustained temperature; boiling makes the meat fibrous and the sauce greasy rather than silky.

Remove the lid, add the drained butter beans, and increase heat to a confident simmer. Cook uncovered for 25-30 minutes, stirring gently every 5 minutes, until the braising liquid reduces to a thick, luscious gravy that coats the oxtail pieces in a glossy curtain. The butter beans will absorb the tamarind-spice braise and become deeply flavored — they are as important as the meat. Discard the thyme stems and whole scotch bonnet (or leave the pepper whole on the plate as a warning to diners). Taste and adjust salt and tamarind. Serve over white rice with fried plantains.

recipes.name: Kerala Tamarind Prawn Curry
steps: Heat the coconut oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the mustard seeds — they will pop and splutter within seconds, scattering against the lid, so have it ready. As soon as the popping slows, add the fenugreek seeds, dried red chiles, and curry leaves in that order. The curry leaves will erupt violently in the hot oil, releasing their aromatic oils in a crackling burst. Stir once and allow 20–30 seconds for the fenugreek to toast to a pale gold.

Add the finely sliced onions to the spiced oil and stir to coat. Cook over medium heat, stirring regularly, for 10–12 minutes until the onions have melted down from their raw volume by more than half and turned a deep, even golden-brown — not blond, not mahogany. Add the garlic and ginger and fry for 2 minutes more, stirring constantly, until the raw smell of garlic cooks out and the mixture becomes sticky and fragrant.

Add the ground turmeric, coriander, and red chile powder to the golden onion base and stir vigorously to combine. Cook the spice mixture in the oil and onion paste for 90 seconds to 2 minutes, stirring constantly. This step — called bhunao in Hindi — fries the ground spices in fat, toasting them and driving off their raw notes. The mixture will look dry and clumpy at first, then loosen slightly as the spice oils release. Add a tablespoon of water if the spices begin to scorch.

Add the tamarind paste and stir it into the masala — it will hiss and sizzle. Pour in the coconut milk and salt, then stir thoroughly to combine everything into a smooth, uniform gravy. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered for 5–6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the gravy has thickened slightly and the raw sour edge of the tamarind has mellowed into the coconut. Taste: the gravy should be sour, warm with spice, lightly sweet from the coconut, and well-salted.

Add the peeled prawns to the simmering gravy in a single layer, pressing them down to submerge. Scatter a few fresh curry leaves over the top. Cook for 4–5 minutes over medium heat, turning the prawns once at the halfway mark, until they are fully pink and just cooked through. Remove from heat immediately — the residual heat of the gravy will continue cooking them if left on the stove. Serve with Kerala red rice, appam, or roti.

recipes.name: Tandoori Chicken

ingredients.name: Bone-in, skin-on chicken pieces (legs, thighs, breasts)
Garlic cloves, grated or minced to paste
Kashmiri chili powder (mild, for color and flavor)
Chaat masala and lemon wedges, to serve

steps: Using a sharp knife, score each piece of chicken to the bone with 3-4 deep parallel cuts (about 1 cm deep) through the thickest part. For breasts, make diagonal cuts across the chest. For legs and thighs, cut down to the bone. This is not optional — without scoring, the marinade sits only on the surface and the thickest parts will undercook before the exterior chars.

Whisk together all marinade ingredients until thoroughly combined — the mixture should be a brilliant red-orange with an even, yogurt-cream consistency. Apply in two stages: first, rub a light coat of just salt, lemon juice, and a pinch of chili into the chicken and rest 20 minutes. Then apply the full yogurt marinade, pressing aggressively into every score and under the skin wherever possible. Cover and refrigerate for at least 3 hours; overnight (up to 24 hours) is significantly better.

Preheat oven to the maximum temperature (500-550 F / 260-290 C) and place a rack in the highest position. Line a sheet pan with foil and set a wire rack on top. Remove chicken from marinade and shake off excess — a thin, even coat is what remains. Arrange on the rack skin-side up. Roast for 20-25 minutes for thighs and legs, 18-22 minutes for breasts, until the marinade is charred at the highest points and the juices run clear. Optional: finish under the broiler for 2-3 minutes for authentic char.

Transfer chicken to a serving platter. Dust immediately with chaat masala — its sour, salty, smoky profile amplifies the marinade. Arrange lemon wedges alongside. Serve with naan or roti, sliced raw onion, and fresh cilantro chutney. The charred edges are the best part — encourage diners to eat them.

recipes.name: Tandoori Leg of Lamb
steps: Using a sharp, narrow boning knife, make deep slashes all over the leg — 6 to 8 cuts per side, each about 3–4 cm deep and angled to reach as close to the bone as possible. Work methodically: score the top, the underside, and the shank end. The goal is to create as much marinade-to-meat contact as possible and to reduce the effective thickness of the leg for more even cooking. Score through any thick fat cap as well.

Mix the lemon juice, half the Kashmiri chilli powder, and the salt into a rough paste. Rub this first marinade aggressively all over the lamb — over the surface, and deep into every slash and score with your fingers. This acid-and-salt first marinade begins breaking down the surface proteins and carrying heat deep into the meat. Rest for 30 minutes at room temperature while you prepare the second marinade.

Whisk together the yogurt, oil, remaining Kashmiri chilli, cumin, coriander, garam masala, turmeric, ginger paste, and garlic paste until smooth and uniformly orange-red. Taste it — it should be bold, fragrant, and slightly salty (the lamb already carries salt from the first marinade). Apply this second marinade all over the lamb, working it deep into every cut and under any loose membrane. Place in a large dish, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for 4–6 hours, or ideally overnight.

Bring the lamb to room temperature 2 hours before cooking. Preheat the oven to 220°C (425°F) with a rack in the upper third. Place the lamb on a wire rack set over a roasting tray (to catch drips and allow air circulation under the meat). Roast at 220°C for 25–30 minutes until the marinade coating is charred and blackened in spots — this char is essential flavour. Meanwhile, heat the ghee in a small pan. After 25 minutes, baste the lamb generously with ghee, then reduce the oven to 180°C (350°F) and continue roasting for 45–60 minutes more (about 20 min per 500g for medium-pink).

Transfer the lamb to a cutting board and tent loosely with foil — do not wrap tightly, which traps steam and softens the crust. Rest for 20 minutes minimum. This is not optional: the internal temperature will rise 2–3°C more (carry-over cooking) and the muscle fibres will relax and reabsorb the juices. A leg cut too soon bleeds on the board and the meat is tough. Use the resting time to scrape the roasting tray drippings into a small pot and reduce with a splash of water for a pan sauce.

recipes.name: Taramasalata
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Pink carp or cod roe (tarama, not the ready-mixed spread)
Stale white bread (crusts removed, soaked in water 5 min)
Mild extra-virgin olive oil (or light olive oil)
Olive oil and black olives (to serve)

steps: Tear the stale white bread (crusts removed) into rough chunks and submerge in cold water for 5 minutes until thoroughly softened. Take handfuls of the soaked bread and squeeze firmly — you want bread that is moist but not waterlogged. Squeezed bread should hold its shape briefly before relaxing. Weigh or measure after squeezing, as excess water throws off the balance of the dip.

Combine the squeezed bread, tarama roe, lemon juice, and grated onion in a food processor. Blend on high for 60 to 90 seconds until completely smooth and uniform. The mixture will be thick and paste-like at this stage — this is the emulsification base. Scrape down the sides once midway through.

With the food processor running on medium speed, drizzle the olive oil in a very slow, steady stream — exactly as when making mayonnaise. The emulsion will visibly lighten and swell in volume as the oil incorporates. After half the oil is in, taste: if too salty, add a splash more lemon; if too thin, add more bread. Finish adding all the oil. Chill before serving.

recipes.name: Tarte au Citron
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: In a food processor or by hand, combine the flour, icing sugar, and salt. Add the cold cubed butter and pulse until the mixture resembles fine sand — no visible butter chunks. Add the egg yolk and 1–2 teaspoons of cold water and pulse until the dough just comes together. Do not overwork. Press into a flat disc, wrap, and refrigerate for 30 minutes. Roll to 3 mm thickness and line a 22–24 cm fluted tart tin with a removable base. Press gently into the flutes, trim the top neatly, and refrigerate for another 20 minutes. Blind-bake at 180°C (355°F) lined with parchment and weights for 15 minutes, then remove weights and bake a further 10–12 minutes until the base is a uniform pale golden-brown.

In a medium bowl, whisk together the eggs, caster sugar, lemon juice, and lemon zest until the sugar is fully dissolved and the mixture is smooth and uniformly pale yellow. Do not beat to foam — this should be whisked just enough to combine. Set the bowl over a saucepan of barely simmering water (bain-marie), making sure the base of the bowl does not touch the water.

Cook the lemon mixture over the bain-marie, whisking constantly with a flexible spatula or whisk, scraping the sides of the bowl frequently. The mixture will slowly thicken. Continue cooking until it reaches 82°C (180°F) on a thermometer, or the nappe stage: when you draw a finger across the back of a spoon coated in curd, it should leave a clean line. This takes 8–12 minutes. Remove from heat immediately and whisk in the cold butter cubes in two additions, waiting for each to incorporate before adding more. The butter is what makes the curd silky rather than just thick.

Strain the finished warm curd through a fine sieve directly into the cooled tart shell. Gently tap the tin on the counter twice to level the surface and release any air bubbles. Transfer to the refrigerator and chill uncovered for at least 2 hours, or until the curd has set to a sliceable consistency. Serve at room temperature — remove from the fridge 20–30 minutes before serving so the curd softens slightly to its ideal silken texture.

recipes.name: Tarte Tatin

ingredients.name: Apples (Granny Smith or Golden Delicious, peeled, cored, quartered)

steps: Sift the flour into a cold bowl. Add the cubed cold butter and rub between your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs with some pea-sized butter lumps remaining — these laminations create flakiness. Add the sugar and salt. Drizzle in the cold water a tablespoon at a time, pressing the dough together with a fork after each addition, stopping as soon as it just coheres when pressed. Do not knead. Press into a flat disc, wrap in plastic, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes.

In a 24cm ovenproof, heavy-bottomed skillet (cast iron or stainless steel), melt the butter over medium heat. Add the sugar in a single even layer. Do not stir. Let the sugar melt and caramelize, tilting the pan gently to encourage even coloring. Add the vanilla bean and a squeeze of lemon juice. When the caramel is a deep, brick-red amber — the color of dark rum — remove from heat. The caramel will continue cooking in the residual heat of the pan, so pull it one shade before you think it is ready.

Working quickly while the caramel is still fluid, arrange the quartered apples tightly in the pan in concentric circles, curved-side down and stem-end toward the center. Pack them very tightly — they will shrink significantly during cooking. Return the pan to medium heat and cook on the hob for 12–15 minutes, occasionally pressing the apples down with a spatula, until the caramel bubbles thickly around them and the apples have softened and begun to turn translucent at the edges. The juices from the apples will combine with the caramel to create the tart's sauce.

Preheat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Remove the pastry disc from the refrigerator and roll it on a floured surface to a circle 2cm larger than the diameter of the pan. Drape the pastry over the apples in the pan, tucking the excess down around the inside edges of the pan to completely enclose the apples. Pierce the pastry once in the center to let steam escape. Bake for 22–28 minutes until the pastry is deep golden-brown and crisp and the caramel is visibly bubbling up around the edges.

This is the decisive moment: place a large, flat serving plate (larger than the pan, with a slight rim to catch caramel) over the top of the pan. In one fast, confident motion, flip the pan and plate together. Hold for 3 seconds, then lift the pan away. Any apple pieces that shift can be gently replaced with a spoon — the caramel is still fluid enough to stick them back. Serve within 20 minutes while the pastry is still crisp, with a scoop of crème fraîche, clotted cream, or vanilla ice cream.

recipes.name: Tea Eggs (Chá Yè Dàn)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Strong brewed black tea (Assam or Yunnan, double strength)
Rock sugar (small piece) or white sugar
Dried mandarin peel (chen pi) or fresh orange peel

steps: Place eggs in a single layer in a saucepan. Cover with cold water by 2 cm. Bring to a full boil over medium-high heat. Once boiling, cover and remove from heat. Let stand for exactly 10 minutes, then transfer to an ice bath for 5 minutes. The eggs should be fully hard-boiled with no grey ring at the yolk — they will be simmered further and need to start fully cooked.

Using the back of a spoon, tap each egg all over its surface to create a fine network of cracks through the shell. The goal is to crack the shell without removing it — the shell must stay on to hold its shape during simmering. Cracks should be dense and close-set across the entire surface, like a cracked glaze on a ceramic piece.

Combine the strong black tea, both soy sauces, star anise, cinnamon, cloves, Sichuan peppercorns, sugar, and mandarin peel in a pot large enough to hold all the eggs in one layer. Bring to a simmer and add the cracked eggs. Simmer gently for 20 minutes — the shells should not bounce around. Remove from heat, let cool to room temperature in the liquid, then refrigerate in the braising liquid for a minimum of 4 hours, or overnight for the deepest color and flavor.

Peel each egg under cold running water, removing the shell fragments and the inner membrane together. The revealed surface should show a striking marble pattern: dark brown-black staining along every crack line set against the pale amber of the stained egg white. Serve whole or halved, at room temperature or cold.

recipes.name: Tempeh Rendang

ingredients.name: Dried red chilies, soaked and drained

steps: Blend the soaked dried chilies, shallots, garlic, ginger, coriander, and cumin into a smooth paste in a food processor or blender. Add a tablespoon of water if needed to get it moving. The paste should be fine-textured, deep brick-red, and smell intensely of raw shallot and warm spice.

Heat coconut oil in a large wok or heavy pot over medium heat. Add the paste and fry, stirring constantly, for 8–12 minutes. The paste will first thin out as moisture evaporates, then darken and deepen in color, and finally begin to separate from the oil — a thin ring of clear oil appears around the paste. This is keluarkan minyak — the oil breaking out. This step develops the foundational flavor.

Add tempeh to the fried paste and stir to coat. Pour in coconut milk, add the lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves, turmeric leaf if using, salt, and palm sugar. Stir to combine. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a medium simmer. Cook uncovered, stirring every 10 minutes to prevent sticking.

Continue simmering uncovered for 1–1.5 hours, stirring every 10 minutes with increasing frequency as the liquid reduces. The coconut milk will pass through several stages: creamy white, then pale yellow, then the coconut fat will separate and the paste will begin to fry in its own oil. This final stage — when the rendang is almost dry and the tempeh is frying in coconut oil — develops the characteristic dark, burnished crust. Keep stirring to prevent scorching. The rendang is done when the tempeh is dark and encrusted and the 'sauce' is more of a thick, dark coating.

Transfer to a serving plate or shallow bowl. Scatter fried shallots over the top. Serve with steamed rice, sambal, and pickled cucumber. Rendang improves overnight — the flavors deepen and the spice coating firms.

recipes.name: Tempeh Sambal (Tempe Kering)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Coconut or neutral oil for frying
Fresh bay leaves (salam leaves if available)

steps: Heat 1 cm of oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. When the oil shimmers and a small piece of tempeh sizzles immediately on contact, begin frying the tempeh slices in a single layer, without crowding. Fry for 3–4 minutes per side until deep golden-brown and crisp on the outside. The tempeh should not be pale — it needs color for the later glazing step to work properly. Drain on a rack, not paper towels.

In the same pan with the remaining tablespoon of oil, add the shallots and cook over medium heat until golden and beginning to caramelize — about 5 minutes. Add the sliced chiles, garlic, lemongrass, and bay leaves. Stir-fry for 3 minutes until the chiles are softened and fragrant. The shallots should be well beyond translucent — approaching crisp and golden — before the kecap manis is added.

Add the fried tempeh to the sambal base. Pour the kecap manis over everything. Toss vigorously over high heat for 2–3 minutes until the kecap manis caramelizes and coats every piece of tempeh in a dark, glossy glaze. The liquid should reduce completely — the pan should be nearly dry. Season with salt if needed (kecap manis is quite salty already). Remove the lemongrass and bay leaves before serving.

recipes.name: Tempura Batter

ingredients.name: Cake flour or low-protein soft flour (sifted)
Ice-cold water (with ice cubes in the jug)
Neutral frying oil (rice bran, sunflower, or canola)

steps: Fill a tall jug with cold water and add a generous handful of ice cubes. Measure 160g of this ice-cold water — include small slivers of ice if they fall in. The water temperature should be at or below 4 C. Cold water is the most critical variable in tempura: it slows gluten development (since gluten forms faster in warm water) and keeps the batter in a state of perpetual instability until it hits the hot oil. Place the jug in the freezer for 5 minutes if your tap water is not cold enough.

Beat the cold egg yolk lightly in a bowl with chopsticks — just 3 or 4 strokes, enough to break it. Pour in the ice-cold water and stir with a single chopstick or the handle of a spoon, just enough to combine. Do not whisk. The goal is a yolk-streaked water, not a smooth emulsion — the streaks of yolk create micro-pockets of richness in the final crust.

Sift the flour and salt into the egg water all at once. Using chopsticks (not a whisk), stir with large, lazy figure-eight strokes — no more than 10 to 12 strokes. The batter should remain visibly lumpy with pockets of dry flour still floating on the surface. This restraint is the entire technique: every additional stir develops gluten and moves you toward a heavy, doughy batter that fries like calamari rings rather than light tempura. Use immediately — the batter deteriorates in minutes as gluten continues to develop even when unstirred. Keep the bowl over or within the tray of ice to maintain temperature.

Heat the frying oil in a heavy-bottomed pot or wok to 175-180 C — use a thermometer. Dip the ingredient (shrimp, sweet potato, broccoli, etc.) briefly in a light dusting of dry flour, shake off the excess, then dip into the cold batter and lower immediately into the oil. Fry in small batches — crowding drops the oil temperature catastrophically. Fry until the batter is set and pale gold, about 2 to 3 minutes. The key visual cue is when the furious initial bubbling subsides to a quieter, more intermittent sizzle. Remove with a spider strainer and drain vertically on a wire rack, never flat on paper towels (which steam the crust soft). Serve within 2 minutes.

recipes.name: Vegetable Tempura

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables: sweet potato (sliced), shiitake, green beans, lotus root, red pepper
Cake flour or all-purpose flour (very cold)
Neutral oil (sesame-sunflower blend or canola) for frying

steps: Prepare vegetables: slice sweet potato 6mm thick, clean shiitake and score the caps, top and tail green beans, slice lotus root 5mm thick, cut red pepper into wide strips. Pat all vegetables completely dry — any surface moisture prevents batter adhesion and causes dangerous oil splatter. Dust lightly with flour (the second function flour serves after structural gluten — it acts as a primer for batter adhesion). Keep everything cold until the moment of frying.

This step must be done RIGHT BEFORE frying — never in advance. Combine the egg yolk with the ice-cold sparkling water and stir briefly. Add both flours at once and stir with chopsticks or a fork only 8–10 strokes. The batter must remain lumpy, floury, and obviously under-mixed. Large dry flour streaks are normal and desirable. Do not be tempted to mix until smooth — gluten development is the enemy of tempura.

Heat the oil to exactly 170–175 C (340–345 F) — use a thermometer. Dip each vegetable piece briefly in the batter (let excess drip for just 1 second) and lower into the oil. Fry in small batches to maintain oil temperature — too many pieces cools the oil and produces soggy results. Fry 2–3 minutes until the batter sets to a very pale, almost white-gold. Drain on a rack. Serve within 2 minutes.

recipes.name: Teriyaki Glaze
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine the soy sauce, mirin, sake, sugar, and ginger slice in a small saucepan. Stir briefly to help the sugar begin to dissolve. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring once more to ensure the sugar has dissolved completely before the liquid reaches a boil. Do not leave unattended at this stage — the sugar content means it can boil over quickly once it gets going. Remove the ginger slice after 2 minutes if using.

Reduce the simmering liquid over medium-low heat, without stirring, until it has reduced by roughly half and has reached a syrupy, glaze-like consistency. This takes 8-10 minutes. Watch carefully in the final 2 minutes — the sugar concentration rises sharply and the glaze can go from perfect to scorched in under a minute. To test: dip a cold spoon into the glaze and tilt it — it should flow in a slow, heavy sheet and coat the spoon in a thin lacquer. Off the heat, it will thicken further as it cools.

recipes.name: Teriyaki Sauce
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Combine soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small, heavy-bottomed saucepan. Stir briefly to dissolve the sugar. At this stage the mixture is thin, dark, and smells strongly of alcohol — the sake and mirin are raw. Set over medium heat and bring to a gentle simmer, stirring once or twice. Allow the alcohol to cook off before reducing: you will notice the sharp alcohol smell soften and sweeten as the sake and mirin cook out, replaced by a rounder, more caramelized fragrance.

Maintain a steady, gentle simmer — not a hard boil — and reduce the sauce for 5–8 minutes, swirling the pan occasionally rather than stirring. The sauce is ready when it coats the back of a spoon thickly and a line drawn through the coating holds for 2–3 seconds. If using cornstarch: mix it with a tablespoon of cold water to form a slurry, then whisk it into the simmering sauce and stir for 30 seconds until thickened and glossy. Remove from heat — the sauce thickens further as it cools.

recipes.name: Pad Krapow Gai (Thai Basil Chicken)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Chicken thigh, minced or coarsely ground
Thai bird's eye chilies, sliced (adjust to tolerance)
Holy basil (krapow) leaves — NOT Thai basil

steps: Combine oyster sauce, fish sauce, and dark soy sauce in a small bowl. Stir to blend. Taste — it should be powerfully salty and savory. This sauce goes in fast at high heat, so having it ready before you start is essential. Never season a stir-fry by shaking bottles over a hot wok.

Heat oil in a wok over high heat until smoking. Add garlic and bird's eye chilies together. Fry for 30-45 seconds, stirring constantly — the garlic will begin to golden at the edges and the chilies will turn the oil bright orange-red. Do not let the garlic burn or the dish will be bitter.

Add minced chicken and break it apart with a spatula immediately. Stir-fry on high heat for 2-3 minutes, pressing the chicken flat against the wok to get color rather than steam. When no pink remains, pour the sauce around the edge of the wok (not over the chicken) — it will sizzle and char slightly before mixing in. Toss to coat.

Remove wok from heat (or reduce to minimum). Add holy basil leaves all at once and toss vigorously for 10-15 seconds. The leaves will wilt almost instantly from the residual heat. Do not overcook them — they should be wilted and dark green, not brown and mushy. Plate immediately over jasmine rice with a fried egg on top.

recipes.name: Thai Basil Fried Rice (Khao Pad Krapao)

ingredients.name: Ground pork (or coarsely hand-chopped pork shoulder)
Bird's eye chilies (prik kee noo), sliced or smashed (3–6 to taste)
Holy basil (bai krapao), leaves picked — Italian basil is a poor substitute

steps: Heat a wok or large heavy skillet over the highest flame until smoke wisps from the surface — 2 minutes minimum. Add 30 g of the oil and swirl immediately. Add the garlic and chilies all at once and stir-fry for 20 seconds until the garlic is gold and the kitchen fills with a sharp, peppery fragrance. Add the ground pork, breaking it up with a spatula. Let it sear undisturbed for 30 seconds, then break and toss. Cook for 2–3 minutes total until no pink remains and the pork has some golden, crumbly edges rather than being pale and steamed.

Add the cold rice to the wok, breaking up any clumps with the spatula before it hits the heat. Pour the fish sauce, oyster sauce, and soy sauce around the edge of the wok (not directly on the rice) so the sauces hit the hot metal and sizzle. Toss everything together vigorously for 2–3 minutes, pressing the rice flat against the wok surface for 20 seconds at a time to allow contact browning, then tossing to redistribute. The goal is every grain coated and slightly toasted, not steamed.

Remove the wok from heat. Add all the holy basil leaves at once and fold them through the rice with 4–5 broad strokes of the spatula. The residual heat of the rice and wok will wilt the basil in 20–30 seconds — you want it collapsed and glossy but not black or slimy. Holy basil wilts much faster than Italian basil and turns bitter if overcooked. The leaves should turn a deep, jewel-like green and release a wave of clove-anise fragrance. Taste and adjust with a few drops more fish sauce if needed.

In a small wok or skillet, heat the remaining 10 g of oil over high heat until it shimmers and just begins to smoke. Crack eggs into the oil and let them fry undisturbed for 60–90 seconds. The whites should blister and puff immediately on contact, forming golden lacey edges while the yolk stays barely set and glossy. Tilt the pan and baste the yolk with hot oil using a spoon. The egg is done when the white is fully set and golden-fringed, the yolk still deep orange and runny. Serve immediately atop the rice.

recipes.name: Pad Kra Pao

ingredients.name: Thai holy basil (kra pao), leaves only
Fried egg (kai dao), one per serving

steps: Combine oyster sauce, fish sauce, soy sauce, and sugar in a small bowl. Stir until the sugar dissolves. Taste and adjust: it should be intensely savory, salty, slightly sweet, and smell powerfully of fermented seafood and caramel. Set beside the stove. In pad kra pao, there is no time for measuring once the wok is hot — everything must be ready before you start.

Heat a wok or large cast-iron pan over the highest possible heat until it begins to smoke. Add the oil and heat for 15 seconds. Add the chilies and garlic simultaneously. Stir-fry, keeping everything moving, for 30-45 seconds. The garlic should be fragrant and just beginning to color at the edges — not burnt. The chilies will release intense capsaicin vapor; ensure ventilation. This step is fast and violent.

Add the ground pork to the wok in one addition. Press it flat against the hot surface and let it sear without stirring for 30-45 seconds until the contact side turns grey-to-caramelized. Then break it up and stir-fry vigorously for 2-3 minutes, pressing and breaking apart any clumps. Pour in the pre-mixed sauce and the water. Continue stir-frying over maximum heat for another minute until the sauce has reduced and coated every piece of meat in a sticky, dark glaze. The pan should sound like it is sizzling furiously — not steaming.

Remove the wok from heat. Add all the holy basil leaves at once and toss rapidly — residual heat will wilt the basil in 15-20 seconds. Holy basil releases its best aroma when it hits heat but is not overcooked: the leaves should be wilted but still intensely fragrant and not uniformly black. Serve immediately over jasmine rice, topped with a fried egg cooked in very hot oil until the edges are crispy and lacy.

recipes.name: Thai Fish Cakes (Tod Mun Pla)

ingredients.name: White fish fillets (tilapia, Spanish mackerel, or snapper), pin-boned
Kaffir lime leaves, central stem removed, finely chiffonade
Long beans or green beans, cut into 3 mm rounds

steps: Cut the fish into rough chunks. Pulse in a food processor until the fish breaks down into a coarse paste — approximately 15–20 short pulses. Do not blend to a smooth puree; you want some texture remaining. Add the curry paste, fish sauce, egg, and cornstarch. Pulse 10 more times to combine. Then switch from pulsing to processing: run continuously for 30–45 seconds. The mixture will visibly change — it begins to gather into itself, pulling away from the bowl sides and becoming sticky and elastic. This is the myosin protein network forming, the same mechanism that makes bouncy fish balls. This step is not optional.

Transfer the fish paste to a bowl. Add the kaffir lime leaf chiffonade and sliced beans. Fold in firmly with a spatula — not gently, but with real pressure to distribute the additions without breaking the protein network already developed. At this stage, many Thai cooks slap the mixture against the bowl 10–15 times: lift and throw the paste back into the bowl to drive out air bubbles and further tighten the network. Refrigerate the paste for 15 minutes — chilling makes shaping much easier.

Heat the oil in a wok or deep pan to 175°C (350°F). Wet your palms with cold water. Scoop 2 heaped tablespoons of paste and form into a flat disc 1.5 cm thick and 7 cm diameter — they should look like hockey pucks, not balls. Slide gently into the oil. Fry 4–5 at a time without crowding. Cook 2–3 minutes per side until deep golden-brown all over. The cakes will float and puff slightly as they cook — a good sign. Test one by cutting in half: it should be cooked through with no translucent center and a dense, bouncy interior texture.

Drain on paper towels for 60 seconds only — too long and they cool and lose their crackle. Arrange on a serving plate. Serve immediately with Thai cucumber relish (ajat): thin-sliced cucumber and shallot in sweet vinegar with crushed peanuts and coriander. The cool, sharp relish is not optional accompaniment — it is the counterpoint the richness demands.

recipes.name: Thai Red Fish Curry
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Firm white fish (snapper or barramundi, skin-on, cut into 5cm pieces)

steps: Spoon 4 tablespoons of the thick cream that has risen to the top of the coconut cream can into a wok or wide pan. Heat over medium-high until it begins to bubble and the cream starts to separate (the oil splits from the solids). Add the red curry paste and fry in the coconut cream for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly, until the paste darkens slightly, the oil separates fully, and the fragrance fills the kitchen. This frying step in coconut cream is the most important step — do not rush it.

Add the remaining coconut cream and stir to combine with the bloomed paste. Add fish sauce, palm sugar, and torn kaffir lime leaves. Stir and taste — adjust the balance of salty (fish sauce), sweet (palm sugar), and heat (curry paste) until it feels harmonious. Add the Thai eggplant. Simmer for 5-7 minutes until the eggplant is just tender but still holds its shape. The sauce should be rich, slightly thickened, and deeply colored.

Nestle the fish pieces into the simmering curry sauce. Reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and cook for 4-6 minutes depending on thickness. Fish is done when it turns opaque throughout and flakes easily when a fork is pressed gently against the flesh. Do not stir after adding fish — the pieces are delicate and will break apart. Gently baste by spooning sauce over the exposed tops once during cooking.

Remove from heat. Tear in Thai basil leaves and stir gently once. Squeeze lime juice over the top. Taste once more for the final balance of salt, sweet, sour, and heat — this is the moment to adjust. Serve immediately over jasmine rice. The basil must go in off the heat to preserve its anise-clove fragrance.

recipes.name: Thai Green Curry Paste
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Dry-toast coriander seeds in a pan over medium heat, swirling constantly.
In a granite mortar, pound chilies, lemongrass, and galangal hardest first — fibers down to threads.
Add shallot, garlic, and cilantro root. Continue pounding until alliums dissolve into the paste.
Add lime zest, shrimp paste, and ground toasted spices. Pound until the paste pulls cleanly from the mortar.

recipes.name: Thai Larb Gai

ingredients.name: Dried chili flakes (prik bon), or to taste
Lemongrass, tender inner stalk only, minced

steps: Place the raw glutinous rice in a dry wok or heavy skillet over medium heat. Toast, stirring constantly, for 5–8 minutes until each grain turns golden-brown and the kitchen fills with a popcorn-like, nutty fragrance. Do not walk away — the transition from golden to burnt takes seconds. Transfer to a mortar or spice grinder and grind to a coarse powder (the texture of fine breadcrumbs). This powder is the secret texture of larb: it absorbs the dressing and gives the dish its characteristic sandy bite.

Heat a wok over high heat until smoking. Add the ground chicken with no oil — the natural fat in the meat is sufficient and oil would cause steaming. Break the meat apart rapidly with a spatula, spreading it thin across the hot wok surface. Cook until just no longer pink, about 3–4 minutes. Do not cook through completely — the residual heat and lime acid will finish it. The goal is barely cooked, still juicy chicken.

Working while the chicken is still very hot (the heat helps the dressing penetrate), add fish sauce, lime juice, dried chili flakes, and sugar. Toss vigorously. Taste immediately — the balance is the dish. It should hit sour first, then salty, then heat building at the back of the throat. Adjust: more lime for brightness, more fish sauce for depth, more chili for fire.

Fold in the shallots, mint, cilantro, scallion, and minced lemongrass. Scatter the toasted rice powder over the top and fold in gently — you want it distributed but not completely buried. Taste one final time. Serve immediately on a plate lined with cabbage leaves, with extra mint and raw vegetables on the side. Larb deteriorates quickly as the herbs wilt and the rice powder hydrates — this is a dish that lives in the moment.

recipes.name: Thai Pad Thai

ingredients.name: Dried sen lek rice noodles (3mm wide)

steps: Place the dried rice noodles in a large bowl and cover with room-temperature water. Soak for 25–30 minutes until pliable and flexible but still slightly firm — they should bend without snapping but still have a distinct resistance when bitten. Drain well. Do not soak in boiling water: boiling softens the noodles too much before they hit the wok, and they will turn to mush under wok heat.

In a small saucepan, combine the tamarind paste, fish sauce, and palm sugar. Heat over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves completely and the sauce is uniform. Taste: it should be a balanced blend of sour, salty, and sweet — adjust with more tamarind for sour, fish sauce for salty, or sugar for sweet. The balance should lean slightly sweet-sour.

Heat a wok over the highest heat possible until it smokes. Add the oil. When the oil shimmers and wisps of smoke appear, add the garlic and shallots — they should sizzle immediately and vigorously. Stir-fry for 30 seconds. Add the dried shrimp if using, toss 15 seconds. Add the raw shrimp in a single layer. Cook 1 minute without moving, then toss. The shrimp should be nearly cooked through but not quite.

Add the drained noodles to the wok. Pour the pad thai sauce over. Toss constantly for 1–2 minutes. Push everything to one side, crack the eggs into the empty side, and scramble quickly until barely set, then fold into the noodles. Add the bean sprouts and green onions, toss twice, and serve immediately. Garnish with peanuts. Serve with extra fish sauce, chili flakes, sugar, and lime wedges at the table.

recipes.name: Thai Peanut Sauce
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Smooth natural peanut butter (or freshly ground roasted peanuts)
Crushed roasted peanuts & sliced red chili

steps: Pour half the coconut milk into a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the red curry paste and garlic and cook, stirring constantly, for 2 to 3 minutes until the paste is fragrant and the oil in the paste begins to separate as tiny slicks at the edge of the pan. This brief frying step — even in coconut milk rather than oil — cooks out the raw smell of dried spice and wakes up the aromatics. The smell shifts from raw and harsh to warm and toasty.

Whisk in the peanut butter and the remaining coconut milk, stirring until completely smooth and uniform. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium-low heat, whisking steadily. The sauce will thicken considerably as the peanut proteins cook and the coconut milk reduces; if it tightens past a slow-flowing consistency, thin with a splash of water or coconut milk. Cook 5 to 8 minutes until the raw peanut taste mellow into a roasted, nutty depth.

Off the heat, stir in the palm sugar until dissolved, then add the fish sauce and lime juice. Taste and adjust: this sauce should hit sweet first, then the savory-salty fish sauce depth, then bright lime, with the heat building slowly at the back. Tune each element in small doses — a teaspoon of lime lifts more than you'd expect, a few drops of fish sauce deepens without pushing it salty. Add water if needed to reach a consistency that clings to a skewer but flows off a spoon. Pour into a bowl, scatter with crushed peanuts and sliced chili, and serve warm.

recipes.name: Som Tum (Thai Green Papaya Salad)
steps: In a large granite mortar and pestle, add the garlic cloves and whole bird's eye chilis. Pound until they are bruised and broken — not a paste, but no longer whole. This releases the allicin in the garlic and the capsaicin oils in the chili without making them disappear into a paste. In som tum, you want visible shards of garlic and chili throughout, not a homogenous sauce. The technique is to pound and tumble, not grind.

Add the dried shrimp to the mortar and pound briefly to break them up. Add the shredded papaya and the long bean pieces. Now use a combined pound-and-toss technique: pound gently with the pestle while using a large spoon to toss the mixture. The goal is to bruise the papaya strands so they absorb the dressing, not to mash them. You want the papaya strands to remain intact but softened and pliable from the pounding. Add the halved cherry tomatoes and give them 2–3 gentle pounds to lightly crush them so they release their juice.

Add the palm sugar, fish sauce, and lime juice to the mortar. Toss and lightly pound everything together to combine. Taste constantly — som tum is about precision balance between the four flavors: sour (lime), salty (fish sauce), sweet (sugar), and umami-hot (chili + fish sauce). Adjust one element at a time: more lime for brightness, more fish sauce for depth and salt, more sugar to soften if too harsh. No two batches are identical — the lime juice and papaya's natural acidity vary. The finished salad should be aggressively seasoned by Western standards — this is intentional.

Transfer the som tum to a plate using tongs, keeping the papaya strands intact and arranged loosely. Pour any remaining dressing from the mortar over the salad. Scatter the crushed roasted peanuts over the top. Serve immediately alongside sticky rice. Som tum does not hold — the salt and acid will continue to wilt the papaya and the salad will be soggy within 30 minutes. Make and eat.

recipes.name: Thiéboudienne (Senegalese Fish & Rice)
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Whole firm fish (thiof, snapper, grouper), scored and cleaned
Yellow onion, one half sliced, one half in stuffing paste
Root vegetables: cassava, carrot, turnip, eggplant
Fermented locust beans (netetou) or dried shrimp

steps: Blend the parsley, garlic, half the onion, half the scotch bonnet, salt, and pepper into a coarse green paste — this is the rof stuffing. Stuff the rof paste into the score marks of the fish, pressing it firmly into the cuts so the paste fills the incisions. Also rub a thin layer over the fish exterior. Let rest for 15 minutes. This step is the singular flavor signature of thiéboudienne — the rof perfumes the flesh from within as the fish braises.

Heat oil in a large, wide pot over medium-high heat. Fry the stuffed fish for 3 minutes per side until the exterior is golden and the rof has crisped slightly. Remove the fish and set aside. In the same pot, fry the remaining sliced onion until golden. Add the tomato paste and fry, stirring, for 10 minutes until it darkens and the oil separates. Add the locust beans or dried shrimp and the remaining scotch bonnet half. Add enough water to cover all vegetables and fish (about 1.5 liters). Return the fish to the pot and bring to a simmer.

Add the root vegetables (cassava, carrot, turnip, eggplant) to the pot around the fish. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook for 20–25 minutes until the fish is cooked through and the vegetables are tender. As elements finish cooking, remove them to a serving platter and keep warm — the cassava and turnip take longer than the eggplant. Reserve ALL the braising stock — it is the most important ingredient in the dish.

Measure the braising stock — you need a ratio of about 1.5 parts stock to 1 part rice. Top up with water if necessary and season the stock well (it should taste slightly salty). Bring the stock to a boil in the wide pot, add the rinsed rice, and stir once. Reduce heat to low. Cover with foil then lid (the tight steam seal from the jollof technique). Cook for 25–30 minutes until all liquid is absorbed and the rice is tender. Then uncover and increase heat for 3–5 minutes to develop the crust.

Traditionally, thiéboudienne is served on a large communal platter: mound the rice in the center, arrange the fish on top (keeping it as whole as possible even if it has broken during cooking), and distribute the vegetables around the rice. Place the crust chips alongside or on top as a crispy bonus. Spoon any remaining braising liquid over the fish. Serve with lime wedges and a side of fermented onion-and-mustard dibi sauce if available.

recipes.name: Tiramisù
steps: Combine the egg yolks, sugar, and salt in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water (a bain-marie). Whisk constantly and vigorously for 5-7 minutes. The mixture will thin, then pale, then thicken as the eggs gently cook to a safe temperature (about 70°C / 160°F). Never let the bowl touch the water or the yolks will scramble. Remove from the heat the moment it falls in thick, pale ribbons.

Loosen the cold mascarpone with a spatula until smooth, then fold it into the cooled sabayon in two additions until uniform. In a separate cold bowl, whip the heavy cream to soft peaks. Fold the whipped cream into the mascarpone mixture gently, from the bottom up, until just combined. Stop the instant it is homogeneous — overworking will collapse the air and make it grainy or split.

Stir the Marsala (or rum) into the cooled espresso in a shallow dish. Working one at a time, dip each savoiardo into the coffee for ONE second per side — a quick in-and-out. Ladyfingers are thirsty; they keep absorbing after they leave the liquid. Arrange the soaked fingers in a single tight layer in the base of your dish, trimming to fit.

Spread half the mascarpone cream evenly over the first layer of soaked savoiardi, smoothing it into the corners with an offset spatula. Build a second layer of dipped ladyfingers on top, then crown it with the remaining cream, swirling the surface smooth or into gentle peaks. Cover and refrigerate.

After the tiramisù has chilled and set (6 hours minimum), dust the surface with cocoa powder through a fine sieve in an even, generous veil — but only just before serving, so it stays dry and matte rather than dissolving into the cream. Cut with a hot, wiped knife for clean slices.

recipes.name: Toasted Farro Salad with Roasted Vegetables
steps: Place the farro in a large dry skillet over medium heat. Toast, stirring constantly, for 4–6 minutes until the grains smell nutty and are golden — some grains may lightly pop. This step is optional but transforms the flavor dramatically. The toasted grains will have a nuttier, more complex flavor after cooking.

Transfer toasted farro to a pot. Cover with generously salted water or stock (3 parts liquid to 1 part farro by volume). Bring to a boil, reduce to a steady simmer, and cook uncovered for 30–40 minutes for whole farro (20–25 for semi-pearled) until the grains are tender but still have a distinct chew — al dente, like a well-cooked barley. Drain any excess liquid.

Toss all the vegetables with a generous amount of olive oil, salt, and chili flakes on a large sheet pan. Spread in a single layer — do not crowd or they will steam. Roast at 220 C (425 F) for 25–30 minutes, turning once halfway, until caramelized and charred at the edges — particularly the cherry tomatoes, which should burst and concentrate.

While both the farro and vegetables are still warm, combine them in a large bowl. Drizzle with remaining olive oil and lemon juice. Add lemon zest, chili flakes, parsley, mint, and toasted nuts. Toss together gently — you want the warm farro to absorb the lemon and oil. Taste and adjust salt, acid, and oil. The salad is excellent warm, but also very good at room temperature.

recipes.name: Tomato Confit
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Aged balsamic vinegar (a few drops, optional)

steps: Preheat the oven to 110 C / 230 F — low, slow, and patient. Halve the plum tomatoes lengthwise and place cut-side up in a single, tight layer in a roasting dish or on a rimmed baking sheet. They should fit snugly — they will shrink considerably. Scatter the unpeeled garlic cloves and thyme sprigs between the tomatoes. Sprinkle the sugar, salt, and pepper evenly over the cut faces. Drizzle the olive oil over everything generously — the oil must coat every tomato face and pool slightly in the dish; it acts as the confit medium, surrounding the tomatoes in fat and preventing them from drying out instead of concentrating.

Roast at 110 C / 230 F for 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours, checking every hour. The tomatoes will slowly lose their water, shrink, and intensify. Their color will shift from bright red to a deeper, more muted red-burgundy. The cut faces will begin to wrinkle and caramelize into a sweet, tacky surface while the olive oil in the dish turns fragrant and gold. In the final 30 minutes, the surfaces may start to lightly caramelize at the edges. Do not rush this with higher heat — the concentration must be gradual to avoid drying to leather before the sugars develop.

Remove from the oven and add a drop of balsamic vinegar over each tomato if using — the residual heat will soften its edge and let it meld with the oil. Allow to cool in the dish. As they cool, the tomatoes will firm very slightly and the oil will thicken with their released sugars and pectins. The garlic cloves can be squeezed out of their skins and stored with the tomatoes — they will be soft, sweet, and completely transformed.

Transfer the tomatoes and all the scented oil to a sterilised jar, ensuring the tomatoes are submerged. The oil is as precious as the tomatoes — use it to dress salads, drizzle over burrata, finish pasta, or brush on grilled bread. Refrigerate and use within 2 weeks. Serve the tomatoes at room temperature or warm for the fullest flavor expression.

recipes.name: Tonkatsu
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Use a meat mallet or the back of a heavy pan to gently pound the cutlet to an even 2cm thickness. Snip the fat and connective tissue band around the edge of the cutlet at 2cm intervals — this prevents the cutlet from curling during frying. Season generously with salt and white pepper on both sides. Let sit at room temperature for 15 minutes.

Set up three shallow containers in sequence: flour, beaten egg, panko. Dredge the cutlet in flour, shaking off every trace of excess — a thick flour coating creates a gummy layer that prevents the panko from crisping properly. Dip in egg, letting excess drip for a full 5 seconds. Press firmly into the panko, turning and pressing again, building up thick, jagged layers. The more aggressively you press the panko, the more dramatic the crust.

Heat oil to 170°C (340°F) in a pot deep enough for the oil to come halfway up the cutlet. Test with a panko crumb — it should sink, bob, then sizzle immediately without browning in under 10 seconds. Lower the cutlet away from you and fry for 4 minutes per side without disturbing. The lower temperature (versus standard deep frying) allows heat to penetrate to the center before the crust over-browns.

Transfer to a wire rack and rest for 3 minutes — never paper towels, which trap steam and soften the crust from beneath. The carryover heat will bring the interior to a perfect 68°C. Slice into 2cm strips with a sharp knife using a single downward press — sawing shatters the crust. Serve immediately with tonkatsu sauce drizzled over or alongside for dipping, and finely shredded raw cabbage.

recipes.name: Tonnato Sauce
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: Add the drained tuna, anchovy fillets, rinsed capers, lemon juice, and white wine vinegar to a blender. The quality of the tuna is the ceiling of this sauce — use the best oil-packed tuna you can find; water-packed tuna produces a grainy, dull result. Blend on high for 60–90 seconds until the mixture is completely smooth. There should be no visible tuna flakes, anchovy pieces, or caper skins. At this stage the mixture will be thick, blond-beige, and intensely savory — almost overwhelmingly salty and sour before the mayo is added.

Add the mayonnaise to the blender with the tuna base. Blend on medium speed for 20–30 seconds until completely combined — do not over-blend at this stage, as the mayonnaise can break under prolonged high-speed blending. The sauce will transform from the stark, too-salty tuna paste into something considerably more rounded, creamy, and pale. The mayonnaise provides the emulsifying structure, fat, and body that ties everything together. Scrape down the sides and blend for 5 more seconds if any unmixed mayo is visible.

Transfer the sauce to a bowl. Stream in the olive oil while whisking by hand — this adds a final layer of richness and adjusts the consistency. The olive oil will loosen the sauce slightly; add only as much as needed to reach the consistency you want: thicker for spreading on a platter of sliced veal, thinner for drizzling over roasted cauliflower or boiled eggs. Season with salt (taste first — the tuna, anchovies, and capers carry a great deal of salt) and white pepper. Taste and adjust acid if needed. Refrigerate immediately; tonnato sauce keeps for 3 days and is always served cold.

recipes.name: Tonnato
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.

ingredients.name: Cold water or cold veal poaching liquid
Capers and lemon zest, for serving

steps: Combine the drained tuna, anchovy fillets, rinsed capers, and lemon juice in a food processor or blender. Process until the mixture becomes a smooth, homogeneous paste, scraping the sides as needed. There should be no visible chunks of tuna — the goal is a completely smooth, dense purée that will blend evenly into the mayonnaise.

With the processor running on low, spoon in the mayonnaise and drizzle in the olive oil. Process briefly — just enough to integrate. Over-processing after adding the mayo can make the sauce gluey. Scrape down and fold once by hand if needed. The sauce should be pale gold, thick, and absolutely smooth.

Add cold water (or cold veal poaching liquid for a more complex flavor) a tablespoon at a time to thin the sauce to a pourable but still coating consistency — it should coat the back of a spoon and fall in a slow ribbon, not run like water. Season with white pepper and salt, tasting carefully since the anchovies and capers have added significant salt. Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes before serving to let the flavors meld.

recipes.name: Torta Caprese
recipes.note: Quantities are proportions by weight (parts). Scale them to the amount you want to make.
steps: If using whole blanched almonds, pulse them in a food processor until they reach a fine, sandy consistency — the texture of coarse cornmeal. Do not over-process: if the almonds become warm and clumping, they are releasing their oils and will turn to almond paste rather than flour. Work in short 3-second pulses, scraping down the sides between each. The goal is a dry, free-flowing nut meal. If using store-bought almond flour, skip this step.

Combine the chopped dark chocolate and butter cubes in a heatproof bowl. Melt together over a gentle bain-marie (a saucepan of barely simmering water, bowl sitting above but not touching the water) or in a microwave in 30-second bursts, stirring between each. The mixture should be completely smooth and glossy — no streaks of unmelted chocolate. Let cool to room temperature, about 10 minutes. Do not use the chocolate mixture while it is still hot, as it will cook the egg yolks in the next step.

Separate the eggs, placing the yolks in one large bowl and the whites in another clean bowl. To the yolks, add the caster sugar and whisk until pale, slightly thickened, and the sugar is mostly dissolved, about 2 minutes. Add the cooled chocolate-butter mixture and whisk to combine. Add the vanilla extract and salt. Fold in the almond flour with a spatula until fully incorporated. The batter will be thick, glossy, and dense. Set aside. In the separate clean bowl, whisk the egg whites with a pinch of salt until they reach soft peaks — they should hold a peak that droops gently at the tip.
